3. ★★★ This lesson says: "What tears down a team is usually the self within." In your own words, explain what common root lies beneath comparison, power-grasping, monopolizing, and standing on the sidelines.

4. ★★ Tuckman said "most teams do not die from the storm, they die from avoiding it." What does this remind you about how you face friction in a team?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it beautifully." If someone's answer is fragmented, help them organize it — don't finish it for them.

Second Transformation | Digesting It into Life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)

Purpose: through Seeing, Hearing, Thinking, Speaking, and Acting, digest the idea into life.

[See] Seeing Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — proud (caring about titles and decision-making power more than others), fearful (carrying everything alone, afraid to delegate), ashamed (constantly comparing oneself to others and withdrawing), wounded (having been overlooked or excluded on a team and choosing to watch from the sidelines). Which one are you most like? What experience made you this way?

[Hear] Hearing God Speak

6. ★★ For each of these four hearts, God has a specific word to say. Find the verse that corresponds to you, read it aloud, then tell the group: where does this verse touch you?

[Think] Thinking It Through

7. ★★ Think back on a team you've been part of — was there a "storming" friction that, looking back, actually made the relationship more real?

[Speak] Saying It Out Loud

8. ★ Finish this sentence in one line: "This lesson tore down which old idea I had about 'teamwork'?" If your honest answer is "none," say that too — that itself is an important discovery.

[Act] Taking a Step

9. ★★ This week, whose hands will you specifically hold up? Say their name, and the one thing you will do for them.

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for members with a wounded heart, particularly those who have been excluded on a team or had credit for their work taken before. If someone cries, pause the discussion and simply be present — don't rush to give answers. If it involves deeper trauma, follow up individually after the meeting and help arrange a referral if needed.

Third Transformation | Transforming It into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily habit.

10. ★★ "Don't ask who will support me — first ask whose hands I can hold up." In your family, whose hands need you to hold them up this week?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "A team that doesn't care who gets the credit can accomplish astonishing things." This week, in what one situation can you actively give the credit to someone else?

13. ★★★ The ten-minutes-a-day practice: this week, pray by name for one team member each day. Say what time each day you will do this.

14. ★★ The 920 practice: identify your "2" (a spiritual companion). This week, share your answer to question 9 with them, and ask them to pray for your practice of teamwork this week. Say their name out loud now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, in three sentences, tell this lesson to someone outside the group — "Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil"; "If they fall, one will lift up his fellow"; "A threefold cord is not quickly broken." Write down now whom you will tell.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, share two things with each other: whose hands you will hold up this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to make our teams work together, help each other up, keep each other warm, and stand together — a cord not quickly broken.

ch18.title: Who Swears to His Own Hurt and Does Not Change — Building and Guarding Trust
ch18.partTitle: Part 4 — Church Culture and Team Unity
ch18.intro:
Grace and peace, brothers and sisters. The last two lessons spoke of culture and team; this lesson turns to something invisible yet load-bearing — trust. Trust is like air: no one notices it while it is present, but everyone suffocates the moment it is gone. Trust is like a bridge: it takes years to build and can collapse in an instant. A church may have the finest vision and the fullest range of gifts, but if there is no trust between people, everything grinds to a halt. The 321 vision says, "People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things." And trust is the foundation of every relationship.

Psalm 15:2,4 — "He who walks blamelessly and does what is right and speaks truth in his heart… who swears to his own hurt and does not change."

sections.heading: 1. Who Shall Sojourn in Your Tent, Who Shall Dwell on Your Holy Hill
sections.html: Psalm 15 asks: who shall sojourn in your tent, who shall dwell on your holy hill? The answer is not how many sacrifices one has offered, but a string of descriptions about honesty: "He who walks blamelessly and does what is right and speaks truth in his heart." The deepest phrase is "speaks truth in his heart" — not merely refraining from lying with the mouth, but refusing to deceive even one's own heart. Many breaches of trust begin with our being dishonest with ourselves first — clearly jealous, yet calling it "concern for the ministry." Verse 4 says, "He swears to his own hurt and does not change." This is the highest measure of trustworthiness — after making a promise, when the cost turns out to be higher than expected, he keeps it still, because his word weighs more than his own interest. The logic of the world is: circumstances have changed, so let's renegotiate. The logic of the holy hill is: because I promised, it still counts even at my own expense. When a community has a few people like this, the foundation of trust becomes solid.

sections.heading: 2. Trust Is the Foundation, Trust Must Be Built, Trust Must Be Guarded
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. Trust is the foundation — both culture and team are built on trust; where there is trust, hard truths can be spoken plainly and tasks can be delegated freely. Trust must be built — trust is not demanded into existence; it is laid brick by brick through a trustworthy life. Trust must be guarded — trust depreciates and can be damaged; it needs daily deposits, and it needs repair after a breach. Distrust is the most expensive hidden tax a community pays: every decision must be explained repeatedly, every motive is re-examined, and everyone spends their energy on self-protection. A team with trust can hand off a task with a single sentence; a team without trust cannot silence suspicion with ten documents.

sections.heading: 3. Four Pillars, Three Ingredients, Five Breaches
sections.html:
The management psychologists Roger Mayer, James Davis, and F. David Schoorman proposed a widely cited model of trust: people judge "whether he can be trusted" by three ingredients — ability: does he have the competence to do the job well; benevolence: does he genuinely wish me well; integrity: is his word consistent with his deed. If any one of these is missing, trust limps: ability without benevolence inspires fear; benevolence without ability makes people hesitant to entrust anything; ability and benevolence without integrity is the most chilling of all. Consider Daniel, who served faithfully in the Babylonian court, in whom no error or fault could be found even by those seeking to destroy him — so trustworthy that even his enemies had to admit it. Interestingly, Scripture's description of a trustworthy person has already covered these three facets: when the early church chose deacons, they sought men "of good repute, full of the Spirit, and of wisdom" — wisdom is ability, being full of the Spirit produces benevolence, good repute testifies to integrity. Gifts can attract people for a season, but only character can let people rest secure for the long haul. Proverbs 11:13 says, "Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered." The loss of trust in a church is rarely due to some spectacular betrayal — more often it is the daily habit of gossip, turning someone's confided weakness into a prayer request passed along to others. Here's a test: how you talk to me about others tells me exactly how you will talk to others about me. The political scientist Robert Putnam, famous for Bowling Alone, proposed the concept of "social capital" — the network of trust between people, which produces real benefit like a form of capital. He further found that modern society's store of trust has been eroding year by year — people increasingly "bowl alone": the forms of activity together still exist, but the deep connection of relationship has been lost.

A trustworthy life stands on four pillars. First, honesty — saying yes when it's yes, not exaggerating results, not hiding difficulties, and admitting mistakes when they happen. Second, discretion — letting others' weaknesses stop with you, being someone others can safely confide in. These first two pillars govern one's "words": a trustworthy person's words are clean. Third, keeping one's word — writing down and following through on commitments; not making promises lightly, and not breaking a promise even at personal cost. Fourth, endurance over time — trust is a function of time: keeping a promise once is a good thing, but keeping promises for ten years is character. These two pillars govern one's "deeds": a trustworthy person's behavior is predictable. In 1 Samuel 18, Jonathan loved David as his own soul and made a covenant with him, stripping off his robe, his armor, his sword, his bow, and his belt, and giving them to David. By worldly calculation, David was the single greatest threat to Jonathan's own throne; yet Jonathan placed his own robe on his rival with his own hands — the height of selfless love. This covenant would later face the harshest test: when Saul hunted David to kill him, Jonathan risked his life to warn him; and when David became king, he remembered this covenant and showed kindness to Jonathan's descendant Mephibosheth. Trust was built in covenant, proved in hardship, and carried on through generations by grace. Many churches' ministries get stuck at one bottleneck: leaders insist on personally reviewing and approving everything — cautious on the surface, but actually a lack of trust underneath, and the result is that co-workers never grow up; whatever they do will be changed anyway, so why not just wait for instructions. Moses's father-in-law Jethro advised him to appoint leaders of thousands and hundreds, delegating tasks to faithful people. Delegation is trust made concrete — if you say you trust someone but refuse to entrust anything to them, what they feel is still distrust. Healthy delegation is not abandonment: it entrusts the task and also entrusts the vision, gives room to try and grace to fail, and shares in carrying the outcome when something goes wrong. Someone trusted this way grows into a leader who can trust others — trust is hereditary.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Trust Rarely Dies of One Great Wrong; It Usually Dies of Many Small Ones
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson too has a passage that must be spoken honestly. The more we emphasize the importance of trust, the more easily people focus only on guarding against being let down by others, without examining how they themselves are slowly leaking away others' trust in them.

Trust rarely dies of one great wrong; it usually dies of repeated small failures, and there are five everyday behaviors. One, gossip — turning a private confidence into news that circulates. Two, broken promises — making promises lightly and not keeping them, missing a visit you promised to make, pushing back a deadline again and again. Three, blame-shifting — when something goes wrong, looking first for someone else's fault; when a person won't admit fault, others are left with no choice but to document everything to protect themselves. Four, two-facedness — praising to someone's face and criticizing behind their back; once a two-faced person is found out, even their praise becomes suspect. Five, concealment — reporting only the good news and never the bad, so people only find out afterward that you already knew. All five are small things, all with excuses ready — but this is exactly how trust leaks away, drop by drop.

Things that must never be said: "I meant no harm, I was just mentioning it casually." "I forgot about it, it's not that big a deal." "He's the one who made me distrustful in the first place, so I'm just protecting myself." These statements rationalize everyday small failures while forgetting that trust is precisely what leaks away through these "no big deals." The 321 vision says, "Only the selfless can be trustworthy." It is not that people full of self don't want to be trustworthy — they simply cannot; the moment self-interest is put on the scale, a promise grows light.

sections.heading: 5. Three Problems in Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
First problem: "In our church, prayer requests often become a legitimate channel for gossip, and things spread from one person to ten, and ten to a hundred." Proverbs 11:13 reminds us: "He who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered." Covering is not covering up sin — it is refusing to turn someone's weakness into gossip material.

Second problem: "When something goes wrong, everyone's first instinct is to distance themselves from responsibility and blame the circumstances or someone else." 1 John reminds us of the importance of self-examination: when a person won't admit fault, others are left with no choice but to document everything to protect themselves. Admitting a mistake is truly the starting point of repairing trust.

Third problem: "Once someone has been let down once, they guard against everyone, preferring to carry everything themselves rather than entrust anything again." George Müller's testimony of nearly sixty years of faith toward God and transparency toward people reminds us that a trustworthy life is built up precisely through promise after promise kept — worth rebuilding again, not shutting down completely.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
To bring this lesson home into the 321 framework, I want to invite you to make three concrete corrections.

First correction: replace "waiting for others to be trustworthy first" with "I will be the first trustworthy brick." The 321 vision says, "Change begins with me." Rather than waiting for a trustworthy environment, ask instead: are my words clean? Does my promise count?

Second correction: replace "I need to review everything myself before I feel at ease" with "make trust concrete through delegation." If you say you trust someone but refuse to entrust anything to them, what they feel is still distrust; healthy delegation entrusts the task and the vision, and shares in carrying the outcome when something goes wrong.

Third correction: replace "one betrayal keeps the account open forever" with "forgiveness is a decision, rebuilding is a process." Colossians 3:13 says that as the Lord has forgiven us, we too must forgive one another; forgiveness opens the door, and rebuilding walks through it step by step. Repairing trust has four concrete steps: acknowledge — don't dodge or defend, name specifically where the wrong was; apologize — real remorse, without adding "but"; correct — clarify what was distorted, make up what was left undone; endure — during the season of repair, every small promise matters more than ever: be on time, do it well, follow through on what you said. Zacchaeus is the finest example: after meeting Jesus, he repaid fourfold anyone he had defrauded — for someone met by grace, restoration is always concrete.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Trust
sections.html:
The same assignment — "building and guarding trust" — placed before different people stirs up entirely different reactions. Let me lay out four hearts side by side; perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Can't resist wanting to highlight one's own contribution in front of others, eager for everyone to see that it was oneself who made a certain good thing happen. Yet Proverbs reminds us: "Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence or stand in the place of the great, for it is better to be told, 'Come up here,' than to be put lower in the presence of a noble" (Proverbs 25:6–7). The proud heart needs to be reminded: true honor is being seen and given, not seized and stood up for oneself.

The Fearful Heart

Having been let down before, builds a high wall against everyone, no longer daring to actively trust or entrust anything important to anyone. Yet the psalmist declares, "The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?" (Psalm 118:6). True security is not refusing to trust people anymore — it is knowing that the one who ultimately holds you up is the faithful God.

The Ashamed Heart

Once gossiped or broke faith with someone and was later found out, and has felt deeply ashamed since, no longer daring to face the person they hurt. Yet the psalmist says, "I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity… and you forgave the iniquity of my sin" (Psalm 32:5). Honest confession does not lead to condemnation but to forgiveness and release.

The Wounded Heart

Was once let down or betrayed by someone deeply trusted, and has since built thick defenses in the heart, finding it hard to be truly open with anyone again. Yet the psalmist promises, "Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved" (Psalm 55:22). The Lord who knows the pain of being betrayed personally invites you to cast this burden on Him.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
Let me use three examples to help us see what this lesson looks like lived out.

First. A co-worker used to blame circumstances or others whenever something went wrong, and over time no one dared partner with him anymore. One day he found the courage to openly admit an obvious mistake at a co-workers' meeting, without adding any "but." Afterward, another co-worker told him privately, "This is the first time I've felt I could really trust you."

Second. A sister had once had her privacy betrayed by a close co-worker during a past ministry, and for years afterward dared not speak from the heart in any small group. The new small-group leader never asked about her past, but simply, through small kept promises over time — arriving on time, following through on what was said — slowly won back her trust. A year later, she shared her weakness openly in her small group for the first time.

Third. A church's treasurer, following George Müller's principles, insisted that every offering, every income and expense, be fully transparent and open for anyone to review. Over the years, the church's giving not only did not decline but grew steadily, because members said, "We know every dollar here is used with complete clarity."

These three stories share one thing in common: rebuilding trust never comes from one beautiful declaration, but from concrete, visible promises kept and honesty practiced again and again. Who can find a faithful person? May each of us be that person others find.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing a mindset are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: use the four pillars of honesty, discretion, keeping your word, and endurance to do a personal self-check, identify your weakest pillar, and this week specifically make up one debt or keep one promise as the first deposit toward rebuilding trust.

I declare that I will be one who walks blamelessly and speaks truth in his heart, who swears to his own hurt and does not change.

I declare that I will lay down gossip, broken promises, blame-shifting, two-facedness, and concealment, and let my words be clean and my promises count.

I declare that forgiveness is my immediate decision, and rebuilding is my continued action, which I will walk through step by step.

I declare that I will no longer wait for others to be trustworthy first — I will be the first trustworthy brick.

Brothers and sisters, may our churches be like Jonathan, giving place to those worthy of trust; like Müller, full of faith toward God and transparency toward people. Trust is the foundation, trust must be built, trust must be guarded — these three are the truest shape of a healthy church. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations trace a path that moves downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind; the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart; the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — a lesson that never reaches the Third Transformation stays stuck at the level of ideas.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority — if time is short, discuss at least this question in each Transformation; ★★ = secondary priority; ★ = discuss only if time allows. The reproduction task marked (Required) must not be skipped; it may be completed at home if needed.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as a Mindset (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the key point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ "He swears to his own hurt and does not change." What does this line remind you about understanding what it means to be trustworthy?

2. ★★ The three ingredients of trust — ability, benevolence, integrity — if any one is missing, trust limps. How does this help you understand your own trustworthiness, or someone else's?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "Trust rarely dies of one great wrong; it usually dies of many small ones." In your own words, name each of these five everyday behaviors.

4. ★★ Jonathan gave David his robe and armor. What does this act remind you about understanding "selfless love"?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it beautifully." If someone's answer is fragmented, help them organize it — don't finish it for them.

Second Transformation | Digesting It into Life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)

Purpose: through Seeing, Hearing, Thinking, Speaking, and Acting, digest the idea into life.

[See] Seeing Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — proud (deflecting blame when something goes wrong, unwilling to admit fault), fearful (afraid of being let down again and guarding against everyone), ashamed (having gossiped or broken faith and being found out, and blaming oneself), wounded (having been betrayed by someone deeply trusted and finding it hard to open up again). Which one are you most like? What experience made you this way?

[Hear] Hearing God Speak

6. ★★ For each of these four hearts, God has a specific word to say. Find the verse that corresponds to you, read it aloud, then tell the group: where does this verse touch you?

[Think] Thinking It Through

7. ★★ Among the people you trust, is there someone like Jonathan or Müller who earned your trust through years of kept promises?

[Speak] Saying It Out Loud

8. ★ Finish this sentence in one line: "This lesson tore down which old idea I had about 'trust'?" If your honest answer is "none," say that too — that itself is an important discovery.

[Act] Taking a Step

9. ★★ This week, which of the four pillars — honesty, discretion, keeping your word, or endurance — will you use to make up a debt of your own? Say what specifically.

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for members with a wounded heart, particularly those who have been betrayed by someone close to them. If someone cries, pause the discussion and simply be present — don't rush to give answers. If it involves deeper trauma, follow up individually after the meeting and help arrange a referral if needed.

Third Transformation | Transforming It into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily habit.

10. ★★ "Rather than wait for a trustworthy environment, be the first trustworthy brick." In your family, what one promise most needs you to keep it this week?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "If you say you trust someone but refuse to entrust anything to them, what they feel is still distrust." In your small group or family, is there something you could let go of and entrust to someone else?

13. ★★★ The ten-minutes-a-day practice: this week, examine each day whether you kept one small promise today. Say what time each day you will do this.

14. ★★ The 920 practice: identify your "2" (a spiritual companion). This week, share your answer to question 9 with them, and ask them to pray for your practice of trust this week. Say their name out loud now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, in three sentences, tell this lesson to someone outside the group — "He who walks blamelessly and does what is right and speaks truth in his heart" may dwell on God's holy hill; "he swears to his own hurt and does not change"; who can find a faithful person — may we be the one others find. Write down now whom you will tell.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, share two things with each other: the debt you will make up or the promise you will keep this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to make us people who walk blamelessly and speak truth in our hearts, becoming that faithful person others find.

ch19.title: A City Set on a Hill Cannot Be Hidden — Becoming a Model of Church Culture
ch19.partTitle: Part 4 — Church Culture and Team Unity
ch19.intro:
Grace and peace, brothers and sisters. The last three lessons spoke of culture, team, and trust; this lesson asks a more personal question: where does all of this first become visible to others? The answer is — it begins with example. Culture is not a document; culture is someone living it out first. No matter how good a value is, if no one visibly lives it, it remains only a slogan on the wall. The first of the 321 vision's three foundations is "Jesus is my example." A community is always searching for a living answer: is this kind of life actually possible? And God's intention is: you and I are meant to be that answer.

Matthew 5:14,16 — "You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden… Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven."

sections.heading: 1. No One Lights a Lamp and Puts It Under a Basket
sections.html: Notice that Jesus does not say, "You must try to shine," but rather, "You are the light of the world" — this is a declaration of identity. Believers already have the life of Christ within; that life naturally shines. The problem is never whether the light exists, but whether it has been covered by a basket. "Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house." This passage also contains a striking balance: the light must shine before others, so that they see your good works — but the result is that people give glory to your Father in heaven, not to you. The purpose of the shining tests the motive behind it: if people praise me after seeing my good work, then I have become a shadow blocking the way. The deepest art of being an example is letting people see you, and yet remember God.

sections.heading: 2. The Demonstration of Life, a Trail Worth Following, the Influence of Light
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. The demonstration of life — teaching tells people what to do; example proves it is possible; people listen to what you say, but they follow what you do. A trail worth following — Paul dared to say "imitate me," because his life was laid open for all to see; an example need not be perfect, but it must be real and traceable. The influence of light — light need not shout; it only needs to shine, and people in the darkness will naturally see the way. There is an old saying: your actions speak so loudly I cannot hear what you're saying. The pulpit preaches humility while the leader grabs the best seat, and the community learns to grab the best seat — lived example is the loudest form of teaching.

sections.heading: 3. Mirror Neurons, Three Degrees of Influence, and the Posture of Running
sections.html:
The Italian neuroscientist Giacomo Rizzolatti's team, while studying monkeys' brains, unexpectedly discovered a peculiar group of neurons: they fired when a monkey grasped food itself, and they fired in exactly the same way when the monkey merely watched another monkey grasp food — as though the brain were internally rehearsing the observed action. This became the famous discovery of mirror neurons. The human brain has a similar mechanism, closely tied to imitative learning and empathy. This confirms an ancient truth: humans are natural imitators — a baby learns its mother tongue without a single lesson; a new co-worker absorbs a community's atmosphere without any training. The question was never whether people are influenced, but by whom: your patience is being copied by someone, and so is your complaining. The sociologists Nicholas Christakis and James Fowler, analyzing decades of large-scale social network data, proposed the famous "three degrees of influence" rule: a person's behavior and emotions spread through their relational network up to three degrees out — your friends, your friends' friends, and your friends' friends' friends. This is the scientific version of leaven and light: in God's design, there is no one who does not influence others — only those who influence for good and those who influence for ill.

In Philippians 3:17, Paul writes a line few people today dare to say: "Brothers, join in imitating me, and keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us." Paul's confidence did not come from his own perfection — in that very same chapter he says he has not already obtained this, or is already perfect, but presses on toward the goal. What is worth imitating is not a flawless achievement but the posture of running. In 2 Thessalonians 3, Paul reminds the church that he never ate anyone's bread without paying for it, but worked and labored night and day — "not because we do not have that right, but to give you in ourselves an example to imitate." The weight of an example is measured by the cost of self-denial. Luke 6:40 says, "A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher." This is the ceiling effect of example: a community's spiritual height rarely exceeds the life-height of its leaders. But this saying also carries hope: if the teacher keeps growing, the disciple's ceiling keeps rising too — and our ultimate teacher is Christ, who has no ceiling at all. Hebrews 13:7 says, "Remember your leaders… and imitate their faith, considering the outcome of their way of life." What is imitated is their faith, not their speaking style; methods go out of date and gifts are hard to copy, but faith can be learned by everyone. James 3:13 says, "Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom." True wisdom is proved not by eloquence but by conduct; not by an overpowering presence, but by meekness. Moses was exceedingly meek, yet could confront Pharaoh; Jesus was gentle and lowly in heart, yet dared to cleanse the temple — meekness is strength under God's control. Example is not found under a spotlight, but in four ordinary settings: the family — the you that your spouse and children see is the real you; the small group — how you listen, how you respond to a wounded member; the workplace — unbelieving colleagues don't read the Bible, they read you; hardship — the peace found in suffering, the silence kept when misunderstood, are the most penetrating light of all. An example with no pulpit is often more powerful than one with a pulpit.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — an Example Doesn't Demonstrate Flawlessness, It Demonstrates Authenticity
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson too has a passage that must be spoken honestly. The more we emphasize how important being an example is, the more easily people conclude that one must be perfect before setting an example, and so either give up entirely or swing toward performance instead.

Many people say: I can't even get my own life together — how can I be an example? This misunderstands the nature of example — an example doesn't demonstrate flawlessness, it demonstrates authenticity: how you get up after falling, how you apologize after wronging someone. A father who can say to his children, "Daddy was wrong just now, please forgive me," teaches a deeper lesson than ten family devotions. A community doesn't need a superhero who never falls — it needs a real person who, by grace, rises after falling. But authenticity must also guard against another extreme — performance. The Pharisees' conduct was performed for an audience: they loved to pray standing at street corners. The test is simple: when no one is watching, are you still the same?

Things that must never be said: "I'm not qualified yet, let me wait until I'm more mature." "No one's watching me anyway." "Being an example means appearing perfect — you can't let people see any weakness." These statements either use imperfection as an excuse not to shine, or twist example into performance. Albert Schweitzer said, "Example is not the main thing in influencing others; it is the only thing." The 321 vision says that through a selfless example, what people see is not the person but Christ — all glory belongs to Jesus, not one bit withheld.

sections.heading: 5. Three Problems in Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
First problem: "It's easy in our church to elevate a certain spiritual elder to near-idol status, treating his every word as authoritative, forgetting that the goal of imitation is Christ, not him." Hebrews reminds us that what we imitate is faith, not the person themselves; an example rooted in self builds a personality cult, but a selfless example points people toward Christ.

Second problem: "Many people think that being an example means looking good in front of others, while privately being someone else entirely." James 3:13 says true wisdom shows itself in good conduct through the meekness of wisdom; the test is whether you are still the same when no one is watching.

Third problem: "What is preached from the pulpit and what is practiced off the pulpit often don't match, and the congregation sees it but no one dares say so." Paul's example in the Thessalonian church was not found on a platform but at the dinner table, in the workshop — the example of culture lives in these small daily things: who washes the dishes first, who arrives on time.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
To bring this lesson home into the 321 framework, I want to invite you to make three concrete corrections.

First correction: replace "wait until I'm perfect to be an example" with "shine today, in whatever position I'm in." The 321 vision says, "Change begins with me." You don't have to wait until you become a leader to live out Christ — start now, as a lamp not put under a basket.

Second correction: replace "grinding out a good testimony through willpower" with "supplying the oil daily through the Spirit, using the heart not the mind." A good testimony maintained by willpower alone is a lamp running low on oil, bound eventually to run dry; the Spirit supplies oil daily, and the light becomes natural, lasting, and unforced.

Third correction: replace "let people see me" with "let people see God through me." The deepest art of being an example is letting people see you, and yet remember God; we are all the moon, not the sun — the light is reflected, not our own. Becoming an example has four directions we can practice daily: staying close to Christ — being a good student first, so as to become a good teacher; opening up our lives — inviting people into our everyday, praying together, serving together, eating together; consistency of word and deed — not teaching what you don't practice, but practicing before you teach; deliberate transmission — entrusting what you have heard and learned to the faithful who can teach others — this is the very path of the final step in the eight steps of change: "reproduction."

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Lamp
sections.html:
The same assignment — "becoming a model of church culture" — placed before different people stirs up entirely different reactions. Let me lay out four hearts side by side; perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Thoroughly enjoys being treated as a role model and followed by others, secretly hoping to gather followers to himself and build his own influence. Yet Paul says, "Am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ" (Galatians 1:10). The proud heart needs to be reminded: a true example points people toward Christ, not toward oneself.

The Fearful Heart

Feels too young, too immature, too full of weakness, and doesn't feel qualified to be anyone's example at all. Yet God said to Jeremiah, "Do not say, 'I am only a youth'; for to all whom I send you, you shall go… Do not be afraid… for I am with you to deliver you" (Jeremiah 1:7–8). God's calling does not look at qualifications — only at whether He is with you.

The Ashamed Heart

Once fell and failed in the faith, and has since felt unworthy to be an example for anyone else to imitate, wanting only to quietly stay hidden. Yet Jesus said to Peter, "I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers" (Luke 22:32). Those who have fallen and turned back are often best able to strengthen others who are falling.

The Wounded Heart

Once fully imitated a spiritual role model, only to discover that person's words and deeds didn't match, and has since regarded any "example" with suspicion and guardedness. Yet the prophet Jeremiah says, "Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, whose trust is the LORD" (Jeremiah 17:7). People will disappoint us, but the Lord who is truly trustworthy never puts to shame those who trust in Him.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
Let me use three examples to help us see what this lesson looks like lived out.

First. A pastor had for years taught forgiveness from the pulpit, while privately remaining cold toward a co-worker who had wronged him. One day his child asked him directly, "Dad, didn't you teach us to forgive?" The question pierced him and led him to seek out that co-worker to reconcile. He said, "I had been teaching others to climb the mountain while standing at the bottom myself."

Second. A young co-worker had been deeply hurt by an elder mentor whose words and deeds didn't match, and had since kept her distance from any "spiritual example" in the church, doubting everything. A new pastor never asked her to imitate him — he simply, over the years, lived out a consistent, everyday example in front of her, and gradually she became willing to trust again.

Third. A sister, because of a public failure in the past, had for years dared not participate in any ministry, feeling she had lost the right to be used. An elder encouraged her: "Peter denied the Lord three times, and later became the one who strengthened his brothers; your own fall will one day be a blessing to someone else." She later became one of the church's most capable companions for weak and struggling members.

These three stories share one thing in common: the power of a true example never comes from perfection, but from an honest turning and continued walking forward after a fall. The world is waiting for a living answer, waiting to read a living letter — may you and I be that answer, that letter.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing a mindset are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: honestly identify the widest gap between what you "say" and what you "do," and this week begin closing it from that point, apologizing to those affected if necessary, so that your life and words become consistent again.

I declare that I am the light of the world; I will let my light shine before others, giving glory to my Father in heaven.

I declare that I need not wait for perfection to shine; when I fall, I will rise by grace and keep running.

I declare that I will stay close to Christ, open my life, live with consistency of word and deed, and deliberately pass my life on.

I declare that I am the moon and not the sun; I will face the source of the light daily, so that people see God through me.

Brothers and sisters, may we all be like Paul, daring to say "imitate me, as I imitate Christ"; and may we all follow Schweitzer's footsteps, leaving behind a trail worth imitating through a lifetime, not merely words. The demonstration of life, a trail worth following, the influence of light — these three are the truest shape of being an example. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations trace a path that moves downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind; the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart; the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — a lesson that never reaches the Third Transformation stays stuck at the level of ideas.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority — if time is short, discuss at least this question in each Transformation; ★★ = secondary priority; ★ = discuss only if time allows. The reproduction task marked (Required) must not be skipped; it may be completed at home if needed.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as a Mindset (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the key point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ "You are the light of the world" is a declaration of identity, not a goal to strive for. What does this remind you about understanding "being an example"?

2. ★★ Mirror neurons and the three degrees of influence both confirm: there is no one who does not influence others. What does this remind you about your everyday life?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "An example doesn't demonstrate flawlessness, it demonstrates authenticity." In your own words, explain the difference between a real example and a performed one.

4. ★★ "We are the moon, not the sun." What does this remind you about the danger of being an example (building a personality cult)?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it beautifully." If someone's answer is fragmented, help them organize it — don't finish it for them.

Second Transformation | Digesting It into Life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)

Purpose: through Seeing, Hearing, Thinking, Speaking, and Acting, digest the idea into life.

[See] Seeing Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — proud (enjoying being imitated while gathering followers to oneself), fearful (feeling too young or unqualified to be anyone's example), ashamed (having fallen and failed before, feeling unworthy to be imitated), wounded (having been hurt by an inconsistent role model and no longer trusting). Which one are you most like? What experience made you this way?

[Hear] Hearing God Speak

6. ★★ For each of these four hearts, God has a specific word to say. Find the verse that corresponds to you, read it aloud, then tell the group: where does this verse touch you?

[Think] Thinking It Through

7. ★★ Think about the example who has most deeply influenced your faith — which trait of their "faith" do you most want to imitate?

[Speak] Saying It Out Loud

8. ★ Finish this sentence in one line: "This lesson tore down which old idea I had about 'being an example'?" If your honest answer is "none," say that too — that itself is an important discovery.

[Act] Taking a Step

9. ★★ This week, which gap between "what you say" and "what you do" will you close? Name it specifically.

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for members with a wounded heart, particularly those who have been hurt by an inconsistent spiritual elder. If someone cries, pause the discussion and simply be present — don't rush to give answers. If it involves deeper trauma, follow up individually after the meeting and help arrange a referral if needed.

Third Transformation | Transforming It into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily habit.

10. ★★ "An angel outside the home, a hedgehog inside it — that's a lamp under a basket." In your family, what is the one thing you most need to align this week?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "Unbelieving colleagues don't read the Bible, they read you." This week, in what specific situation can you let a colleague see Christ?

13. ★★★ The ten-minutes-a-day practice: this week, examine each day whether your words and deeds were consistent today. Say what time each day you will do this.

14. ★★ The 920 practice: identify your "2" (a spiritual companion). This week, share your answer to question 9 with them, and ask them to pray for your consistency of word and deed this week. Say their name out loud now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, in three sentences, tell this lesson to someone outside the group — "You are the light of the world; a city set on a hill cannot be hidden"; "Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works"; "and give glory to your Father who is in heaven." Write down now whom you will tell.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, share two things with each other: the gap you will close this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to make us the lamp not put under a basket, so people see God through us.

ch20.title: Encourage One Another and Build One Another Up — The Art of Encouragement and Gratitude
ch20.partTitle: Part 4 — Church Culture and Team Unity
ch20.intro:
Grace and peace, brothers and sisters. Part Four comes to its final lesson. We have spoken of culture, team, trust, and example — today we add one final brick, and the gentlest one of all: encouragement and gratitude. Consider: when was the last time you sincerely praised a co-worker? When was the last time you said thank you to God, or to a person, for the grace around you? Many communities lack neither truth nor gifts — what they lack is words that lift each other up and eyes that see grace. The 321 vision's path of service — spirit, understanding, life, service, God — ends at "God": everything is what God has accomplished in Christ, so give thanks in all things and give all glory to Jesus.

1 Thessalonians 5:11 — "Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing."

sections.heading: 1. But Barnabas — a Life of Encouragement
sections.html: His given name was Joseph, but the apostles called him Barnabas — which means "son of encouragement," because encouragement was the mark of his life. When Saul was converted and went up to Jerusalem, the disciples were all afraid of him and did not believe he was truly a disciple; Scripture records four precious words: "But Barnabas took him" — he alone welcomed this man everyone else avoided, brought him to the apostles, and told them how the Lord had appeared to him on the road. Without that one act of welcome from Barnabas, there would have been no Apostle Paul later on. He later also gave a second chance to Mark, who had abandoned the mission halfway through — that young man went on to write the Gospel of Mark. Barnabas was content to play a supporting role, yet he made possible the ministries of two writers of Scripture. A church needs preachers; it needs Barnabas even more.

sections.heading: 2. Encouraging Words, a Grateful Life, the Ministry of Barnabas
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. Encouraging words — a good word makes the heart glad; the church ought to be the most encouraging community in the whole world. A grateful life — giving thanks in all things is not mere politeness, it is spiritual eyesight, seeing that everything is grace God has given in Christ. The ministry of Barnabas — using encouragement to build others up, content to play a supporting role. The word "build up" is originally a term for construction — putting people up brick by brick. Tearing down is easy; one cold word is enough. Building up requires laying bricks day after day. Paul says "one another," "each other" — this is not a leader's privilege but every believer's calling.

sections.heading: 3. A Good Word Gladdens the Heart, the Bucket and the Dipper, the Science of Gratitude
sections.html:
Proverbs 12:25 says, "Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad." Anxiety is like a heavy weight, bending a person's heart so he cannot straighten up. All around us are people like this: the smile behind their service may conceal a bent-down heart. And the remedy, remarkably, is cheap — just one fitting good word. Donald Clifton, one of the founders of positive psychology, proposed the "Bucket and Dipper" theory: everyone carries an invisible bucket, full of energy when it's full, drained and discouraged when it's empty; every word of affirmation and thanks fills someone else's bucket, and every word of contempt and mockery dips water out of it. Research further shows: the one who fills others' buckets finds their own bucket filling too. The father of psychology William James said, "The deepest craving in human nature is the need to be appreciated." Hebrews 3:13 says, "Exhort one another every day, as long as it is called 'today,' that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin." A heart does not harden overnight — it hardens day by day, in days when no one checks in.

The psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough conducted a classic gratitude experiment: subjects were divided into groups, one asked to write down several things they were grateful for each week, one to write down troubles, and one to write neutral events. After several weeks, the gratitude group showed markedly higher well-being, fewer physical complaints, better sleep, and a greater willingness to help others. The church has sung "Count Your Blessings" for hundreds of years — science has only now caught up. Paul, writing to the Philippian church from prison, opens: "I thank my God in all my remembrance of you." For Paul, remembering and thanking were linked — the moment he thought of the brothers and sisters in Philippi, what rose up in his heart was not their faults, but the grace of God upon them. Ten lepers cried out to Jesus for mercy and were cleansed on the way, but Scripture says, "Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice, and fell on his face at Jesus's feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan." The other nine were likely not evil people — just too caught up in their excitement; they received the grace but left the giver of grace behind. 1 Thessalonians 5 says, "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you." Encouragement is a learnable art: be specific — "you're great" is a courtesy, but "I saw you kneel down yesterday and listen to that child all the way through, and I saw Jesus's gentleness in you" is a building block; be timely — while it is still called today, say it the moment you see it; be genuine — flattery seeks to gain something from the other person, encouragement seeks to build the other person up; point to God — "I thank God for you" outweighs "you're amazing"; the former builds faith, the latter can unwittingly feed pride. A grateful eye is trained one step at a time: counting — writing down a few things you're grateful for every day; speaking it — bringing that gratitude directly to the person; being grateful in hardship — deliberately finding something to be thankful for even in difficult days; giving thanks in everything — reaching the maturity where you no longer need a reason to be grateful, when thanksgiving becomes as natural as breathing.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — a Jealous Tongue Cannot Speak Words That Build Up
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson too has a passage that must be spoken honestly. The more we emphasize the need to encourage one another, the more easily people assume it just takes a few nice words to say, without examining why they are so reluctant to give praise in their own hearts.

Why are some people stingy with praise? Often because of the self — afraid that praising someone else will make them look better, afraid that affirming someone else will make oneself look worse. A jealous tongue cannot speak words that build up. Encouragement also requires discernment: criticize privately, face to face; praise publicly, for all to hear — many communities do exactly the opposite. And encouragement is not manipulation — using praise to buy compliance turns encouragement into a tool; and gratitude is not performance either — giving thanks before others while complaining in one's heart; God searches the heart.

Things that must never be said: "He should already know I appreciate him, I don't need to say it out loud." "Too much praise will make people prideful." "If I praise someone else, I'll seem less important myself." These statements lock appreciation forever inside the heart, forgetting that appreciation kept locked inside comforts no one. The 321 vision says, "Only the selfless can encourage generously." A selfless person is different: when someone else is built up, he is truly glad, because his focus is on Jesus, not on himself.

sections.heading: 5. Three Problems in Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
First problem: "Our culture tends to keep praise locked in the heart, feeling it's awkward to say it out loud, or fearing it will make the other person prideful." Proverbs 12:25 reminds us that a good word makes the heart glad — such a cheap remedy, and yet we are so often stingy in giving it.

Second problem: "In church, people often only speak up when someone makes a mistake, and stay silent for long stretches when someone is faithfully serving." The bucket-and-dipper theory reminds us: the real reason many co-workers leave is that their bucket ran empty — physical tiredness can be recovered with one good night's sleep, but an empty bucket stays empty no matter how much you sleep.

Third problem: "After receiving grace, we often rush ahead, rarely turning back to thank God or people." Only one of the ten lepers turned back to give thanks, and Jesus's three heartbreaking questions still linger: where are the other nine? Gratitude is what turns grace received into a relationship walked out.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
To bring this lesson home into the 321 framework, I want to invite you to make three concrete corrections.

First correction: replace "keeping appreciation inside" with "speaking the good word out loud." This week, speak a specific, sincere word of affirmation to three people, and remember to point them to God: "I thank God for you."

Second correction: replace "standing by and watching" with "being the one who says, 'But Barnabas.'" The 321 vision says, "Change begins with me." Find someone near you who is discouraged, has withdrawn, or has been misunderstood, take the initiative to welcome them, and give them a second chance at the door.

Third correction: replace "finding fault with everything" with "giving thanks in everything." Giving thanks in everything doesn't mean everything is good — it means that within everything, there is something to be thankful for, because we know God reigns over all things. See how Jesus built people up: while Simon was still unstable, Jesus already called him Cephas, meaning the Rock; the moment Nathanael approached, Jesus said, here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit; when a widow gave two small coins, Jesus publicly declared that she had given more than all the others. Jesus's eyes always saw the treasure God had placed within a person — He is history's greatest encourager, and we can encourage others because we have first been encouraged by Him.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Good Word
sections.html:
The same assignment — "encouragement and gratitude" — placed before different people stirs up entirely different reactions. Let me lay out four hearts side by side; perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Secretly envies a co-worker who receives praise, feeling that affirming someone else makes oneself look inadequate, and so is stingy with words of praise. Yet James says, "Where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice" (James 3:16). The proud heart needs to be reminded: a jealous tongue cannot speak words that build up — it only blocks the whole community from being built up together.

The Fearful Heart

Wants very much to praise or thank someone, but is afraid it will seem insincere, or be mistaken as flattery, and so ends up saying nothing at all. Yet the psalmist says, "I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears" (Psalm 34:4). A sincere good word need not be feared, because God can deliver us from our fear of how others see us.

The Ashamed Heart

Feels like a constant failure, never good enough, and so doesn't feel worthy to praise or encourage anyone else, nor deserving of any affirmation. Yet the psalmist says, "He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities" (Psalm 103:10). God's grace does not treat us according to our failures, and we need not stop building others up because of them.

The Wounded Heart

Was rarely praised or encouraged growing up, and was often criticized and put down instead, and since then has not known how to speak words that build others up, nor known how to believe others' praise. Yet the prophet Isaiah promises, "A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench" (Isaiah 42:3). The Lord who will not break a bruised reed is personally healing the thirst in your heart that has never been watered.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
Let me use three examples to help us see what this lesson looks like lived out.

First. A co-worker had for years felt a pang whenever someone else was praised, even secretly looking for their flaws. One day she honestly confessed this jealousy to her spiritual companion, who prayed with her. After that, she deliberately practiced praising one co-worker specifically every week. She said, "Strangely, the more I spoke of others' good, the less bitterness I felt in my own heart."

Second. A brother, having rarely been praised by his parents as a child, grew up throwing himself into ministry without expecting any affirmation, and did not know how to encourage others either. An elder began speaking one specific, good word to him every week, and after several months, he too gradually learned to say the same kinds of things to others. He said, "It turns out I wasn't incapable — no one had ever shown me how."

Third. A small group used to spend its review meetings picking out faults, and the atmosphere was heavy. The group leader began ending every gathering by inviting each person to specifically thank one group member for one thing. Half a year later, a member said, "Now we look forward to coming, because we know we'll be seen."

These three stories share one thing in common: a culture of encouragement and gratitude never comes from one moving declaration, but from specific, sincere appreciation spoken out loud again and again. May the dipper in our hands fill someone else's bucket every single day.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration: Reviewing Part Four
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing a mindset are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: begin a gratitude list — every night before bed, write down three things you're thankful for that day, and offer a short prayer of thanks to God, for seven days, and see what changes in your eyes.

Having reached this point, the five lessons of Part Four, "Church Culture and Team Unity," together form a complete picture: shaping a healthy church culture — culture is the air a community breathes, and love for one another is the mark of a disciple; fostering team cooperation — members coordinating, standing together, helping each other up, a cord of three strands not quickly broken; building and guarding trust — honesty, discretion, keeping one's word, endurance — trust is the foundation of everything; becoming a model of church culture — culture needs a face, you are the light of the world; the art of encouragement and gratitude — encouraging one another, building one another up, giving thanks in everything. Culture is the air, team is the body, trust is the foundation, example is the light, and encouragement is the voice within the household — together they form a spiritual family, the earthly embryo of a system belonging to God. May everyone who walks in encounter Christ.

I declare that I will encourage one another and build one another up, speaking out the appreciation in my heart without holding back.

I declare that I will give thanks in everything, like the Samaritan who turned back to give thanks, turning grace received into a relationship walked out.

I declare that I will be a "But Barnabas" for those around me, the first to reach out in welcome when everyone else is watching from a distance.

I declare that the dipper in my hand will fill someone else's bucket every day, so that Jesus receives all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, may our churches be like Barnabas, building others up; like the Samaritan who turned back to give thanks, turning grace into relationship. Encouraging words, a grateful life, the ministry of Barnabas — these three are the warmest voice of a spiritual family. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations trace a path that moves downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind; the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart; the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — a lesson that never reaches the Third Transformation stays stuck at the level of ideas.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority — if time is short, discuss at least this question in each Transformation; ★★ = secondary priority; ★ = discuss only if time allows. The reproduction task marked (Required) must not be skipped; it may be completed at home if needed.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as a Mindset (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the key point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ "But Barnabas" welcomed Saul, whom everyone else feared. What does this line remind you about the power of encouragement?

2. ★★ The "Bucket and Dipper" theory says every affirming word fills someone's bucket, and every cold word dips it out. What does this remind you about the way you speak?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "A jealous tongue cannot speak words that build up." In your own words, explain what lies at the root of being stingy with praise.

4. ★★ Of the ten lepers healed, only one turned back to give thanks. What does this remind you about the difference between "receiving grace" and "giving thanks"?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it beautifully." If someone's answer is fragmented, help them organize it — don't finish it for them.

Second Transformation | Digesting It into Life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)

Purpose: through Seeing, Hearing, Thinking, Speaking, and Acting, digest the idea into life.

[See] Seeing Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — proud (envying someone praised and being stingy with words), fearful (afraid praise will seem insincere, so saying nothing), ashamed (feeling unworthy to praise or encourage anyone), wounded (rarely praised growing up and not knowing how to encourage others). Which one are you most like? What experience made you this way?

[Hear] Hearing God Speak

6. ★★ For each of these four hearts, God has a specific word to say. Find the verse that corresponds to you, read it aloud, then tell the group: where does this verse touch you?

[Think] Thinking It Through

7. ★★ Is there a good word someone once said to you that you still remember, and that still shapes you today?

[Speak] Saying It Out Loud

8. ★ Finish this sentence in one line: "This lesson tore down which old idea I had about 'praise and gratitude'?" If your honest answer is "none," say that too — that itself is an important discovery.

[Act] Taking a Step

9. ★★ This week, to whom will you speak a specific, sincere good word? Say their name, and what you will say.

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for members with a wounded heart, particularly those rarely affirmed and often criticized while growing up. If someone cries, pause the discussion and simply be present — don't rush to give answers. If it involves deeper trauma, follow up individually after the meeting and help arrange a referral if needed.

Third Transformation | Transforming It into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily habit.

10. ★★ "Tearing down is easy; one cold word is enough. Building up requires laying bricks day after day." In your family, what good word most needs to be said this week?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "Criticize privately, face to face; praise publicly, for all to hear." In your small group, which often-overlooked member could you publicly praise this week?

13. ★★★ The ten-minutes-a-day practice: this week, write down three things you're grateful for every night before bed. Say what fixed time you will do this.

14. ★★ The 920 practice: identify your "2" (a spiritual companion). This week, share your answer to question 9 with them, and ask them to pray for your practice of gratitude this week. Say their name out loud now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, in three sentences, tell this lesson to someone outside the group — "Encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing"; "A good word makes the heart glad"; "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances." Write down now whom you will tell.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, share two things with each other: the good word you will say this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to make our church a spiritual family that encourages one another and builds one another up.

ch21.title: Make Disciples of All Nations — Building a Discipleship System
ch21.intro:
Grace and peace, brothers and sisters. Today we begin a new part: Discipleship and Leadership Development. In the last part we built the church's home — culture, team, trust, example, encouragement. But the deepest joy of a home is that life is born, grows, matures, and then bears children of its own within it. Before He ascended, Jesus did not leave us the command to "make decision-makers of all nations," nor "make gatherings exciting" — He said, "make disciples of all nations." A church can have many activities and no disciples; many listeners and no followers. The problem is often not that people are unwilling, but that the church has no road that carries people to maturity.

Matthew 28:19–20 — "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age."

sections.heading: 1. All Authority in Heaven and on Earth Has Been Given to Me
sections.html: In the original grammar of this passage, there is only one main verb — "make disciples"; "go," "baptizing," and "teaching" are all participles clustered around it. The bullseye of the Great Commission is not how many places were visited or how many events were held, but how many disciples were formed. And the goal of teaching is "observe" — not knowing what the Lord commanded, but doing what the Lord commanded; the report card of discipleship is not found in a notebook, but in a life. Notice how the Great Commission is bracketed: before it, "all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me"; after it, "I am with you always, to the end of the age." Discipleship's deepest resource is not curriculum — it is Immanuel.

sections.heading: 2. The Mission of Making Disciples, Jesus's System, the Path of Multiplication
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. The mission of making disciples — the core of the Great Commission is forming people into disciples, not gathering a crowd, but shaping life. Jesus's system — the Lord Himself demonstrated the complete path: calling, presence, sending, and oversight. The path of multiplication — four generations passing the torch, turning addition into multiplication. Activities are points; a system is a road. Without a road connecting the points, people drift between activities. A system must answer four questions: after someone believes, where do they go next? Who walks with them? What does maturity look like? And once mature, whom do they lead? A church that cannot answer these four questions may have plenty of excitement, but no disciples.

sections.heading: 3. Scaffolding, Deliberate Practice, and the Multiplication of Four Generations
sections.html:
The educational psychologist Lev Vygotsky proposed the famous theory of the "zone of proximal development": every learner has two levels — what they can do independently, and what they can do with the support of someone more experienced; the zone between the two is precisely where growth happens. Effective teaching is like building scaffolding: supporting a person where they cannot yet reach, and gradually removing the scaffolding once they can stand on their own. Mark 3 records that Jesus "appointed twelve … so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach" — He placed His deepest investment in a few, because He was looking not at how many attended over three years, but at the gospel movement thirty years later. The purpose of this appointment had two layers: first presence, where life is shaped in relationship; then sending, where growth is proven through mission. The psychologist Anders Ericsson spent his career studying how top performers are made, and his conclusion overturned intuition: what produces mastery is not talent, nor even hours logged, but "deliberate practice" — setting clear, small goals at the edge of one's ability, practicing with full focus, and receiving real-time coaching feedback. Ten thousand hours of practicing an instrument produces vastly different results depending on whether there was coaching feedback or aimless playing. Why does someone attend church for thirty years and yet their life still looks like their third year of faith? Because there was only repetition, never deliberate practice.

2 Timothy 2:2 — "What you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also." Four generations stand within this one verse: Paul taught Timothy, Timothy entrusted it to faithful people, and the faithful people taught others in turn. This is exactly where a discipleship system should be evaluated: not "how many people have you brought in," but "have the people you brought in started bringing others?" Do the math: an evangelist who leads a thousand people to Christ every day would, in thirty years, reach about eleven million people — astonishing. But another person spends a whole year bringing just one person to the point of being able to disciple others; the two of them each disciple one more, doubling every year: by year ten, only 1,024 people — far behind. But by year thirty, over a billion. Addition looks impressive at the start; multiplication has boundless staying power. Ephesians 4 says the Lord gave the five-fold offices "to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ" — a pastor's calling is not to complete all the ministry on behalf of the congregation, but to equip the congregation to minister themselves. In late-eighteenth-century England, children under the Industrial Revolution worked in factories on weekdays and roamed the streets on Sundays. The newspaper publisher Robert Raikes did not merely lament the state of society — he hired godly women to gather these children on Sundays and teach them to read and memorize Scripture. That is how Sunday school was born. Within four years it had spread across England, and within decades its students numbered in the millions; many later preachers and missionaries first started as children in Sunday school. Its genius was not in the depth of its curriculum, but in the reproducibility of its system: a fixed time, simple materials, ordinary teachers — it did not depend on a genius speaker, so it could spread everywhere. A complete path of discipleship also stands on four pillars: truth — Scripture is my standard, teaching truth step by step; life — Jesus is my example, dealing with the self and practicing selflessness; relationship — life is transmitted through relationship, one-on-one companionship, the covering of spiritual parents; mission — being sent out is half of growing, letting people grow through bearing responsibility.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Discipleship Has No Wholesale, Only Retail
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson too has a passage that must be spoken honestly. The more we emphasize a system, the more easily people assume that if the process is well designed, discipleship will simply happen on its own, forgetting that behind every system are still living, individual people.

Colossians 1 says, "Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ." In this short passage Paul says "everyone" three times — discipleship has no wholesale, only retail: every life has different breaches and a different pace, requiring all manner of wisdom to be applied individually. Paul also says honestly that he "toils" — the original word is a term for a wrestler struggling in the arena; forming a person is never easy. But he adds, "struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me" — toil without power leads to burnout; power without toil is just talk.

Things that must never be said: "We just need to build a good system, and people will naturally be formed." "The curriculum's already written, just follow it." "He can't keep up — that's his own problem." These statements reduce discipleship to a process, forgetting that its deepest core is a pair of hands, one at a time, willing to lead someone by the hand. The 321 vision says discipleship is the construction project of a system belonging to God — every selfless disciple gained is another inch of real territory added to God's kingdom.

sections.heading: 5. Three Problems in Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
First problem: "It's easy in our church to equate discipleship with taking a class — as soon as the homework is turned in, it's considered done, with no real follow-up on the person's life." A Bible study class addresses "not knowing"; discipleship must address "not being able to" — dealing with the self and practicing selflessness, letting Christ take shape in the heart.

Second problem: "Pastors carry every ministry themselves, unwilling to raise anyone up, so the church's growth gets capped by the leader's own stature." Ephesians 4 reminds us that the five-fold offices exist to equip the saints, not to complete every task on the saints' behalf.

Third problem: "People tend to pour resources into holding events and chasing attendance, but rarely ask whether these people are actually leading anyone." Addition looks impressive at the start; multiplication has boundless staying power — may we be a church with the vision to pursue multiplication: slower, but able to change the world.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
To bring this lesson home into the 321 framework, I want to invite you to make three concrete corrections.

First correction: replace "waiting for the church to roll out a complete system" with "reconnecting myself to the chain first." In the four-generation chain of 2 Timothy 2:2, every believer should hold two positions: someone is leading you, and you are leading someone. The 321 vision says, "Change begins with me."

Second correction: replace "a one-time course" with the four-step rhythm of "I do, you watch; I do, you help; you do, I help; you do, I watch." Demonstrate first, then give them a role, then hand the lead role to them, and finally let go completely — once this four-step cycle completes, one generation has passed to the next. You can also draw a clear growth map for your church: from seeker to new believer, someone reads the gospel with them; from new believer to growing believer, laying the foundation of small group and devotional life; from growing believer to co-worker, discovering gifts and beginning to serve; from co-worker to spiritual elder, becoming a spiritual parent who reproduces the next generation. Don't wait for a perfect blueprint before starting — a system is walked into being, not drawn on paper.

Third correction: replace "an anxious season" with "diligently laying the road and entrusting it to God." I planted, Apollos watered, but only God gives the growth; let people be people, faithfully laying the road and walking alongside; let God be God, He is the one who grows the life.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Chain
sections.html:
