The same assignment — "building a discipleship system" — placed before different people stirs up entirely different reactions. Let me lay out four hearts side by side; perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Feels that having been a believer for many years already makes him mature enough, no longer needing anyone to shepherd or accompany him, wanting only to lead others while unwilling to be led himself. Yet 1 Corinthians says, "If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know" (1 Corinthians 8:2). The proud heart needs to be reminded: the more mature a life becomes, the more it knows it still needs to be shepherded.

The Fearful Heart

Genuinely wants to begin discipling a new believer, but is afraid of being inadequate and disappointing the other person's trust, and so keeps putting off that first step. Yet Paul says, "Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God" (2 Corinthians 3:5). Discipling others has never depended on our own ability, but on God's power.

The Ashamed Heart

Once tried to disciple someone and it ended in failure, and has since felt unworthy to try again, carrying a deep sense of having wasted that time. Yet the prophet Joel promises, "I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten" (Joel 2:25). God can restore the years we thought were wasted — past failure is not the final word.

The Wounded Heart

Was once overlooked or abandoned by their own spiritual parent or coach, and has since guarded against any discipleship relationship, afraid to entrust themselves to anyone again. Yet the psalmist says, "Father of the fatherless … is God in his holy habitation… God settles the solitary in a home" (Psalm 68:5–6). The God who is a Father to the fatherless in His holy dwelling is Himself placing you in a true spiritual family.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
Let me use three examples to help us see what this lesson looks like lived out.

First. A brother had walked alone for over a decade since coming to faith, feeling he already understood the doctrine and didn't need anyone to shepherd him. When he later hit a major low point in life, he realized he had no spiritual elder nearby he could speak honestly with. He then took the initiative to seek out an elder for counsel. He said, "I thought I was mature enough — really, I had just never been truly accompanied."

Second. A sister had once discipled a new believer, but her methods were rigid, and the person eventually left the church; she had not dared try again since. Years later, a pastor encouraged her to start again and walked with her through the four-step rhythm. She said, "This time, I finally understood that leading someone isn't about handing them the answers — it's about walking with them."

Third. A small group used to operate as separate individuals, with no one taking the initiative to accompany one another. The leader began practicing the chain of 2 Timothy 2:2: he first sought counsel from an elder, and at the same time began accompanying a new-believer member. Half a year later, that new believer had begun reading Scripture with another newcomer. The leader said, "It turns out a chain really can extend itself."

These three stories share one thing in common: the true beginning of discipleship never waits for a perfect system — it starts with reconnecting yourself to that chain first. Disciples are not taught into being; they are led into being.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing a mindset are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: write down two names — "who is leading me" and "who am I leading." If either slot is empty, this week begin praying for that position and take the first concrete step.

I declare that I will make disciples of all nations, not merely gathering a crowd, but shaping life.

I declare that I will reconnect myself to the four-generation chain — someone leads me, and I lead someone.

I declare that I plant, I water, but it is God who makes the life grow; I will be diligent, not anxious.

I declare that I will present everyone mature before God, striving with all His energy that powerfully works within me.

Brothers and sisters, may we all be like Jesus, placing our deepest investment in a few; and may we all learn Paul's resolve, presenting everyone mature before God. The mission of making disciples, Jesus's system, the path of multiplication — these three are the truest shape of a discipleship system. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations trace a path that moves downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind; the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart; the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — a lesson that never reaches the Third Transformation stays stuck at the level of ideas.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as a Mindset (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the key point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ The Great Commission has only one main verb — "make disciples." What does this remind you about the purpose of the church's existence?

2. ★★ "Addition looks impressive at the start; multiplication has boundless staying power." What does this remind you about how a church should invest its resources?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "Discipleship has no wholesale, only retail." In your own words, explain the relationship between a system and individual accompaniment.

4. ★★ "Presence without sending raises hothouse believers; sending without presence burns out and dries up workers." What does this remind you about the rhythm of discipleship?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it beautifully." If someone's answer is fragmented, help them organize it — don't finish it for them.

ch22.title: The LORD Sees Not as Man Sees — How to Discover and Develop New Leaders
ch22.intro:
Grace and peace, brothers and sisters. Last lesson we laid a road of discipleship for the church; this lesson asks: among those walking this road, who is the leader God has prepared for the next relay leg? And how should we develop them? Every generation of the church cries out about a "shortage of co-workers" — but the problem is often not that God has not prepared people, but that we lack the eyes to discover them: David was in the sheep pen in Bethlehem, Elisha was driving oxen in the field, Timothy was an unknown in Lystra — God's leaders are often hidden in corners no one notices, waiting for a pair of eyes that can see. Today let us ask the Lord first to change how we see people: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.

1 Samuel 16:7 — "But the LORD said to Samuel, 'Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.'"

sections.heading: 1. The Eighth One Who Was Left Out
sections.html: Samuel was sent to Bethlehem to anoint a new king, and the moment he saw Eliab's tall stature, he thought to himself: surely the LORD's anointed stands before Him. Notice — this was the old prophet who had anointed Saul and had seen countless people! Yet God stopped him: "Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him." Jesse paraded seven sons before Samuel, but did not even think to call David back — not even David's own father considered this shepherd boy a candidate. Yet God had seen the heart in the wilderness: the faithfulness of fighting lions and bears for the flock, the hunger for God expressed through the harp. God's list is often different from man's — don't only look for leaders on the platform; go look in the sheep pen.

sections.heading: 2. God's Vision, a Spiritual Standard, Development by Grace
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. God's vision — man looks at appearance, God looks at the heart; discovering leaders means laying down a résumé-shaped way of seeing. A spiritual standard — from Jethro to the apostles, Scripture's criteria for selection are clear and consistent, and character always ranks above ability. Development by grace — a leader does not automatically grow simply by being chosen; like Elijah casting his cloak over Elisha, they need a calling, companionship, and encouragement. A church can survive a shortage of funds, but not a break in the leadership line — the most painful line in Judges is, "there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD." A generational break often takes only one generation of neglect.

sections.heading: 3. Four Marks, the Peter Principle, and the Heart of a Spiritual Parent
sections.html:
The management scholar Douglas McGregor proposed the famous Theory X and Theory Y: Theory X assumes people are naturally lazy and avoid responsibility; Theory Y assumes people long to grow and are willing to take responsibility. He pointed out something crucial: a leader's assumptions become self-fulfilling — treat people according to Theory X, and they really do become more passive; treat people according to Theory Y, and their potential is awakened. Moses judged the people alone until he was utterly exhausted, and his father-in-law Jethro issued Scripture's first leadership selection checklist: "Look for able men from all the people, men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe." Of the four qualifications, only one concerns ability; three concern character. The management scholar Laurence Peter proposed the humorous yet penetrating "Peter Principle": in a hierarchical organization, people keep being promoted because they perform well in their current role, until they reach a position they cannot handle. Churches often fall into this same trap — someone who sings well is made worship leader; someone eager to serve is made a department head — but leading people and doing a task well are two entirely different gifts. Acts 6 records that when the early church selected deacons, the standard was "men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom" — there is no position in the church that says "spirituality not required." Though the heart is examined only by God, it reveals itself through four observable marks: faithfulness — finishing well with no one watching; hunger — an appetite for the Word of God; self-denial — going the extra mile while others rest; influence — people naturally willing to listen to and follow them.

After receiving his commission on Mount Horeb, Elijah found Elisha plowing a field and "cast his cloak upon him" — the prophet's cloak was a symbol of office, and this act was a public calling. Elisha's response was total: he slaughtered a pair of oxen and used the plowing equipment as firewood to cook the meat for the people — turning the tools of his livelihood into fuel for a sacrifice, cutting off any road back. Timothy was young, introverted, and often timid; Paul reminded him: "Do not neglect the gift you have." A gift is real, but it does not ignite on its own — it can be smothered by timidity, cooled by neglect, like a fire in a furnace slowly dying down. Paul said to the Corinthian church, "For though you have countless guides in Christ, you do not have many fathers." A guide teaches a skill, charges a fee, and watches performance. A father gives life, pays a cost, and loves the person themselves. If developing new leaders is only about courses and evaluations, what is produced is hired hands; only the heart of a spiritual parent can produce leaders with real life in them. In 1855, an ordinary Boston Sunday school teacher named Edward Kimball worried about a shoe-store apprentice in his class. He paced back and forth outside the shop door, nearly losing his nerve to go in; once inside, in a stockroom stacked with shoeboxes, he stammered his way through a message about the love of Christ. That day, eighteen-year-old Dwight Moody came to faith — he later became an evangelist spanning two continents, leading hundreds of thousands to Christ. Obedience matters more than eloquence; showing up matters more than being perfect. The path of development has four elements: giving opportunity — letting people grow through bearing responsibility; giving cover — putting them on stage while standing behind them; giving feedback — specifically affirming what is right and honestly pointing out what could be better; giving space — allowing them to be different from you, even to surpass you.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Saul Could Not Bear David
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson too has a passage that must be spoken honestly. The more we emphasize discovering and developing leaders, the more easily people assume the problem lies entirely in a lack of method, without examining whether their own hearts have already grown unable to bear someone stronger than themselves.

The root of a shortage of co-workers often lies within ourselves. The first obstacle: not letting go — senior co-workers doing everything themselves, which looks like responsibility on the surface but is a lack of peace underneath. The second obstacle: fear of being surpassed — seeing a rising talent's outstanding gifts feels not like joy but like a threat; Saul glaring at David the moment he heard "David has struck down his ten thousands" is exactly this sickness. The third obstacle: misplaced standards — rushing to use whoever has ability, skipping the testing of character; the result is that a gift lifts a person to a height that character cannot support, and the fall injures many.

Things that must never be said: "It's not that I won't let go — they're really just not ready yet." "Who I promote is my own business, I don't need a standard." "There'll be a successor sooner or later, let's just let it happen naturally." These statements dress the self up as caution or casualness, while avoiding the real fear and jealousy in one's own heart. The 321 vision says, "Only the selfless dare raise up someone stronger than themselves." John the Baptist said, "He must increase, but I must decrease" — this is a declaration of selflessness.

sections.heading: 5. Three Problems in Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
First problem: "It's easy in our church to judge someone's leadership potential by education, eloquence, or family background, overlooking the testing of character." In Jethro's checklist, one part concerns ability, three parts concern character — this is the reminder left to us by Scripture's first leadership selection checklist.

Second problem: "Senior co-workers often do everything themselves, and younger people are left forever watching from the sidelines, never getting a chance to step onto the field." The path of development requires giving opportunity, cover, feedback, and space — without a chance to step onto the field, even the best seedling can only sit on the bench.

Third problem: "Churches tend to reward the most eye-catching performers while rarely noticing those who quietly and faithfully do small things." Do you want to discover tomorrow's preacher? Look at who most faithfully wipes down the table today.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
To bring this lesson home into the 321 framework, I want to invite you to make three concrete corrections.

First correction: replace "man looks at appearance" with "seeking God's vision." The 321 vision says, "Change from a human viewpoint to God's viewpoint." Ask the Lord to help us go look in the sheep pen, to find the eighth one who was left out.

Second correction: replace "fear of being surpassed" with "He must increase, but I must decrease." Developing a successor is an exercise in laying down power; when one generation of leaders is willing to become a ladder, the next generation can stand taller than this one.

Third correction: replace "quietly admiring in your heart" with "walking over and casting the cloak." This week, specifically tell the person you have noticed: I see the hand of God on you. Jesus saw the crowds like sheep without a shepherd, and said to His disciples: the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest. The first act of raising up workers is prayer, because the workers are sent by the Lord, not manufactured by us — our discovering is finding what the Lord has already chosen; our developing is joining what the Lord is already doing.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Vision
sections.html:
The same assignment — "discovering and developing new leaders" — placed before different people stirs up entirely different reactions. Let me lay out four hearts side by side; perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Sees a rising talent's outstanding gifts and feels not joy but threat, secretly suppressing anyone stronger than himself while only promoting the compliant and mediocre. Yet Paul says, "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Galatians 5:26). The proud heart needs to be reminded: suppressing someone stronger than yourself ultimately crushes the future of the whole community.

The Fearful Heart

Has been called by God to take on greater ministry, but grows timid because of youth, introversion, or lack of experience, repeatedly shrinking back from receiving the cloak. Yet the psalmist says, "Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD!" (Psalm 27:14). The strength God gives grows steady within the hearts of those who wait for Him.

The Ashamed Heart

Like David, feels like the "eighth one" not even his own father thought of, deeply convinced in his heart of hearts that he is not good enough, not worth God using. Yet the psalmist says, "You knitted me together in my mother's womb… I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psalm 139:13–14). How wonderfully God made you — His vision never follows the order of man's list.

The Wounded Heart

Has always longed to be seen, to be developed, but no one has ever cast that cloak over them, and has since carried the wound of being forgotten, no longer daring to hope for discovery. Yet the prophet Isaiah promises, "Can a woman forget her nursing child… Yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands" (Isaiah 49:15–16). You have never been forgotten by the true Father — He has engraved you on His palms.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
Let me use three examples to help us see what this lesson looks like lived out.

First. A senior pastor had for years done everything himself, with the pulpit almost entirely his alone. When illness once made preaching impossible, he was forced to let a young co-worker take the pulpit, and the congregation's response was surprisingly good. Reflecting afterward, he said: "I thought I was being responsible; in fact I had been blocking the very people God wanted to raise up."

Second. A young brother, being introverted by nature, had for years had a gift for ministry but never dared take on greater responsibility. An elder noticed him, took the initiative to invite him to serve together, and reminded him of the gift God had given whenever he shrank back. Years later, he became one of the church's most trusted small-group leaders.

Third. A sister had always felt unvalued at home growing up, and continued to feel she was never the one who mattered in church either. A senior co-worker noticed her quiet, faithful service and told her directly, "I see the hand of God on you." She remembered that line for the rest of her life, and it became the starting point of her own willingness to develop others.

These three stories share one thing in common: the true beginning of discovering leaders never waits for a perfect evaluation system — it comes from eyes willing to pay attention, and a mouth willing to speak up. In your own community there is a David tending sheep, an Elisha plowing a field, a Moody in a shoe store waiting for one visit.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing a mindset are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: using the four marks of faithfulness, hunger, self-denial, and influence, quietly observe your community for one week, write down two or three names — paying special attention to that "eighth one who was left out" — and pray for these names every day.

I declare that I will seek God's vision, not looking at outward appearance, but at the heart God has made within.

I declare that I will no longer fear being surpassed; I will joyfully say: He must increase, but I must decrease.

I declare that I will walk over and cast the cloak, telling the one God has chosen, with my own mouth: I see you.

I declare that I will carry the heart of a spiritual parent, passing on life, not merely knowledge.

Brothers and sisters, may we all be like Samuel, willing to have our vision corrected by God; and may we all learn Elijah's courage, taking the initiative to approach the one plowing in the field. God's vision, a spiritual standard, development by grace — these three are the truest shape of discovering and developing new leaders. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.html:

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it beautifully." If someone's answer is fragmented, help them organize it — don't finish it for them.

Second Transformation | Digesting It into Life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)

Purpose: through Seeing, Hearing, Thinking, Speaking, and Acting, digest the idea into life.

[See] Seeing Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — proud (feeling threatened by others' outstanding gifts and wanting to suppress them), fearful (called but timid because of youth or introversion, shrinking back), ashamed (feeling like the unvalued "eighth one"), wounded (longing to be discovered but never being seen, and being hurt by it). Which one are you most like? What experience made you this way?

[Hear] Hearing God Speak

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for members with a wounded heart, particularly those who felt unvalued from childhood and longed to be discovered but never were. If someone cries, pause the discussion and simply be present — don't rush to give answers. Third Transformation | Transforming It into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily habit.

10. ★★ "The 920 practice: your children and your group members may be a David God has hidden." In your family, which of someone's qualities will you specifically affirm this week?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "Do you want to discover tomorrow's preacher? Look at who most faithfully wipes down the table today." Is there someone quietly faithful like this in your small group?

13. ★★★ The ten-minutes-a-day practice: this week, pray each day for the names on your observation list. Say what time each day you will do this.

14. ★★ The 920 practice: identify your "2" (a spiritual companion). This week, share your answer to question 9 with them, and ask them to pray for your observation and invitation this week. Say their name out loud now.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, share two things with each other: the person on whom you will cast the cloak this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to give us His vision, to see the vessels He has hidden in the corners.

ch23.title: Give Him Some of Your Authority, So That the People Will Obey — Developing Leaders Across Generations
ch23.intro:
Grace and peace, brothers and sisters. The last two lessons spoke of the road of discipleship and the eyes to discover leaders; this lesson faces a longer-term issue — passing the torch across generations. God's work crosses generations: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — three generations carrying the same promise; Moses and Joshua, Elijah and Elisha, Paul and Timothy — two generations handing off the same torch. The most beautiful scene in a church is not the brilliance of one generation, but several generations walking together within the same vision; a church's deepest hidden danger is not outward persecution, but the torch being dropped between two generations. Today let us learn from the handoff between Moses and Joshua.

Numbers 27:18,20 — "So the LORD said to Moses, 'Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him… You shall invest him with some of your authority, that all the congregation of the people of Israel may obey.'"

sections.heading: 1. Lest the Congregation of the LORD Be as Sheep That Have No Shepherd
sections.html: The background of this passage is deeply moving: God told Moses that he would not enter the Promised Land. Moses did not plead for himself, but asked God to appoint someone to lead the congregation, "that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd" — with the end of his life in sight, what weighed on him was not his own legacy, but the flock's tomorrow. God's instructions for the handoff involved four actions: lay your hand on him — identity affirmed and blessed; set him before the priests and all the congregation — a public establishment; charge him — passing on mission and experience; invest him with some of your authority — the hardest step of all: genuinely dividing power and standing over to him. So many transitions fail at this last step: the position is given, but the honor is withheld. Moses gave completely, and so Joshua received securely.

sections.heading: 2. The Laying On of Hands for the Next Runner, a Double Portion of Spirit, the Recounting Across Generations
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. The laying on of hands for the next runner — Moses laid his hand on Joshua's head before everyone and gave him a share of his authority; passing on leadership needs public confirmation and real delegation. A double portion of spirit — Elisha asked that a double portion of Elijah's spirit rest on him; a healthy succession does not seek merely to preserve what came before, but to exceed it. The recounting across generations — telling the excellent deeds of the LORD to the next generation; faith is a relay of storytelling that never breaks. In a relay race, the mistake rarely happens on the straightaway — it happens in the handoff zone; when the fire of revival goes out, it is rarely at the peak, but in the gap between two generations handing off. Passing the baton is a stretch of running together, not a single ceremony of transfer.

sections.heading: 3. Generativity, a Double Portion of Spirit, and the Relay of Generations
sections.html:
The developmental psychologist Erik Erikson divided the human lifespan into eight stages, and he called the challenge of the second half of life "generativity versus stagnation": in the latter half of life, a person either turns toward nurturing the next generation, and their life becomes rich through giving it away, or falls into stagnation, circling endlessly around their own achievements and comfort. A life that gives itself away is the life that flourishes; a torch that is passed on is the torch that does not go out. Before Elijah was taken up into heaven, he offered Elisha a blank check: ask what I shall do for you before I am taken from you. Elisha did not ask for peace or position — he asked that "a double portion of your spirit be on me." "Double portion" in the Law referred to the firstborn's inheritance right; what he asked for was the inheritance of a spiritual firstborn. And the one passing the baton must have a heart big enough to celebrate that double portion — when Joshua asked Moses to stop two men from prophesying, Moses said, "Would that all the LORD's people were prophets!" The sociologists Neil Howe and William Strauss studied centuries of generational change and proposed a generational theory: roughly every twenty years forms a new generation, each shaped by the major events of its formative years. Generational difference is not about who is right and who is wrong — it is that different soils of the times grow different fruit trees; the root cannot say to the branch, "I have no need of you," nor can the branch say to the root, "I have no need of you."

Psalm 78 says, "We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD, and his might, and the wonders that he has done… that they should arise and tell them to their children." At least four generations stand together in this one chain of storytelling; methods go out of date, but stories never do. 2 Timothy 1 records: "I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well." Three generations, one and the same sincere faith; family gave Timothy the root of faith, and Paul gave him the wings of ministry. Joel 2:28 says, "Your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions." Every generation has a part; no generation is skipped over. The older generation holds the roots; the middle generation holds the beams; the younger generation holds the fire — roots without fire grow rigid, fire without roots burns crooked, and beams standing alone will collapse under the weight. In his old age, the apostle John shepherded the churches around Ephesus, and among his disciples was a young man named Polycarp, who heard with his own ears John's accounts of walking with the Lord. Polycarp later became bishop of Smyrna and shepherded the church for over half a century; at eighty-six he was brought to execution, and when the magistrate urged him to curse Christ and live, he said, "Eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me?" — and he went to his death calmly. Polycarp in turn raised up Irenaeus, one of the most important apologists of the early church. Jesus — John — Polycarp — Irenaeus: a living version of four-generation succession. From Moses's example we can distill the four actions of passing the baton: laying on of hands — a public confirmation; honor — a real delegation of authority; walking together — accompanying through the transition; blessing — a willing stepping-down, retreating to the position of intercessor, not remaining a puppet-master behind the curtain.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Two Kinds of Failure in the Handoff Zone
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson too has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because the most dangerous moment in a succession is often not the day of farewell, but the stretch of road where two generations hand off to each other.

The first kind of failure belongs to the older generation: holding on and refusing to let go. The reasons sound spiritual — "the young ones still aren't mature enough," "let's wait and observe a bit longer" — but "a bit longer" turns into ten years. The deeper cause is often the self: identity bound up in a position, so that letting go of power feels like losing oneself. The second kind of failure belongs to the younger generation: unable to wait. Seeing the older generation's limitations, they rush to overthrow them, speaking of their predecessors with contempt. Absalom is the classic example — winning people's hearts at the city gate, usurping his father's throne, and destroying himself in the process. Elisha's path was entirely different: he poured water in service for years, staying by Elijah's side without a step's distance right to the very end. The spiritual law is clear: those who honor the previous generation inherit the estate; those who despise the previous generation lose the blessing.

Things that must never be said: "They're still not mature, let's wait a bit longer." "Times have changed, that old approach is outdated." "I've given my whole life to this position, how could I just let it go." These statements dress the self up as caution or progress, while avoiding the real work of the handoff zone. The 321 vision says, "Only selflessness can bring the next generation to fullness." When two selfish people meet, it is the story of Saul and Absalom; when two selfless people meet, it is the story of Moses and Joshua.

sections.heading: 5. Three Problems in Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
First problem: "Churches often treat generational differences as a spiritual problem to be condemned — the older generation feels the young aren't reverent enough, and the young feel the older generation can't keep up." Most of these are cultural differences, not disagreements about truth — treating cultural differences as spiritual failings is the most common killer of cross-generational partnership.

Second problem: "The older generation often hands over the position while keeping the honor to themselves, still wanting a say in every decision." God instructed Moses to "invest him with some of your authority, that all the congregation of the people of Israel may obey" — so many successions fail at this exact last step.

Third problem: "The story of faith is rarely told at home or in church, and the younger generation knows only rules, not the acts of God." Psalm 78 reminds us that faith has always been just one generation away — if this generation does not tell it, the next generation will not know it.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
To bring this lesson home into the 321 framework, I want to invite you to make three concrete corrections.

First correction: replace "holding on and refusing to let go" with "laying on of hands, honor, walking together, blessing." The 321 vision says, "Humility is laying down power and returning to one's own place." When the older generation gives completely, the younger generation can receive securely.

Second correction: replace "unable to wait, rushing to overthrow" with "serving, honoring, asking for a double portion." Elisha's résumé begins with pouring water on Elijah's hands — before becoming a leader, he was first a servant.

Third correction: replace "each generation talking past the other" with "telling it to the next generation." This week, find a young person or an elder and either tell or listen to an account of God's work, continuing the chain of storytelling.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Torch
sections.html:
The same assignment — "developing leaders across generations" — placed before different people stirs up entirely different reactions. Let me lay out four hearts side by side; perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Ties identity and worth entirely to a position, feeling that letting go and passing the baton would mean losing one's own significance, and so keeps refusing to truly let go. Yet the psalmist says, "For not from the east or from the west and not from the wilderness comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psalm 75:6–7). The proud heart needs to be reminded: rising and falling are both in God's hands — there is no need to prove your worth by clutching a position.

The Fearful Heart

Has been entrusted with greater responsibility, but keeps putting off truly taking hold of it, afraid of being inadequate and disappointing the older generation's expectations. Yet God said to Joshua (and to every successor): "It is the LORD who goes before you. He will be with you; he will not leave you or forsake you. Do not fear or be dismayed" (Deuteronomy 31:8). What leads you forward is not your own ability, but the God who goes ahead of you.

The Ashamed Heart

Once could not wait and rushed to prove himself, seizing a position through improper means, and has since felt deep regret and self-blame over how he acted. Yet the psalmist says, "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17). What God values is a returning heart, not a life sentenced forever to past regret.

The Wounded Heart

Has always longed to be affirmed and honored by the older generation, but has been consistently overlooked or belittled, and has since carried this grievance, finding it hard to trust cross-generational relationships again. Yet the prophet Malachi promises, "He will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers" (Malachi 4:6). God Himself will mend the broken heart between generations — He sees your grievance.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
Let me use three examples to help us see what this lesson looks like lived out.

First. A senior pastor had led a church for over thirty years, always reluctant to pass the baton, always saying "we still need to observe a bit longer." Only when a serious illness forced him into recovery did a young co-worker fully lead the church for the first time — and the result went surprisingly well. He later admitted, "I thought it was for the church's good; really, I just couldn't bear to let go."

Second. A young co-worker, dissatisfied with the older generation's way of leading, privately rallied other co-workers to set up a rival faction, and the ministry eventually split, which he came to regret deeply. Years later he took the initiative to apologize to that elder, and the two reconciled. He said, "I learned that only those who honor the previous generation can bear to inherit the estate."

Third. A sister, having longed to be entrusted with responsibility in her youth but always overlooked, later became a leader herself, and made a point of especially nurturing young people who were easily overlooked. She said, "Because I know what that feeling of being overlooked is like, I don't want anyone else to go through it."

These three stories share one thing in common: passing the torch across generations never comes from one perfect handover ceremony, but from both sides, day after day, choosing honor over grasping, and choosing service over rushing ahead. The torch in our hands has been passed down all the way here; now it is our turn to ask: where is the next pair of hands?

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing a mindset are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: this week, visit or call a spiritual elder, bringing two questions — over the years, what has been the most wonderful thing God has done in your life? What is the one thing you most want to pass on to our generation? Simply listen, and write down what you hear.

I declare that I will be like Moses, genuinely giving honor to the next generation, giving completely, and stepping down willingly.

I declare that I will be like Elisha, pouring water in service to the end, honoring the previous generation, asking for a double portion of the spirit.

I declare that I will tell the excellent deeds of the LORD to the next generation, so that the chain of storytelling never breaks with me.

I declare that both generations will let Jesus be King; our handoff is not a transfer of power, but a continuation of the same Lord.

Brothers and sisters, may we all be like Moses, concerned for the flock's tomorrow rather than our own legacy; and may we all learn Elisha's faithfulness, pouring water in service and honoring to the end. The laying on of hands for the next runner, a double portion of spirit, the recounting across generations — these three are the truest shape of developing leaders across generations. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations trace a path that moves downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind; the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart; the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — a lesson that never reaches the Third Transformation stays stuck at the level of ideas.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority — if time is short, discuss at least this question in each Transformation; ★★ = secondary priority; ★ = discuss only if time allows. The reproduction task marked (Required) must not be skipped; it may be completed at home if needed.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as a Mindset (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the key point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ What weighed on Moses was not his own legacy but the flock's tomorrow. What does this remind you about the motive behind succession?

2. ★★ "The position is given, but the honor is withheld" is the step where succession most easily fails. What does this remind you about real delegation?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "The handoff zone rarely fails on the straightaway — it fails at the curve." In your own words, explain the failures the older and younger generations are each prone to.

4. ★★ "The root cannot say to the branch, 'I have no need of you,' nor can the branch say to the root, 'I have no need of you.'" What does this remind you about generational difference?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it beautifully." If someone's answer is fragmented, help them organize it — don't finish it for them.

Second Transformation | Digesting It into Life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)

Purpose: through Seeing, Hearing, Thinking, Speaking, and Acting, digest the idea into life.

[See] Seeing Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — proud (identity tied to a position, unwilling to truly let go), fearful (afraid of being unworthy to take up the baton and putting it off), ashamed (having rushed and grasped at a position before, and regretting it), wounded (overlooked and belittled by the older generation, carrying that grievance). Which one are you most like? What experience made you this way?

[Hear] Hearing God Speak

6. ★★ For each of these four hearts, God has a specific word to say. Find the verse that corresponds to you, read it aloud, then tell the group: where does this verse touch you?

[Think] Thinking It Through

7. ★★ Has a spiritual elder ever genuinely given you "honor," or have you ever given it to someone younger like this?

[Speak] Saying It Out Loud

8. ★ Finish this sentence in one line: "This lesson tore down which old idea I had about 'cross-generational succession'?" If your honest answer is "none," say that too — that itself is an important discovery.

[Act] Taking a Step

9. ★★ This week, which elder will you visit, or which young person will you tell a story to? Say their name.

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for members with a wounded heart, particularly those overlooked, belittled, or had credit taken by the older generation. If someone cries, pause the discussion and simply be present — don't rush to give answers. If it involves deeper trauma, follow up individually after the meeting and help arrange a referral if needed.

Third Transformation | Transforming It into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily habit.

10. ★★ "The 920 practice: learn from Lois and Eunice, living out sincere faith at home." In your family, how can you tell an account of God's work this week?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message asked: "Who is my Joshua? How much honor have I given him?" If you are leading a ministry, which decision-making authority could you genuinely hand over this week?

13. ★★★ The ten-minutes-a-day practice: this week, pray each day for someone from the older or younger generation. Say what time each day you will do this.

14. ★★ The 920 practice: identify your "2" (a spiritual companion). This week, share your answer to question 9 with them, and ask them to pray for your practice of succession this week. Say their name out loud now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, in three sentences, tell this lesson to someone outside the group — "Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit"; "lay your hand on him"; "you shall invest him with some of your authority, that all the congregation may obey." Write down now whom you will tell.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, share two things with each other: the person you will visit upward or tell a story to downward this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to help us all hand the torch steadily into the next runner's hands.

ch24.title: Until Christ Is Formed in You — Spiritual Formation in Discipleship
ch24.intro:
Grace and peace, brothers and sisters. In the last three lessons we laid a road, found people, and passed on the torch — but what is the very core of all of this? If discipleship is only about finishing a course, filling a position, or lining up a successor, then all we have built is a well-running organization. Paul captured the core of discipleship in a mother's words: "My little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you." Spiritual formation is letting Christ take shape within a person — not an accumulation of knowledge, not a polishing of behavior, but a reshaping of life. The 321 vision says: five layers of change from the inside out — mindset, life, lifestyle, relationships, ministry — and the order cannot be reversed.

Galatians 4:19 — "My little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you!"

sections.heading: 1. What You Signed Was Not a Teaching Contract, But a Mother's Resolve
sections.html: The Galatian believers had already been born again, and yet Paul says he must suffer birth pains "again" — because though they had the life of Christ, the shape of Christ had not yet grown within them. The original word for "formed" is the term used for the formation of an embryo: the life already carries the seed of Christ, but it still needs to grow Christ's own features — His heart, His disposition, His responses. This is discipleship's deepest goal: not shaping people into what the church needs, but letting Christ grow His own shape within a person. And Paul chose the most painful metaphor in the world — the pain of childbirth. Shaping a life means weeping in intercession, enduring pain while waiting, and picking someone up again and again as they repeatedly stumble. Anyone doing discipleship should be prepared: what you signed was not a teaching contract, but a mother's resolve.

sections.heading: 2. Christ Formed, Channels of Practice, a Life United to the Vine
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. Christ formed — the goal of formation is not "becoming better," but "becoming more like Christ." Channels of practice — life cannot command itself to grow, but it can position itself within the channels through which grace flows: the Word, prayer, community, obedience. A life united to the vine — a branch need not strain to bear fruit; it need only remain on the vine. We must discern several kinds of very convincing counterfeit "growth": inflated knowledge — more and more Bible knowledge, and not a bit of temper changed; busy activity — a schedule packed seven days a week, and a spirit growing emptier by the day; chasing experiences — one conference after another, arriving fast and leaving fast. True spiritual growth has only one mark: becoming more like Jesus.

sections.heading: 3. Neuroplasticity, a Tree Planted by Streams of Water, and Abiding in Him
sections.html:
The neuroscientist Michael Merzenich was a pioneer of research into "neuroplasticity." The scientific community once believed the adult brain was fixed; his experiments proved that the brain remains plastic throughout life — repeated, focused practice can genuinely rewire neural circuits. The excitement of a single conference cannot rewire a circuit; only daily practice reshapes a life. Romans 8:29 says, "For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son." God's ultimate purpose in saving us is to shape us into the image of Christ — this reframes how we read our circumstances: prosperity is formation, and hardship is formation too. The spiritual theologian Richard Foster, in Celebration of Discipline, points out that spiritual disciplines like meditation, prayer, fasting, and solitude do not themselves produce life — they are "the means by which we place ourselves before God"; what truly changes a person is God's grace. Another mentor, Dallas Willard, added a crucial line: "Grace is not opposed to effort; it is opposed to earning." Psalm 1 says, "His delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night. He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither." Rushing through one chapter a day is worth less than chewing on one verse for an entire day.

John 15 says, "Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing." A branch never grits its teeth and strains to "squeeze out" grapes — it does only one thing: stay connected to the vine; the sap flows through it, and fruit naturally comes out. In a seventeenth-century Paris monastery, a lay brother named Lawrence, who did menial work, spent thirty years washing pots and cooking in the kitchen, practicing the presence of God — doing every small task out of love for God. He said, "I possess God as tranquilly in the noise and clatter of my kitchen … as if I were upon my knees before the altar." Luke 5:16 has only one sentence: "But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray." That word "but" carries tremendous weight: at the very height of ministry's momentum, Jesus withdrew. The power for ministry is not replenished among the crowds — it is replenished before the Father. Formation flows through four channels of grace: the Word — meditating day and night; prayer — the practice of withdrawing to the wilderness; community — life polished through relationship; obedience — hearing and immediately doing. The fastest shortcut to spiritual formation is saying "yes" the instant you sense the Spirit's prompting. Peter's parting words say, "But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ." Growth runs on two tracks: growing in grace, experiencing the Lord's grace ever more deeply and treating others with ever more kindness; growing in knowledge, knowing the Lord Himself ever more truly. Missing either one leads to imbalance: knowledge without grace grows a cold, rigid teacher; passion without knowledge grows an easily deceived child. Those who make disciples must also remember their own place: we are midwives, not the author of the life; the most important thing we can do is bring people to the source, teaching them to read Scripture and hear the Spirit themselves, rather than depending on us for everything. Successful discipleship means the disciple needs you less and less, and needs the Lord more and more.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Three Very Convincing Detours
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson too has a passage that must be spoken honestly. The more we emphasize spiritual formation, the more easily people mistake certain seemingly spiritual behaviors for real growth.

There are three detours that look spiritual. Error one: inflated knowledge — equating spiritual life with Bible knowledge; the more Bible study, the sharper the judgment of others; Scripture says knowledge puffs up, but only love builds up. Error two: busy activity — equating spiritual life with the volume of service; Martha was distracted with much serving, her heart troubled and anxious, but the Lord said Mary had chosen the good portion. Error three: chasing experiences — chasing meetings, chasing anointing, chasing feelings; like Peter on the mountain of transfiguration saying "it is good for us to be here," while the Lord led him back down the mountain toward the road of the cross. What these three errors have in common: they all stop at "what did I gain," never advancing to "what am I becoming."

Things that must never be said: "I read my Bible more than anyone, I must be very spiritual." "My schedule is packed seven days a week, how could I not be growing?" "I just went to a conference with amazing anointing." These statements treat knowledge, busyness, and experience as proof of spiritual growth, while avoiding the one true mark: am I more like Jesus? The 321 vision says formation must go all the way to selflessness — the self is the root of the fall, and the process of Christ being formed is the process of "I" gradually stepping down while Christ gradually takes the throne.

sections.heading: 5. Three Problems in Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
First problem: "It's easy in our church to treat someone with rich Bible knowledge as the most spiritual role model, while overlooking their temper and how they treat others." Love builds people up; knowledge that never lands in obedience is only spiritual fat.

Second problem: "People tend to measure someone's commitment by how busy their service schedule is — the busier, the more praised, while quiet solitude is met with suspicion instead." Yet Jesus withdrew to desolate places to pray — the power for ministry is not replenished among the crowds, but before the Father.

Third problem: "Many believers turn devotional life into a grinding chore, failing again and again, blaming themselves, and giving up, feeling they will never measure up." Fruit is not squeezed out — it flows out; the Lord's command is not "bear more fruit," but "abide in me."

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
To bring this lesson home into the 321 framework, I want to invite you to make three concrete corrections.

First correction: replace "straining fruit out through willpower" with "abiding in Him." The 321 vision says, "Selflessness lets Jesus live within." Not visiting the Lord once a week, but dwelling with Him constantly.

Second correction: replace "service that only exhales, never inhales" with "withdrawing is inhaling, going out is exhaling." This week, follow the Lord's example of "but" — on the busiest day, deliberately set aside half an hour to withdraw to a quiet place.

Third correction: replace "replacing presence with busyness" with "keeping all four channels flowing daily." The Word, prayer, community, obedience — with all four in place, the shape of Christ forms day by day. 2 Corinthians says, "And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit." The mechanism of transformation is not desperate imitation, but focused beholding — a person gradually comes to resemble what they gaze upon. Those who gaze on Christ daily are transformed into Christ's shape — this is the work of the Spirit, not a self-improvement grind.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Formation
sections.html:
The same assignment — "spiritual formation" — placed before different people stirs up entirely different reactions. Let me lay out four hearts side by side; perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Feels that rich Bible knowledge and strong Bible-study skill equal spiritual maturity, secretly looking down on members whose knowledge falls short of his own. Yet Paul says, "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up" (1 Corinthians 8:1). The proud heart needs to be reminded: knowledge without love is merely decoration for self-conceit.

The Fearful Heart

Is afraid to stop serving and step away into quiet solitude, feeling it would make them look less committed, unable to keep up with everyone else, and so never dares to truly withdraw to the wilderness. Yet God said to Moses and the Israelites, "The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent" (Exodus 14:14). Real battle is sometimes stillness, not ceaseless busyness.

The Ashamed Heart

Fails again and again at spiritual disciplines, resolving and then falling, falling and then blaming themselves, feeling they can never truly change. Yet Paul once cried out the same way: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!" (Romans 7:24–25). Even Paul went through this struggle — the way out is not gritting your teeth harder, but thanking the Lord who saves us.

The Wounded Heart

Was once required to meet harsh devotional standards in a certain community, judged as not spiritual enough at the slightest lapse, and has since felt fear and resistance toward the very word "discipline." Yet Jesus says, "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest… for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:28–29). True discipline finds rest in the Lord's gentleness and lowliness — it is never crushed under legalism.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
Let me use three examples to help us see what this lesson looks like lived out.

First. A brother with rich Bible knowledge often corrected others' interpretations in small group, but rarely cared for the lives of group members. One day someone gently asked him, "With all that study, has your temper actually gotten any better?" The question stung, and it led him to re-examine the direction of his own "growth."

Second. A sister who served extremely busily, taking part in nearly every church activity, grew more and more parched and exhausted inside. She began following the Lord's example of "but," deliberately setting aside a completely quiet time each week — not to accomplish anything, simply to draw near to the Lord. She said, "I had always thought busyness meant spirituality; in fact I had already run dry."

Third. A brother had failed again and again for years in his devotional life, and had at one point given up any regular habit entirely, feeling deep self-blame. A spiritual companion walked with him to restart using "ruminative meditation" — choosing just one verse and chewing on it daily. Half a year later, he said, "I finally understand — fruit isn't squeezed out, it flows out."

These three stories share one thing in common: true spiritual formation never comes from more knowledge, more busyness, or more experiences — it comes from the daily discipline of abiding in the Lord. May we all carry a mother's resolve for one another, until Christ is formed in each of our hearts.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing a mindset are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: choose one verse and ruminate on it every day this week — read it three times in the morning, chew on it whenever it comes to mind during the day, and write down one takeaway at night, experiencing the difference between meditating day and night and simply having read it.

I declare that I will abide in the Lord, letting fruit flow naturally from a life united to Him, no longer straining it out.

I declare that I will be planted by streams of water, meditating on God's word day and night, bearing fruit in its season, my leaf never withering.

I declare that I will learn the Lord's rhythm — withdrawing is inhaling, going out is exhaling — replenishing my strength for ministry before the Father.

I declare that I will gaze on Jesus, letting the Spirit gradually shape me into the image of His Son, from one degree of glory to another.

Brothers and sisters, may we all be like Brother Lawrence, practicing the presence of God in the most ordinary of positions; and may we all learn Jesus's rhythm, withdrawing to the wilderness and also walking among the crowds. Christ formed, channels of practice, a life united to the vine — these three are the truest shape of spiritual formation. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations trace a path that moves downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind; the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart; the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — a lesson that never reaches the Third Transformation stays stuck at the level of ideas.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority — if time is short, discuss at least this question in each Transformation; ★★ = secondary priority; ★ = discuss only if time allows. The reproduction task marked (Required) must not be skipped; it may be completed at home if needed.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as a Mindset (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the key point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ The original word for "formed" is the term for an embryo taking shape. What does this remind you about the difference between "spiritual formation" and "accumulating knowledge"?

2. ★★ "Fruit is not squeezed out, it flows out." What does this remind you about the way sanctification works?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "Inflated knowledge, busy activity, chasing experiences" are three very convincing counterfeits of growth. In your own words, explain the one mark of true growth.

4. ★★ Jesus, at His busiest moment, "but" withdrew to the wilderness to pray. What does this remind you about the rhythm of withdrawing and going out?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it beautifully." If someone's answer is fragmented, help them organize it — don't finish it for them.

Second Transformation | Digesting It into Life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)

Purpose: through Seeing, Hearing, Thinking, Speaking, and Acting, digest the idea into life.

[See] Seeing Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — proud (assuming rich knowledge equals spiritual maturity), fearful (afraid quiet solitude will look uncommitted), ashamed (failing again and again at devotional discipline and blaming oneself), wounded (judged before by harsh devotional standards). Which one are you most like? What experience made you this way?

[Hear] Hearing God Speak

6. ★★ For each of these four hearts, God has a specific word to say. Find the verse that corresponds to you, read it aloud, then tell the group: where does this verse touch you?

[Think] Thinking It Through

7. ★★ Have you known a "Brother Lawrence" type — someone living out the presence of God in the most ordinary of positions?

[Speak] Saying It Out Loud

8. ★ Finish this sentence in one line: "This lesson tore down which old idea I had about 'spiritual growth'?" If your honest answer is "none," say that too — that itself is an important discovery.

[Act] Taking a Step

9. ★★ This week, which of the four channels — the Word, prayer, community, obedience — will you reopen? Say specifically what that means.

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for members with a wounded heart, particularly those who have been judged or crushed by harsh spiritual standards. If someone cries, pause the discussion and simply be present — don't rush to give answers. If it involves deeper trauma, follow up individually after the meeting and help arrange a referral if needed.

Third Transformation | Transforming It into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily habit.

10. ★★ "The kitchen can be a sanctuary, washing dishes can be worship, as long as the heart is turned toward God." In your family, which ordinary chore could become this week a practice of God's presence?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "The fastest shortcut to spiritual formation is saying yes the instant you sense the Spirit's prompting." What specific prompting of the Spirit have you noticed this week?

13. ★★★ The ten-minutes-a-day practice: this week, ruminate on the same verse each day. Say what time each day you will do this.

14. ★★ The 920 practice: identify your "2" (a spiritual companion). This week, share your answer to question 9 with them, and ask them to pray for your spiritual practice this week. Say their name out loud now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, in three sentences, tell this lesson to someone outside the group — "I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you"; "abide in me, and I in you"; "apart from me you can do nothing." Write down now whom you will tell.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, share two things with each other: the channel of grace you will reopen this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to help us all abide in Him, until Christ is formed in each of our hearts.

ch25.title: The Lord Added to Their Number Day by Day — The Link Between Discipleship and Church Growth
ch25.intro:
Grace and peace, brothers and sisters. Part Five comes to its final lesson. Having walked through four lessons — laying a road, finding people, passing on the torch, and forming life — someone may have been wondering all along: after all this effort spent slowly forming lives, will the church still grow large? Could discipleship make the church "deep" but "small"? Today let us answer together, from Scripture and from fact: discipleship not only does not hinder growth — it is precisely the root of a church's genuine, healthy, lasting growth. The early church had no growth strategy, only the life of disciples — and Scripture records: "The Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved."

Acts 2:47 — "Praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved."

sections.heading: 1. Three Thousand People Entered Immediately into the Life of Disciples
sections.html: On the day of Pentecost, three thousand people were baptized in a single day — the largest growth explosion in church history. But look at the very next verse: they "devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers" — three thousand people did not become three thousand spectators; that very day they entered into the life of disciples: teaching of truth, connection in relationship, a life of worship. The growth did not overwhelm the church, because the pillars of discipleship were already standing that same day. Now look at the grammar of verse 47: "The Lord added to their number day by day" — the subject of the growth is the Lord, not the apostles' strategy. This sets the tone for the entire study of church growth: we are responsible for health, the Lord is responsible for growth; we make disciples, the Lord adds the numbers. Reverse the order, and you are using human methods to do the Lord's work.

sections.heading: 2. Life Brings Growth, Quality Before Quantity, a Multiplied Harvest
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. Life brings growth — growth is the natural phenomenon of a healthy life; a healthy child naturally grows taller, a healthy church naturally grows; if growth stalls, ask about health first, not method. Quality before quantity — Jesus's order was depth before breadth: three years invested in twelve people, and only then the three thousand of Pentecost. A multiplied harvest — a single grain of wheat that dies produces many grains; slow at the start, surging later. Pursuing growth is not worldly — longing for the world to be saved is God's own heart; the problem lies in the order. Depth and breadth are not a choice — they are a sequence: go deep, and breadth follows naturally; chase only breadth, and in the end you get neither.

sections.heading: 3. Natural Church Development, a Grain of Wheat, and the Faith of a Mustard Seed
sections.html:
The German church researcher Christian Schwarz led a large-scale survey spanning dozens of countries and over a thousand churches, published as Natural Church Development. He found: churches with long-term healthy growth need not have a famous pastor or a large-scale program, but they consistently score high on eight quality characteristics — empowering leadership, gift-oriented ministry, passionate spirituality, functional structures, inspiring worship service, holistic small groups, need-oriented evangelism, and loving relationships. His central metaphor comes from farming: a farmer cannot pull the seedling to make it grow taller — he can only improve the soil; once the soil is good, growth happens naturally. Acts 6:7 says, "And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith." A shallow message attracts shallow followers; only a deep life can pierce a hardened heart. The day after Jesus fed the five thousand, the crowds surged toward Him again, but the Lord saw through it: "You are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves." A crowd can gather for bread, and it can scatter for the lack of it; what the Lord counts are those who take up the cross and follow.

Ephesians 4 is the most complete anatomy of church growth: the source of growth is "holding fast to the head, Christ"; the mechanism of growth is "every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly"; the mode of growth is "growing," organic and gradual, never inflated overnight. Discipleship is precisely the work of turning listeners into limbs of a body. When some Greeks asked to see Jesus, He said instead: "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit." A church that seeks only to preserve itself remains a single grain; only a church willing to die will multiply. Matthew 13 says, "The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed… which is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants." Do not despise small beginnings: a discipleship group of three, one family's altar — mustard-seed thinking does not look at present size, but at the life within. At the end of the nineteenth century, the missionary John Nevius proposed the three-self principle: self-propagating, self-governing, self-supporting — not raising believers into long-term recipients, but training them as disciples from the very first day of their faith. This approach was fully adopted in Korea and produced one of the rare growth miracles in mission history. Discipleship's fruit has four dimensions: growth in depth — disciples rooted in truth, so the church does not scatter when storms come; growth in health — everyone serving, everyone helping each other, so co-workers no longer burn out; growth in numbers — every disciple a witness, the 920 practice carrying the gospel into their own network of relationships; growth in influence — disciples scattered into workplaces, families, and communities, being salt and light. Some pit discipleship against evangelism: discipleship tends the inside, evangelism tends the outside. In fact the Great Commission fuses the two into one: "go" is evangelism, "make disciples" is discipleship. The most powerful evangelistic network is precisely the relational network of disciples — Andrew found his brother Simon, Philip found Nathanael. A single evangelistic event reaches one evening; a hundred disciples practicing 920 are a hundred relational networks running year-round.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — the False Growth of Swapped Seats and a Filled Room
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson too has a passage that must be spoken honestly. The more we emphasize that a church should grow, the more easily people mistake certain seemingly successful numbers for real revival.

Some growth doesn't count on the kingdom's ledger. The first kind: swapped-seat growth — the numbers really did increase, but mostly transferred in from other churches; the kingdom as a whole did not grow, only the flock relocated. The second kind: filled-room growth — using events and giveaways to draw a crowd; the scene is lively, but empty and cold once it's over. The common flaw in both kinds of false growth: only counting "who came," never counting "who grew." The path to healing is switching to a different scoreboard: ask less "how many came today," and more "how many people believed and were baptized this year? How many entered discipleship? How many have begun leading others?"

Things that must never be said: "Our church has more people, so we must be more blessed." "Fewer people must mean we're not doing enough." "As long as the event is exciting enough, people will stay." These statements treat numbers as the sole measure of spiritual life, while avoiding the true order between health and growth. The 321 vision says, "We are responsible for health; the Lord is responsible for growth." It is the Lord who adds people, the Lord who makes the word prosper, the Lord who builds the church.

sections.heading: 5. Three Problems in Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
First problem: "Churches tend to quietly compare their attendance numbers against each other, and churches or pastors with fewer people often feel inferior." What God values is not numbers, but those who take up the cross and follow; a church's health cannot be measured by the number of seats in its sanctuary.

Second problem: "People tend to use events and giveaways to draw a crowd, while rarely investing in the discipleship work that truly matures people." Schwarz's research reminds us: a farmer cannot pull the seedling to make it grow taller — he can only improve the soil; once the soil is good, growth happens naturally.

Third problem: "Small-group leaders are often reluctant to divide their groups, and co-workers are reluctant to delegate authority, and so the church stays stuck in place." What small-group leaders are often most reluctant to do is split the group — but a grain of wheat unwilling to fall into the ground remains, forever, a single grain.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
To bring this lesson home into the 321 framework, I want to invite you to make three concrete corrections.

First correction: replace "chasing speed over depth" with "depth first, then breadth." The 321 vision says, "Depth and breadth are not a choice — they are a sequence." Go deep, and breadth follows naturally; chase only breadth, and in the end you get neither.

Second correction: replace "only counting who came" with "switching to a different scoreboard." How many unbelievers am I earnestly praying for this year? How many people am I currently accompanying in their growth? Has the person I'm leading begun to lead others? On the road to Caesarea Philippi, Jesus declared: "I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." It is "my" church, and the builder is "I" — if the pressure of growth leaves you gasping for breath, return first to this verse: the rise and fall of the church ultimately rests on the Lord's shoulders, not yours.

Third correction: replace "unwilling to divide" with "a grain of wheat willing to fall into the ground." Send your best co-workers out to plant new works; divide off mature small groups to multiply — on the road of growth, there is always a threshold of "dying" to cross.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Harvest
sections.html:
The same assignment — "discipleship and church growth" — placed before different people stirs up entirely different reactions. Let me lay out four hearts side by side; perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Secretly judges the success or failure of a ministry by church attendance numbers, feeling that a larger church must be more blessed, more spiritual. Yet the prophet Jeremiah says, "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom… but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD" (Jeremiah 9:23–24). The proud heart needs to be reminded: what is truly worth boasting about has never been numbers, but knowing God.

The Fearful Heart

Is afraid the road of discipleship is too slow, that the church will be left behind by the times and overtaken by other rapidly growing churches, and so is constantly anxious inside. Yet the psalmist says, "Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain" (Psalm 127:1). The building of the church ultimately rests in God's hands, not in our anxious rush to keep pace.

The Ashamed Heart

Because the ministry or small group they lead has few members, secretly feels ashamed, afraid to mention it to others, and feels like a failed servant. Yet Jesus said to His disciples, "Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom" (Luke 12:32). God never measures the kingdom He gives by numbers; He is delighted to entrust the whole kingdom to a seemingly small flock, valuing faithfulness, not scale.

The Wounded Heart

Has experienced the "swapped-seat" or "filled-room" kind of church growth before — watching crowds rise and fall — and has gradually grown discouraged, even losing hope in the very word "growth." Yet God promises, "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). God's heart toward the church, and toward you, has always been one of peace and hope.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
Let me use three examples to help us see what this lesson looks like lived out.

First. A pastor had for years secretly envied a nearby church with a large membership, feeling his own small church had little value. He later met a co-worker who had once served at that large church but had left it, and learned that discipleship there was nearly nonexistent. He said, "It turns out God isn't looking at how many people are in my church, but whether the disciples I've formed have truly grown."

Second. A small-group leader was always reluctant to send out mature members to start new groups, and as a result his group's numbers stagnated for years.
