Write down right now who you will tell it to.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, tell each other two things: the conversation you will take the initiative to open this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to help us all be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.

ch32.title: Kind to Everyone — How to Handle Conflict Between Leader and Congregation
ch32.partTitle: Part 7 — Communication and Church Relationship Management
ch32.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. Today is the second lesson of Part 7. Last lesson we learned the skills of communication; today we face a harder scene — when communication has already come too late, and conflict has already happened, where should a leader stand? Conflict in the church cannot be avoided: disagreement, mismatched expectations, hurt and misunderstanding — all of it happens even in the community that most loves the Lord. The question is not whether the church will have conflict, but whether, when conflict comes, the leader chooses to contend or chooses to be gentle. The 321 vision says: humility overcomes pride — the deepest battlefield of conflict is often not in the other person, but in our own heart.

2 Timothy 2:24: "The Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil."

sections.heading: 1. Miriam Spoke Against Him, and Moses Interceded for Her
sections.html: Numbers 12 records one of the sharpest conflicts in Scripture: Moses's sister Miriam and brother Aaron began to slander him because he had married a Cushite woman, even asking, "Has the LORD indeed spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us also?" What a wounding attack — from his closest family, aimed at the very heart of his calling. But the text goes right on to say, "Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth." God himself intervened to vindicate Moses, and Miriam was struck with leprosy — and how did Moses respond? He immediately cried out on her behalf: "O God, please heal her." The one who had been attacked was the first to intercede for the attacker — this is the highest model for handling conflict: not settling who was right first, but interceding first for the one who wounded you.

sections.heading: 2. The Wisdom of Stepping Back, the Speed of Reconciliation, and the Slowness of Contending
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, the wisdom of stepping back — meekness is not weakness, but the kind of "more than all people" heart Moses had, handing the right to vindicate himself over to God. Second, the speed of reconciliation — the Lord Jesus taught that when you discover a brother has something against you, go quickly to be reconciled — don't delay. Third, the slowness of contending — 2 Timothy says the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome; the more a leader is in the right, the more he must learn to be right without contending for it. Together these three form the church's most fundamental posture toward conflict: meek intercession, proactive reconciliation, refusing to quarrel.

sections.heading: 3. Nonviolent Communication, Early Reconciliation, and the Example of Our Spiritual Forebears
sections.html:
Proverbs 17:14 cuts to the point: "The beginning of strife is like letting out water, so quit before the quarrel breaks out." The image of letting out water is remarkably precise — once a small crack becomes a breach, it can no longer be stopped; conflict is always easiest to handle the moment it first begins to show, not after it has already flooded the whole church. The psychologist Marshall Rosenberg developed "nonviolent communication," pointing out that most conflict escalates because people habitually speak in "judgmental language" — "you always..." "you never..." — language that backs the other person into a defensive corner and only provokes counterattack. He recommended a formula of "observation plus feeling plus need" instead: rather than saying "you don't care about the brothers and sisters at all," say "I noticed this wasn't followed up, and I feel worried, because I really care whether our members are being cared for." Trading accusation for openness gives the other person room to solve the problem together, rather than rushing to defend themselves.

In Matthew 5:23–24, the Lord Jesus places reconciliation before worship: "So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift." This verse overturns the common instinct to "worship first, deal with relationships later" — the Lord says: worship is incomplete while a relationship remains unreconciled. 2 Timothy 2:24–25 then gives the method: "The Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance." A leader's goal in handling conflict is not to win, but that "God may perhaps grant them repentance" — handing sovereignty over the outcome back to God, and taking responsibility only for offering gentleness.

Church history holds a beloved story of reconciliation: the eighteenth-century preachers George Whitefield and John Wesley once had a sharply public theological conflict, at times becoming virtual strangers to one another. But neither let their theological disagreement become a personal attack; years later, as Whitefield lay dying, he specifically left instructions that Wesley — the very man who had once debated him fiercely — should preach his funeral sermon. Wesley agreed without hesitation, and honored his once-sparring spiritual co-worker sincerely from the pulpit. Two of the eighteenth century's most influential evangelists spent a lifetime demonstrating what it means to say "views can differ while respect never does" — contention ends in meekness, not in whoever persuades whom.

Handling conflict also involves an often-overlooked discipline — digesting criticism. When receiving sharp criticism, the first instinct is usually self-defense, rushing to explain, rushing to clarify; but a truly mature leader first discerns whether there is a grain of truth inside the criticism. Even if the other person is ninety percent mistaken, there may still be that one-tenth worth heeding; picking out that portion to receive, and handing the rest over to God, means neither denying yourself wholesale nor being wholly crushed. And a good apology usually contains four elements: stating specifically what was done wrong, rather than glossing over it vaguely; acknowledging the harm caused, rather than rushing to explain the reasons; stating how things will change, rather than an empty "sorry"; and giving the other person time, rather than demanding immediate forgiveness. Missing even one of these four elements makes an apology easily feel like a formality.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Being Wronged Does Not Decide Who Is Righteous
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because in the middle of conflict, the hardest thing is often not the principle, but the grievance of "I'm clearly in the right — why should I be the one to bow first?"

The moment Miriam slandered Moses, Moses stood entirely on the side of being right — he had done nothing wrong; Miriam was the one at fault. But Moses did not wait for her to apologize first before he was willing to forgive, and he did not even wait for God to finish judging before he opened his mouth to intercede. This teaches us a piercing lesson: interceding first for the one who hurt me is not because they were right — it is because I choose not to let bitterness live in my heart. Many conflicts in the church drag on into years-long knots of the heart not because the principle was unclear, but because both sides are waiting for the other to bow first — and the meek person is willing to bow first, yet that does not mean he has conceded defeat; he simply chooses not to let contention define this relationship.

Words that must never be said: "I've done nothing wrong, why should I apologize first?" "Let's just drop it and never mention it again" (while never truly letting it go inside). "I'm not fighting with him, I'm just stating the facts" (spoken in a tone already full of judgment). True reconciliation is not about who concedes first — it is both sides being willing to hand their bitterness over and let God take charge of judging.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "The church treats conflict as an enormous taboo — the moment someone raises a different opinion, they are labeled as 'causing division,' so the real problems that no one dares to touch only circulate privately, eventually turning into suspicion across the whole community, and even causing some once-faithful co-workers to quietly leave rather than risk being labeled." Healthy conflict handling does not eliminate different opinions; it gives different opinions a safe path to be heard.

The second question: "Between the eldership and the congregation, conflict is often left to fade with time rather than truly resolved by sitting down together, so the surface looks fine while each side privately carries a wound, and the same pattern of conflict repeats itself years later." Early reconciliation outweighs delayed, cold avoidance.

The third question: "Face culture makes public admission of fault extremely difficult; even when someone privately knows they were wrong, they will wrap it in various justifications and only manage a reluctant 'I didn't mean it,' leaving the other person unable to feel any real sincerity in the apology." A sincere, specific apology outweighs a vague, roundabout explanation.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "waiting for the other to apologize first" for "Moses-style intercession." Rather than waiting for the other to bow first, intercede first before God for the one who hurt you, and hand the bitterness over.

The second correction: exchange "delayed, cold avoidance" for "go quickly to be reconciled to your brother." The beginning of strife is like letting out water — the earlier you stop it, the smaller the cost.

The third correction: exchange "contending for what's right" for "being kind to everyone." The more a leader is in the right, the more he must learn to hand sovereignty over the outcome back to God, without contending for it.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Conflict
sections.html:
The same conflict that needs to be faced, set before different people, stirs completely different responses. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Believes its own judgment must be correct, and the moment conflict arises rushes to prove the other person wrong, unwilling to hear any counsel. Proverbs says: "Whoever isolates himself seeks his own desire; he breaks out against all sound judgment." (Proverbs 18:1) The proud heart needs to be reminded: the start of contention is often not a lack of clear reasoning, but a heart unwilling to bow.

The Fearful Heart

Is afraid to face conflict, and the moment the atmosphere turns tense, chooses to avoid and hide, preferring to pretend nothing happened rather than deal with it directly. After Adam sinned in the garden: "I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself." (Genesis 3:10) Avoidance cannot resolve conflict; it only widens the distance.

The Ashamed Heart

Because it once spoke harsh words or did something hurtful in a past conflict, it carries deep self-reproach, not knowing how to face it, and can only cover the shame with avoidance. The psalmist says: "My iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me... my wounds stink and fester because of my foolishness." (Psalm 38:4–5) Acknowledging your own wound is where healing begins.

The Wounded Heart

Was hurt by a trusted co-worker or friend — a pain deeper and harder to heal than the attack of a stranger. The psalmist laments: "It is not an enemy who taunts me... but it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend." (Psalm 55:12–14) God understands how deep this kind of wound goes, and is willing to heal it himself.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. Two elders disagreed sharply over the direction of a ministry, arguing fiercely at a meeting until their faces turned red, and afterward each deliberately avoided the other, leaving the church atmosphere tense and even drawing other co-workers into uncertainty over which side to stand on. Later, one of them took the initiative to invite the other for coffee, opening with, "This has made things tense between us, and I don't want that — can we start over?" The other paused, surprised, then let his guard down too, and the two rebuilt a friendship that had lasted for years of co-working together.

The second. A church member felt overlooked in a ministry assignment and carried the resentment silently for a long time, never telling the pastor, only complaining privately to others — the pastor had no idea until the rumor eventually reached him and he realized the problem had been dragging on for nearly a year, leaving the church shrouded in a low, indefinable tension. The pastor initiated an honest conversation, saying sincerely, "Thank you for letting me know. I'm sorry it took this long to hear it, and I'd like to hear the whole story from you." That conversation lasted nearly two hours, during which the pastor mostly sat quietly and listened, rarely interrupting to explain. After that conversation, this member not only recommitted to ministry but became one of the pastor's most trusted intercessors.

The third. A newly appointed elder was publicly questioned about his competence by a senior member during a meeting, and the wound cut deep enough that he considered stepping down from ministry altogether. He later chose to follow Moses's example — instead of striking back, he specifically interceded for that member during a prayer meeting. A few months later, that member sought him out to apologize, and the two grew even closer than they had been before the conflict.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: identify one conflicted relationship you are currently avoiding, and this week take the first step — if you were wrong, apologize sincerely; if you were wronged, first intercede for the other person before God, then reach out to seek reconciliation.

I declare: I will learn the meekness of Moses, interceding for those who hurt me.

I declare: I will stop strife early, not letting it spread like water let loose.

I declare: I will be kind to everyone, handing sovereignty over the outcome back to God.

I declare: let Jesus be King, so I do not contend, but seek only what brings God glory; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may we all be meek like Moses, quick to reconcile as the Lord Jesus taught, so the church becomes a community that can still intercede for one another and embrace one another even in the midst of conflict. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.html:

Closing (5 minutes)

ch33.title: God Shows No Partiality — Cross-Cultural Communication and Inclusion
ch33.partTitle: Part 7 — Communication and Church Relationship Management
ch33.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. Today is the third lesson of Part 7. Today's church is more "diverse" than any era before it — people of different nationalities, different generations, different languages, and different cultural backgrounds sit together in the same worship hall. What a beautiful picture this is, yet it also brings real tension: different habits, different ways of expressing things, even different understandings of what "godliness" even looks like. The gospel was always meant to cross every boundary — if the church cannot first cross culture within itself, how can it proclaim the gospel to all nations? The 321 vision says: let Jesus receive all the glory — not let any single culture claim the highest seat.

Acts 10:34–35: "So Peter opened his mouth and said: 'Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.'"

sections.heading: 1. A Vision on the Rooftop Broke Through Peter's Boundaries
sections.html: Acts 10 records the early church's most dramatic cross-cultural breakthrough: Peter was praying on a rooftop when he saw a vision — a great sheet descending from heaven, filled with every kind of creature that Jewish law considered unclean, and a voice said to him, "Rise, Peter; kill and eat." Three times Peter refused: "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean." But God answered, "What God has made clean, do not call common." Not long after the vision ended, the men Cornelius had sent arrived at the door — a Gentile centurion, in a house no Jew was ever supposed to enter. Peter later admitted openly, "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean." God tore down the wall inside Peter's heart before he could ever walk through that door.

sections.heading: 2. Setting Aside Superiority, Learning to Listen, and Living Out Unity
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, setting aside superiority — God shows no partiality; no single culture can claim itself as the standard of godliness, for anyone who fears the Lord and does what is right is acceptable to him. Second, learning to listen — cross-cultural communication is not merely speaking a language the other person understands; it means being willing to first understand the other person's cultural logic, so that good intentions don't backfire into harm. Third, living out unity — in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek; unity does not erase difference, it means being of one heart within difference. Together these three form the truest testing ground for the church to live out the universal nature of the gospel.

sections.heading: 3. Cultural Dimensions Theory, the Jerusalem Council, and a Missionary's Humility
sections.html:
The Dutch scholar Geert Hofstede spent years researching cultural differences among multinational corporations and proposed the well-known "cultural dimensions theory," showing that different cultures have systematic differences along dimensions such as power distance, individualism versus collectivism, and tolerance for uncertainty — not a matter of right or wrong, but of differing perspectives. His research reminds us that many "cultural conflicts" within churches are, in fact, not spiritual problems at all, but different cultural defaults: some cultures are accustomed to direct expression of opinion, others to indirect and understated expression; some cultures value efficient decision-making, others value thorough consultation. Without understanding this layer of difference, it is very easy to misread another's cultural habits as unspiritual or disobedient.

Acts 15 records the early church's most important council: after Gentiles came to faith, must they keep the Jewish law? This was a dispute serious enough to split the church. James concluded at the Jerusalem Council, "Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God." The church did not require Gentile believers to first become Jews before they could believe; it retained only a few basic moral requirements. This decision had far-reaching implications: the gospel need not be carried by any single cultural shell — its core truth can, and should, be expressed in different cultural languages. In 1 Corinthians 9:22, Paul himself demonstrates this principle: "I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some." This was not principle-less pandering — it was, for the sake of the gospel, a willingness to set aside his own cultural comfort and enter the other person's situation.

Matteo Ricci, who came to China as a missionary in the sixteenth century, is a famous witness to this lesson. He did not require the Chinese to become Europeans before they could believe; instead he spent years studying Chinese language, Confucian classics, and Chinese customs, wore the robes of a Confucian scholar, observed the etiquette of Chinese literati, and explained the core truths of the faith in language familiar to the Chinese — winning great respect even among the scholar-official class. Though his missionary path later sparked the theological debates known as the Chinese Rites Controversy, he left behind a lesson still worth pondering today: to respect a culture is not to compromise the truth; true humility is a willingness to set aside the comfort of your own culture and put on the language the other person can understand.

Revelation 7:9 paints an ultimate picture: "After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb..." Worship in heaven does not mean all cultures vanish, leaving only one uniform style — it means people from every nation, tribe, and language stand together in worship, each still carrying their own identity. This picture reminds the church: cross-cultural effort is not waiting for a destination where "everyone finally becomes the same" — it is rehearsing, here on earth, the picture of "all nations worshiping together." Every encounter in the church where someone is willing to set aside cultural superiority and actively listen is a rehearsal of this ultimate picture.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Unity Is Not Sameness, but Love Within Difference
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because the word "unity" is most easily misunderstood as "everyone becoming the same."

Galatians 3:28 says: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus." This verse has never meant that differences of culture, gender, or identity are erased — it means these differences no longer determine one's standing or qualification for salvation. 1 Corinthians 12 uses the analogy of the body: the eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of you"; each member has a different shape and function, yet they belong to one body — the body's unity is actually built upon the members' differences, and if every member became identical, the body itself would be crippled and incomplete. If the church understands unity as "everyone must become like me," it is, in fact, forcibly whittling every member into the same shape — that is not unity, that is assimilation.

Words that must never be said: "This is just how our church's culture is, people who aren't used to it need to adapt on their own." "Their way of expressing things just isn't spiritual enough." "This is our tradition, it doesn't need to change." True unity is members of different cultures each serving in their own role, together building one body — not requiring every member to grow into the same shape.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "First-generation immigrants and the second generation in the church show clear gaps in language, thinking, and worship style, yet often each remains committed to separate congregations or gatherings, lacking real dialogue or integration, forming two worlds within the church that are invisible yet truly exist." Cross-generational dialogue requires both sides to be willing to step out of their comfort zone first.

The second question: "Facing brothers and sisters from different nationalities and church backgrounds, people habitually use 'we've always done it this way' as the standard of judgment, unconsciously treating their own cultural habits as spiritual orthodoxy." Biblical truth is absolute, but its cultural expression is diverse — the two must not be confused as one.

The third question: "Ministry opportunities and voice are often concentrated in the hands of the same cultural group, and newcomers with a different accent or background, even with real gifting, are not easily seen or invited." The church must actively create space so that members of every cultural background can exercise their gifts.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "cultural superiority" for "God shows no partiality." No single culture can claim itself as the standard of godliness — anyone who fears the Lord and does what is right is acceptable to him.

The second correction: exchange "demanding assimilation" for "unity, not sameness." Unity means members with different functions belonging to one body, not requiring every member to grow into the same shape.

The third correction: exchange "clinging to our own way" for "becoming all things to all people." For the sake of the gospel, be willing to set aside cultural comfort and be the first one willing to cross over.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Crossing
sections.html:
The same cross-cultural encounter, set before different people, stirs completely different responses. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Unconsciously assumes its own cultural habits are the standard, believing others' ways always need "improving" to be considered orthodox. Peter was once this way too: "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation." (Acts 10:28) The proud heart needs to be reminded: cultural habit is not the same as the truth of the faith.

The Fearful Heart

Is afraid to engage unfamiliar cultures and people, feeling the other person too different, too foreign, and would rather stay within its own familiar small circle. The spies who scouted Canaan reported, "We seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them." (Numbers 13:33) Fear magnifies difference into a gap that feels impossible to cross.

The Ashamed Heart

Because its culture, language, or background differs from the mainstream, feels lesser, and dares not voice its needs. Acts records, "The Hellenists murmured against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution." (Acts 6:1) The church should actively see and actively care for those pushed to the margins.

The Wounded Heart

Was once excluded, misunderstood, or even mocked because of cultural difference, and carries a deep wound about the very idea of "fitting in." The psalmist laments, "By the waters of Babylon, there we sat down... How shall we sing the LORD's song in a foreign land?" (Psalm 137:1, 4) God understands that loneliness of feeling foreign and out of place.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A church had for years been made up mostly of first-generation immigrants, with both worship and preaching conducted in the mother tongue, and the second-generation young people gradually felt out of place, their numbers dwindling year by year. The elder board eventually decided to try bilingual worship and invited the younger generation to help plan part of the service — some of the elders felt unaccustomed to it at first, but months later, the church saw the long-missing sight of generations worshiping together once again.

The second. A new immigrant brother had just joined the church, and because his accent and way of expressing himself were different, he sensed impatient glances a few times when sharing in his small group, and gradually stopped speaking up. One member noticed and made a point of saying after his next share, "Thank you for sharing — I really want to hear more of what you think." That simple sentence gave the brother back the courage to speak up in the group again.

The third. A church's ministry positions had long been filled by the same group of people, and a sister from a different cultural background, though gifted, had never been invited to serve. An elder eventually noticed and invited her to join the worship team; she hesitated at first, but through serving discovered she was truly needed, and has now become an indispensable member of the worship team.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: reach out to a member whose cultural background is different from your own — invite them for coffee this week and simply listen to their story, without judging or comparing, just listening.

I declare: I believe God shows no partiality — anyone who fears the Lord and does what is right is acceptable to him.

I declare: I will set aside cultural superiority and become all things to all people.

I declare: I will live out unity, not sameness — each serving in our own role, belonging to one body.

I declare: let Jesus receive all the glory, so the church becomes a home where all nations and all peoples can worship; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may our church become a community that truly crosses culture and lives out unity, where people of every nation and tribe can worship the God who shows no partiality. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

10. ★★ "Listen more, judge slowly, ask first." In your own family, is there a tension arising from generational or cultural difference this week that these three practices could address?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about in your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "Ministry opportunities and voice are often concentrated in the hands of the same cultural group." Is there a gifted member in your church who hasn't been seen, whom you could actively invite to serve?

13. ★★★ A ten-minute daily discipline: this week, intercede each day for a member of a different cultural background from yours — name who it is for and what time you will pray.

14. ★★ The 920 discipline: identify your own "2" (spiritual companion); this week invite them to actively get to know a new friend or someone of a different background together. Say their name out loud right now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, tell this lesson to someone outside the group in three sentences — God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him; there is neither Jew nor Greek, for you are all one in Christ Jesus; I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some. Write down right now who you will tell it to.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, tell each other two things: the member you will actively reach out to this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to make our church a home where all nations and all peoples can worship.

ch34.title: With One Mind and One Voice, Glorify God — Building Harmony Within the Leadership Team
ch34.partTitle: Part 7 — Communication and Church Relationship Management
ch34.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. Today is the fourth lesson of Part 7. The previous three lessons dealt with communication and conflict between leaders and the congregation; today we turn our focus to another often-overlooked scene — inside the leadership team itself. If co-workers are not at peace with one another, the church can hardly be truly at peace; when elders and deacons quarrel, it is more destructive than the congregation quarreling, because they are the very group that should be most of one mind. The 321 vision says: only the self-emptied can be unified — a team's harmony has never come from a well-tuned system; it comes from each person being willing to set self aside first.

Romans 15:5–6: "May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus, that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ."

sections.heading: 1. Euodia and Syntyche, the Discord Paul Named by Name
sections.html: Philippians 4:2–3 contains a passage rarely preached, yet strikingly real: Paul names two female co-workers in his letter — "I entreat Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to agree in the Lord." These two had labored alongside Paul for the gospel, yet were now so at odds that Paul had to address it publicly in a letter to mediate. Paul did not avoid this awkward subject, nor did he simply split the blame equally between them; he goes on to ask his "true companion" to help them — Paul understood deeply that if a team's rift went unaddressed, it would drag down the whole church's witness. This passage reminds us: even within the church Paul planted and deeply loved, discord between co-workers was a real thing; the question is not whether a team will ever have friction, but whether, when friction appears, someone is willing to step forward and build a bridge.

sections.heading: 2. Fair Positioning, Mutual Deference, and the Declaration of One Accord
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, fair positioning — when Paul mediated between Euodia and Syntyche, he did not take sides; he appealed to both from the height of the gospel, calling them to be of one mind. Second, mutual deference — Romans says to outdo one another in showing honor, not thinking of yourself more highly than you ought. Third, the declaration of one accord — with one mind and one voice, glorify God: true unity in a team is not agreement on every opinion, but everyone's focus being aligned on the same point, all fixed on God. Together these three form the foundation on which a church's leadership team can serve together for the long haul.

sections.heading: 3. The Robbers Cave Experiment, Mutual Deference, and Unity Under a Greater Vision
sections.html:
Paul's way of mediating between Euodia and Syntyche holds a threefold wisdom: fairness — he took no side, "entreating" both women equally; positioning — he reminded them to "agree in the Lord," pulling their focus away from their disagreement and back to the shared Lord; and bridge-building — he asked his "true companion" to help mediate between them, rather than demanding they reconcile out of thin air on their own. This threefold wisdom is still the most practical path for team mediation today: don't rush to determine who is right and who is wrong; first pull everyone's eyes back to the shared vision, then find the right person to build a bridge.

The social psychologist Muzafer Sherif conducted the famous "Robbers Cave Experiment": he divided a group of boys who had never met into two teams, first letting competition between them generate intense hostility and conflict, then trying various ways to dissolve it — simple contact and social mixers had little effect. What truly dissolved the hostility was designing a shared task that neither team could complete alone and that required cooperation — such as fixing the water supply together. Once the two teams had a shared goal, the hostility genuinely melted away. This experiment confirms biblical wisdom: the most effective way to dissolve a team's rift is often not demanding both sides "make up," but giving them a greater vision that requires unity to accomplish — and the church's mission is exactly this kind of shared task, far transcending any personal grievance.

Romans 12:10 says: "Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor." 1 Peter 3:8 adds: "Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind." Together these two verses sketch the most concrete shape of team harmony: not that no one expresses an opinion, but that after expressing it, one knows how to defer; not that there is no friction, but that after friction, one knows how to show sympathy. In Genesis 13, when Abram's herdsmen and his nephew Lot's herdsmen quarreled, Abram — though he could have claimed the land first by right of age and as the heir of the promise — instead let Lot choose first: "If you take the left hand, then I will go to the right, or if you take the right hand, then I will go to the left." What generosity of spirit — setting aside his own right of priority, and receiving in return an even greater promise of blessing from God. In psychology there is the well-known "Franklin effect": someone you have once asked a favor of is actually more likely to develop goodwill toward you, because people tend to align their feelings with their own actions — a reminder that a team's rift can sometimes be re-bridged through a small, mutual request that shows they still need one another.

In John 17, before his crucifixion, the Lord Jesus prayed urgently for the disciples' unity: "That they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us." The Lord did not pray for the disciples' eloquence, talent, or ministry results — he specifically prayed for their unity, which shows how much weight unity carries in the Lord's eyes. This also reminds every leader on a team: the greater vision is never only the church's mission — it is the very unity the Lord himself prayed urgently for. When a team develops a rift, it is worth pausing to remember: the Lord once prayed urgently for this very relationship.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — A Rift Left Unattended Is the Real Wound
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because a rift within a team is most easily rationalized as "let's wait and see," or "let's not make a big deal of it," and the result is years of delay.

Paul openly named and addressed the discord between Euodia and Syntyche, showing that the church's tradition is not to hide a rift between co-workers and pretend nothing happened, but to face it early and build a bridge early. So many cracks in church teams actually began as a very small misunderstanding, and because it was never resolved early, it accumulated day after day until it became a knot in the heart that even those involved can no longer explain. The path to reconciliation between co-workers actually shares the same principles as reconciliation between individuals: first lower the hostility, find a shared vision, then invite a suitable third party to mediate — the difference is only that, because co-workers must serve together long-term and depend on one another, the cost of delay is usually far greater than an ordinary interpersonal conflict, because it directly drags down the whole team, even the entire church's ministry.

Words that must never be said: "It's such a small thing, it'll fade with time." "It's fine as long as we get along on the surface." "Don't bring this up in front of the co-workers — don't air the family's dirty laundry." A truly healthy team has the courage to face a rift the moment it appears, rather than letting it ferment in silence.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "When elders develop a knot between them, they habitually express their dissatisfaction through silence, coldness, and reduced interaction, without ever saying it outright — the surface stays polite, but meetings always feel strangely tense, and the progress of ministry suffers as a result." Honest confrontation outweighs surface-level peace.

The second question: "In the team, senior co-workers' words carry particular weight, and newer co-workers, even with a different opinion, dare not voice it face to face — over time, team decisions look unanimous but are really only a few voices speaking." True unity means everyone can safely voice a different thought.

The third question: "The line between co-workers' personal friendship and their official ministry duties grows blurred — personal grudges are brought into meetings, and disagreements from meetings are carried back into personal relationships, the two tangled together and growing more confused the more one tries to sort them out." Learning to keep ministry disagreements separate from personal friendship is an important mark of a mature team.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "reconciling alone out of thin air" for "inviting someone to build a bridge." Paul asked his "true companion" to help Euodia and Syntyche — a team's rift need not be carried alone; the right third party can be invited to mediate.

The second correction: exchange "competing for priority" for "mutual deference." Abram let Lot choose the land first, setting aside his own right of priority, and received an even greater blessing from God in return.

The third correction: exchange "letting small matters drag on" for "facing it early." Have the courage to face a rift the moment it appears, rather than letting it grow larger in silence.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Team
sections.html:
The same team that needs to be of one mind, set before different people, stirs completely different responses. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Is used to arguing within the team over whose opinion is better, whose contribution is greater, secretly treating co-workers as objects of comparison and competition. The disciples were once this way too: "A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest." (Luke 22:24) The proud heart needs to be reminded: a team is not a ring for ranking who is greater — it is a partnership sharing the same yoke.

The Fearful Heart

Is afraid a co-worker will be more affirmed or more gifted than itself, feels a secret unease, and even deliberately keeps its distance from that person. Saul was once this way toward David: "Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him greatly... And Saul eyed David from that day on." (1 Samuel 18:8–9) Fear turns a co-worker into an imagined threat.

The Ashamed Heart

Because it once wronged a co-worker or did something to hurt the team in the past, feels deep shame, does not know how to face it, and can only deliberately avoid that person. When Joseph's brothers faced the one they had once sold, "his brothers could not answer him, for they were dismayed at his presence." (Genesis 45:3) Joseph, though, chose to embrace, forgive, and reconcile.

The Wounded Heart

Was once deeply hurt by a co-worker's words or decisions — a pain sharper than criticism from an outsider, because the other person was once on the very same side. Proverbs says: "A brother offended is more unyielding than a strong city, and quarreling is like the bars of a castle." (Proverbs 18:19) God knows the weight of this kind of wound, and is willing to step in and heal it himself.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. Two district co-workers held firmly opposing views over a resource allocation decision, and afterward always deliberately avoided each other's opinions in meetings, even privately courting other co-workers to take sides, leaving the church atmosphere tense. A senior elder eventually took the initiative to invite both to a meal, reminding them, "We share the same yoke — we're not competitors." Only then were the two willing to sit down together, rediscover their shared vision, and get the ministry moving smoothly again.

The second. A new young co-worker raised a different view from a senior co-worker's during a meeting and immediately sensed a subtle awkward silence, and afterward never dared to speak up on his own again, only complaining privately to friends after meetings. The team chair eventually noticed this pattern and made a point of setting aside time in every meeting to ask each co-worker for their thoughts one by one — the young co-worker gradually found the courage to speak up in meetings again, and the team's decisions became more well-rounded as a result.

The third. A pair of elders developed a rift years ago over a disagreement about a church ministry, and though they continued to work together on the surface, they kept each other at a distance inwardly for years. It was only when the church faced a major crisis, forcing them into close cooperation, that they rediscovered each other's strengths through facing the difficulty together, and their years-old knot quietly dissolved through that collaboration.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: think of a co-worker on your team who feels distant from you or with whom you have a rift, and this week take the initiative to invite them for coffee, simply reconnecting — without rushing to solve everything, first rebuilding the warmth of the relationship.

I declare: I will defer to others, not thinking of myself more highly than I ought.

I declare: I will face rifts in my team early, not letting them ferment in silence.

I declare: I will be of one mind and one voice, pulling our focus back from our differences to our shared Lord.

I declare: let Jesus be King, so our team follows the example of Christ Jesus, of one mind glorifying God; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may the God of endurance and encouragement grant our leadership team to live in harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus, that together we may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations move downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind, the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart, and the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — without reaching it, this lesson stays at the level of an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority, cover at least this question in each phase if time is short; ★★ = secondary priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked (Required) must not be skipped and may be completed at home.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as an Idea (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ Paul publicly named and mediated the discord between Euodia and Syntyche rather than hiding it. What does this prompt you to understand about how the church should face discord between co-workers?

2. ★★ Sherif's Robbers Cave Experiment found that what truly dissolved hostility was a shared task that required cooperation. What does this prompt you to understand about how the church's mission can help a team reconcile?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "True unity in a team is not agreement on every opinion, but everyone's focus being aligned on the same point." In your own words, explain the difference between "agreeing on opinions" and "aligning on focus."

4. ★★ Abram let Lot choose the land first, setting aside his own right of priority. What does this prompt you to understand about how "mutual deference" can dissolve a team's dispute?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it well." If someone speaks in fragments, help them organize their thought — don't finish it for them.

Second Transformation | Digesting It into Life (about 35 minutes · the core of this lesson)

Purpose: through Seeing, Hearing, Thinking, Speaking, and Acting, digest the idea into life.

[See] See Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — Proud (used to arguing over whose opinion is better, whose contribution is greater), Fearful (afraid a co-worker will be more affirmed, secretly uneasy), Ashamed (once wronged or hurt the team in the past, deeply ashamed and avoidant), Wounded (deeply hurt by a co-worker's words or decisions). Which are you most like? What experience made you this way?

[Hear] Hear God Speak

6. ★★ God has one sentence for each of these four hearts. Find the verse that matches you, read it aloud, then tell the group: where does this sentence touch you?

[Think] Think Through the Obstacle

7. ★★ In a team you are part of now or have been part of before, is there a rift that has never truly been resolved? What has kept it unaddressed?

[Speak] Say It Out Loud

8. ★ Finish this sentence in one line: "This lesson tore down which old idea I had about 'my team's co-workers'?" If your answer is "none," say that honestly too — that itself is an important discovery.

[Act] Take a Step

9. ★★ This week, which co-worker will you actively invite to reconnect and rebuild the warmth of your relationship? Name the specific person.

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for wounded-type members, particularly those deeply hurt by a co-worker's decision or words and still unreconciled today. If someone weeps, pause the discussion and sit with them first — don't rush to give answers. If deeper trauma surfaces, follow up individually after the meeting and help arrange a referral.

Third Transformation | Transforming It into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily practice.

10. ★★ "Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor." In your own family, on what matter will you actively defer rather than compete for priority this week?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about in your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "Have the courage to face a rift the moment it appears, rather than letting it ferment in silence." Is there a relationship you need to face early rather than continue to delay?

13. ★★★ A ten-minute daily discipline: this week, intercede each day for your team or co-workers, asking the Lord of endurance and encouragement to make everyone of one mind and one voice. Name what time you will pray.

14. ★★ The 920 discipline: identify your own "2" (spiritual companion); this week actively invite them to pray together for your team's unity. Say their name out loud right now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, tell this lesson to someone outside the group in three sentences — May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus, that together you may with one voice glorify God; outdo one another in showing honor; have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind. Write down right now who you will tell it to.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, tell each other two things: the co-worker you will actively reconnect with this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to make our team of one mind and one voice, glorifying God.

ch35.title: Not to Please Man, but to Please God — Managing the Congregation's Expectations
ch35.partTitle: Part 7 — Communication and Church Relationship Management
ch35.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. Today we come to the final lesson of Part 7, "Communication and Church Relationship Management." We have learned to communicate, resolved conflict, crossed culture, and strengthened our team; now, last of all, we must face something that presses on a leader's shoulders year after year, yet is rarely spoken of plainly — the congregation's expectations. Everyone has expectations of a pastor: preach well, visit well, counsel well, be available at a moment's notice, never grow tired. When expectations go unmet, they become disappointment; disappointment, accumulated, becomes criticism. How does a leader stand steady between the expectations of the many and the commission of God? The 321 vision says: let Jesus be King — not let expectation be king.

1 Thessalonians 2:4: "But just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts."

sections.heading: 1. Everyone Is Looking for You, Yet the Lord Says: Let Us Go Elsewhere
sections.html: Mark 1 records the most successful evening of ministry: the whole town of Capernaum gathered at the door, and the Lord healed many who were sick. Early the next morning, the crowds came looking again, and the disciples said, "Everyone is looking for you." Those five words are the success every servant of the Lord dreams of. But look at the Lord's answer: "Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out." The Lord was not carried along by need — he was led by his calling. This unlocks the deepest bind every servant faces: need is limitless, but calling has direction — not every need is your calling. And the key to discerning it is in the verse just before: "And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed." The place where the Lord discerned the voice of the crowd from his true calling was not in the crowd, but in the wilderness. Direction is discerned in prayer, not scheduled onto a calendar.

sections.heading: 2. Weighing the Load of Expectation, Anchoring in Pleasing God, and Honest Boundaries
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, weighing the load of expectation — everyone is looking for you: expectation is part of ministry, but expectation left unchecked can crush a leader and distort ministry itself; even Jesus once faced a crowd who wanted to force him to be king. Second, the anchor of pleasing God — only one seat sits on the bench that judges ministry. Third, honest boundaries in communication — learn the Lord's own phrase, "that is why I came out": state your calling clearly, and make your boundaries plain. Let's first say the balanced thing: it is entirely healthy for a congregation to have expectations of its leaders — sheep looking to their shepherd is only natural; the problem is not expectation itself, but expectation left unchecked. Managing expectation is not refusing the flock — it is turning both sets of eyes to look at God together.

sections.heading: 3. Psychological Contract Theory, the Snare of Fearing Man, and the Anchor of Our Spiritual Forebears
sections.html:
The organizational psychologist Denise Rousseau developed "psychological contract theory": beyond any formal agreement, there is an unwritten contract living inside people's minds — a one-sided expectation, never spoken aloud, yet genuinely governing their emotions; when it is violated, the person feels not ordinary disappointment but something close to betrayal — even though the other party never actually promised any such thing. Churches are full of these invisible contracts: "the pastor should remember my name," "I gave an offering, so the church should adopt my suggestion" — no one ever says these things aloud, yet everyone keeps score in their own heart. What a pastor "violates" is often a contract in someone else's mind that he never even saw. The remedy: bring hidden expectations into the light — ask actively, respond clearly, put it in writing. Spoken expectations can be aligned; hidden expectations can only explode.

Proverbs 29:25 says: "The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe." A "snare" is a hunter's trap — the more the caught animal struggles, the tighter it binds. The fear of man works exactly this way: afraid of disappointing the congregation, you agree to everything; the more you agree to, the higher expectations rise; the higher expectations rise, the less you dare to say no — until ministry becomes a performance, and rest becomes a guilt. Many a leader's exhaustion is not from too much work, but because half of that work was done only to keep from disappointing someone. The way out is in the second half of the verse: safety, because the judge on the bench has changed — no longer a thousand pairs of watching congregational eyes, but a single pair of eyes that tests the heart. Paul left an eternal anchor for every servant of the Lord in Galatians 1:10: "If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ." 1 Thessalonians 2:4 gives three pillars: the qualification comes from God, the content is set by God, and the evaluation is done by God. Human expectation returns to its proper place: an important reference, not the highest standard.

A. W. Tozer, the pastor called "the prophet" of the twentieth century, left a much-quoted line: whoever fears God need never again fear any man; whoever does not fear God will find himself having to fear everyone. Tozer pastored for decades, never once tailoring his pulpit to popular taste, and yet he fed generations of believers — because what he preached was not what people wanted to hear, but what God wanted said. This is the deepest secret of managing expectations: not learning the art of saying no, but changing the audience in your heart — a person who performs for only one audience, for a lifetime, cannot be swept away by a full house's gaze. Chinese culture places great weight on relationships and face, and the pressure of "it's too awkward to refuse" is especially heavy. But expectations sustained by sheer force always collapse eventually; trust built on honesty can last forever.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Only One Seat Sits on the Bench of Ministry
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because "not pleasing man" is easily misunderstood as "not caring about anyone's feelings at all."

In 1 Samuel 8:7, God said to Samuel, "They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them." The people wanted a king they could see, to replace the King they could not see — the deepest misalignment of expectation is placing what belongs to trust in God onto a human being instead. It's the same today: when a congregation treats its pastor as an all-powerful support, it is, in essence, crowning a man king; when a leader accepts this without question, he is accepting a crown that was never his to wear. But this verse also comforts Samuel: a faithful leader can still be rejected, and being rejected does not mean being cast off by God. In 1 Corinthians 4:3–4, Paul lists three courts — the judgment of others, his own judgment, and the Lord's judgment — and he recognizes only the last one: "I do not even judge myself... It is the Lord who judges me." Living inside the congregation's grading system means every day is a day of judgment; living inside the Lord's judgment means there is only one Judge, and that Judge is full of grace.

Words that must never be said: "If everyone's unhappy, I must have done something wrong." "If I just try hard enough, I can make everyone happy." "I can't rest, because the congregation needs me." True freedom is knowing that the qualification, content, and evaluation of ministry all rest in God's hands — people's opinions are an important reference, not the highest standard.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "The church treats its pastor as an all-around superman — expert at preaching, counseling, administration, and visitation, working year-round without rest, and criticized at the slightest shortfall, while no one ever asks how many hours he actually slept that week." No human being of flesh and blood can carry that list — even Moses needed Jethro to remind him.

The second question: "The church is treated like a service industry — the songs must suit one's taste, the sermon must fit one's palate, and if not satisfied, one simply switches churches — forgetting that Ephesians says the role of pastors and teachers is to equip the saints for the work of ministry, each doing their own part, not to serve the congregation in their place." A consumer mindset is quietly eroding the essence of the church.

The third question: "Voices of criticism are always louder than voices of intercession; the congregation rarely tells the pastor directly what he did well, but often discusses privately what fell short, leaving the servant of the Lord living for years under an indefinable low pressure." Showing consideration for the pastor is a discipline the congregation needs to practice too.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "pleasing man" for "pleasing God." The qualification, content, and evaluation of ministry all rest in God's hands — a person's expectations are an important reference, not the highest standard.

The second correction: exchange "accepting everything" for "honest communication." Learn the Lord's own phrase, "that is why I came out" — state your calling clearly, and make your boundaries plain.

The third correction: exchange "the audience's verdict" for "the teammate's participation." Translate "you should do this" into "let's do this together" — once expectation turns into participation, the complainer becomes a co-worker.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Expectation
sections.html:
The same congregational expectation, set before different people, stirs completely different responses. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Believes it understands how things should be done better than anyone, even better than God's own will, and rushes to act on its own rather than seeking God first. Peter was once this way too, restraining the Lord: "Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, 'Far be it from you, Lord!'" (Matthew 16:22–23) The proud heart needs to be reminded: well-meaning insistence can also become a stumbling block to God's will.

The Fearful Heart

Is afraid of others' opinions, afraid of losing applause, and so dares not voice its true convictions, preferring to cater to the crowd's expectations instead. Many of the authorities believed in Jesus at that time, "but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God." (John 12:42–43) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: the glory of man does not last, but the glory of God endures forever.

The Ashamed Heart

Once violated a principle it clearly understood in its heart just to please the crowd, and afterward feels deep self-reproach, feeling it has let God down. Saul confessed: "I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD and your words, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice." (1 Samuel 15:24) God is willing to receive an honest confession and help you stand again.

The Wounded Heart

Was deeply pierced by the congregation's criticism and dissatisfied words, feeling that nothing it does is ever good enough, carrying an unspeakable grievance inside. The psalmist cries out: "For wicked and deceitful mouths are opened against me... they encircle me with words of hate." (Psalm 109:2–3) God sees these unspeakable grievances, and is willing to vindicate you himself.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A minister spent years saying yes to every request — replying to messages within seconds, attending every event — until one day he broke down in tears in the middle of a sermon, and only then realized he had long since been crushed under the congregation's expectations. He later learned to set aside one completely uninterrupted block of time each week and honestly told the elder board about his own boundaries — and the quality of his ministry improved as a result.

The second. A deacon could never bring himself to say no to a new ministry invitation, afraid that refusing would disappoint someone, until one day he found himself holding five positions at once, doing none of them well. He later learned to explain, graciously and firmly, "I'm not able to take this on right now, but I'd be glad to pray for it" — and gradually rediscovered both the joy and the fruit of ministry.

The third. A church member repeatedly criticized the church for not caring enough for its elderly members. The pastor did not rush to explain, but instead answered, "Thank you for seeing this need — would you be willing to start this with me?" Six months later, this critic became the core co-worker of the elder care ministry, and the church gained a blessed new team of servants along with it.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration: Reviewing Part Seven
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: write down your own "that is why I came out" — sit quietly before the Lord and write, in one or two sentences, the direction he has entrusted to you; then look at your calendar: how much of this week's busyness falls within that direction? If you are a member of the congregation, your discipline is this: intercede specifically for your pastor three times this week, and turn one expectation of the church into one act of actual participation.

Having come this far, the five lessons of Part 7, "Communication and Church Relationship Management," together trace one path of relationship. Effective communication skills for the church — quick to hear, slow to speak, only such speech as is good for building up. How to handle conflict between leader and congregation — learn the meekness and intercession of Moses, go quickly to be reconciled, for the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome. Cross-cultural communication and inclusion — God shows no partiality, unity rather than sameness, being the first one willing to cross over. Building harmony within the leadership team — deferring to one another, letting no rift outlast a month, kneeling down to pray together. And today, managing the congregation's expectations — not to please man, but to please the God who tests our hearts alone. Five lessons, one thread: every lesson about relationship is, in the end, a lesson about life — first life, then relationship, then ministry; humility overcomes pride; only the self-emptied can be unified.

I declare: I will please God, not man — the qualification, content, and evaluation of ministry all rest in God's hands.

I declare: I will communicate honestly, stating my calling clearly and making my boundaries plain.

I declare: I will turn the audience into teammates, letting expectation become co-laboring participation.

I declare: let Jesus be King, not expectation; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may our church become a church that listens, a church that reconciles, a church that crosses over, a church of one accord, a church that looks only to God. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
