ch36.title: Faithful in the Very Little — The Basic Principles of Church Financial Management
ch36.partTitle: Part 8 — Financial Management and Resource Stewardship
ch36.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. Today we open a new part: Financial Management and Resource Stewardship. In the last part we cared for relationships between people in the church; in this part we care for something else often misunderstood, yet deeply spiritual — money. Many believers frown the moment "the church talks about money," feeling that a spiritual place should have nothing to do with worldly calculation. But one of the subjects the Lord Jesus spoke about most in his earthly life was, in fact, money. Money is not the enemy of the spirit — a mistreated heart toward money is. The 321 vision says: let Jesus be King, including letting Jesus be King over our money.

Luke 16:10: "One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much."

sections.heading: 1. He Stole Nothing, Yet the Master Called Him "Wicked and Slothful"
sections.html: Matthew 25 records a parable in which the Lord defines what it means to be a faithful steward. A master was going on a journey and entrusted his property to his servants — one received five talents, one two, one a single talent, each according to his own ability. Those with five and two talents went and traded with them and doubled their money; the one with a single talent went and dug in the ground and hid his master's money. When the master returned, he praised the first two as "good and faithful," but rebuked the third as "wicked and slothful." Notice: the servant with one talent did not squander it, nor did he steal it — he returned it intact. Yet the master still condemned him: not the sin of waste, but the sin of burial; not a lack of caution, but a refusal to take a risk, a refusal to put it to use. The most common failure in church financial management is rarely embezzlement or extravagance — far more often, it is fearful burial: locking offerings away in a conservative drawer, afraid to invest in ministry, afraid to cultivate a vision.

sections.heading: 2. The Identity of a Steward, the Principle of Faithfulness, and the Discipline of Honesty
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, the identity of a steward — everything belongs to the LORD: the church's property has never been "ours"; it is entrusted to us. Second, the principle of faithfulness — giving account according to ability: the parable of the talents teaches us that faithfulness has nothing to do with the size of the amount, and everything to do with whether it was used to the fullest. Third, the discipline of honesty — doing everything according to order, walking in the light: the very system by which money is managed is itself a spiritual testimony. The Lord Jesus said, where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. A financial statement is, in truth, the most honest physical checkup of a church's faith — where the offerings go is where the vision truly is; how the budget is drawn up is how the values are truly revealed.

sections.heading: 3. Mental Accounting Theory, a Contest of Faithfulness Rather than Talent, and Larry Burkett's Reminder
sections.html:
Before calculating a single cent, we must first establish who the true owner is. Psalm 24 declares: "The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell therein." Haggai puts it even more directly: "The silver is mine, and the gold is mine." A church's treasurer is not the owner of its property, but a steward appointed by the Owner; a committee is not the final authority over decisions, but an executor entrusted with a task. The behavioral economist Richard Thaler proposed the theory of "mental accounting": people do not treat all money as the same money — they mentally sort it into different "accounts" — a paycheck account spent cautiously, a lottery-winnings account spent without a second thought. It is worth dividing the annual budget into three main accounts — "ongoing operations," "ministry development," and "reserve and risk" — each with a clear proportion and stated purpose, giving donors peace of mind while also reminding leaders: a reserve is not an excuse to avoid actually stewarding the ministry.

Look carefully at this: the praise given to the servant who earned five talents and the praise given to the servant who earned two talents are word for word identical — "Well done, good and faithful servant." The master did not grade by the absolute amount earned; he rewarded by the degree of faithfulness. This is an enormous freedom for the church: the financial faithfulness of a small church and the financial faithfulness of a large church are equally precious in the Lord's eyes. Paul's line is remarkably short: "It is required of stewards that they be found faithful." The standard by which a steward is evaluated is not cleverness, not efficiency, not return on investment — it is faithfulness. Faithfulness is not an abstract adjective; it takes concrete shape: books that are clear and can withstand scrutiny; funds used in a way consistent with the donor's intent; nothing diverted, nothing delayed, nothing left vague; and when facing uncertainty, choosing to ask cautiously rather than act unilaterally.

When Paul was raising a collection to support the Jerusalem church, he deliberately arranged for several people to travel together and witness the process: "We aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord's sight but also in the sight of man." Paul was not afraid that he himself would truly err — he did not even want to leave room for suspicion. The basic rules of church finance should include at least three: division of duties — no one who handles money decides alone; regular reporting — a public overview of finances; and external review — a second person reviews significant transactions. In the late twentieth century, the American businessman Larry Burkett was originally a corporate finance executive; after being called, he founded a financial education ministry and spent his life teaching believers to manage money by biblical principles. He repeatedly preached one central conviction: God does not truly need our money — he needs our hearts; financial discipline is a tool God uses to shape character and build faith. He especially emphasized: the root problem of church finance is rarely the system — it is the mindset. Teach first, then manage.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Excessive Caution Wears the Coat of Prudence
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because the most common financial temptation in a church is rarely blatant embezzlement — far more often, it is burial disguised under the banner of "caution."

Temptation one: burial — like the servant with one talent, storing up offerings, unwilling to invest in gospel ministry, watching the account balance grow year after year while the vision makes no progress at all; excessive caution wears the coat of prudence, but underneath it is unbelief and fear. Temptation two: vagueness — years without a formal financial report, income and expenses recorded by feel, the deacon board and the congregation unable to clearly say where the money actually went; vagueness is not always born of malice, but vagueness itself is a breach. Temptation three: self-interest — personal and church funds not clearly separated, church resources used to favor "one's own people" first, financial decisions used as a tool to consolidate connections or status. These three temptations, in truth, share one root disease: treating what belongs to God as one's own.

Words that must never be said: "It's safer to save it up first, don't take a risk on ministry." "Everyone trusts me anyway, we don't need that many people checking." "I'll just handle this myself, no need to trouble anyone else." True faithfulness is not returning the money buried and intact — it is taking the risk in faith to steward what God has entrusted to us.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "The church habitually keeps offerings in fixed deposits or as cash reserves, unwilling to invest in new ministry — vision is proposed year after year, yet the budget stays just as conservative year after year, until the vision eventually becomes only a slogan on the wall." Faith-driven stewardship is not recklessness — it is daring to take one step beyond visible resources, guided by vision.

The second question: "Financial decisions have long been concentrated in the hands of a few senior members — the younger generation, even with a clear vision and a concrete proposal, finds it very hard to reach the budget discussion table, leaving the church's resource allocation disconnected from the needs of the times." Where counselors are many, there is safety — collective deliberation outweighs monopoly by a few.

The third question: "A culture that values relationships makes financial co-workers reluctant to ask one another for a cross-check, feeling that checking implies distrust — so the system exists in name only, and when a real problem finally happens, no trace can be found." Rules are not distrust of anyone — they are a protective wall built for faithful people.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "burial and conservatism" for "stewarding according to ability." Excessive caution wears the coat of prudence, but underneath it is unbelief and fear; faithfulness means putting it to work, not returning it untouched.

The second correction: exchange "vague bookkeeping" for "doing everything according to order." Regular reporting, multiple hands, external review — let the system become a protective wall for faithfulness, and a testimony to those outside the church.

The third correction: exchange "self-interested calculation" for "consistent with the Owner's heart." When managing finances, the question is whether it is consistent with the Owner's heart, not what benefit it brings to me.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Trust
sections.html:
The same property entrusted by God, set before different people, stirs completely different responses. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Views the property it possesses as earned entirely by its own ability and effort, forgetting the blessing and provision of God behind it all. The prophet Hosea pointed out this very pride in Ephraim: "Ephraim has said, 'Ah, but I am rich; I have found wealth for myself; in all my labors they cannot find in me iniquity or sin.'" (Hosea 12:8) The proud heart needs to be reminded: boasting of a lifetime of clean, self-made wealth is often precisely the beginning of blindness to one's own debt to God.

The Fearful Heart

Frets constantly over how much or how little it has, always worrying whether tomorrow will be enough, and so dares not give, dares not invest, needing to hold everything in its own hand to feel safe. Yet the Lord says: "Do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink... your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things." (Matthew 6:25, 32) Your heavenly Father knew your need long before you ever spoke a word.

The Ashamed Heart

Because it once managed money poorly, or once broke someone's trust over money, feels deep shame, believing it is no longer fit to be trusted with any property. The dishonest manager thought to himself: "I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg." (Luke 16:3) Yet God is still willing to use again anyone willing to repent and learn faithfulness anew.

The Wounded Heart

Was once financially wronged by a trusted friend or co-worker — a pain deeper than a stranger's deceit, and one that leaves a lingering wariness toward anyone who handles money afterward. Nehemiah records the people suffering financial exploitation at the hands of their own kin: "The people and their wives raised a great outcry against their Jewish brothers." (Nehemiah 5:1) God understands the pain of being exploited by your own people, and is willing to vindicate those who were wronged himself.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A church had for years kept most of its offerings in fixed deposits, and every vision proposal was shelved with "let's wait and see," until a young co-worker finally worked up the courage to ask directly at a deacon board meeting, "What exactly are we afraid of?" That question left the elders in the room silent for a long time. The church eventually released a portion of its reserve to support a new ministry, and the results far exceeded expectations, prompting everyone to rethink the cost of excessive caution.

The second. A financial co-worker had once been questioned by members over unclear bookkeeping, felt deep shame, and at one point considered stepping down from ministry. He later took the initiative to invite another co-worker to reconcile the books together every month, and reported openly to the deacon board. Two years later, he had become the church's most trusted financial gatekeeper. He said, "I learned that being willing to be checked builds trust far better than trying to prove myself."

The third. A brother had lent money years ago to a close friend in the church who never paid it back, and the relationship grew distant as a result — after that, he kept his distance from any ministry that involved handling money. An elder later reminded him, "One person's broken trust doesn't mean everyone will do the same." He worked up the courage to rejoin financial ministry, and through the process he not only rebuilt his trust in people but also experienced God's healing anew.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: honestly examine your own financial situation — are you living within your means, giving consistently, living in the fear of "burial" or the loss of control of "extravagance"? And actively find out about the church's financial situation — if a financial report exists, take time to read it; if none exists, gently suggest establishing a habit of regular reporting.

I declare: I will be faithful in the very little, for the measure of faithfulness is not the amount but the effort.

I declare: I will do everything according to order and walk in the light, letting the system become a protective wall for faithfulness.

I declare: I will bury nothing, but steward in faith what God has entrusted to me.

I declare: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus be King over my money too; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may we all become good and faithful stewards, using every portion of what God has entrusted to us for the glory of his name. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

ch37.title: Devote Ourselves to Prayer and the Ministry of the Word, and Also Manage This Matter Well — Resource Allocation and Ministry Development
ch37.partTitle: Part 8 — Financial Management and Resource Stewardship
ch37.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. This is the second lesson of Part 8. The last lesson established the identity of a steward and the principle of faithfulness; today we face a difficulty every church eventually meets — resources are always limited, while needs keep growing. The early church faced this exact same difficulty. Acts 6 records the church's first dispute arising from "distribution" — not over doctrine, but over the daily distribution of food. The 321 vision says: the one purpose is to build a system that belongs to God, and building such a system cannot be separated from the reasonable allocation of resources.

Acts 6:3–4: "Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word."

sections.heading: 1. The Disciples Were Increasing, Yet a Group of Widows Was Quietly Overlooked
sections.html: Acts 6:1 says: "Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution." Notice the opening of this verse: "in these days when the disciples were increasing in number." A church's difficulties often do not appear in a season of decline — they surface in a season of growth. As numbers grew, the supply system that had once run on relationships and informal understanding began to develop cracks. Widows were the most vulnerable group in that society, and the daily distribution was tied directly to whether they had enough to eat. It is reasonable to assume this was not intentional favoritism on the apostles' part, but that a language and cultural divide caused one group to be overlooked first. The neglect was structural, and the solution had to be structural too. It is worth noting that the text does not hide this conflict — a healthy community is not one without complaints, but one willing to face complaints honestly and treat them as an opportunity for improvement.

sections.heading: 2. Seeing the Overlooked Need, Establishing Roles by Gifting, and Resources That Serve the Mission
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, seeing the overlooked need — church growth is often accompanied by overlooked corners, and seeing the need is the starting point for allocating resources. Second, establishing roles by gifting — choosing people of good repute, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to manage the matter, putting the right people in the right positions. Third, resources serving the mission, not the mission serving resources — the ultimate purpose of every allocation is to keep the core mission from being drowned by minor matters. Many think resource allocation is purely a management discipline, unrelated to the spiritual life; but Acts 6 tells us that whether this is handled well is directly tied to whether the word of God flourishes and the number of disciples multiplies.

sections.heading: 3. The Pareto Principle, LeTourneau's Testimony, and the Wisdom of Letting Vision Determine Allocation
sections.html:
The apostles' response deserves close attention: "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables." They did not force themselves to manage everything at once — they openly admitted this was not right. This is great wisdom and great humility — acknowledging that one's own calling and capacity have limits is not dereliction of duty; it is honesty. The solution was to choose from among the full number of the disciples seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom — and notably, the congregation chose them while the apostles laid hands on them and appointed them: delegating authority, not abandoning it. The Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto observed that eighty percent of Italy's land was held by twenty percent of the population, and later generations named this the "Pareto principle": in many systems, roughly eighty percent of the results come from roughly twenty percent of the input. An honest inventory often reveals that a church calendar packed full of activities is not necessarily packed with the key twenty percent. But this must be used with caution: the church is not a business — just as the number of neglected widows was small, the church still put its full effort into fixing the problem. The Pareto principle can be applied to efficiency, but it must never be used to measure the value of a person.

The twentieth-century American inventor and industrialist R. G. LeTourneau experienced bankruptcy and a renewal of his faith in his youth, and vowed to give faithfully for the rest of his life. As his business prospered, the proportion he gave kept rising, eventually reaching ninety percent of his income given to missions and gospel ministry — what came to be called the "reverse tithe." He often said, "I shovel it out, and God shovels it back — but God has a bigger shovel." He never regarded his company's resources as his own personal accumulation, but as a tool for advancing gospel ministry — resources are meant to serve the mission, not the mission to serve resources. Many churches, when drawing up their budgets, habitually look first at where last year's money went and simply continue the same pattern this year — this is inertial allocation, not vision-driven allocation. The healthy order should be reversed: first clearly define the church's vision and mission, then ask how resources should be allocated. Vision is the sieve, and resources are the water — without a sieve, water flows wherever the terrain happens to lead, not according to any intention. The church's most precious resource is not only its property, but the time and gifting of its brothers and sisters — if eighty percent of the ministry load is pressed onto twenty percent of the core co-workers, the same kind of rupture recorded in Acts 6 will eventually appear again, except this time the ones who collapse from exhaustion will be burned-out co-workers.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Efficiency Is a Tool, Love Is the Goal
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because the Pareto principle is so appealing when discussed with enthusiasm, it can easily turn a church's resource allocation into a cold performance review.

A visit that only weighs input against output loses the warmth of shepherding; a ministry casually cut simply because its numbers are small may be cutting off a group precious in God's sight. Efficiency helps us use resources more wisely; love ensures we never treat people as numbers. In truth, efficiency and love are not in conflict — rightly understood, efficiency exists precisely to let more love be exercised. Appointing seven deacons was done precisely to make the food distribution more efficient, so that every single widow could be cared for more properly. Healthy resource allocation is loving people wisely: clear systems and priorities ensure that love is never lost to disorder, and never turns cold in the name of efficiency.

Words that must never be said: "Too few people are involved in this ministry to be worth the resources." "That group's voice is too quiet — let's serve the louder voices first." "Use the numbers to rank who matters." True resource allocation is loving people wisely — never calculating people away.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "Church ministry resources are long concentrated on ministries with large numbers and loud voices; groups that are marginal, vulnerable, or quiet are rarely actively noticed, even when their needs are real." When a church's resource allocation only serves the mainstream, the convenient, and the loud, it drifts from the consistent heart of Scripture.

The second question: "Core co-workers carry multiple roles for years on end, unwilling to delegate and unwilling to train new people, so the church's growth is capped by the physical stamina and time of a handful of co-workers." The healthy way is to follow the apostles' example: identify needs early, establish roles, and let the weight of ministry be spread across suitable shoulders.

The third question: "Major resource adjustments are often decided privately by a small few and only announced afterward; even when the congregation has real questions, they hesitate to raise them directly, and can only speculate and discuss privately." A transparent, consultative process — even when the outcome cannot satisfy everyone — is far more likely to be accepted by the majority.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "inertial continuation" for "letting vision determine allocation." Ask first what kind of church we want to become, then ask how the money should be allocated — don't let the budget become a copy of last year's.

The second correction: exchange "superhero-style ministry" for "establishing roles and spreading the load." Identify needs early, choose people by gifting, and don't let a handful of core co-workers burn out.

The third correction: exchange "closed-door decisions" for "openness and transparency." Explain the reasoning to the relevant co-workers beforehand, and encourage them to offer input — rather than announcing the outcome afterward.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Allocation
sections.html:
The same limited resource, set before different people, stirs completely different responses. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Secretly believes its own ministry matters more than others', even angling for a more prominent position and a larger share when resource allocation is discussed. The mother of two of the disciples once asked the same way: "Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom." (Matthew 20:21) Yet the Lord Jesus taught: "When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor." (Luke 14:8) The proud heart needs to be reminded: securing a prominent position is not the same as securing importance in God's eyes.

The Fearful Heart

Fears its own share will not be enough, and so tends to hold back more, unable to fully trust the system and process of allocation. When the Israelites gathered manna in the wilderness, "some left part of it till the morning, and it bred worms and stank." (Exodus 16:19–20) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: God's faithfulness to provide day by day is more trustworthy than the false security of holding a little extra in your own hand.

The Ashamed Heart

Feels its own need is not important enough to bother speaking up for, preferring to silently endure the shortage rather than let others see its lack. Ruth, gleaning in Boaz's field for the first time, said: "Why have I found favor in your eyes, that you should take notice of me, since I am a foreigner?" (Ruth 2:10) Yet God delights to actively look after the needs that no one dares to voice, through the people he has already prepared.

The Wounded Heart

Has carried an overly heavy ministry burden alone for a long time, without receiving matching support, and has accumulated deep, unspoken grievance and exhaustion inside. Moses once cried out to God: "The burden of all this people is too heavy for me... Kill me at once." (Numbers 11:14–15) Yet God sent seventy elders to help Moses share that overwhelming burden.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A church had for years invested most of its resources in Sunday worship and pulpit ministry, leaving children's and youth ministry chronically short-staffed, until a parent worked up the courage to raise the issue in a meeting — only then did the church realize that these children with "the smallest voice" had been overlooked for far too long. A dedicated children's ministry team was established shortly after, and resources and staffing gradually followed.

The second. An elder had personally carried the roles of finance, administration, and visitation for years, never once asking to share the load, until a sudden hospitalization revealed that the entire operation nearly ground to a halt because of one man. After recovering, he finally agreed to establish a supporting role and hand off part of the work to a newly trained co-worker. He said, "I used to think holding everything together was faithfulness — now I understand that letting someone else have the chance to grow is faithfulness too."

The third. A group of new immigrant believers, due to language and cultural barriers, had rarely been actively invited into the church's core ministry for years, and resource-allocation discussions always seemed to pass them by. An elder later took the initiative to understand their situation and established a cross-cultural ministry team, handing over part of the resources and roles to them. This once-marginalized group later became one of the church's most vibrant ministry teams.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: spend time this week honestly reviewing whether there is a group being overlooked in resource allocation, in your ministry or your church. Write it down, and go ask directly: who have I been overlooking?

I declare: I will actively see overlooked needs, not waiting for complaints to surface before responding.

I declare: I will establish roles by gifting, not letting a few people carry the whole burden alone.

I declare: I will let resources serve the mission, not let the mission serve resources.

I declare: let Jesus be King, letting resources flow fairly to every corner God values; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may our church become a church that sees the weak, coordinates by gifting, and moves its resources tightly around its mission, devoting itself to prayer and to the ministry of the word. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations move downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind, the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart, and the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — without reaching it, this lesson stays at the level of an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority, cover at least this question in each phase if time is short; ★★ = secondary priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked (Required) must not be skipped and may be completed at home.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as an Idea (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ The conflict of Acts 6 happened in a season when "the disciples were increasing in number," not in a season of decline. What does this prompt you to understand about the blind spots that often accompany church growth?

2. ★★ The Pareto principle points out that about eighty percent of results come from about twenty percent of the input, but it cannot be used to measure a person's value. What does this prompt you to understand about how a church balances efficiency and love?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "Rightly understood, efficiency exists precisely to let more love be exercised." In your own words, explain why efficiency and love are not in conflict.

4. ★★ LeTourneau said, "I shovel it out, and God shovels it back — but God has a bigger shovel." What does this prompt you to understand about "resources are meant to serve the mission, not the mission to serve resources"?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it well." If someone speaks in fragments, help them organize their thought — don't finish it for them.

Purpose: through Seeing, Hearing, Thinking, Speaking, and Acting, digest the idea into life.

[See] See Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — Proud (secretly believes its own ministry matters more, angles for a larger share), Fearful (fears its own share won't be enough, tends to hold back more), Ashamed (feels its needs aren't important enough to voice), Wounded (has carried an overly heavy burden alone without matching support). Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, tell each other two things: the overlooked person you will actively care for this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to make our church a church that sees the weak and moves its resources tightly around its mission.

ch38.title: Not Only in the Lord's Sight but Also in the Sight of Man — Financial Transparency and Building Trust
ch38.partTitle: Part 8 — Financial Management and Resource Stewardship
ch38.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. This is the third lesson of Part 8. The first two lessons spoke of a steward's faithfulness and the allocation of resources; today we speak of a discipline just as important, yet often overlooked — trust. No system, however sound, can stop a congregation's quiet suspicion about finances from eroding the church's unity. The 321 vision says: only the self-emptied can be unified. Transparency is not a sign of doubting a faithful person — it is the wisdom that protects everyone and builds trust across the whole community.

2 Corinthians 8:21: "For we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord's sight but also in the sight of man."

sections.heading: 1. He Stole Nothing, Yet He Fell Dead at the Apostles' Feet
sections.html: Acts 5 records: "But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, and with his wife's knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles' feet." Notice the heart of the matter — Ananias and Sapphira were under no obligation to give the full price of the land; that was entirely their own choice. Peter's rebuke to Ananias was: "While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal?" The problem was never how much they kept back — it was pretending to give it all while secretly keeping a portion. It was concealment. It was deceit. Peter's rebuke went deeper still: "You have not lied to man but to God." Ananias heard these words, fell down, and breathed his last. Through this event, God established a solemn principle for the early church: financial honesty is a non-negotiable foundation of the church's testimony.

sections.heading: 2. Money Easily Breeds Suspicion, the Solemn Warning of Integrity, and the Fruit of Holding All Things in Common
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, money easily breeds suspicion, and a system builds trust — Paul arranged for several people to travel together and handle the collection, leaving a verifiable trail. Second, the solemn warning of integrity — the tragedy of Ananias and Sapphira deceiving the Holy Spirit warns us of the danger of concealment. Third, transparency produces the fruit of holding all things in common — the early church, trusting one another, gave freely and willingly, accomplishing a beautiful testimony. Building trust takes a very long time; a single act of concealment or suspicion can destroy years of accumulated trust in an instant. Today's lesson is to turn transparency from a slogan into a concrete, workable system and habit.

sections.heading: 3. O'Neill's Theory of Trust, Barnabas's Example, and Buffett on Reputation
sections.html:
2 Corinthians 8:20 says: "We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us." Paul deliberately arranged for several brothers to travel alongside him and escort the funds — not because he distrusted anyone, but because he deeply understood that money easily invites suspicion; even with a clear conscience himself, he actively avoided leaving any room for someone to find fault. Notice the phrase "aim at" — this is not a passive stance of answering if someone happens to ask; it is actively arranging things in advance so that no one needs to ask at all. The British philosopher Onora O'Neill, who spent years studying the nature of trust, offered a thought-provoking insight: modern society often mistakenly assumes that building trust means declaring more loudly that we are trustworthy; but what truly builds trust is not more declarations — it is verifiable information, letting people check the facts for themselves rather than relying on a simple "trust me." Verifiability can be broken down into three practical layers: open information, transparent process, and feasible auditing — without all three, transparency easily becomes a mere formality.

In contrast to Ananias's concealment, Acts 4 records a beautiful picture: "Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common." Being of one heart and soul was not forced by command — it was built up day by day through open, honest dealing with one another over money. There was a Levite named Barnabas, whom the apostles called Son of Encouragement; he owned a field, sold it, and brought the full amount and laid it openly at the apostles' feet — no concealment, no keeping back a portion while pretending to give it all. Barnabas and Ananias faced the same exact situation, yet made entirely different choices: one gave everything openly, the other concealed a portion; one became a model of encouragement to the whole church, the other became one of church history's most sobering warnings. The investor Warren Buffett has a widely quoted line: "It takes twenty years to build a reputation and five minutes to ruin it." Financial integrity cannot wait until a problem arises to be repaired — it must be built as a habit and a system that can withstand scrutiny long before any crisis.

The Lord Jesus himself is the most perfect example of walking in the light. 1 John says, "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all." Throughout his life, the Lord never avoided scrutiny — he taught openly, performed miracles openly, and even invited the doubting Thomas to personally examine his risen body. He had no secret to hide, because everything about him was in complete alignment with the will of God. The ultimate root of financial transparency is not a management technique — it is following the example of the One who has no darkness in him at all and stands unafraid in the light. 1 John goes on to say, "If we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another." If a church is willing to walk in the light as the Lord Jesus did, not only will its finances grow clearer — the fellowship between its people will grow deeper and more genuine too.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Integrity Is Not Built by a Policy Document
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because a culture of integrity has never been built by a policy document — it is built through a leader's personal example, accumulated day after day.

If a church's leaders themselves are vague about finances and refuse to be reviewed, yet demand honesty and transparency from co-workers, such a demand will be hard for anyone to accept. If leaders are willing to openly disclose the funds they themselves handle, and submit to the same standard of review, this kind of leading-by-example humility carries far more persuasive weight than any rule or regulation. No leader is perfect and error-free; an occasional financial slip or misjudgment does not necessarily destroy trust. What truly determines whether trust survives is how a mistake is handled afterward — is it honestly admitted and immediately corrected, or glossed over and vaguely dismissed? The former can actually deepen a congregation's trust in its leader.

Words that must never be said: "We're a church of trust, we don't need that much auditing." "I have a clear conscience about this, no need to explain it." "This amount is too small to bother clarifying." True trust is not built by declaration — it is built by verifiable information, reliable commitments, and the character to admit and correct a mistake honestly.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "The church treats a public audit of the books as distrust of a long-serving co-worker, and that co-worker also feels that being asked to reconcile accounts is a loss of face — so the system exists in name only, and when a real problem finally happens, no trace can be found." Rules are not distrust of anyone — they are a protective wall built for faithful people.

The second question: "Major financial decisions are often settled privately within a small circle and only announced to the congregation afterward; even when members have real questions, they hesitate to raise them directly, and can only speculate privately." A transparent, consultative process — even when the outcome cannot satisfy everyone — is far more likely to be accepted by the majority.

The third question: "Leaders, after making a mistake, habitually handle it by 'making the big matter small and the small matter disappear,' afraid that admitting fault will damage their authority — so small oversights accumulate into deep suspicion until it all erupts years later at once." Admitting a mistake honestly, correcting it immediately, and explaining it openly actually deepens a congregation's trust in its leader.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "just trust me" for "verifiable information." A clear financial statement builds genuine trust far more effectively than any appealing slogan.

The second correction: exchange "passive explanation" for "actively walking in the light." Don't wait for suspicion before explaining — arrange things beforehand so no one needs to ask.

The third correction: exchange "protecting one's image" for "self-emptied integrity." A self-emptied person is willing to lay their own books, decisions, and motives out in the open, because there is no hidden self-interest left to protect.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Review
sections.html:
The same public review of accounts, set before different people, stirs completely different responses. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Believes it has always been honest and needs no one to review what it handles, even taking a request for review as a personal insult. Yet Jesus describes the rich man who trusted only his own judgment: "Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry." (Luke 12:19) The proud heart needs to be reminded: self-confidence cannot substitute for verifiable evidence.

The Fearful Heart

Though it has done nothing truly wrong, it instinctively grows tense and defensive at any review, afraid of being misunderstood or suspected, even looking for reasons to avoid it. Yet Proverbs says: "The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion." (Proverbs 28:1) One with a clear conscience can face any scrutiny without fear.

The Ashamed Heart

Once made a financial error, and after being found out, felt so deeply ashamed it believed it could never again face the brothers and sisters of the church with a raised head. The prophet once said, "As the thief is shamed when caught... so shall they be shamed." (Jeremiah 2:26) But those who confess and correct their fault can still win back trust — they need not live forever in shame.

The Wounded Heart

Once trusted someone in a time of hardship, only to be financially betrayed by that very person — a wound that leaves it wary of any relationship involving money ever since. Proverbs warns: "Trusting in a treacherous man in time of trouble is like a bad tooth or a foot that slips." (Proverbs 25:19) God understands the pain of being betrayed, and is willing to personally rebuild your trust in people.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A treasurer had served the church faithfully for years and was deeply trusted, yet consistently resisted having other co-workers reconcile the accounts alongside him, feeling it implied distrust. It was only after an unintentional bookkeeping error caused a misunderstanding that he realized actively welcoming review was, in fact, the best way to protect himself. He then began inviting two co-workers to reconcile the quarterly books together, and found his ministry burden actually lightened as a result.

The second. An elder once made a misjudgment on a ministry expense that led to a small loss. At first he wanted to handle it quietly, but later decided to explain the situation openly at a deacon board meeting and propose a remedy. Once the congregation learned of it, far from losing trust in him, they respected him even more for his honesty. He said, "I learned that admitting a mistake wins people's hearts far better than hiding it."

The third. A brother had once borrowed church funds years ago for temporary use but delayed repaying them. When discovered, he felt deep shame and at one point considered leaving the church. A pastor later approached him, received his repentance, and walked alongside him as he confessed to the deacon board and set up a repayment plan. Years later, he became the church's most steadfast advocate for full financial openness, his life itself a testimony to the renewal that repentance brings.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: in a matter you are responsible for, actively clarify to the relevant people something you could easily have left vague — practice aiming at what is honorable, explaining it clearly before anyone even asks.

I declare: I will aim at what is honorable, not only in the Lord's sight but also in the sight of man.

I declare: I no longer need to protect an image that cannot withstand scrutiny — I am willing to be reviewed.

I declare: I will become a verifiable, trustworthy steward, letting trust be built through honesty.

I declare: let Jesus be King, and let my books stand up to his examination; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may our church become a community unafraid of the light, aiming always at what is honorable, so that trust grows ever more steadfast through honesty and transparency. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations move downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind, the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart, and the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — without reaching it, this lesson stays at the level of an idea.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as an Idea (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ The problem with Ananias and Sapphira was not keeping back money, but pretending to give it all. What does this prompt you to understand about the difference between "concealment" and "deceit"?

Purpose: through Seeing, Hearing, Thinking, Speaking, and Acting, digest the idea into life.

[See] See Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — Proud (believes it has always been honest, needs no review), Fearful (though never truly wrong, grows tense and defensive at any review), Ashamed (once made a financial error, believes it can never hold its head up again), Wounded (once trusted someone who then betrayed it financially). Which are you most like? What experience made you this way?

9. ★★ This week, to whom will you actively clarify something you could easily have left vague? Name the specific person.

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for wounded-type members, particularly those once financially betrayed by someone they trusted and still guarded today. If someone weeps, pause the discussion and sit with them first — don't rush to give answers. If deeper trauma surfaces, follow up individually after the meeting and help arrange a referral.

10. ★★ "Trust is accumulated, not declared." In your own family, is there a small matter this week you should explain more proactively and clearly, rather than leaving it vague?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about in your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "If leaders are willing to openly disclose the funds they themselves handle and submit to the same standard of review, this humility carries more weight than any rule." Is there something you handle that you could proactively open up for review?

13. ★★★ A ten-minute daily discipline: this week, practice "actively walking in the light" on one small matter each day — explain it proactively rather than waiting to be asked. Name what time you will practice this.

14. ★★ The 920 discipline: identify your own "2" (spiritual companion); this week honestly share with them something you once concealed or left vague. Say their name out loud right now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Write down right now who you will tell it to.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, tell each other two things: the matter you will actively clarify this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to help us all become a community that aims at what is honorable.

ch39.title: God Loves a Cheerful Giver — How to Raise Funds to Support Church Ministry
ch39.partTitle: Part 8 — Financial Management and Resource Stewardship
ch39.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. This is the fourth lesson of Part 8. The first three lessons spoke of a steward's faithfulness, the allocation of resources, and financial transparency; today we face a discipline many church leaders both look forward to and dread — how to raise the funds that support the ministry God has entrusted to us. The moment fundraising is mentioned, many immediately think of emotional manipulation or moral pressure; but Scripture shows us a completely different picture — cheerful giving sparked by vision. The 321 vision says: let Jesus be King, including letting Jesus be King over our money and the motives behind our giving. Self-emptied giving is not an obligation forced out of us — it is cheerful willingness stirred by vision.

2 Corinthians 9:7: "Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver."

sections.heading: 1. Moses Actually Told the People to "Stop Giving"
sections.html: Exodus 36 records: "The people brought much more than enough for doing the work that the LORD had commanded us to do. So Moses gave command, and word was proclaimed throughout the camp, 'Let no man or woman do anything more for the contribution for the sanctuary.' So the people were restrained from bringing, for the material they had was sufficient to do all the work, and more." This is an extraordinarily rare scene in Scripture — craftsmen actually asking Moses to give an order for the people to stop giving, because the materials had already exceeded what could be used. The most common problem in church fundraising today is pleading with a congregation to give more; Exodus records the reverse problem — so much given that it had to be stopped. What could move a people who had just come out of slavery, owning almost nothing, to give so generously it exceeded what was even needed? The answer lies in the verses before: Moses clearly conveyed God's heart — to build a tabernacle for the LORD, that God's presence might dwell among the people. The vision was specific, the goal was clear, the meaning was profound, and the people's hearts were moved to give cheerfully — even beyond what was asked.

sections.heading: 2. Vision Sparking Cheerful Giving, the Example of the Macedonian Churches, and the Call of Wisdom
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, vision sparking cheerful giving — when the tabernacle was being built in Exodus, the materials the people brought exceeded what was needed, because the vision was clear and moving. Second, the example of the Macedonian churches — in extreme poverty they still overflowed in a wealth of generosity, even begging earnestly for the favor of taking part. Third, the call of wisdom outweighing the pressure of emotion — truly healthy fundraising appeals to a clear vision and need, not guilt or comparison. Raising funds to support ministry is, at its heart, a pastoral opportunity — inviting the congregation to participate in God's great work, practicing faith and generosity, and experiencing the genuine joy that giving brings.

sections.heading: 3. Dunn's Happiness Research, Generosity in the Midst of Hardship, and the Mindset of Sowing
sections.html:
Exodus 35 records: "Every one whose heart stirred him, and every one whose spirit moved him, brought the LORD's contribution to be used for the tent of meeting." A clear vision naturally sparks generosity — it needs no emotional manipulation, no social pressure. The psychologist Elizabeth Dunn and her research team found that spending money on others brings a more pronounced and more lasting sense of happiness than spending money on oneself — an effect observed across many different cultures around the world. This echoes Paul's teaching from a distance — God loves a cheerful giver, and cheerful giving that God loves carries its own reward of joy. But note carefully — this should never be turned upside down: the motive for giving should never ultimately be to obtain psychological happiness; it should come from a heart that loves God and loves people, and joy is only the byproduct that follows.

2 Corinthians 8 records: "In a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity." The Macedonian churches were going through affliction and severe testing, in extreme poverty — yet in that very condition, they overflowed in a wealth of generosity, completely overturning the myth that "one must be wealthy before one can be generous." Paul specifically noted that the Macedonians gave "beyond their means" — beyond what any rational calculation of their capacity could support. Even more striking, they were not passively receiving an invitation to give — they were "begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints." The root of it all: "They gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us by the will of God." The secret of the Macedonian churches' generosity was never fundraising technique — it was that they had already given their entire lives to the Lord first. 2 Corinthians 9:6 says: "Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully." Understanding giving as sowing means the sower does not calculate the return the moment the seed is planted — it is done in faith, trusting that God will, in his own way, use these gifts to bear the fruit he considers good.

The Lord Jesus himself personally defined what constitutes the most valuable offering. He sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into it, and many rich people put in large sums. A poor widow came and put in two small copper coins. Jesus said to his disciples, "This poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on." What God measures in giving has never been the absolute size of the amount — it is the heart of complete, unreserved dependence behind the gift. This is a profound reminder for every church leader: the focus of a fundraising ministry should never ultimately be the target amount reached — it should be guiding each person to give themselves wholeheartedly to the Lord, just as that poor widow did.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Giving Is Not a Transaction, It Is Worship
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because church history has no shortage of examples of emotionally pressured fundraising: exaggerating a crisis, manufacturing guilt, publicly comparing who gave more, implying that not giving means being unspiritual.

These tactics may produce results in the short term, but they erode the congregation's trust in the church, and distort the cheerful willingness that giving was always meant to have. In contrast, the call of wisdom clearly presents the need and the vision, hands the decision back to each individual, and entrusts it to God's own work within their hearts. When Paul was raising funds, he deliberately held up the example of the Macedonian churches to encourage the Corinthian believers, while also clearly stating: "I say this not as a command." He appealed to the power of example and vision, not the force of apostolic authority — inspiring the heart, never manipulating it; sharing vision, never forcing a decision.

Words that must never be said: "God has done so much for you, how can you not give?" "So-and-so gave this much, what about you?" "If this ministry doesn't get enough funding soon, it will have to close." A truly healthy call honestly presents the real need, without exaggeration or concealment, letting the congregation respond freely, guided by clear information and a moved heart.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "The church habitually wraps fundraising in a sense of indebtedness, framing giving as repayment for God's grace — over time this breeds spiritual fatigue and resistance, turning worship into a transaction." What God loves is cheerful, willing giving — not a number squeezed out under pressure.

The second question: "Publicly praising top donors and using numeric rankings to stir up comparison turns giving from worship of God into a performance for others, and can even leave those who give less feeling secretly inferior." Give as you have decided in your own heart — not reluctantly, not under compulsion.

The third question: "The church rarely teaches a biblical view of money in ordinary times, and only talks about giving heavily when a specific ministry needs funds, leaving the congregation feeling that the church only thinks of them when it needs money." The healthy approach weaves the teaching of giving into everyday spiritual formation, taught consistently throughout the year.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "emotional pressure" for "clear vision." Rather than designing a more effective pressure tactic, invest that energy into clearly communicating the vision.

The second correction: exchange "performance and comparison" for "deciding in one's own heart." What God looks at has never been the amount given — it is the heart of complete, unreserved dependence.

The third correction: exchange "giving as transaction" for "giving as worship." Self-emptied giving is not a performance — it is the natural overflow of love; all the glory belongs to the God who supplies all things.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Offering
sections.html:
The same call to give, set before different people, stirs completely different responses. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Likes to be seen and praised when giving, even secretly hoping to have its name specially mentioned. Yet the Lord Jesus taught: "When you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you... Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward." (Matthew 6:2) The proud heart needs to be reminded: giving done to be seen has already collected its reward on earth.

The Fearful Heart

Fears there won't be enough left after giving, and so calculates again and again, endlessly hesitant to sow in faith. Moses, too, once shrank back when called: "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?" (Exodus 3:11) Those who overcalculate whether they're qualified enough or have enough often forget that it was never their own ability doing the sending.

The Ashamed Heart

Feels its ability to give is too small compared to others, and so simply gives nothing at all, preferring to avoid the occasion entirely rather than feel inferior. Yet Paul says: "If the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have." (2 Corinthians 8:12) God does not look at the size of the amount — he looks at the willingness of the heart.

The Wounded Heart

Was once manipulated by someone under the guise of zeal, and so instinctively guards against and distrusts any invitation to give or participate. Paul once warned the Galatian church: "They make much of you, but for no good purpose. They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them." (Galatians 4:17) God understands the wound of being used, and is willing to rebuild your trust in a genuine call.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A church's building fund had made little progress for years, until it changed its approach — instead of using rankings to stir motivation, it clearly showed the congregation how many families and children the completed building would serve. Within just a few months, giving exceeded expectations. One member said, "Before, it felt like a demand. This time, it felt like being invited to take part in something beautiful."

The second. A brother, with limited income for years, always felt his giving was too small to offer, and so quietly avoided any occasion involving giving. He was deeply moved when a pastor specifically mentioned the story of the widow's two small coins in a sermon, and began to give cheerfully according to his own ability. He said, "I finally understand — God doesn't look at how much I gave, he looks at whether I gave it wholeheartedly."

The third. A sister had once been pressured at another church with the message that "not giving means you're unspiritual," and afterward remained wary of any call to give, at one point even considering leaving church life altogether. She later joined a church that clearly stated its needs and never applied pressure, and rediscovered the cheerful willingness giving was always meant to have. She said, "I realized giving can be joyful — not the kind of pressure I used to imagine."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: honestly examine your own giving — is it out of cheerful willingness, or out of habitual obligation or guilt? Bring what you discover before God and ask him to renew your heart. And follow the spirit of the poor widow's two small coins — this week, in one small matter, practice giving wholeheartedly and without reservation.

I declare: I will be a cheerful giver, for God loves a cheerful giver.

I declare: I will give myself to the Lord first — my financial giving is the natural overflow of a life wholly given.

I declare: I will sow in faith without calculating the return, trusting God to use it to bear beautiful fruit.

I declare: let Jesus be King, and let my giving return to the essence of worship; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may our church become a community that clearly communicates its vision, honestly invites participation, and lets giving return to the essence of worship. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations move downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind, the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart, and the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — without reaching it, this lesson stays at the level of an idea.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as an Idea (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ When the tabernacle was being built, the people gave so much that Moses had to order them to stop. What does this prompt you to understand about "the clarity of vision determines the intensity of giving"?

2. ★★ Dunn's research found that spending money on others brings more lasting happiness than spending it on oneself. What does this prompt you to understand about the relationship between giving and joy?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "Giving is not a transaction, it is worship; not a performance, it is the natural overflow of love." In your own words, explain which matters more to God — the motive behind a gift, or its amount?

4. ★★ The Macedonian churches "gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us by the will of God." What does this prompt you to understand about "the secret of generosity is not fundraising technique, but a life wholly given"?

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — Proud (likes to be seen and praised when giving), Fearful (fears there won't be enough left, endlessly hesitant to sow), Ashamed (feels its giving is too small, so gives nothing), Wounded (once manipulated under the guise of zeal, guards against any call to give).
