In pairs, tell each other two things: the small matter in which you will practice giving wholeheartedly this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to help us all become cheerful givers.

ch40.title: First Sit Down and Count the Cost — Risk Control in Financial Management
ch40.partTitle: Part 8 — Financial Management and Resource Stewardship
ch40.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. This is the final lesson of Part 8, "Financial Management and Resource Stewardship." We have walked through a steward's faithfulness, the allocation of resources, financial transparency, and cheerful giving; today we take up the last piece of the puzzle — risk control. A church that focuses only on expansion and giving, without learning to prepare for rainy days, will eventually be hurt by an unexpected storm. Wise preparation has never been a sign of weak faith — it is the foresight a faithful steward ought to have. The 321 vision says: the one purpose is to build a system that belongs to God, and a system able to withstand testing needs wise risk control as its foundation.

Luke 14:28: "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?"

sections.heading: 1. An Ant with No Boss Taught Us the Most Practical Lesson in Money Management
sections.html: Proverbs 6 says: "Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise. Without having any chief, officer, or ruler, she prepares her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest." What makes these verses so remarkable is that the ant has no outside authority urging her on at all, yet she still actively prepares food in summer and gathers her supply at harvest. This gives the church an extremely important reminder about financial management: truly healthy risk control should not depend on the pressure of external auditing to be carried out — it should come from an inner sense of responsibility that actively prepares for the future. The ant's wisdom lies in discerning the seasons — preparing in abundance so there is something to rely on in scarcity. Waiting for a crisis to arrive before scrambling to respond is usually already too late.

sections.heading: 2. The Wisdom of Preparing for Rainy Days, an Honest System of Internal Controls, and Casting Our Cares Without Anxiety
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, the wisdom of preparing for rainy days — the ant preparing food in summer, and Joseph storing up grain in the years of plenty, are both far-sighted acts of responsibility toward the future. Second, an honest system of internal controls — the offering chest and counting procedure established in the days of King Joash allowed the flow of money to withstand scrutiny. Third, casting our cares without anxiety, while still preparing wisely — Philippians teaches us that faith and wisdom walk hand in hand; even as we cast our burden on God, we still fulfill our own responsibility. Having walked through a steward's faithfulness, the allocation of resources, financial transparency, and cheerful giving, today's lesson on risk control is precisely about placing the lessons of the previous four within a structure able to withstand the test of time.

sections.heading: 3. Joseph's Grain Stores, the Swiss Cheese Model, and King Joash's Offering Chest
sections.html:
Genesis records that after Joseph interpreted the dream, he proposed a plan to Pharaoh: "Let him take the fifth part of the produce of the land of Egypt during the seven plentiful years... That food shall be a reserve for the land against the seven years of famine." Joseph did not stop merely at the level of prophecy — he immediately proposed a concrete, workable plan of action. Genesis records: "Joseph stored up grain in great abundance, like the sand of the sea, until he stopped measuring it, for it could not be measured." This large-scale, systematic reserve not only saved Egypt itself, but allowed Joseph's own family, and even the surrounding nations, to survive the famine. The psychologist James Reason proposed the well-known "Swiss cheese model" to explain how major accidents happen in complex systems: each layer of protection is like a slice of cheese full of holes — normally the holes in each layer sit in different places, so a gap in one layer is blocked by another; but when the holes of every layer happen to line up, risk can pass straight through unimpeded. This gives the church a very practical reminder: don't rely on a single line of defense. The healthy approach is to build multiple layers of protection — clear systems, multiple hands, regular reviews, external audits — layered one upon another.

2 Chronicles records: "So the king gave command, and they made a chest and set it outside the gate of the house of the LORD... And when the Levites saw that there was much money in the chest, the king's secretary and the officer of the chief priest came and emptied the chest and took it and carried it back to its place." King Joash, in order to repair the temple, established an offering chest placed outside the temple gate, allowing the people to freely deposit their gifts, which prevented the possibility of anyone secretly manipulating the funds. This is precisely a model of a sound internal control system — every cent that moved had a clear, traceable record. This kind of internal control was not because anyone doubted a particular official's faithfulness — it was because it was deeply understood that even faithful people need the protection of a system. The Lord Jesus said, "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?" Faith and calculation are not mutually exclusive — true faith includes the wisdom to honestly face reality and prepare responsibly. Some believers equate "acting by faith" with "no need to prepare" — but this idea does not actually match the teaching of Scripture. Joseph storing grain in the years of plenty was itself an act of wisdom that came from God; neglecting such wisdom actually comes closer to testing God than trusting him.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — True Security Is Not in a Bank Account, but in the God Who Supplies All Things
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because preparation and hoarding are separated by a single line, and the key is the self.

Preparation rooted in self easily slides into hoarding — piling up ever more reserves while remaining unwilling to invest in ministry, even turning "security" into the true object of the heart's trust, replacing dependence on God. Paul says in Philippians: "Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God." This verse is often misread to mean there is no need to plan at all, but what Paul means by "do not be anxious" is a heart not bound by worry — not the abandonment of every reasonable behavioral preparation. Healthy church financial management is, at the same time, casting every burden on God through prayer and supplication, and diligently carrying out risk assessment, building systems, and stockpiling resources.

Words that must never be said: "Our faith is strong enough, we don't need reserves." "I'll just carry this alone, no need for handover documents." "It hasn't happened yet, so no need to plan a contingency." A truly healthy view of faith wholeheartedly depends on God's provision on the one hand, and faithfully applies the wisdom God has given to make responsible preparation on the other.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "The church treats building a reserve fund or a risk-control mechanism as a sign of weak faith, preferring to prepare nothing at all rather than risk being misunderstood as unspiritual — and the result is being caught helpless the moment a storm hits." Joseph storing grain in the years of plenty was exactly the foresight a faithful steward should have — not a lack of faith.

The second question: "A critical financial position has depended on the same co-worker for years, with no handover documents or backup person ever established — and the moment that co-worker suddenly leaves or falls ill, the entire operation nearly grinds to a halt." Every critical financial position should have clear handover documents and a backup person in place.

The third question: "Even when the church has a contingency plan, it is often just a document locked in a filing cabinet, never updated for years, never actually rehearsed or reviewed." Risk control is not a one-time project — it is a living system that requires ongoing maintenance.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "faith without preparation" for "preparation with wisdom." Joseph storing grain in the years of plenty was the foresight a faithful steward should have — it was not testing God, but the wisdom of reverencing God.

The second correction: exchange "a single line of defense" for "multiple layers of protection." Clear systems, multiple hands, regular reviews, and external audits, layered one upon another, are what can truly withstand testing.

The third correction: exchange "security in the bank account" for "security in God." A self-emptied steward, on the one hand, diligently makes wise preparation, and on the other hand, clearly knows that true security is not in the number in a bank account, but in the God who supplies all things.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Preparation
sections.html:
The same preparation for the future, set before different people, stirs completely different responses. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Feels full of confidence about its plans for the future, yet forgets in both word and heart that everything rests in God's hands, as if tomorrow must surely unfold exactly according to its own arrangement. James warns: "Yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring... As it is, you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil." (James 4:13–16) The proud heart needs to be reminded: one who cannot even be certain of tomorrow has little reason to boast that their own plan is foolproof.

The Fearful Heart

Is filled with anxiety about the future, constantly worrying over things that have not yet happened, unable to find peace even after making reasonable preparations. Yet the Lord Jesus says: "Do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble." (Matthew 6:34) God invites you to exchange excessive worry for trust, one day at a time.

The Ashamed Heart

Because of a past financial miscalculation or bad decision, feels deep shame, and no longer dares to take on any responsibility for planning or risk. Proverbs advises someone who put up security for a friend and fell into financial trouble: "When you have come into the hand of your neighbor, go, hasten, and plead urgently with your neighbor." (Proverbs 6:1, 3) Facing a past mistake with humility is the starting point for a fresh beginning, not a permanent shame.

The Wounded Heart

Once experienced a sudden financial disaster, and the unexpected loss left a deep wound, leaving it filled with insecurity about the future ever since. After losing all his property in a single day, Job still declared: "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." (Job 1:21) God can, even after the deepest loss, still give a worship that is not shaken by material things.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A church had never built up a reserve fund in all its years, until a sudden roof repair crisis caught it completely off guard, forcing an emergency appeal to the congregation — a scramble that brought no small measure of stress. The church later established an emergency reserve fund system, and years later, when a similar mishap occurred, the church handled it with composure. An elder said, "This time we weren't panicking — we were calmly following the plan."

The second. A financial co-worker had managed the church's accounts alone for years without ever establishing handover documents, until a sudden hospitalization revealed that no one even knew the basic account passwords, throwing operations into temporary disarray. After recovering, he took the initiative to compile complete handover documentation and train a backup co-worker. He said, "I used to think I was indispensable — now I understand that was actually a risk to the church."

The third. A brother once caused a significant loss to the church through a mistaken financial decision, and felt deep shame, at one point considering stepping away from all financial ministry. A pastor later encouraged him to face it honestly, explain it to the deacon board, and propose improvements. Far from condemning him, the church, through that very experience, built a far more robust review process. He said, "One mistake became the starting point for the whole church to grow more sound."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration: Reviewing Part Eight
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: conduct a simple risk inventory for yourself or the team you serve, writing down three "what ifs" and their possible responses; follow the example of the ant, and begin preparing on your own initiative before anyone ever asks you to.

Having come this far, the five lessons of Part 8, "Financial Management and Resource Stewardship," together form one complete lesson. The basic principles of church financial management — everything belongs to the LORD, and we are only entrusted stewards. Resource allocation and ministry development — see the overlooked need, and let resources serve the mission. Financial transparency and building trust — aim at what is honorable, and let integrity become the foundation. How to raise funds to support church ministry — vision sparks cheerful, willing giving. And today, risk control in financial management — prepare for rainy days, and cast our cares without anxiety. These five lessons interlock to form one complete, God-honoring system of church financial management. May our church become a community that is both faithful and transparent, both generous and prudent, both trusting in God and wisely applying his wisdom.

I declare: I will follow the example of the ant, actively preparing before anyone asks me to.

I declare: I will build multiple layers of protection, not relying on any single mechanism or person.

I declare: I will be anxious about nothing, casting every burden on God through prayer and supplication.

I declare: let Jesus be King — my security is not in a bank account, but in the God who supplies all things; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may we all become good and faithful stewards, faithful in the very little and faithful in much, until the day the Lord returns. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
