Third Transformation | Transforming It into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily practice.

10. ★★ "Every critical position should have clear handover documents and a backup person." In your own family, is there an important matter only you know about that has never been clearly explained to anyone else?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about in your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "Prayer is not a substitute for planning, and planning is not an insurance policy that substitutes for prayer." Is there something in your life where you have only prayed without preparing diligently, or only prepared without casting it in prayer?

13. ★★★ A ten-minute daily discipline: this week, pray over one thing that worries you each day using the phrase "be anxious about nothing" — name what time you will practice this.

14. ★★ The 920 discipline: identify your own "2" (spiritual companion); this week review each other's risk inventory together and pray for one another. Say their name out loud right now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, tell this lesson to someone outside the group in three sentences — Which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it; be anxious about nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God; the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. Write down right now who you will tell it to.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, tell each other two things: the risk inventory you will conduct this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to help us all become good and faithful stewards, wisely prepared and wholly entrusted to him.

ch41.title: Filled with the Spirit of God — How the Church Can Use Technology to Advance Its Ministry
ch41.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. Beginning with this lesson, we enter Part 9, "Technology and Church Modernization" — five lessons reflecting on how the church can serve faithfully in this rapidly changing digital age. This is the first lesson, and we must ask the most fundamental question: whose is technology, really? Is it a worldly tool the church reluctantly has to touch, or is it, from the start, a gift that comes from God, that can be filled with God's Spirit and used to build his house? Exodus gives us an unexpected answer.

Exodus 35:30–31: "Then Moses said to the people of Israel, 'See, the LORD has called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and he has filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability, with intelligence, with knowledge, and with all craftsmanship.'"

sections.heading: 1. A Craftsman God Called by Name Himself
sections.html: This is an extraordinary scene in Scripture: before God ever called a prophet, a judge, or a king to build the tabernacle, he first called a craftsman "by name." Bezalel was not a priest, not a prophet — he was a craftsman skilled in working gold, silver, bronze, precious stones, and wood. The text specifically emphasizes that God did not merely "permit" him to work — God "filled him with the Spirit of God," giving him ability, intelligence, and knowledge to do every kind of work — the very same language later used to describe prophets and judges being filled with the Holy Spirit. God himself placed the skill of craftsmanship and the filling of the Spirit in the very same sentence. This gives the church today an extremely important starting point for using technology: the ability to work with technology and craft is not, in itself, a worldly, second-rate gift — it can be wisdom given by God, filled by the Spirit of God.

sections.heading: 2. Gifting Is Given by God, Direction Determines Good or Evil, and the Focus Remains on Jesus, Not the Tool
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, the gift of technology and craftsmanship is, in itself, wisdom given by God — Bezalel was filled with the Spirit of God, and used his skilled hands to build God's house. Second, the very same gift, pointed in the wrong direction, becomes an idol — Aaron used those same skilled hands to cast the golden calf. Third, no matter how the tools change, the focus remains on Jesus, never on the tool itself — the core of the gospel has never changed; only the medium of proclaiming it has. As we enter this series, we are not asking whether technology is good — we are asking what we are using technology for.

sections.heading: 3. Bezalel and the Golden Calf: The Same Two Hands, Two Directions
sections.html:
Exodus goes on to record that Bezalel and his assistant Oholiab, using the wisdom God had given them, made the ark of the covenant, the mercy seat, the lampstand, and the altar — every piece pointing to God's presence and redemption. Yet in that very same book, there is another pair of skilled hands — Aaron's. The people pressed Aaron, saying, "Up, make us gods." Aaron "received the gold from their hand and fashioned it with a graving tool and made a golden calf." In the original language, Bezalel's "work" and Aaron's "fashioning" use nearly the same set of craft vocabulary — technically almost no difference at all. The only difference was that one pair of hands worked for God's glory, and the other worked to satisfy the people's immediate anxiety and desire. This gives the church today a profound reminder about using technology: software, platforms, and algorithms are, in themselves, neither good nor evil — the key always lies in who we are using them for: to build God's house, or to forge a calf that can be seen and worshiped immediately.

Church history has repeated this pattern again and again. Gutenberg's invention of movable-type printing allowed the Bible, for the first time, to be printed in large quantities and spread into the hands of common people, directly fueling the Reformation — Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses spread across all of Europe within just a few weeks, carried by that era's most advanced technology. In the early twentieth century, radio allowed the voice from the pulpit, for the first time, to cross city walls and mountains and reach the bedsides of the sick and the remote countryside. Every shift in medium has, in its time, been questioned as "worldly, dangerous" — yet looking back, each one became a vessel through which God expanded the boundaries of the gospel. The media theorist Marshall McLuhan offered the thought-provoking insight that "the medium is the message" — the medium itself, quietly and unconsciously, shapes how content is received; it is never merely a neutral channel. This reminds the church that choosing which platform to proclaim the gospel on has never been purely a technical decision — it is also a spiritual discernment.

Every tool the church uses today — livestreaming systems, online giving platforms, member databases, social media accounts — stands at this very same fork in the road. They can be modern-day tabernacle instruments, faithfully pointing to God's presence, or they can quietly become modern-day golden calves, a stage for a church or a leader to prove and inflate themselves. The key to discernment has never been how advanced a tool is — it is toward whom the heart using that tool is turned.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — When We Begin to Be Infatuated with Numbers Rather Than the God Who Is Worthy of Worship
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because building the tabernacle and casting the golden calf are separated by a single line, and the key is the self.

Using technology out of self easily leads to treating view counts, likes, and share rates as the sole measure of whether a ministry has "succeeded" — and to unconsciously adjusting the content and direction of a message to chase better numbers, catering to what the algorithm favors rather than what pleases God. This is the modern-day golden calf — not a deliberate betrayal of God, but a substitute forged with one's own hands, in anxiety and comparison, something that can be seen and praised immediately.

Words that must never be said: "This post's numbers aren't good — is our ministry failing?" "That other church has more livestream viewers than us, we must be doing something wrong." "Just make the headline more sensational, and we'll attract more people." A truly healthy view of technology knows clearly that the ultimate standard for measuring ministry is never the number on the screen — it is whether this helps people draw closer to Jesus.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "Church leaders treat follower counts and view numbers as proof of spiritual success — greatly encouraged when the numbers look good, discouraged when they slip, unconsciously letting the algorithm determine the direction of shepherding." Bezalel was filled with the Spirit of God in order to build God's house, not to please the crowd in front of him.

The second question: "The church rushes to keep up with every new piece of technology, but never stops to ask whether this tool truly helps people draw closer to Jesus, or merely makes the scene look more lively." Choosing technology requires spiritual discernment, not just following the technical trend.

The third question: "A leader is buried twenty-four hours a day in notifications and messages, yet never deliberately establishes a boundary of 'digital sabbath,' letting the time meant for solitude with God be quietly eroded by technology." Even Bezalel, who built the tabernacle, worked under the commandment of the Sabbath — restraint in work is what makes it sustainable.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "numbers are proof of success" for "numbers are only a reference tool." The true standard is whether this helps people draw closer to Jesus — not the like count on the screen.

The second correction: exchange "adopting technology by trend" for "choosing technology by spiritual discernment." Before introducing any new tool, ask first: is this to build God's house, or to satisfy the crowd's immediate anxiety?

The third correction: exchange "being led by notifications" for "deliberately establishing a digital sabbath." A self-emptied leader can freely use technology, and can just as freely set it down, because what he depends on has never been the numbers — it is the God who called him by name.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Tool
sections.html:
The same piece of technology, set before different people, stirs completely different responses. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Longs to accomplish something great with technology, so that its own name will be remembered and celebrated. Yet the Preacher looked back on all the resources he had spent building for himself: "I made great works. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself." (Ecclesiastes 2:4) The proud heart needs to be reminded: wisdom truly used by God is for God's name, not for one's own.

The Fearful Heart

Grabs hold of every new piece of technology in a hurried panic, afraid of falling behind the times, afraid of becoming obsolete — like the people who panicked when Moses delayed coming down the mountain: "Up, make us gods who shall go before us." (Exodus 32:1) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: choices made out of panic are usually the furthest from God.

The Ashamed Heart

Because it is unskilled at operating new technology, feels it has fallen behind the times and become a burden to the church, and would rather hide in a corner than admit it needs help — like Adam hiding from God: "I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself." (Genesis 3:8) The ashamed heart needs to be reminded: admitting your own weakness is not shameful — it is the starting point for honestly facing God.

The Wounded Heart

Has once been misunderstood or wounded by cruel words online, or feels like nothing more than a dispensable number inside a vast digital system, never truly remembered by anyone — like the psalmist's lament: "I have been forgotten like one who is dead... I have become like a broken vessel." (Psalm 31:12) Yet God himself calls every single person by name — no one is only a set of data in his eyes.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A small rural church had worried for years about not being able to keep its young people, and later tried recording its Sunday messages as short videos and posting them online. The view count was dismal at first, and the pastor nearly gave up. Six months later, a young person working far from home, who hadn't set foot in a church for years, happened to scroll past one of the videos and reconnected with the pastor from his hometown church — he now attends regularly online. The pastor said, "We weren't doing it for the traffic — we were doing it so those children who had drifted far away could still hear one familiar greeting."

The second. A minister once rode an emotional rollercoaster with the view count of every post — elated when the numbers were good, doubting his own calling when they were poor. He later began deliberately praying before publishing anything, and stopped refreshing the backend statistics repeatedly afterward. He said, "I learned that my job is to sow faithfully — what happens with the numbers is God's business."

The third. An elderly deacon had no confidence operating the church's online systems and, for a long time, was afraid to volunteer for related ministry, worried he would hold the team back. A young co-worker later took the initiative to invite him to learn together, and the two paired up — the elder's shepherding experience and the younger person's technical skill complementing each other. Now this deacon can independently handle basic online tasks. He said, "I discovered that admitting I didn't know something actually gained me a co-worker."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: examine one digital tool you or your church currently uses, and honestly ask whether it is helping people draw closer to Jesus or merely making the numbers look better. And set aside a period of "digital sabbath" for yourself — deliberately not checking notifications, alone with God.

I declare: I will be a servant filled with the Spirit of God, able to do skilled work — not a craftsman seeking his own name.

I declare: my standard for using technology is whether it helps people draw closer to Jesus, not the number on the screen.

I declare: I will deliberately establish a boundary of digital sabbath, so my time alone with God is not eroded by technology.

I declare: let Jesus be King — no matter how the medium changes, the focus of my ministry stays on Jesus; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may we all become servants like Bezalel — filled with the Spirit of God, faithfully using our gifts to build God's house. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations move downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind, the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart, and the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — without reaching it, this lesson stays at the level of an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority, cover at least this question in each phase if time is short; ★★ = secondary priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked (Required) must not be skipped and may be completed at home.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as an Idea (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ God called Bezalel "by name" and filled him with the Spirit of God, giving him wisdom to do every kind of work. What does this prompt you to understand about "the gift of craft and technology can also be a spiritual gift"?

2. ★★ Bezalel building the tabernacle and Aaron casting the golden calf used the very same craft skills, yet pointed in entirely opposite directions. What does this prompt you to understand about "the tool itself is neither good nor evil — the key is the direction"?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "The ultimate standard for measuring ministry is never the number on the screen — it is whether this helps people draw closer to Jesus." In your own words, explain the difference between these two standards.

4. ★★ McLuhan said "the medium is the message" — the medium itself shapes how content is received. What does this prompt you to understand about the importance of a church's choice of platform?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it well." If someone speaks in fragments, help them organize their thought — don't finish it for them.

Second Transformation | Digesting It into Life (about 35 minutes · the core of this lesson)

Purpose: through Seeing, Hearing, Thinking, Speaking, and Acting, digest the idea into life.

[See] See Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — Proud (longs to accomplish something great with technology so its own name is remembered), Fearful (grabs new technology in a panicked hurry, afraid of falling behind), Ashamed (unskilled at new technology, feels it is holding the church back, dares not admit it needs help), Wounded (once misunderstood or hurt online, or feels like a dispensable number in a vast system). Which are you most like? What experience made you this way?

[Hear] Hear God Speak

6. ★★ God has one sentence for each of these four hearts. Find the verse that matches you, read it aloud, then tell the group: where does this sentence touch you?

[Think] Think Through the Obstacle

7. ★★ In your habits with technology (social media, messaging apps, ministry tools), is there one that is actually chasing visible numbers rather than helping people draw closer to Jesus?

[Speak] Say It Out Loud

8. ★ Finish this sentence in one line: "This lesson tore down which old idea I had about 'technology and spirituality'?" If your answer is "none," say that honestly too — that itself is an important discovery.

[Act] Take a Step

9. ★★ This week, what specific "digital sabbath" period will you set for yourself? Name the time and the method.

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for wounded-type and ashamed-type members, particularly those once hurt online or made to feel inferior for being unskilled with technology. If someone weeps, pause the discussion and sit with them first — don't rush to give answers. If deeper trauma surfaces, follow up individually after the meeting and help arrange a referral.

Third Transformation | Transforming It into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily practice.

10. ★★ "The purpose a tool exists for is to help people draw closer to Jesus." In your own family, this week, does how you use your phone or tablet draw your family closer or push you further apart?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about in your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "The true standard is whether this helps people draw closer to Jesus, not the like count on the screen." Is there a piece of technology you currently use that needs to be re-examined by this standard?

13. ★★★ A ten-minute daily discipline: this week, turn off phone notifications for ten minutes each day and be quiet before God alone — name what time you will practice this.

14. ★★ The 920 discipline: identify your own "2" (spiritual companion); this week share your technology habits with each other and remind one another in prayer. Say their name out loud right now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, tell this lesson to someone outside the group in three sentences — The LORD called him by name and filled him with the Spirit of God, giving him wisdom to do skilled work; the purpose a tool exists for is to help people draw closer to Jesus; no matter how the medium changes, the focus stays on Jesus, not on the tool itself. Write down right now who you will tell it to.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, tell each other two things: the digital sabbath period you will set this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to make us all servants filled with his Spirit, faithfully using our gifts to serve people without being bound by our tools.

ch42.title: The Word Became Flesh — Building a Model for Integrating Online and Offline Church
ch42.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. This is the second lesson of Part 9. Last lesson we reflected on technology itself; this lesson faces a tension that touches daily life much more closely: as more and more people choose to join Sunday worship through a screen, how should the church understand the relationship between "online" and "offline"? Should online gathering be treated as a reluctant substitute, or as a new door God has opened for this age? Hebrews gives us a clear reminder and a clear calling.

Hebrews 10:24–25: "And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near."

sections.heading: 1. A Gathering That Must Not Stop
sections.html: The word "meet together" in the original Greek is ἐπισυναγωγή (episynagōgē), a word carrying the sense of being actively, deliberately gathered — not a casual, optional encounter, but the action of a people being called together by one and the same Lord. The author specifically warns against making a "habit" of neglecting to meet — the original implies that once absence becomes routine, the heart drifts further and further from the community, until a person no longer even notices anything is wrong. This verse was written for the early church, facing persecution and the ever-present danger of scattering, yet two thousand years later it unexpectedly speaks with striking precision into our own situation: when a screen makes "attending" so easy, absence becomes just as easy — so easy that a person can drift away without ever noticing it happened.

sections.heading: 2. Online Is a New Door God Has Opened; the Incarnation Is Our Foundation; Online Is the Bridge, Offline Is Home
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, online church is a new door God has opened for this age — a response to a real pastoral need, not a reluctant compromise. Second, the Word became flesh, reminding us that real presence can never be replaced — John's declaration is the deepest theological foundation for how we think about the relationship between online and offline. Third, online is the bridge and offline is home — a healthy model of integration lets online be the starting point of connection, and offline be the destination of commitment. The question the church faces today is not "should we have an online presence" — it is "how do online and offline fulfill each other."

sections.heading: 3. A New Door: From the Printing Press and Radio to Online Gathering
sections.html:
Church history has repeatedly seen moments when "a new door opened." Gutenberg's printing press allowed the Bible, for the first time, to be printed in great quantity; the radio of the twentieth century carried the voice of the pulpit across city walls to the bedside of the sick. Today's online gathering is simply the next step on that very same trajectory — it responds to real and concrete pastoral needs: the wanderer living far from home who cannot regularly return to church; the elderly member whose mobility keeps them from going out; the seeker still watching from a distance, not yet ready to step through the church door. For these people, online gathering is not a second-rate substitute — it is a door God himself has opened, so that the gospel can reach people it otherwise could not reach.

But John's Gospel reminds us that this door cannot replace something else at the very core. John 1:14: "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth." In the original, "flesh" is σάρξ, referring to a real, concrete, flesh-and-blood body; "dwelt" is σκηνόω, its root related to "pitching a tent" — describing God himself "pitching his tent" to dwell among people, not observing from a distance, but drawing near in presence. This is one of the deepest mysteries at the very center of the Christian faith: God chose to reveal himself to humanity through a real body, a real presence. This gives the church a profound reminder: however far technology advances, real bodily presence always carries a power that can never be fully replaced — a hand held, a real embrace, weeping together, sharing a meal together — these are graces a screen finds difficult to fully reproduce. The psychologist Sherry Turkle, in her research on what she calls "alone together," observes that while digital connection can bring convenience and the illusion of companionship, it often stays at a shallow level, unable to replace the real intimacy that requires vulnerability and eye contact. Acts 2 records that the believers of the early church "day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes" — that daily, real, face-to-face fellowship is the original shape of κοινωνία (koinōnia, communal fellowship).

The original word behind "encouraging one another" is παρακαλέω (parakaleō), which literally means "to come alongside" — an active action of drawing near and staying close beside someone, not a distant blessing or a "like" tapped from far away. This is precisely the deepest calling of a healthy online-offline integration model: whether a person walks in through a screen or through the church's front door, the church must actively "come alongside" them, rather than passively waiting for them to walk in on their own. One pastor once described the change in his own church this way: "We used to only care whether the camera picture was clear. Later we understood that what actually matters is whether anyone is willing to walk over to the person on the other side of that screen." That reminder is worth every church building an online ministry pondering again and again.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Online Is Not the Destination, It Is the Bridge Home
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because convenience and commitment are separated by a single line, and the key is the self.

Using online gathering out of self easily lets a person hide behind the screen, enjoying the feeling of "participating" while never being willing to step into a real relationship — never needing to be seen in their weakness, never needing to be asked for commitment, never needing to face the vulnerability that comes with eye contact. Over time, this kind of "participation" lets a person believe they are already part of the church, when in reality they have remained standing outside the door the whole time. The healthy principle is: online is the bridge, offline is home — a bridge exists so that people can walk toward home, not so that people can stay on the bridge forever.

Words that must never be said: "Watching online is enough for me, I don't need to join an in-person group as well." "It counts as attending either way, so it doesn't matter if I show up late or leave early." "I'm just looking for now — I don't need anyone to know I'm here." A truly healthy model of integration actively invites every online member to walk toward a real, face-to-face relationship.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "The church treats online gathering as a reluctant, second-rate option, secretly believing 'only those who are truly committed come in person,' leaving online members feeling like second-class members who can never be fully accepted." Online gathering is a door God has opened — not a second-rate compromise.

The second question: "The church has a large number of long-term 'invisible members' who only ever watch online, and no one has ever actively reached out to them — the pastoral team cannot even name them." Know every member by name, no matter which door they came in through.

The third question: "The church pours all its resources into improving its livestream technology, but overlooks that what actually moves an online member toward offline commitment is people actively inviting and accompanying them — not better camera equipment." Technology can draw people to the door; what actually keeps them is a real relationship.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "online is second-rate" for "online is a door God has opened." Responding to the real needs of those who live far away, who are less mobile, or who are still watching from a distance is God's mercy, not a reluctant compromise.

The second correction: exchange "online is enough" for "online is the bridge, offline is home." A bridge exists so that people can walk toward home; a healthy church actively invites every online member to walk toward real commitment.

The third correction: exchange "unable to name them" for "actively reaching out by name." A self-emptied pastoral team is willing to spend the effort to know and reach out to every single person who comes in through a screen, one by one.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Door
sections.html:
Facing the choice between online and offline, different people carry completely different reactions in their hearts. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Loves to boast about the church's livestream numbers and reach, treating the scale of online gathering as proof of spiritual achievement — like David, who after counting the people, was struck with remorse in his heart: "I have sinned greatly in what I have done." (2 Samuel 24:10) The proud heart needs to be reminded: numbers have never been what God weighs most — faithfulness is.

The Fearful Heart

Afraid of being seen, afraid of being judged, afraid of the cost of stepping into a real relationship, and so would rather hide behind the screen for a long time — like the disciples that Easter night, "the doors being locked... for fear of the Jews." (John 20:19) Yet Jesus came and stood among them, walking through the locked door himself, and said, "Peace be with you." He came in person to that very door that was shut.

The Ashamed Heart

Because of past failure or a sense of owing something, feels unworthy to walk into a physical church community, and can only watch from far away on the other side of a screen — like the prodigal son's confession within himself: "I am no longer worthy to be called your son." (Luke 15:19) Yet his father saw him while he was still a long way off, and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.

The Wounded Heart

Has been hurt before within a real community, and now would rather keep a distance, participating only from far away through a screen, unwilling to risk drawing near again — like Elijah's lonely lament in the wilderness: "I, even I only, am left." (1 Kings 19:10) Yet God did not abandon him — he came himself to the very wilderness where Elijah was, and gently asked him, "What are you doing here?"

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A young man had, for years, secretly watched the church's livestream late at night, never commenting, never revealing who he was, until a staff member noticed the repeated anonymous viewing pattern and reached out with a private message. The two gradually built a real conversation. Six months later, this young man stepped through the church's front door for the very first time and said, "I had been waiting a long time for that greeting."

The second. An elderly member with limited mobility had for years been able to attend Sunday worship only online. The pastor deliberately arranged for small group members to visit him regularly at home, truly connecting his online and offline experience of church. The elder said, "The screen lets me hear the message; your visits let me truly feel I am still part of this family."

The third. A church that had once poured most of its budget into livestream equipment found its congregation's growth stalled regardless. It later adjusted its strategy, forming a dedicated team to actively reach out to every visitor who had watched online for more than a month. Within six months, noticeably more new faces appeared at in-person gatherings. The pastor said, "It turns out technology only sets the stage — what actually brings people in is one warm phone call."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: identify one member or friend you know who has long participated only online, and actively send them a message of greeting, inviting them to one day join in a real gathering.

I declare: I will treat online gathering as a door God has opened, not a second-rate compromise.

I declare: I will actively invite every person who comes in through a screen to walk toward a real, face-to-face commitment.

I declare: I will know every member by name, no matter which door they came into the church through.

I declare: let Jesus be King — he became flesh and dwelt among us, and I too am willing to be truly present with others; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may we all become a church that both makes good use of the door of online gathering and cherishes real, offline presence. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations move downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind, the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart, and the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — without reaching it, this lesson stays at the level of an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority, cover at least this question in each phase if time is short; ★★ = secondary priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked (Required) must not be skipped and may be completed at home.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as an Idea (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ The original word for "meet together," ἐπισυναγωγή, carries the sense of being actively, deliberately gathered, and the author specifically warns against making it a "habit" to neglect meeting. What does this prompt you to understand about how absence gradually becomes a habit?

2. ★★ John's Gospel says "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" — God chose to reveal himself to humanity through a real body. What does this prompt you to understand about "real presence can never be replaced"?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "Online is the bridge, offline is home; a bridge exists so that people can walk toward home, not so that people can stay on the bridge forever." In your own words, explain what this sentence means.

4. ★★ Sherry Turkle's research shows that digital connection often stays at a shallow level, unable to replace the real intimacy that requires vulnerability and eye contact. What does this prompt you to understand about the limits of online relationship?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it well." If someone speaks in fragments, help them organize their thought — don't finish it for them.

Second Transformation | Digesting It into Life (about 35 minutes · the core of this lesson)

Purpose: through Seeing, Hearing, Thinking, Speaking, and Acting, digest the idea into life.

[See] See Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — Proud (loves to boast about the church's livestream numbers and reach, treating scale as proof of spiritual achievement), Fearful (afraid of being seen or judged, would rather hide behind the screen), Ashamed (feels unworthy to walk into a physical community because of past failure, can only watch from far away), Wounded (once hurt within a real community, now keeps a distance). Which are you most like? What experience made you this way?

[Hear] Hear God Speak

6. ★★ God has one sentence for each of these four hearts. Find the verse that matches you, read it aloud, then tell the group: where does this sentence touch you?

[Think] Think Through the Obstacle

7. ★★ Is there someone around you who has long participated only online but has never truly been cared for? What has kept you from reaching out to them?

[Speak] Say It Out Loud

8. ★ Finish this sentence in one line: "This lesson tore down which old idea I had about 'online gathering'?" If your answer is "none," say that honestly too — that itself is an important discovery.

[Act] Take a Step

9. ★★ This week, which member or friend who has long participated only online will you actively reach out to? Name the specific way you will do it.

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for wounded-type and ashamed-type members, particularly those who have been hurt in a real community or who feel unworthy because of past failure. If someone weeps, pause the discussion and sit with them first — don't rush to give answers. If deeper trauma surfaces, follow up individually after the meeting and help arrange a referral.

Third Transformation | Transforming It into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily practice.

10. ★★ "Online is the bridge, offline is home." In your own family this week, is there a digital conversation that could actually become a real, face-to-face one?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about in your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "Know every member by name, no matter which door they came in through." How many members who participate only online can you actually name?

13. ★★★ A ten-minute daily discipline: this week, spend ten minutes each day praying for someone who participates only online, and write down their name — name what time you will practice this.

14. ★★ The 920 discipline: identify your own "2" (spiritual companion); this week visit or reach out together to one online member. Say their name out loud right now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, tell this lesson to someone outside the group in three sentences — Do not neglect to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encourage one another; the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth; online is the bridge, offline is home. Write down right now who you will tell it to.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, tell each other two things: the online member you will reach out to this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to make us a church that is both a bridge that makes good use of technology and a community that cherishes real presence.

ch43.title: Witnesses to the End of the Earth — The Challenges and Opportunities of Digital Evangelism
ch43.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. This is the third lesson of Part 9. In the last two lessons we reflected on technology as a tool for ministry and how online and offline can be integrated; today we step into a much wider picture — how the frontier of evangelism has, again and again, been reopened by technology. The promise of Acts 1:8, two thousand years later, is now being fulfilled inside our phones, in a way the disciples of that day could never have imagined.

Acts 1:8: "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth."

sections.heading: 1. A Circle That Keeps Expanding Outward from Jerusalem
sections.html: The last words Jesus spoke to his disciples before his ascension sketch out a map that keeps expanding outward: from Jerusalem, to all Judea, to Samaria, to the end of the earth. In that day, "the end of the earth" was, for the disciples, an almost unimaginably distant concept — walking, riding a donkey, sailing a ship, a person could spend a lifetime and never cross more than a few nations. Today, "the end of the earth" carries a completely different weight for the first time: a phone and a network connection can, in theory, carry a word of testimony to any corner of the globe within seconds. The vision God gave the church has never changed — only the time it takes to reach the end of the earth has.

sections.heading: 2. Every Believer Is a Witness, Information Overload Is a New Challenge, and the Focus Remains on Jesus, Not the Traffic
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, every believer is a "witness" — the original word μάρτυς does not mean only full-time ministers can testify; it means every person who bears witness to Christ through their own life and words. Second, information overload is the new thorn of this age — Paul reminds us to walk carefully, because the days are evil. Third, the focus always remains on Jesus, not on the traffic — the true fruit is that God causes the growth, not our algorithm strategy. As we enter the terrain of digital evangelism, we must see both the opportunity and honestly face the challenge.

sections.heading: 3. Seed Among Thorns, the Areopagus in Athens, and Keeping the Focus on Jesus
sections.html:
The original word for "witness," μάρτυς (martys), is the very root that later became the word "martyr" — its original meaning was a person willing to testify to what he believed with his own life, not merely someone relaying information. This reminds us that the core of digital evangelism does not lie in how sensational or clickable the content is, but in whether the person sharing it is truly living out the life they are testifying to. In Matthew 13's parable of the sower, the Lord Jesus specifically mentions that some seed fell among thorns, "and the thorns grew up and choked them"; he explains that the thorns represent the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches. The American scholar Herbert Simon offered the insight of the "attention economy": a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention — when a person is bombarded by endless information, notifications, and headlines, they find it increasingly difficult to truly digest and deeply consider any message at all, including the gospel message. Ephesians 4:14 warns against being "tossed to and fro... by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes" — the original scheming and craftiness, put in today's terms, corresponds directly to algorithmic manipulation, fake news, and sensational headlines competing for clicks.

Acts 17 records Paul standing at the Areopagus in Athens, facing a city full of idols and Greek intellectuals who knew nothing of the gospel. He did not directly rebuke their ignorance — he first quoted the altar "to the unknown god" they were familiar with, and the words of their own poets, as an entry point, and only then turned the conversation toward the true God. This is an extremely important model: Paul was willing to first understand the other person's situation and language before he could effectively proclaim the truth. In 1 Corinthians 9, Paul says: "To the weak I became weak... I have become all things to all people." This gives the church today an extremely important reminder for using new media to evangelize: adjusting the form of expression and choosing a suitable platform does not mean compromising the content of the gospel — new media is a tool, not the main character; the focus is always on Jesus, never on the traffic. Philippians 2's teaching on "self-emptying" is precisely the theological root of the 321 vision's "selflessness," reminding every person who proclaims the gospel online to stay alert, lest digital evangelism quietly become a stage for building a personal brand and a personal image. Galatians 6:14 and John 12:32 point to the very same focus: "And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself." In 1 Corinthians 3, Paul says: "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth." Let people be people, and let God be God — we sow and water faithfully, and entrust the final fruit to the God who gives the growth.

The media available to the church and to believers today are far richer than in Paul's time — text, images, short video, livestreaming; every format can carry the gospel, and every format can also be twisted into a tool for pursuing attention alone. The key to discernment has never been the medium itself, but whether the heart using that medium still simply and purely longs for more people to know the Lord who is worthy of worship.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — When Testimony Becomes Performance, and the Gospel Becomes Traffic
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because testimony and performance are separated by a single line, and the key is the self.

Building digital evangelism out of self easily and gradually shifts the focus from "testifying to Christ" to quietly "building myself" — sharing a faith testimony while secretly hoping to be seen by more people, to be praised, even adjusting the way a testimony is told, for the sake of traffic, to make oneself seem more charismatic, more worth following. Over time, this kind of ministry blurs the line between whether a person is testifying to Christ, or using Christ to testify to themselves.

Words that must never be said: "This testimony's numbers aren't good enough, I need a more sensational way to tell it." "That other account has more influence than mine, I must be doing something wrong." "As long as the traffic is high enough, whether the gospel content is accurate doesn't really matter." A truly healthy view of digital witness knows clearly: I plant, I water, but it is God — not my content strategy — who gives the growth.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "Believers treat the follower count and engagement rate of their personal social media as proof of their own spiritual influence, unconsciously letting the content of their testimony increasingly cater to what the algorithm favors rather than remain faithful to the truth." The focus is on Jesus, not on the traffic.

The second question: "The church is accustomed to proclaiming the gospel in one single, fixed way, and has never seriously considered that people of different ages and situations need different entry points and different language." Paul in Athens was willing to first understand the other person's situation before proclaiming the truth.

The third question: "Facing information online where truth and falsehood are hard to tell apart, believers often forward things without verifying them, even using unconfirmed content to 'defend the faith,' which instead damages the church's credibility as a witness." Walk carefully, and do not fall into the deception of cunning schemes.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "building a personal brand" for "faithfully being a witness to Christ." Using new media without self means keeping the focus on Jesus, not on oneself.

The second correction: exchange "one single, fixed way of proclaiming" for "the wisdom of meeting people where they are." Follow Paul's wisdom in Athens, willing to understand the other person's situation and language before proclaiming the truth.

The third correction: exchange "forwarding without verifying" for "verifying carefully before sharing." Truthfulness is the most basic foundation of any testimony — never sacrifice accuracy for the sake of attention.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Testimony
sections.html:
Facing the act of bearing witness online, different people carry completely different reactions in their hearts. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Loves to publicly display its own spiritual achievements and zeal for ministry before others, secretly hoping to be seen and praised — like what the Lord Jesus himself warned against: "Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them." (Matthew 6:1) The proud heart needs to be reminded: a true testimony does not need an audience's applause.

The Fearful Heart

Afraid that publicly declaring their faith online will bring judgment, mockery, or labeling, and so always chooses silence. Yet Jesus said to his disciples: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell." (Matthew 10:28) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: what truly deserves reverence has never been the judgment of a stranger on the other side of the screen.

The Ashamed Heart

Because of past failure or weakness, feels unworthy to testify for Christ, deeply afraid that others will dig up the past, and so dares not openly declare their faith — like Paul's reminder to Timothy: "Do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord." (2 Timothy 1:8) God can use a witness who honestly admits weakness far more than one who performs perfection.

The Wounded Heart

Has once suffered sharp criticism, mockery, or even personal attacks online for openly declaring their faith, and feels deeply wounded, now filled with fear at the thought of sharing their faith again — like Jeremiah's lament: "The word of the LORD has become for me a reproach and derision all day long." (Jeremiah 20:8) Yet God still chose this very wounded prophet, and continued speaking his word through him.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A young person shared, over a long period, his own process of overcoming internet addiction on social media, at first simply to keep a record for himself. He unexpectedly received many private messages from strangers saying they were struggling with the very same thing. He said, "I never set out to build any kind of following — I was just being honest, and God used it to reach people I never imagined."

The second. A minister had long used the exact same approach to evangelize people of every age, with limited results. He later learned from Paul's wisdom in Athens and adjusted his entry point for younger audiences, starting from life situations they were familiar with before guiding the conversation toward the core of the gospel — the response noticeably improved. He said, "The content wasn't compromised — I simply became willing, at last, to first understand their language."

The third. A believer once publicly forwarded an emotionally charged message without verifying it, and was later shown that the content was inaccurate, leaving them deeply embarrassed and remorseful. Since then, they have practiced verifying the source before sharing anything, and publicly apologized to friends and corrected the record. They said, "I discovered that being careful is also a responsible way of loving the gospel."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: this week, before sharing any piece of information, spend one minute verifying its source; and honestly write down one testimony of your own — not for traffic, only for testifying to Christ.

I declare: I will be a true witness to Christ, not a performer building a personal brand.

I declare: I will verify carefully, never sacrificing accuracy for attention, and be a witness who discerns and builds people up.

I declare: I plant, I water, but it is God, not my content strategy, who gives the growth.

I declare: let Jesus be King — everything I share online keeps its focus on Jesus, not on the traffic; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may we all become faithful witnesses, in Jerusalem, in all Judea, in Samaria, to the end of the earth, until the day the Lord returns. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations move downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind, the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart, and the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — without reaching it, this lesson stays at the level of an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority, cover at least this question in each phase if time is short; ★★ = secondary priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked (Required) must not be skipped and may be completed at home.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as an Idea (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ The original word for "witness," μάρτυς, is the root that later became "martyr," meaning a person willing to testify to what he believes with his own life. What does this prompt you to understand about "a testimony is more than relaying information"?

2. ★★ Simon proposed that "a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention." What does this prompt you to understand about the new kind of "thorns" facing evangelism today?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "New media is a tool, not the main character; the focus is always on Jesus, never on the traffic." In your own words, explain what this sentence means.

4. ★★ Paul at the Areopagus in Athens first quoted words familiar to his audience as an entry point, and only then proclaimed the truth. What does this prompt you to understand about "adjusting the form is not the same as compromising the content"?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it well." If someone speaks in fragments, help them organize their thought — don't finish it for them.

Second Transformation | Digesting It into Life (about 35 minutes · the core of this lesson)

Purpose: through Seeing, Hearing, Thinking, Speaking, and Acting, digest the idea into life.

[See] See Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — Proud (loves to publicly display spiritual achievement, secretly hoping to be seen and praised), Fearful (afraid that declaring faith online will bring judgment and mockery, so chooses silence), Ashamed (feels unworthy to testify for Christ because of past failure), Wounded (once suffered sharp criticism online for declaring their faith, deeply wounded). Which are you most like? What experience made you this way?

[Hear] Hear God Speak

6. ★★ God has one sentence for each of these four hearts. Find the verse that matches you, read it aloud, then tell the group: where does this sentence touch you?

[Think] Think Through the Obstacle

7. ★★ Have you ever chosen silence online, afraid of judgment, instead of declaring your faith? What made you hold back at that moment?

[Speak] Say It Out Loud

8. ★ Finish this sentence in one line: "This lesson tore down which old idea I had about 'digital evangelism'?" If your answer is "none," say that honestly too — that itself is an important discovery.

[Act] Take a Step

9. ★★ This week, which real, personal testimony of faith will you try to share? Name the specific content or the person you have in mind.

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for wounded-type and fearful-type members, particularly those who have been attacked online for declaring their faith publicly. If someone weeps, pause the discussion and sit with them first — don't rush to give answers. If deeper trauma surfaces, follow up individually after the meeting and help arrange a referral.

Third Transformation | Transforming It into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily practice.

10. ★★ "The content wasn't compromised — I simply became willing to first understand their language." In your own family, this week, how could you share one sentence of faith in language your family members would actually understand?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about in your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "Verify carefully, never sacrificing accuracy for attention." This week, how can you remind yourself to verify a source before sharing anything?

13. ★★★ A ten-minute daily discipline: this week, spend ten minutes each day praying for someone you want to reach but haven't yet — name their situation and what time you will practice this.

14. ★★ The 920 discipline: identify your own "2" (spiritual companion); this week share with each other and check the testimony content you each plan to tell. Say their name out loud right now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, tell this lesson to someone outside the group in three sentences — You will receive power, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth; do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord; I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. Write down right now who you will tell it to.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, tell each other two things: the testimony content you will share this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to make us all faithful witnesses, with the focus always on Jesus, never on the traffic.

ch44.title: Faithful in the Smallest Digital Detail — Digital Management Skills for the Church Leader
ch44.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. This is the fourth lesson of Part 9. In the first three lessons we reflected on how technology can advance ministry, integrate online and offline, and expand the frontier of evangelism; today we step into the most real, daily reality on the desk of every pastor, elder, and small group leader — administration. Membership lists, care records, meeting notices — this tedious but unavoidable work has, for most churches today, moved onto phones and into the cloud. Digital tools are a rich gift this age has given the church, and also a tightrope that must be walked carefully.

Luke 16:10: "One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much."

sections.heading: 1. The Early Church's First Administrative Crisis
sections.html: Acts records that as the number of disciples in Jerusalem multiplied explosively, the burden of administration exploded right along with it — the Hellenist widows "were being neglected in the daily distribution." This was no small problem — those being neglected were the most vulnerable people in the church. The twelve apostles did not brush the problem aside, nor did they simply grit their teeth and carry the entire administrative burden themselves — they honestly admitted: "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables," and so they chose seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, to take specific charge of this work. Administrative neglect most often first wounds the people in a church who are most easily overlooked; if a church today lacks proper management, the very first people to be let down will, again, be the families who need care most and are most easily missed.

sections.heading: 2. Administrative Effectiveness Is a Grace, Knowing Cannot Be Replaced by Data, and the Tool Is a Means, Not the Master
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, digital tools help the effectiveness of shepherding and administration — a membership database, a care-tracking system, can free leaders from tedious administration to focus more fully on spiritual shepherding. Second, the convenience of data cannot replace real care — a fully completed information sheet does not equal truly knowing a person's heart. Third, use tools without self, to serve people, rather than being bound by tools — a tool is a means for serving people; if a leader becomes hostage to a system and its notifications, they lose the very purpose of ministry. No church today can fully avoid digitization — the question has never been whether to use technology, but how to use it faithfully.

sections.heading: 3. Devoted to Prayer and the Ministry of the Word, the Good Shepherd Who Knows by Name, and Newport's Deep Work
sections.html:
The word "devote" in the original Greek is προσκαρτερέω, meaning to commit steadily and wholeheartedly, with full, undivided attention, to one thing. When the apostles chose others to manage the distribution of food, they were not casually handing off administration as second-rate work — they understood deeply that only by getting administration properly organized and entrusted to the right people could prayer and the ministry of the word receive the kind of full, undivided commitment they truly needed. The passage immediately continues: "And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem." Many churches today that use a membership database, a care-tracking system, or a cloud collaboration tool are living out precisely the wisdom of this passage — handing off what is tedious but necessary to the right systems and the right people, so pastors can devote themselves fully to prayer, the ministry of the word, and real shepherding. One senior pastor shared that he used to spend nearly six hours a week manually organizing visitation records, often delaying care for families that truly needed it because of misremembered or missed entries; after switching to a shared care-tracking system, those six hours were compressed to under one hour, and the time saved went toward visiting two or three more families.

But John 10 reminds us that no tool can replace the good shepherd himself. The Lord Jesus said: "I know my own and my own know me." The original word for "know" is γινώσκω, referring not merely to information-level "knowledge that this person exists," but to an experiential, relational knowing, carried by intimacy and commitment. A complete membership record can note a person's name, birthday, and family situation, but it can never automatically produce the kind of knowing that understands why he couldn't sleep last night. A database is a good shepherd's tool, but it can never replace the good shepherd himself. The American scholar Cal Newport, in his theory of "deep work," points out that truly deep-focus ministry requires an uninterrupted, sustained stretch of attention; yet attention that is continually fragmented by notifications is severely weakened in its ability to enter that deep state — over time, a person may stay busy all day and yet remain stuck at a shallow, fragmented level. Mark's Gospel records that right after the disciples returned from a mission trip, the crowds were so great they "had no leisure even to eat," yet Jesus invited them: "Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while" — even the Lord who became flesh personally set a boundary of retreat and rest for his disciples.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Every Box on the Form Was Checked, but the Heart Never Truly Showed Up
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because efficiency and faithfulness are separated by a single line, and the key is the self.

One small group leader once shared that he carefully recorded every visit to every group member in an app, marking a green checkmark each time one was completed. One day, a member finally worked up the courage to confide a long-buried marital struggle, and only then did he realize that although his visitation records were perfectly tidy, that visit itself had been little more than a mechanical greeting before he hurried off to the next task. Every box on the form had been checked, but the heart truly willing to stop and listen all the way through had never actually shown up.

Words that must never be said: "My visitation records are all checked off, so I've fulfilled my duty of care." "The system will remind me who needs care, I don't need to remember myself." "How fast I reply to messages is proof of how faithful my ministry is." Truly healthy digital management is letting the tool help us find that one person faster, and then genuinely, wholeheartedly staying with them.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "Leaders treat the numbers of visits logged and messages marked as read as the sole proof of whether they've been faithful in shepherding, and rarely honestly ask themselves how many of those interactions truly had a heart present in the other person's story." An efficiency metric can record how many times something happened, but it cannot record whether the heart was truly present.

The second question: "Leaders are led around twenty-four hours a day by notifications — sermon preparation and prayer get interrupted before ten minutes pass — the days feel busy and exhausting, yet nothing ever feels truly accomplished." If every notification is allowed to interrupt at any moment, the end result may be an empty shell of efficiency, having lost the very depth of presence that shepherding needs most.

The third question: "The church rushes to introduce every kind of digital system, but never trains the senior co-workers unfamiliar with technology, who then gradually withdraw from ministry because they cannot keep up, needlessly losing precious pastoral experience." Introducing tools should help more people serve together, not filter out those who are willing but not technically skilled.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "checking the box means duty fulfilled" for "even after checking the box, still truly stay." An efficiency metric can record the number of visits made, but it cannot record whether the heart was truly present.

The second correction: exchange "always on call to respond" for "deliberately setting aside a period of deep focus." Follow the example of Jesus, who actively withdrew to pray in a solitary place, so that he could return to a busy ministry with a restored heart.

The third correction: exchange "technology filtering out co-workers" for "technology accompanying co-workers in learning together." Let every person willing to serve, whether skilled with technology or not, be accompanied and equipped together.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Administration
sections.html:
Facing digital administrative management, different people carry completely different reactions in their hearts. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Loves to boast about the efficient system it built with its own hands, secretly treating the system's success as its own glory — like Nebuchadnezzar's boast: "Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty?" (Daniel 4:30) The proud heart needs to be reminded: even the finest system is only a channel for the wisdom God gives — never one's own glory.

The Fearful Heart

Feels the administrative burden is too heavy to carry alone, yet is afraid to ask for help, fearing it will look incapable — like what Moses' father-in-law Jethro observed: "You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone." (Exodus 18:18) God is glad to provide co-workers to share the burden — he never intends for anyone to grit their teeth and carry it alone.

The Ashamed Heart

Because of a past administrative mistake or falling behind on how a system works, feels deeply ashamed and dares not take on related ministry again — like the tax collector's prayer: "God, be merciful to me, a sinner!" (Luke 18:13) Yet God receives a heart that humbly admits its weakness far more than an appearance of perfection.

The Wounded Heart

Has felt like nothing more than a piece of recorded data inside a vast administrative system, with no one truly remembering the effort given — like Job's lament: "He has put my brothers far from me... my intimate friends have forgotten me." (Job 19:13–14) Yet God knows every faithful servant by name — not one act of labor is ever forgotten by him.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A pastor once had his phone buzzing with notifications all day long, his sermon preparation and prayer interrupted before even ten minutes had passed. He later practiced turning off non-urgent notifications, spending the first part of each morning in uninterrupted prayer and Scripture reading before checking any messages, and silencing and putting away his phone entirely during visits and counseling. He said, "I can finally hear someone all the way through their story now, without rushing to check my phone."

The second. A small group leader once treated every "checkmark" in the visitation app as proof that shepherding was complete, until one member's confession made him realize his heart had not truly been present. He changed his approach: after every visit, instead of rushing to check the box, he now sits quietly for a few minutes and reflects on what the conversation truly touched. He said, "The checkmark stopped mattering — what matters is whether I truly heard him."

The third. An older deacon, long unfamiliar with the church's newly introduced cloud system, felt increasingly left behind and nearly withdrew from ministry. A younger co-worker then took the initiative to invite him to learn together, and the two of them shared the work of care records — the elder's shepherding experience and the younger person's technical skill complementing one another. He said, "It turns out I didn't have to figure it all out alone, and I didn't need to feel ashamed and withdraw just because I didn't understand something."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: take stock of every digital tool you currently use, and honestly ask which ones truly help shepherding, and which ones are only consuming your attention; and set aside a fixed period of silence for yourself, and keep it faithfully for one week.

I declare: I will be faithful even in the smallest digital details, not letting efficiency replace a truly present heart.

I declare: I will deliberately set aside periods of undistracted focus, and return to shepherding with a restored heart.

I declare: I will accompany every co-worker willing to serve but not skilled with technology, and never let a tool filter out a faithful person.

I declare: let Jesus be King — my identity and worth are not measured by an empty notification bar, but by being the servant he has entrusted to faithfully shepherd his flock; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may we all become faithful stewards who make good use of technology without being ruled by it. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Purpose: through discussion, drive the point of this lesson into a clear idea.
