ch45.title: All Things Are Lawful, but Not All Things Build Up — The Ethical Challenges Technology Brings
ch45.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. This is the final lesson of Part 9, "Technology and Church Modernization." We have walked together through advancing ministry, integrating online and offline, expanding the frontier of evangelism, and faithfulness in a leader's administration; today we face the deepest, and most easily overlooked, question of this whole series — what ethical challenges has technology actually brought us? Artificial intelligence can write text indistinguishable from the real thing; deepfake technology can replicate a person's voice and face; social media algorithms fight day and night for our attention. Paul's reminder, two thousand years later, remains the sharpest standard of judgment we have.

1 Corinthians 10:23: "'All things are lawful,' but not all things are helpful. 'All things are lawful,' but not all things build up."

sections.heading: 1. An Ancient Commandment Becomes the Earliest Line of Defense Against a Deepfake Age
sections.html: Exodus 20:16, the ninth of the Ten Commandments: "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor." God, at Mount Sinai, entered into covenant with a people who had just been freed from slavery in Egypt — this newborn community had no king, and what held the community together at its most basic level was trust in one another. False witness in ancient times happened at the city gate, in the presence of judgment; today's false witness happens inside a video, a recording, a message. Deepfake technology can replicate a person's face and voice, making the figure on the screen say things they never said; scam rings use AI to replicate a family member's voice, weeping and begging an elderly relative to wire money. The commandment has not become outdated — only the tool of bearing false witness has changed, from a mouth to an entire algorithm. John 8:44 records the Lord Jesus pointing out that the root of falsehood is not merely a technical problem, but a spiritual one: "When he lies, he speaks out of his own character, for he is a liar and the father of lies." AI and deepfake technology have no moral will of their own — they are tools being used; when a person chooses to use these tools to fabricate a lie, the one they are imitating is precisely the father of lies. 1 John 4:1 reminds us: "Test the spirits to see whether they are from God." Verifying sources, taking a moment before sharing, honestly disclosing the use of AI assistance in any content, and teaching the next generation to discern deepfake content — this wisdom of discernment is equipment the church of this generation cannot afford to be without.

sections.heading: 2. AI and Data Ethics, the Competition for Attention, and Establishing Boundaries of Discernment
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, the challenge of AI and data ethics — artificial intelligence, deepfake technology, and the collection and use of personal data bring unprecedented difficulties around authenticity and privacy. Second, the tension between technology addiction and spiritual life — phones and social media continually compete for our attention, quietly eroding the space for prayer, Scripture reading, and devotion. Third, how the church can establish ethical boundaries for using technology — not resisting or banning technology, but testing everything, keeping only what builds up people, builds up community, and glorifies God. Today we must ask a deeper question: I am able to do this — but should I?

sections.heading: 3. It Was Not Only Martha Who Was Anxious and Troubled, Intermittent Reward, and Whether We Are Building or Tearing Down
sections.html:
Luke 10 records that Martha was distracted with much serving, her heart anxious and troubled, and Jesus gently said: "Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her." In the original, "anxious and troubled" is two words, one describing a heart pulled apart by many things, the other describing inner turmoil and unrest; and the good portion Mary chose is singular and undivided. Today, the "many things" have taken on a new name — notifications: unread message dots, feed updates, the next episode that autoplays, each one competing for our limited attention. Studies show that the average user unlocks their phone more than eighty times a day, and the notification mechanisms of many apps directly borrow the principle of intermittent variable reward — not knowing whether the next message will be interesting makes it harder to stop checking than if every check were rewarded. This mechanism is deliberately designed and repeatedly tested and optimized for the single purpose of holding on to more and more of our time. Attention is the currency of love; whoever receives the most of our attention takes the throne of our heart.

Corinth was, in its day, the most prosperous and diverse commercial city, and Paul did not simply hand the church a list of prohibitions — he gave a much deeper standard: not only asking what is lawful, but asking, does this benefit people? Does it build them up? In the original, "helpful" is συμφέρει (sympherei), meaning advantageous, bringing good; "build up" is οἰκοδομεῖ (oikodomei), whose root is precisely "house" — its original meaning is to construct a building. Using this image, we can reframe the question: is the way I use a piece of technology building something up in my life, or is it quietly tearing something down — tearing down my ability to focus, tearing down my real connection with God and with people? The American media theorist Neil Postman proposed the theory of technopoly — a culture can move from a tool-using culture to a technopoly, a stage in which technology itself is treated as the supreme value and standard, and begins to define what is real and what matters, while people often remain completely unaware of it happening. This is precisely the modern, technology-clothed shape of the very "self" that the 321 vision's "selflessness" seeks to overcome.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Without Noticing, Letting the Phone Take the Throne That Belongs Only to Christ
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because using and being used are separated by a single line, and the key is the self.

Using technology out of self, at its core, runs on the logic of "can this satisfy me right now" — instant information, instant entertainment, the instant thrill of being seen. Gradually, technology shifts from being a tool to becoming the center of life, without a person even noticing it happening. When a person unconsciously believes checking their phone is more urgent than reading Scripture, and scrolling a feed feels more real than praying, technology has already taken, in that person's life, the very throne that belongs only to God.

Words that must never be said: "Everyone else is sharing this anyway, it doesn't matter whether it's actually true." "It's just entertainment, it doesn't count as wasted time." "I used AI to help write this, I don't need to say so." A truly healthy view of technology ethics knows that all things are lawful, but not all things build up, and not everything can be brought before God with the honest words, "this is for your glory."

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "Believers forward emotionally charged messages of unknown origin without verifying them, even using them to judge others, damaging the church's credibility as a witness." Test the spirits to see whether they are from God.

The second question: "Many believers honestly admit that the first thing they touch each day is not the Bible, but their phone — devotion has become something squeezed in only if there's time left over." The good portion Mary chose is not automatically preserved — it must be chosen freshly, deliberately, every single day.

The third question: "The church uses AI to help produce promotional materials or images, but does not honestly disclose it, letting the congregation mistakenly believe the content is entirely human-made, unintentionally damaging the church's integrity." Authenticity is a line the church cannot compromise on, no matter what technology it uses.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "accepting everything at face value" for "always testing it first." Verifying sources and taking a moment before sharing is equipment this generation's believers cannot afford to be without.

The second correction: exchange "reaching for the phone first" for "reaching for Scripture first." In the first ten minutes after waking, pray to God before picking up the phone, reclaiming the first place that rightfully belongs to him.

The third correction: exchange "all things are lawful" for "all things build up." Ask not only whether something is legal, but whether it is building something up in your life, and whether it is done for God's glory.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Discernment
sections.html:
Facing the ethical challenges of technology, different people carry completely different reactions in their hearts. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Becomes absorbed in cultivating a carefully curated image online, gradually mistaking that image for who they really are. Yet Proverbs reminds us: "Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD, and turn away from evil." (Proverbs 3:7) The proud heart needs to be reminded: the image on the screen has never been the same thing as who you truly are in God's eyes.

The Fearful Heart

Cannot resist checking their phone again and again, afraid of missing a message, afraid of being left out of the group, tightly gripped by that insecurity. Yet the prophet declares to the fearful of heart: "Say to those who have an anxious heart, 'Be strong; fear not!'" (Isaiah 35:4) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: that fear of being left behind should not be fed by a phone — it should be brought before God and laid down.

The Ashamed Heart

Deeply ashamed over technology addiction or having been deceived by false information, and chooses to cover it with more disguise and concealment, like Adam and Eve after they sinned: "And they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths." (Genesis 3:7) Yet God is willing to come himself to those who are hiding, to seek them and call out to them, not to condemn them.

The Wounded Heart

Has been deceived and hurt by fabricated messages or a false show of concern, and has lost trust in both people and technology, as Proverbs says: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy." (Proverbs 27:6) God can discern who a true friend is, and can heal a heart wounded by deception.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. An elderly member received a phone call in a voice strikingly like his grandson's, weeping and begging for an urgent wire transfer — fortunately, the family recognized in time that it was an AI-generated scam voice. Since then, the whole family has learned together to verify sources and set up a family password. He said, "It turns out even a voice can be fake — our family reminds each other of that now, more than ever."

The second. A believer told herself every night, "just five more minutes of scrolling," only to find an hour had passed and her prayer and Scripture reading time had been squeezed out again and again. She later began charging her phone outside her bedroom and using a real alarm clock instead. She said, "In that first ten minutes of morning, coming back to God, I realized how long it had been since I had truly been still."

The third. A church had used AI to help produce promotional graphics and text without actively disclosing it, until a member noticed and raised a question. The church then established a standard: any content produced with AI assistance would be honestly disclosed going forward. The pastor said, "Honest disclosure isn't a hassle — it's the most basic respect we owe our congregation."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration: Looking Back on Part Nine
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: this week, honestly track how many hours you spend on your phone each day, and honestly ask yourself how much of that time truly built up your life; and charge your phone outside your bedroom, giving the first ten minutes of each morning to prayer and Scripture reading.

Having come this far, the five lessons of Part 9, "Technology and Church Modernization," together form one complete lesson: how the church can use technology to advance its ministry — the wisdom of being filled with God's Spirit, where direction determines good or evil; building a model for integrating online and offline church — online is the bridge, offline is home; the challenges and opportunities of digital evangelism — the focus is on Jesus, not the traffic; digital management skills for the church leader — faithful even in the smallest digital detail; and today, the ethical challenges technology brings — all things are lawful, but not all things build up. These five lessons interlock to form a complete godly system for the church to serve faithfully in the age of technology. May our churches become communities that are neither left behind by the times, nor quietly defined and ruled by the very tools of this age.

I declare: I will always test the spirits, never accepting everything at face value, and never forward unverified information for the sake of attention.

I declare: I will reclaim the first ten minutes of every morning, praying to God before I pick up my phone.

I declare: all things are lawful, but I will choose only what builds up people, builds up community, and glorifies God.

I declare: let Jesus be King — I will not let any technology take the throne that belongs only to Christ; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may our churches become communities whose focus is on Jesus, defined by truth rather than by algorithms, until the day the Lord returns. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

ch46.title: As for Me and My House — Advancing a Ministry of Healthy Families
ch46.partTitle: Part 10 — Family Ministry and Marriage Counseling
ch46.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. Beginning with this lesson, we enter Part 10, "Family Ministry and Marriage Counseling" — five lessons reflecting on the church's most basic, yet most easily overlooked, object of ministry: the family. Because in the end, no matter how advanced the technology the church uses or how refined its administration, what it ultimately serves is still real, living people, and nearly every person comes from a family. Today, let us return to the most fundamental question: what place does the family hold in God's eyes?

Joshua 24:15: "But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."

sections.heading: 1. It Is Not Good for the Man to Be Alone: A Community Older Than the Church
sections.html: Genesis 1 records God's six days of creation, each one declared "very good"; but in chapter 2, the only "not good" statement in the entire creation narrative suddenly appears — "It is not good that the man should be alone." This does not mean Adam had done anything wrong — it is God himself pointing out that even a whole, well-made human being, made "very good," remains "not good" if left utterly alone. It is worth noting that all of this took place in Eden, thousands of years before the founding of Israel, before the Law of Moses, before the birth of the New Testament church. The family is the very first community God established in human history, older than any religious institution or organization. When the church's ministry forgets this order, it easily gets things backward.

sections.heading: 2. The Family Is the Foundation, the Church Equips, and the Home Connects to the Community
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, the family is the first community God established, and the starting point of all ministry. Second, the church's ministry should be built on the family as its foundation, not replace it — a healthy family nurtures a healthy church, and the church's role is to equip and support every family, not to take over every function a family is meant to fulfill. Third, how the church can concretely advance a ministry of healthy families — through family small groups, premarital counseling, parenting classes, and intergenerational activities, putting principle into the calendar. May God lead us to set our gaze once again on the dinner table of every family.

sections.heading: 3. Bowen's Family Systems, Self-Differentiation, and Joshua's Declaration
sections.html:
Genesis 2:24: "Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh." In the original, "hold fast" is dabaq, meaning to cling tightly; "become one flesh," basar echad, describes a real, concrete union of life. The American psychiatrist Murray Bowen proposed "family systems theory," pointing out that a family is not simply a collection of independent individuals gathered together, but an emotionally interconnected system — like a web laced with nerves, where pulling on any single thread sends a tremor through every other part. One member's anxiety is rarely an isolated event; it ripples through the whole family, and one member's change — especially an increase in "self-differentiation," the capacity to remain emotionally close to family while still maintaining a clear sense of self — can often move the entire family system toward greater health. This echoes Paul's image of the body in 1 Corinthians 12: if one member suffers, all the members suffer together. Many loving churches, seeing a child lacking some family function, eagerly step in to supply it, and over time the family loses the very opportunity and ability to exercise that function for itself. The truly healthy direction is not "the church does it, the family watches," but "the church equips, the family does it."

Joshua 24:15: in his later years, Joshua gathered the whole assembly at Shechem and gave them his final challenge. As a national leader, what he valued most, what he was most willing to pledge himself to, was not the achievements of his office, but the direction of his own family's worship: "But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." Today many believers serve wholeheartedly at church, yet lack that same patience and commitment at home. In Acts 16, when Paul and Silas were imprisoned at Philippi, the jailer asked, "What must I do to be saved?" and received this answer: "You will be saved, you and your household." In the original, "household" is oikos — once the gospel truly enters a person's life, it rarely stops with that one person; it ripples outward, touching the entire family system.

Decades of research in developmental psychology consistently show that the attachment relationship a person forms in early childhood with their primary caregiver deeply shapes how they build trust and face intimacy for the rest of their lives, an influence that often lasts a lifetime and can even pass across generations. These findings, in another vocabulary, simply confirm a truth Genesis declared long ago: the family is the deepest, earliest place where a life is shaped. Only when the roots are firm can the branches flourish — if the church truly hopes to build up healthy believers, it cannot bypass the family, the most fundamental starting point of all.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — When the Church Takes Over Everything a Parent Should Do
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because love and overstepping are separated by a single line, and the key is the self.

Church ministry done out of self can, in its enthusiasm, unconsciously overstep its bounds, taking over the diligent instruction that belongs to parents and doing it entirely on the church's behalf. Over time, the family becomes more dependent on the institution rather than more healthy. This kind of enthusiasm eventually leads parents to feel that their child's spiritual education is "being handled," freeing themselves to stay silent about faith at home.

Words that must never be said: "The Sunday school teacher teaches better than I do, so I don't need to say more at home." "The kids come to church every week anyway, so the spiritual education is the church's job now." "I'm too busy — family will have to wait until the ministry stabilizes." A truly healthy view of family ministry is the church equipping the family, so the family can return to the place it was always meant to stand.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "Parents send their children to church and assume the spiritual education is now handled, never mentioning God at home again." The church's one hour is meant to add to a parent's six days and six nights of teaching — never to replace it.

The second question: "The church becomes so enthusiastic that it excludes parents entirely from their child's spiritual growth, handling everything itself." One Sunday school class cannot replace a family.

The third question: "The church's family ministry stays at the level of holding a single event — lively for a day, everyone scatters the next, and the family's real underlying issues are never truly touched." A sustained relationship is worth more than a one-time event.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "the church does it, the family watches" for "the church equips, the family does it." Helping every family member grow in self-differentiation is how the whole family system truly moves toward health.

The second correction: exchange "scattered events" for "structured companionship." A regularly meeting family small group, systematic premarital counseling, and parenting classes designed by stage of life offer a sustained relationship, not merely a one-time piece of knowledge or an emotional moment.

The third correction: exchange "each family sweeps its own doorstep" for "connecting into a larger spiritual family." Husband and wife submit to one another in Christ, and family after family prays for and supports one another.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Home
sections.html:
Facing one's own family, different people carry completely different reactions in their hearts. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Treats one particular child in the family as the favorite, using favoritism to shape a hierarchy within the home, unknowingly planting the seeds of jealousy and division — like Jacob's favoritism toward Joseph: "Now Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his sons... But when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peacefully to him." (Genesis 37:3–4) The proud heart needs to be reminded: favoritism within a family has never once bought real unity.

The Fearful Heart

Because of fear for a child's safety or future, transforms that fear into excessive control and anxious watchfulness — like Moses' mother: "And when she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months... she took for him a basket made of bulrushes and daubed it with bitumen and pitch. She put the child in it and placed it among the reeds by the river bank." (Exodus 2:2–3) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: God can, in the very depths of our deepest fear, watch over and prepare a way of escape himself.

The Ashamed Heart

Because of a major loss or lack the family has once experienced, feels the family is not as good as others, carrying deep shame and bitterness — like Naomi's lament: "Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me... the LORD has brought me back empty." (Ruth 1:20–21) Yet God, in what looked like an empty family, prepared an unexpected restoration and lineage himself.

The Wounded Heart

Carries deep scars from deception or mistreatment within the family, letting that wound shape every family relationship that comes after — like Esau's plea to his father: "Have you but one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, O my father." And Esau lifted up his voice and wept. (Genesis 27:38) God can heal a wound passed down through generations of a family, and grant a fresh opportunity for reconciliation.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A couple discovered they had, without realizing it, always praised their older son while overlooking their younger son's efforts, and the younger son gradually grew silent and withdrawn. After honestly facing this, they began deliberately creating moments in which each child was seen individually. The younger son gradually became willing to share his heart again. The mother said, "I finally understood that favoritism doesn't have to be malicious to still wound someone."

The second. A mother, after her child was diagnosed with special needs, lived for a long time in anxiety and overprotection, until a sister from the church prayed with her and helped her learn to loosen her grip and entrust the child to God. She said, "I can finally open my fist and truly place my child in God's hands, not just my own."

The third. In one family, the father died young, and the mother raised two children alone, feeling for years that her family was "incomplete" and never daring to invite anyone over. Later, in a family small group, she gradually opened up, and discovered many other families carried their own kinds of brokenness and struggle. She said, "It turns out I didn't need to wait for my family to become perfect before I was worthy of being loved and accepted."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: this week, actively pray together with the family members you live with, even if it's just a short word of thanksgiving and request before a meal; and actively have one genuine conversation with a member of a different generation in your family.

I declare: I will follow Joshua's example, declaring that as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

I declare: I will practice self-differentiation in my family, remaining closely connected while maintaining clear, healthy boundaries.

I declare: I will let the church equip me rather than replace me, being the first shepherd of my children.

I declare: let Jesus be King — my family will connect into Christ's larger spiritual family; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may every family be able to declare, as Joshua did: as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations move downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind, the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart, and the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — without reaching it, this lesson stays at the level of an idea.

Purpose: through discussion, drive the point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ The only time God says "not good" in the creation narrative is "It is not good that the man should be alone" — spoken before the fall. What does this prompt you to understand about God's original intention for the family?

2. ★★ Bowen points out that a family is an emotionally interconnected web, and one member's change can often move the whole system. What does this prompt you to understand about "helping one person is helping the whole family"?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "The truly healthy direction is not the church does it, the family watches, but the church equips, the family does it." In your own words, explain the difference between these two models.

4. ★★ The pledge Joshua valued most in his later years was not the achievements of his office, but "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." What does this prompt you to understand about where service truly begins?

ch47.title: Just as Christ Loved the Church — Biblical Principles for Marriage Counseling
ch47.partTitle: Part 10 — Family Ministry and Marriage Counseling
ch47.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. This is the second lesson of Part 10. Last lesson we reflected on the family's place in God's heart; today we step into a subject that is closest to home, and also the most easily misunderstood — marriage. Many couples who once deeply loved each other and gladly entered a covenant find, years later, only exhaustion and defensiveness left between them — not because love has died, but because they no longer know how to love, having heard Scripture's teaching skewed. Today, let us return to the Bible's original design and see clearly, once again, this most commonly misread passage in Ephesians 5.

Ephesians 5:25: "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her."

sections.heading: 1. The LORD God Made a Helper: Taken from the Side, Standing Shoulder to Shoulder
sections.html: Genesis 2:18: "Then the LORD God said, 'It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him.'" In the original, "helper" is not a lesser role — the Old Testament repeatedly uses this very word to describe God himself as Israel's helper. God caused Adam to fall into a deep sleep, and took a rib from him to build the woman — not taken from his foot, implying she was to be trampled underfoot; not taken from his head, implying she was to rule over him; taken from his side, to stand shoulder to shoulder with him. Adam's first reaction upon seeing her is a poem: "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh" — the deepest recognition of kinship. The very first scene of marriage is God himself, with his own hand, bringing Eve before Adam — God himself acting as the matchmaker.

sections.heading: 2. Marriage's Sacred Design, the Order of Mutual Submission, and Forgiveness Amid Conflict
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, the sacred design of marriage — two becoming one flesh is not a human civilizational invention, but God's original intent. Second, correctly understanding the order of mutual submission — the husband is to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, which is an active, sacrificial love; the wife's respect is a response of trust to that sacrificial love, never a license the husband can use to make demands. Third, the practice of conflict and forgiveness in marriage — biblical wisdom is not to avoid conflict, but to face it honestly and forgive one another, following Christ's example of forgiving the church.

sections.heading: 3. The Husband's Self-Emptying, the Wife's Respect, and the Cry of Attachment
sections.html:
The passage in Ephesians 5 most often taken out of context is precisely its opening: "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ." Many people quote this passage starting from verse 22, "Wives, submit to your own husbands," but skip right past verse 21, "submitting to one another." Grammatically in the original, the phrase in verse 22 concerning "wives" has no independent verb "submit" of its own — it flows directly from verse 21 as one specific application of it. The command given to husbands is "love," appearing three times, in the present-tense imperative in the original — not a one-time feeling, but a continuous action, chosen freshly every single day; and immediately after comes "gave himself up for her," using the very same set of words the New Testament uses to describe Christ's sacrificial death on the cross. In verse 33, Paul's word for the wife is "respect, reverence," which is a different word entirely from "submit" in verse 22 — the wife's response is trust and respect for her husband's sacrificial love, not obedience forced out by command. This passage never once gives the husband a line that says, "you may demand your wife submit to you" — the command given to the husband is always and only one thing: to love, to give himself up.

Ephesians 4:26–27: "Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil." In the original, the existence of anger itself is permitted — it never says one must never be angry; what is truly forbidden is letting the anger carry through into sin. Many of a marriage's wounds do not come from one enormous conflict, but accumulate from countless nights of anger allowed to fester. Verses 31-32 continue: "Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you." "Forgiving" in the original shares the same root as "grace" — the forgiveness the Bible teaches is not a transactional pardon that waits until the other deserves it or apologizes first; it follows the pattern of God's unconditional forgiveness of us in Christ. The psychologist Sue Johnson, in developing "emotionally focused therapy," points out that what a couple appears to be arguing about on the surface is often not the real issue at all; underneath is something she calls "the cry of attachment" — when one partner does not feel seen or needed by the other, they express, through anger, blame, or the silent treatment, a question they cannot bring themselves to say out loud: do you still care about me? This strikingly echoes Ephesians' teaching: when a husband becomes sensitive to the deep cry underneath his wife's emotion, and when a wife is willing to respond with respect, a secure attachment is built.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — When a Verse Is Used as a Weapon
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because citing and misusing are separated by a single line, and the key is the self.

It is not uncommon in marriage counseling to witness this scene: a husband, in the middle of an argument, throws out the line, "the Bible says wives should submit to their husbands," while never once mentioning his own calling to love his wife and give himself up for her; a wife, worn down by long-endured grievance, is taught to endure just a little more, while no one ever asks: has her husband lived out that sacrificial love for her? When a verse is stripped of its premise, leaving only the half-sentence that benefits one side, this is no longer obeying Scripture — it is exploiting Scripture.

Words that must never be said: "The Bible says you must submit to me, so you can't object." "We can't let the sun go down on our anger, so you're going to admit you're wrong today, period." "Forgiveness means pretending nothing happened." A truly healthy view of marriage is that the husband is called to give himself up like Christ first, and the wife's respect is a response won by that love, not obedience wrung out by a verse.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "Husbands habitually quote 'wives should submit to their husbands' to demand obedience, while rarely examining whether they themselves have first given themselves up like Christ to love." Who is the one called to act first? It is the husband, following Christ's example of self-giving love.

The second question: "When a couple argues, both wait for the other to be the first to bow the head and apologize — the standoff can drag on for weeks or even months." The question is never who should bow first, but who is called to be like Christ first.

The third question: "Many young couples enter marriage with a 'let's just try it and separate if it doesn't work' mindset, letting every conflict include leaving as an option." A ring has no exit — the covenant of marriage was never designed with a convenient door left open for separation.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "demanding the other apologize first" for "being like Christ, giving myself up to love, first." A husband holds no authority to demand his wife submit — he holds only one calling: to love first, to give himself up first.

The second correction: exchange "the logic of fairness" for "the logic of grace." Forgiveness does not wait for the other to deserve it — it follows the example of the Lord who forgave us first, while we did not yet deserve it.

The third correction: exchange "arguing over who is right" for "listening for each other's cry of attachment." The next time an argument starts heating up, ask first: "Are you feeling unseen by me right now?"

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Marriage
sections.html:
Facing the tensions within marriage, different people carry completely different reactions in their hearts. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Habitually demands that a spouse serve and obey their wishes, while being gentle and courteous toward everyone else, harsh and difficult only at home — like Nabal's arrogant response to David's messengers: "Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants these days who are breaking away from their masters. Shall I take my bread and my water and my meat that I have killed for my shearers and give it to men who come from I do not know where?" (1 Samuel 25:10–11) The proud heart needs to be reminded: the person closest to you at home is the very last person who should be treated with harshness.

The Fearful Heart

Afraid to show real weakness and need in front of a spouse, and so protects itself with lies or defensiveness, harming the trust within the marriage instead — like Abraham's fear: "I thought, 'There is no fear of God at all in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.' Besides, she is indeed my sister." (Genesis 20:11) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: real honesty protects a marriage far better than self-protection ever can.

The Ashamed Heart

Because of a past broken promise or debt owed within the marriage, feels deep shame and dares not face a spouse, even hiding behind avoidance — like David's prayer of confession: "For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me... Against you, you only, have I sinned." (Psalm 51:3–4) Yet God is glad to receive a heart that honestly repents, and grants the grace of a fresh start.

The Wounded Heart

Feels their contribution in the marriage or family has long gone unnoticed, carrying an unspoken grievance building up inside — like the Shulammite's lament: "My mother's sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept." (Song of Songs 1:6) Yet God sees every unnoticed act of giving, and is willing to himself heal that long-aggrieved heart.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A couple had gone around and around in a standoff over who should apologize first, until the husband, in prayer, was reminded: "You've been waiting every day for her to respect you first, but you've never once given yourself up for her like Christ did." He began actively listening to his wife's grievances. Weeks later, his wife said, "It isn't that he demanded I submit — it's that he loved me to a point I began wanting to draw close to him."

The second. A wife, deeply hurt by her husband's past broken promise, had for a long time protected herself with the silent treatment, until one deep conversation, when she finally said, "It's not that I don't want to forgive — I'm afraid of being hurt again." Her husband honestly admitted his wrongdoing and kept rebuilding trust through his actions. A year later, his wife said, "Forgiveness isn't a single decision — it's a road we've walked together."

The third. A couple often fought over whose turn it was to do the dishes. After a deeper conversation, they discovered what the wife truly meant was, "I'm so exhausted, how is it you never seem to notice?" and underneath the husband's defensiveness was, "I try so hard, yet you always feel it isn't enough." Once they learned to pause the argument and simply ask each other, "Do you feel like I haven't seen you?" the temperature of the conflict dropped immediately.

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: this week, find a quiet moment and simply ask your spouse: is there anything lately you wish I saw more, or cared about more? Then just listen — first understand the real cry underneath their emotion.

I declare: I will be like Christ, giving myself up to love, first — not waiting for the other to yield first.

I declare: I will forgive by the logic of grace, not clutching the ledger of fairness.

I declare: I will listen for my spouse's real cry underneath their emotion, not only hear the argument on the surface.

I declare: let Jesus be King — my marriage will become the truest testimony to Christ's love for the church; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may our marriages become the truest testimony to that love — just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

ch48.title: Manage His Own Household Well — The Challenge of Balancing Family and Ministry
ch48.partTitle: Part 10 — Family Ministry and Marriage Counseling
ch48.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. This is the third lesson of Part 10. In the previous two lessons we talked about the family's importance in God's heart, and about tending a marriage well; today we must face a tension that nearly every earnest servant, sooner or later, has to reckon with — as a church's ministry grows more numerous and more heavy, does our family, without our even noticing, become the thing sacrificed? Scripture speaks with striking directness about the qualifications of a church leader.

1 Timothy 3:4–5: "He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?"

sections.heading: 1. The Overseer's Qualification: How Well a Home Is Run Is the Hardest Thing to Hide
sections.html: When Paul wrote this letter, Timothy was shepherding the church at Ephesus and needed to appoint overseers and deacons. Among the qualifications Paul lists for an overseer, one stands out sharply: not eloquence, not breadth of knowledge, but managing his own household well. In the original, "manage" is προΐστημι, meaning to stand at the front, to lead, to take responsibility for oversight — the very same root used to describe an elder who manages the church well. Paul deliberately used the identical verb, showing that running a household and leading a church are not two entirely different skill sets, but the same faithfulness and wisdom, applied in two different settings. In writing to Titus about the qualifications for elders, and in his requirements for deacons, Paul likewise mentions managing children and one's own household well — this shows that it is not an isolated condition attached to one special office, but Scripture's consistent, universal requirement for every church leader.

sections.heading: 2. The Family Must Never Be Sacrificed, Boundaries Are Wisdom, and the Home Itself Is a Field of Ministry
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, ministry must not come at the cost of sacrificing the family — Scripture's qualifications for church leaders clearly include managing one's own household well. Second, the wisdom of boundaries and time management — being busy is not the same as being faithful; leaders need to discern what is a true calling and what is overcommitment. Third, the family itself is the most important field of ministry — serving family members is not a private matter apart from ministry; it is a field of service God has entrusted, equal in weight to, and even prior to, church ministry.

sections.heading: 3. Redeeming the Time, Clark's Work-Family Boundary Theory, and Lois and Eunice
sections.html:
Ephesians 5:15–16: "Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil." In the original, "making the best use of" is ἐξαγοράζω, literally meaning to buy back, to redeem — a commercial term carrying the sense of paying a price to actively reclaim something. Time will not be well used automatically unless we actively, at a cost, redeem certain moments and set them apart for the people they belong to; family time is precisely the part most in need of being redeemed. The psychologist Sue Campbell Clark proposed "work/family border theory," pointing out that people cross back and forth between the domains of work and family every day, and when the boundary is too blurred, it produces role confusion and psychological exhaustion. The healthy approach is to deliberately build clear yet flexible boundaries, and cultivate the ability to become a skilled "border-crosser," able to focus fully within each role rather than being pulled at simultaneously by both. True diligence, wisely understood, is knowing when to cross the boundary wholeheartedly, returning home fully present as a husband, wife, or parent.

The "diligent instruction" of Deuteronomy 6, in the original shanan, literally means to sharpen, to whet — like a whetstone repeatedly sharpening a blade's edge. A servant of God who gives all their diligence to the church pulpit, but never brings that same patience home, again and again sharpening a child's faith, leaves the very blade that most needs sharpening the dullest of all. In 2 Timothy 1:5, Paul mentions that Timothy's faith first lived in his grandmother Lois, and then in his mother Eunice. This young leader, later called by Paul his true child, whose influence has echoed through church history, had his faith's very first cradle not in some great gathering, but in his own home. Many of the faithful workers the church relies on today, like Timothy, were first watered with the seed of faith by a faithful family member, day after day.

Healthy boundaries are a concrete discipline: phone on silent at the dinner table, full presence with family; a fixed family day every week with no ministry scheduled; genuine rest during vacation, not on standby for church messages at all hours. These boundaries may look like they slow certain ministries down, but in fact they are what makes it possible for service to continue, healthily, for the long run — a servant who burns out and whose family falls apart, for lack of boundaries, ultimately has far less to give the church than one whose boundaries are clear, whose family is stable, and who can serve for the long haul.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Knowing Every Name in the Church, but Not the Latest Thing on a Child's Heart
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because being busy and being faithful are separated by a single line, and the key is the self.

It is not hard to find this scene: a servant of God can name dozens of church members by heart, yet cannot answer what difficulty their own child recently faced at school; can plan every detail of a church event with great care, yet hasn't had a real heart-to-heart with their spouse in weeks. This is not a lack of love for the church — it is that the priority of service has, without anyone noticing, become misplaced.

Words that must never be said: "Serving God's kingdom matters more than anything, my family should understand." "The church needs me, so it's like this for now — I'll make it up to my family later." "I've given the church my best hours, so my family should be satisfied with what's left." A truly healthy view of ministry is being faithful at home first, and then carrying that proven faithfulness from home into the church.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "Servants of God unconsciously pour the most time into church ministry that earns immediate applause, while pushing family life, which earns no applause at all, to the very last place." Your family will never applaud you, but they quietly keep count of every time you were absent.

The second question: "Church leaders sacrifice family for the sake of ministry results over the long term — this sacrifice is rarely one enormous decision, but the accumulation of countless small ones: it's like this for now, I'll make it up later." If the church matters more than family, sooner or later the cost will show.

The third question: "Servants of God have never honestly communicated their family time boundaries with co-workers or the church, letting ministry invitations endlessly encroach on family time without limit." Setting boundaries is not selfishness — it is the wisdom that lets service continue in a healthy way for the long run.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "proving my worth through ministry results" for "confidently giving my most tender side to my family first." A self-emptied servant does not need to prove their worth through the results of their ministry.

The second correction: exchange "boundless busyness" for "deliberately crossing the boundary." Serve wholeheartedly at the office and at church, and when you come home, truly come home — don't let a sense of responsibility endlessly bleed into the dinner table.

The third correction: exchange "seeking the church's kingdom first" for "managing my own household well first, then caring for God's church." The two have never been opposites — both require careful, cherished attention.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Priority
sections.html:
Facing the tension between ministry and family, different people carry completely different reactions in their hearts. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Loves to display its faithfulness and zeal at church before others, while turning a blind eye to how often it is absent at home — like the practice of the Pharisees: "They do all their deeds to be seen by others... and greetings in the marketplaces." (Matthew 23:5,7) The proud heart needs to be reminded: true faithfulness needs no audience — it begins at home.

The Fearful Heart

Afraid that declining a church invitation will disappoint others or be seen as insufficiently committed, and so keeps agreeing to more ministry than it can bear — like Martha, growing resentful amid her frantic serving: "Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, 'Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?'" (Luke 10:40) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: if frantic service costs you your place sitting at the Lord's feet, that busyness itself needs to be reexamined.

The Ashamed Heart

Because of a past failure or negligence in raising children, feels deep shame, even avoiding any conversation about family at church — like Eli's regret over indulging his sons: "for he knew that his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them." (1 Samuel 3:13) Yet God is willing to grant the grace of a fresh start, and to redeem lost time.

The Wounded Heart

Carries a wound from childhood, having felt that parents valued the church more than themselves — neglected and left out in the cold — a wound that still shapes their relationships today, like Leah's longing to truly be valued by her husband: "Because the LORD has looked upon my affliction; for now my husband will love me." (Genesis 29:32) God himself sees every child who has ever felt they were never given priority, and can heal that deep wound.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A pastor's grown child grew distant from the church, until, in a deep conversation, the child finally said: "As a kid, I felt the church mattered more than I did." The pastor was struck with remorse, actively worked to repair the relationship, and from then on deliberately placed his family's important days at the very top of his calendar. Years later, the relationship between father and son gradually healed.

The second. A sister who had served for years, unable to say no to any invitation, lived in chronic exhaustion, and her family felt deeply neglected. She later learned to honestly express boundaries to her co-workers, setting aside one family day every week. She said, "I finally understood that setting boundaries isn't a lack of commitment — it's what lets service go the distance."

The third. A deacon, busy with church ministry, had not had a real heart-to-heart conversation with his wife for years, until one remark from her woke him up. Since then, he sets aside fifteen uninterrupted minutes every day to listen fully to what his wife shares. He said, "It turns out the deepest ministry begins with really listening to the person who sleeps beside me."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: this week, have an honest conversation with your spouse or family about time and boundaries; and do one concrete thing for your family — a fully present dinner, or a long-overdue apology or word of thanks.

I declare: I will manage my own household well, being a consistent example in word and deed for my children and spouse.

I declare: I will actively redeem the time, reclaiming the moments that belong to my family instead of letting them slip away.

I declare: I will become a servant who knows how to cross the boundary well, fully engaged in ministry and fully present at home.

I declare: let Jesus be King — I will stop proving my worth through ministry results, and confidently give my most tender heart to my family first; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may we all manage our own households well, and faithfully care for the church God has entrusted to us, until the day the Lord returns. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The Three Transformations move downward. The First Transformation drives the point into the mind, the Second Transformation carries it from the mind into the heart, and the Third Transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the Third Transformation — without reaching it, this lesson stays at the level of an idea.

First Transformation | Internalizing It as an Idea (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the point of this lesson into a clear idea.

1. ★ Among the qualifications Paul lists for an overseer is "managing his own household well," using in the original the same word as "an elder who manages the church well." What does this prompt you to understand about "running a household and leading a church are the same kind of ability"?

2. ★★ "Making the best use of the time" in the original carries the sense of paying a price to actively redeem — time will not be well used on its own. What does this prompt you to understand about family time needing to be deliberately reclaimed?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "Be faithful at home first, and then carry that proven faithfulness from home into the church." In your own words, explain what this order means.

4. ★★ Clark points out that a truly healthy person is one who deliberately crosses boundaries, rather than letting the responsibilities of both worlds bleed into each other. What does this prompt you to understand about the importance of boundaries?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "being able to say it," not "saying it well." If someone speaks in fragments, help them organize their thought — don't finish it for them.

12. ★★ The message said: "Setting boundaries is the wisdom that lets service continue in a healthy way for the long run." This week, what specific boundary could you propose to your church or co-workers?

Write down right now who you will tell it to.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the time you will redeem this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to help us faithfully manage the family he has entrusted to us, and faithfully manage the church he has entrusted to us.

ch49.title: Teach Your Children Diligently — The Church's Role in Parent-Child Education
ch49.partTitle: Part 10 — Family Ministry and Marriage Counseling
ch49.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. This is the fourth lesson of Part 10. In the first three, we talked about the ministry of healthy families, biblical principles for marriage counseling, and how to balance the tension between family and ministry; today, we must face a question that has caused many parents anxiety — will my child come to faith one day? What can the church do about it? Deuteronomy places the responsibility for teaching children clearly on parents, not on priests or institutions.

Deuteronomy 6:6–7: "And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise."

sections.heading: 1. Moses' Parting Charge: A Chain of Responsibility That Bypasses No Institution
sections.html: Deuteronomy is the farewell address Moses gave to the new generation of Israel, just before they were to enter the land of Canaan. Moses knew that if this new generation did not hear and see God's work for themselves, directly from their parents, they would easily lose their way amid the idol culture of Canaan. Deuteronomy 6 first declares the Shema — "The LORD our God, the LORD is one" — and the very next command is addressed, not to priests, not to Levites, but to every parent in Israel. In the original, "teach diligently" is shanan, whose root meaning is to sharpen, to whet, used to describe sharpening a blade or an arrowhead, extended to mean repeatedly, carefully, engraving and instilling something; "command" is tsavah, meaning to order, to solemnly entrust. Together, these two words paint an extremely clear picture: God solemnly commands, and parents are to teach diligently — this is a chain of responsibility handed directly from God into the hands of parents, with no priest and no institution standing in between.

sections.heading: 2. The Family Is the Front Line, Modeling Matters More Than Telling, and the Church Equips Rather Than Replaces
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, the family is the front line of passing on the faith, and the church's role is to assist, not to replace — Deuteronomy 6 clearly places the responsibility for teaching children on parents. Second, modeling matters more than telling — the manner of teaching Deuteronomy describes is sitting, walking, lying down, rising, a continuous demonstration woven into daily life, and the reality of a parent's own life speaks more persuasively than any spoken instruction. Third, how the church can concretely support parents — Sunday school, family equipping classes, intergenerational activities: the church's role is to become a resource and a support behind parents, not to take over their responsibility.

sections.heading: 3. The Meaning of "Talk," Baumrind's Authoritative Parenting, and Equipping the Saints
sections.html:
"Talk" in the original, dabar, means to speak, to converse — describing the natural verbal exchange that happens in daily life, not a formal, one-directional lecture. The parent-child faith education Deuteronomy describes is, in its essence, relational: what a child receives from their parents is not merely a set of doctrinal knowledge, but, in countless everyday conversations, a gradual absorption of how their parents see God, how their parents rely on God, and the shape of life that flows from it. The American developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind, through long-term observational research, distinguished several major parenting styles: the authoritarian style demands much but lacks warmth; the permissive style is full of warmth but lacks principle; she specifically pointed out that the authoritative style, which combines high warmth and responsiveness with high standards and principle, tends to raise children who develop the healthiest confidence, self-discipline, and relational skills. Looking back at Deuteronomy 6, parents on the one hand clearly command God's words — this is principle and boundary; on the other hand, they proclaim these words in the most everyday, intimate moments of sitting, walking, lying down, and rising — this is warmth and presence. What children notice most keenly, from the very beginning, is often not their ears but their eyes — a father can verbally teach his child to be honest, yet casually lie while filing his taxes, and the child sees this far more deeply than they hear the lesson. Children first see, before they are willing to hear.

Ephesians 4:11–12: "And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers, to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ." In the original, "equip," katartismos, literally means to mend something back to a complete, whole state — the same word used for a fisherman mending his nets. The church's office is to mend and equip God's people fully, so that they can function healthily in their own roles — not to replace them in performing that function. If the church takes over the responsibility that belongs to parents, the result is not a mended net — it is taking the entire net away from the fisherman so he never has to cast it again. The church's role is to stand behind parents, as a resource and support they can always rely on, not to stand in front of them and take over what they should be doing themselves.

One pastor once shared that his deepest imprint of faith as a child was not any particular verse a Sunday school teacher had taught, but one image: when his father's business once suffered a major setback, he got up in the middle of the night, and passing his parents' bedroom door, saw a sliver of light beneath it — his father, kneeling by the bed, praying quietly for his family, for the way ahead, for a long time. He has never forgotten that silhouette. Not a single word was spoken to him directly, and yet it told him, more deeply than any sermon ever could, that this God was real. In a moment of crisis, what a child sees is a parent's prayer; the silent example is often the deepest imprint of all.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — One Sunday School Class Cannot Replace a Family
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because equipping and replacing are separated by a single line, and the key is the self.

Some parents send their children to church and think, now the spiritual education is being handled, and stop mentioning God at home entirely; other churches, in their enthusiasm, exclude parents entirely from their child's spiritual growth, taking over everything themselves, which instead leaves parents feeling they have no place to contribute. Both of these imbalances stray from the healthy picture.

Words that must never be said: "The kids go to Sunday school every week, I don't need to say more at home." "The teachers at church know the Bible better than I do, teaching the kids is their job." "Nobody taught me when I was growing up, so I don't know how to teach my kids either." A truly healthy view of parent-child education is that one Sunday school class cannot replace a family; the church exists to be a support to parents, not their replacement.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "Parents entirely offload the responsibility for spiritual education onto the church, staying silent about God at home." The native soil of faith has always been at home.

The second question: "Parents verbally teach their children one set of values, while living out something entirely different in their own lives, so what the child receives is not the words, but the pattern of behavior." Telling tells a child what they should do; modeling shows a child what is actually possible.

The third question: "The church becomes so enthusiastic that it marginalizes parents' role, handling everything itself, leaving parents feeling they are not qualified to participate." The church's role is to equip, not to replace.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "sent to church, job done" for "diligent instruction, kept on the heart." Parents are the first shepherd their child will ever have.

The second correction: exchange "telling comes first" for "modeling comes first." Children see first, before they are willing to hear; the reality of a life outweighs a thousand spoken words.

The third correction: exchange "the church takes over everything" for "the church equips the parents." Resources are not a transfer of responsibility — walk alongside parents, teaching the next generation together.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Instruction
sections.html:
Facing the task of teaching one's children, different people carry completely different reactions in their hearts. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Treats a child's grades or behavior as proof of their own parenting success, boasting of it before others, while overlooking the true foundation of a life of faith. Yet God rebuked Eli: "Why then do you scorn my sacrifices and my offerings that I commanded for my dwelling, and honor your sons above me by fattening yourselves on the choicest parts of every offering of my people Israel?" (1 Samuel 2:29) The proud heart needs to be reminded: what is truly worth boasting about is not a child's performance, but knowing the true and living God.

The Fearful Heart

Because of fear that a child will one day drift from the faith or go astray, lives day after day in anxiety and excessive control, like the worry Proverbs describes: "A foolish son is a grief to his father, and bitterness to her who bore him." (Proverbs 17:25) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: anxious control cannot buy a child's faith — only entrusting them to God, alongside diligent teaching, bears real fruit.

The Ashamed Heart

Because of a child's rebellion or waywardness, feels like a failed parent, even too ashamed to speak of family difficulties at church — like Proverbs' warning: "The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother." (Proverbs 29:15) Yet God is willing to grant grace and wisdom for a fresh start, even within a parenting journey that looks like failure.

The Wounded Heart

Carries a wound of feeling estranged and out of place, having never sensed a family's faith as real while growing up — like the psalmist's lament: "I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's sons." (Psalm 69:8) Yet God is willing to himself take in every child who has ever felt lonely and alienated within their own family.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A father had served enthusiastically at church for years, but rarely brought up faith at home, until his grown child asked him, "Why have you never once shared your own faith with me?" That question shook him awake. Since then, he sets aside time each week to share his own weakness and dependence on God with his child, and his child said, "Knowing that Dad struggles too makes faith feel a lot more real."

The second. A mother, after her child was diagnosed with a learning difficulty, lived in chronic anxiety, trying every discipline method with little success. Later, a sister from church prayed with her and helped her learn the wisdom of authoritative parenting, holding warmth and boundaries together. She said, "I finally understood that love and principle aren't opposites — they can be given at the same time."

The third. A church once ran Sunday school with great fanfare, but rarely equipped the parents. It later shifted direction and launched a family-equipping class, teaching biblical parenting principles and parent-child communication skills. One father who attended said, "I finally know what I can do at home myself, beyond just bringing my kids to church."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: this week, find a meal when the whole family is together, and actively begin a conversation about God, letting talk of God's word become a natural part of family life.

I declare: I will teach my children diligently, keeping God's word on my heart, sharpening their faith again and again.

I declare: I will live out the reality of modeling, letting my children see first, so they will be willing to hear.

I declare: I will gladly let the church equip me, rather than offloading the responsibility for teaching entirely onto the church.

I declare: let Jesus be King — my family and my church, together, will entrust my children's faith to the true and living God; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may our families and our churches, together, entrust our children's faith to the true and living God. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
