ch50.title: Seek the Welfare of the City — Connecting Family Ministry to the Community
ch50.partTitle: Part 10 — Family Ministry and Marriage Counseling
ch50.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. This is the final lesson of Part 10, "Family Ministry and Marriage Counseling." Over the past four lessons, we moved from the foundation of a ministry to healthy families, through the biblical principles of marriage counseling, the balance between ministry and family, and the church's role in parent-child education, and the focus has gradually moved from building up the family internally toward the final question we must ask today: where should a family, once well built, ultimately go? The answer is not to stay home and enjoy it, but to follow the example of the exiled people of Israel — even while living in a foreign land, they were to seek the welfare of that city.

Jeremiah 29:7: "But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare."

sections.heading: 1. Faith in a Land of Exile: Settling Down and Blessing Others, at the Same Time
sections.html: Jeremiah 29 records that the king of Babylon had carried the people of Judah into exile, relocating them to a foreign land. All they could think of was one thing: when could they return to Jerusalem? At the time, false prophets said they would return soon, but Jeremiah sent a letter that said not "flee quickly," but "settle down": "Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce... Take wives and have sons and daughters... that you may be multiplied there, and not diminished." God commanded the exiled people not to live with a temporary mindset, always ready to leave, but to live earnestly in a situation they never wanted — this was the exiled people's first lesson in faith. Then comes the truly startling line of Jeremiah's letter: "Seek the welfare of the city." In the original, "seek" is דָּרַשׁ, an active pursuit, an inquiry; "welfare" is שָׁלוֹם (shalom), whose meaning goes far beyond the absence of war — it is comprehensive flourishing and well-being. Being blessed has never been the destination — it is the starting point from which one is sent out to bless others.

sections.heading: 2. The Family Is Not a Fortress, Hospitality Is a Daily Practice, and the Church Weaves a Network of Blessing
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, the family is not an isolated fortress, but should become a blessing to the community — following the example of the exiled people's resolve to seek the welfare of the city. Second, the open home: hospitality and care extended to neighbors — a family willing to open its door is, in itself, the truest testimony of the gospel. Third, the church's overall strategy: from individual families to a community network — the church equips, connects, and mobilizes each family, forming a network that blesses the community, rather than each family fighting alone. Over the past four lessons, we built the family, this house, from the foundation to the roof; today, we open its front door.

sections.heading: 3. Practicing Hospitality Eagerly, the Shape of the Early Church, and Asset-Based Community Development
sections.html:
In Romans 12, right after laying out the great doctrine of justification by faith, Paul writes a series of concrete reminders for daily life: "Seek to show hospitality." In that era, the Roman Empire had no modern hotel system — if a Christian traveler had no brother or sister to open their door, they had almost nowhere to go. Hebrews 13:2 says: "Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." In the original, "hospitality" is φιλοξενία, made up of the words for "love" and "stranger" — literally, "love of strangers"; "seek" carries a root meaning of pursuing, chasing after — not a passive response, but an active search for opportunities to welcome someone. Acts 2 records that after Pentecost, three thousand people were baptized in a single day — and the answer was not to build one enormous hall, but two settings running side by side: the public gathering at the temple, and the breaking of bread in individual homes: "day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes... And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved." From the very beginning, the church has been a network woven together from open homes.

The American scholar John McKnight, of Northwestern University, proposed "asset-based community development," abbreviated ABCD. Traditional community renewal is needs-driven — an outside institution arrives with resources, lists what the community lacks, and tries to fix it, but this model gradually turns residents into passive recipients of aid. McKnight argued for a wiser approach: first discover the assets the community already possesses — every resident's gifts, every family's connections and resources — and then connect those assets to one another, turning residents from recipients into active participants. The church can concretely do three things: discover what gifts and resources each family already has; connect gifted families with neighbors in need; and mobilize and send out each family to live out a blessing to their neighbors along the ordinary paths of their daily lives.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Don't Wait Until Someone Has Fallen to Open Your Door for the First Time
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because safety and isolation are separated by a single line, and the key is the self.

Today's urban living structures naturally push families toward isolation — living in a high-rise for ten years without ever learning the neighbor's name, social media keeping us warmly connected to friends far away while having no contact at all with the person downstairs. A family shaped by self keeps its time and resources entirely to itself, and its front door slowly rusts shut, becoming an isolated island — until someone actually falls, and only then, for the very first time, does that door finally open, and the neighbor gets met.

Words that must never be said: "I can barely keep up with my own family, I have no energy left for the neighbors." "Strangers are risky, it's safer to just keep the door closed." "I'll show hospitality once I'm ready — once the house is bigger, once I have more time." A truly healthy view of family is that settling down and blessing others were always meant to be the same thing, not two separate steps. Today, find one small thing, and begin.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "Families think of hospitality as the exclusive job of the church's welcoming team, rather than the natural, daily calling of every Christian family." Welcoming travelers is the natural, daily calling of every Christian family.

The second question: "When the church promotes community service, it habitually starts by drawing up a list of needs to fill, without ever taking stock of the gifts and resources each family already has." Every community is not a list of needs to be filled — it is a mine of assets waiting to be discovered.

The third question: "Many healthy families are content with their own piety at home, but never connect that health outward to their neighbors and community." A group of individually pious but mutually disconnected families still adds up only to isolated families, not a church.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "take care of myself first" for "settling down and blessing others happen at the same time." Don't wait until you're "ready" before you start blessing others.

The second correction: exchange "passively waiting for someone to knock" for "actively pursuing hospitality like a chase." A stranger may be carrying, unknown to you, a messenger from God.

The third correction: exchange "filling the community's list of needs" for "connecting the assets each family already has." Connect the gifts God has already placed in every family, letting service become a natural overflow of life.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Front Door
sections.html:
Facing the act of opening one's home, different people carry completely different reactions in their hearts. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Busy accumulating more property and space, leaving no room at all for neighbors, treating the expansion of the home as a symbol of achievement — like the prophet's warning: "Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land." (Isaiah 5:8) The proud heart needs to be reminded: a home's value lies not in how much it has accumulated, but in whether it still leaves room for others.

The Fearful Heart

Afraid of becoming entangled with a stranger or a neighbor in need, and so would rather go out of the way than risk getting involved — like the avoidance of the priest and the Levite: "Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side." (Luke 10:31) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: the true neighbor is the one who stopped, not the one who hurried away.

The Ashamed Heart

Because of their family's circumstances, health, or situation, feels not presentable enough, deeply unworthy of receiving hospitality, and dares not invite anyone into their own home — like Mephibosheth's self-deprecating response: "What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?" (2 Samuel 9:8) Yet God is glad to give the seat of highest honor to those who feel themselves unworthy.

The Wounded Heart

Once had a good-faith gift betrayed or mocked by a neighbor or friend, and has grown cold ever since, shutting the door and never trying again — like the discouragement of Nehemiah's workers amid the rebuilding: "The strength of those who bear the burdens is failing. There is too much rubble. By ourselves we will not be able to rebuild the wall." (Nehemiah 4:10) Yet God can, in the most discouraging moment, grant the strength to rise up and keep building.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A sister had lived in a new community for six months when the elderly neighbor living alone across the hall fell in the middle of the night and knocked on her door for help — and only then did she meet this neighbor for the first time. Since then, she has regularly invited that elder over for meals. She said, "I finally understood that I don't have to wait until someone falls to open my own door."

The second. A family had once been taken advantage of after showing hospitality to a stranger, and had kept their door shut ever since, refusing to try again, until their church small group prayed with them and helped them learn wise, thoughtful openness. They became willing to invite neighbors into their home again, this time with clear boundaries and wisdom. They said, "Openness isn't naivety — it's courage carried with wisdom."

The third. A church had always rushed to fill every gap in the community's needs, gradually depleting its resources and manpower, until it switched to mapping its assets instead, discovering members who were skilled bakers, plumbers, and retired couples willing to drive neighbors to appointments. The church wove these gifts into a network of service. One elder said, "It turns out we were never short on resources — what we lacked was the vision to connect them."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration: Looking Back on Part Ten
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: this week, sit down with your family and honestly list what gifts and resources you have to offer; and at least once this month, actively invite a neighbor over for a meal.

Having come this far, the five lessons of Part 10, "Family Ministry and Marriage Counseling," together form one complete lesson: advancing a ministry of healthy families — the family is the first community God established, and the church equips rather than replaces; biblical principles for marriage counseling — the husband is called to give himself up like Christ, first; balancing the tension between family and ministry — managing one's own household well is the truest foundation of all service; the church's role in parent-child education — the church equips parents, it does not replace them; and today, connecting family ministry to the community, moving our gaze from inside the front door to what lies beyond it. These five lessons interlock to form one complete path: foundation, pillar, order, transmission, extension. May every one of our families become a starting point that is both blessed, and a blessing to others.

I declare: I will follow the example of the exiled people, seeking the welfare of the city I live in even as I settle down.

I declare: I will actively pursue hospitality like a chase, letting my front door exist for more than just my own family.

I declare: I will see the gifts my own family already has, and connect them to the neighbors who truly need them.

I declare: let Jesus be King — my family will become a channel of living water that God sends into the community; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may we no longer shut our homes into isolated islands, but follow the resolve of the exiled people, seeking the welfare of the city where we live, until the day the Lord returns. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

sections.html:

Closing (5 minutes)

ch51.title: To the End of the Earth, as My Witnesses — The Necessity of Engaging in Global Missions
ch51.partTitle: Part 11 — Global Missions and the Church's Calling
ch51.intro:
Peace to you, brothers and sisters. Beginning today, we enter Part 11, the final part of the entire "Church Leadership" fifty-five-lesson series: "Global Missions and the Church's Calling." Over the past ten parts, we began at the foundation of servant leadership and journeyed through vision, crisis, culture, discipleship, spiritual health, communication, finance, technology, and family — this path has, in fact, been a journey from the inside out the whole way: first building a life, then building relationships, and finally, inevitably, moving toward a calling. Today, we must ask a question many believers have never seriously asked themselves: does global missions truly have anything to do with me?

Acts 1:8: "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth."

sections.heading: 1. The Commissioning on the Mountain: Doubt Still Present, the Command Already Given
sections.html: Matthew 28 records that the risen Jesus appeared to the eleven disciples on a mountain in Galilee. The text honestly records a line often overlooked: "And when they saw him they worshiped him, but some doubted." This was the most important commissioning in church history, and yet the disciples did not stand there full of unwavering confidence — some bowed down, and some still carried doubt in their hearts. Jesus did not wait for the doubt to disappear before issuing the Great Commission — he spoke right into the moment while doubt was still present: "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations." In the original, "make disciples" is the Greek verb μαθητεύσατε, the single core command of the whole sentence; "all nations" is πάντα τὰ ἔθνη, and ἔθνος is the very root of the English word "ethnic," referring to every people group, every nation, without regard to geography or culture. From the very beginning, this command left no room for any people group to be exempt.

sections.heading: 2. Every Believer Is on the List, the Order of Geographic Expansion, and a Commission Shared by the Whole Body
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, the Great Commission is the calling of every believer, not the exclusive privilege of a select few especially called — the command is addressed to "you," the whole body of disciples, not a small group of professional missionaries. Second, Acts 1:8 gives a clear geographic order: Jerusalem, all Judea, Samaria, to the end of the earth — the expansion of the gospel has an order, but no end point; "the end of the earth" in the original, ἔσχατος τῆς γῆς, is the very root of the English word "eschatology," and missions is tightly bound to the culmination of redemptive history. Third, missions is a commission shared by the whole body together, not the solitary task of one finger — Paul, in 1 Corinthians 12, uses the image of the body for the church: the missionary is often the hand reaching outward, yet the whole body must together supply the blood and strength that hand needs. Today, let us together face the question: does this have anything to do with me?

sections.heading: 3. Compassion Before Strategy, the Bystander Effect, and the Church's Silence
sections.html:
Matthew 9 records that Jesus saw the crowds, "and he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd." In the original, "compassion" is σπλαγχνίζομαι, whose root refers to the inward organs churning in pain — a compassion arising from the deepest place, one that cannot be suppressed. Jesus then said to his disciples: "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest." The original words for "laborers," ἐργάτης, and "send out," ἐκβάλλω, are worth noting — the latter is the very same verb Jesus used when casting out demons, carrying a force nearly equivalent to a strong push. God sending out laborers is never a lukewarm invitation — it is an urgent, forceful sending. The starting point of a calling has never been strategy — it is compassion, coming before strategy.

In 1964, the murder of Kitty Genovese in New York shocked the nation, and sociologists afterward discovered that multiple witnesses heard her cries for help, yet no one called the police. The psychologists Bibb Latané and John Darley conducted a famous series of experiments in 1968: when a subject was left alone in a room that filled with smoke, they reported the problem almost immediately; when more people were placed in the same room, the proportion willing to report dropped sharply — this became known as "the bystander effect," where responsibility is diluted by the number of people present, and everyone assumes "someone else will surely do it." Does the church today, facing global missions, not often fall into this very same collective silence? Missions funding sits at the bottom of the budget sheet; praying for the nations is the item most easily skipped at prayer meeting — because we quietly assume some other church, some other organization, will surely take care of it. The only way to break the bystander effect is to assign responsibility concretely to one person, one family, one church — never leave it with a vague "everyone."

In fact, the very first person in human history to truly cross a cultural boundary was not Paul, and not any of the apostles — it was Jesus Christ himself. Philippians 2:6–8 says: "Though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross." In the original, "emptied himself" is ἐκένωσεν, whose root means "to pour out" — describing Christ actively laying down his original glory and status, crossing the most distant cultural chasm of all, between heaven and earth, becoming the likeness of man, dwelling among us. He is the first, and the most complete, cross-cultural missionary of all — every believer today willing to take a step forward is walking a road he walked first.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — The Great Commission Is Not Someone Else's Project, It Carries Every Disciple's Name
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this lesson also has a passage that must be spoken honestly. Because absence and observing are separated by a single line, and the key is the self.

Many believers think of the Great Commission as "someone else's project" — that is the missionary's calling, the mission agency's specialty, the passion of a select few especially zealous people; the most they themselves do is give a little at a fundraiser, and consider their duty fulfilled. A self-centered heart safely places itself in the bleachers, using "I don't have that gift" to exclude itself from the list, forgetting that Jesus, from the very beginning, said "you."

Words that must never be said: "Missions is for missionaries — I just need to serve at home." "I don't have the gift for languages or that kind of heart, this isn't my calling." "I've already given a little money, I've done my part." A truly healthy view of missions is that every believer is on the Great Commission's list — only the post is different, never a reason for absence.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "The church narrows missions down to the exclusive vocation of a select few especially called, and most of the congregation considers it to have nothing to do with themselves." The Great Commission is addressed to "you" — not to "them."

The second question: "The church's missions concern stays at the level of a distant, vague 'all nations,' never becoming concrete, never landing on a specific person or people group's name." When responsibility has no concrete name, it easily dilutes and dissipates across a crowd.

The third question: "The church habitually places missions funding and prayer at the very end of the calendar, and when budgets tighten, missions is often the first thing sacrificed." If compassion stays only at the moment it is felt, and is never translated into a priority on the calendar, it remains nothing but empty words.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "missions is someone else's business" for "my name is on the Great Commission's list." The command has always been addressed to "you," the whole body of disciples.

The second correction: exchange "vague nations" for "one concrete person." Find one concrete people group or individual, and make your prayer and concern land on them.

The third correction: exchange "compassion that ends at feeling moved" for "compassion translated onto the calendar." Pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers, and pray the Lord to send out you and me too, to become people who no longer merely observe.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Same Sending
sections.html:
Facing the Great Commission, different people carry completely different reactions in their hearts. Let me hold up four hearts against each other — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Having labored for years in their own post, feels entitled to enjoy comfort, and grows resentful when others are sent far away — like the laborer who worked all day in the vineyard, complaining: "These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat." (Matthew 20:12) The proud heart needs to be reminded: the more grace one has received, the more one should be willing to be sent — not more entitled to refuse.

The Fearful Heart

At the mere thought of facing unfamiliar language, culture, and unknown danger, is bound first by fear, and would rather stay in a familiar, safe place — like Jonah, who heard the call to Nineveh, yet rose up and fled in the opposite direction: "But Jonah rose up to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD." (Jonah 1:3) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: the ship that flees from a calling never sails beyond God's sight.

The Ashamed Heart

Because of past weakness or retreat in bearing witness to their faith, feels unworthy to ever again be used by God to testify to the nations — like the deep self-reproach Peter carried after denying the Lord three times: "And he went out and wept bitterly." (Matthew 26:75) Yet God is glad to entrust the heaviest calling once again to the very one who once fell but was willing to repent.

The Wounded Heart

Has once suffered rejection or even persecution for participating in ministry and evangelism, carrying a scar from it, and since then dares not take another step outward — like Paul at Lystra, stoned and dragged out of the city, thought to be dead: "They stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead." (Acts 14:19) Yet God can make the very place where one seemed to fall the starting point from which they rise again and continue on.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A brother had for years felt that missions had nothing to do with him, until, at a church missions Sunday, he truly heard for the first time the name and population of an unreached people group. That night he lay awake, and he said, "I finally understood — for thirty years, I thought that list belonged to someone else."

The second. A family, out of fear of an unfamiliar environment, had for years declined every invitation to cross-cultural service, until a short-term mission trip was suddenly short a member, and they, against their instincts, agreed to go for one week. When they came back, the content of the whole family's prayers had completely changed. They said, "The moment the fear vanished wasn't when the danger passed — it was when we finally stood there in person."

The third. A church had for years placed its missions budget at the very bottom of the sheet, squeezed year after year by other line items, until the board of elders decided to make missions funding a priority rather than the leftover amount. One elder said, "It turns out when the order changed, the whole church's temperature of prayer changed right along with it."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing our thinking are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: this week, look up an unreached people group whose name you have never heard before, write down their name and population, and begin praying for them.

I declare: my name is on the Great Commission's list — I will no longer treat missions as someone else's project.

I declare: I will turn a vague notion of "all nations" into one concrete name, remembering them daily in prayer.

I declare: I will translate compassion into a priority on my calendar, no longer letting missions stay only at a moment of feeling moved.

I declare: let Jesus be King — I will become a laborer who has been sent out, no longer merely observing; all glory belongs to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may we no longer think of missions as someone else's business, but hear these very words Jesus spoke to "you," and gladly become his witnesses to the end of the earth. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

12. ★★ The message said: "Break the bystander effect by assigning responsibility concretely to one person." This week, how could you turn a vague concern for missions into a concrete action?

13. ★★★ A ten-minute daily discipline: this week, spend ten minutes each day praying for one specific unreached people group or missionary — name what time you will practice this.

14. ★★ The 920 discipline: identify your own "2" (a missionary or an unreached people group); this week bring your support to them through one concrete action. Say their name or people group out loud right now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, tell this lesson to someone outside the group in three sentences — But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth. Write down right now who you will tell it to.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, tell each other two things: the missionary or people group you will pray for this week, and who you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to make every one of us his witnesses to the end of the earth.

ch52.title: I Have Become All Things to All People — The Challenges and Strategies of Cross-Cultural Missions
ch52.partTitle: Part 11 — Global Missions and the Church's Calling
ch52.intro:
Grace and peace, brothers and sisters. In the last lesson we confirmed that your name is already on the roster of the Great Commission. Today we need to face an honest question: once you actually step across the line, what waits ahead is not only the barrier of language, but differences buried deep in the substrate of culture — ways of thinking so ingrained that even the people who hold them often cannot see them. Corinth was the busiest commercial port city on the Mediterranean of its day, where peoples, languages, and beliefs of every kind converged. It was in exactly this setting that Paul wrote one of the most important confessions of cross-cultural ministry in all of Scripture.

1 Corinthians 9:22–23: "To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some. I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings."

sections.heading: 1. A Confession from a Commercial City: I Was Willing to Change Myself to Win Some
sections.html: In 1 Corinthians 9:19–23, Paul uses the pattern "to the ___ I became ___" five times in succession, covering the Jews, those under the law, those outside the law, and the weak — the underlying Greek verb γίνομαι, "to become," appears in the perfect tense, underscoring that this was not a momentary performance but a genuine, sustained state of entering another person's world. Yet immediately following, one clause draws a clear boundary: "under the law of Christ" — what Paul adjusted was external form and custom; he never once compromised the core truth of the gospel. This is precisely the most delicate lesson of cross-cultural ministry: what may change is the form; what may never change is the core.

sections.heading: 2. The Real Challenge Is Worldview; the Four Dimensions of Cultural Intelligence; Equal Partnership, Not One-Sided Giving
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, the true challenge of cross-cultural missions is rarely language or customs, but a difference in worldview buried so deep that even the person who holds it is barely aware of it. Second, in 2003 scholars P. Christopher Earley and Soon Ang proposed the theory of "Cultural Intelligence," or CQ, comprising four dimensions — metacognitive, cognitive, motivational, and behavioral — and Paul's whole life is a living demonstration of all four. Third, healthy cross-cultural ministry builds equal partnership with local believers, not one-sided giving — Galatians 2 records Paul, Barnabas, and the pillar leaders in Jerusalem extending the right hand of fellowship to one another, a division of labor, not a hierarchy of superior and subordinate. Missions history holds painful lessons on this point, and it also shows us a better road.

sections.heading: 3. Peter's Withdrawal at Antioch; the Four Dimensions of CQ; Listening Before Teaching
sections.html:
Galatians 2 records a heartbreaking episode. Peter had been eating together at the same table with Gentile believers in Antioch, but when certain men came from James in Jerusalem, belonging to the circumcision party, he withdrew and drew back, fearing those of the circumcision. Two Greek words are worth noting: ὑπέστελλεν, "he withdrew," and ὑπόκρισις, "hypocrisy" — the very root of the English word hypocrisy, literally meaning "to act behind a mask." Paul confronted him to his face because he was "not walking uprightly, not in step with the truth of the gospel" — the underlying word ὀρθοποδέω literally means "to walk a straight path." That even an apostle who had already received a vision confirming that God had cleansed the Gentiles could shrink back into the comfort of his own culture under group pressure reminds us that cross-cultural retreat is rarely a matter of theological understanding — it is far more often a matter of fear in the heart.

Earley and Ang's theory of cultural intelligence names four dimensions: metacognitive CQ, the capacity to notice and reflect on one's own cultural assumptions; cognitive CQ, knowledge and understanding of other cultures; motivational CQ, the inner drive to engage a cross-cultural setting; and behavioral CQ, the practical capacity to adjust one's speech and conduct to the situation at hand. Paul is a living demonstration of all four — he was fully aware of his own cultural assumptions as a Pharisee, and he could shift fluently, with fitting language and imagery, between the Jewish synagogue and the Gentile marketplace. The first lesson of cross-cultural ministry is rarely to rush to speak and teach; it is to first grow quiet and listen for a long season — to learn how a culture understands shame and honor, family and authority, so the seed of the gospel can be planted in real soil, rather than in soil the missionary has merely imagined.

"Contextualization" is a lesson often discussed in cross-cultural ministry — simply put, delivering an unchanging gospel truth in a form the local culture can understand. One missionary, newly arrived in a region that honored royalty, discovered that bowing before elders and honored persons was an ordinary expression of respect there, carrying no religious worship at all, and so adjusted the posture and language of teaching and worship rather than insisting on forms familiar only in the missionary's own home culture. Another missionary, by contrast, mistook customs that were purely cultural for pagan worship and insisted on banning them outright, building an unnecessary wall in the hearts of local believers. Discerning which elements are an adjustable cultural shell and which are a non-negotiable core of faith is the most practical training ground for the "metacognitive" and "cognitive" dimensions of cultural intelligence.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — Cultural Adaptation Is Not Compromising Truth; It Is Taking Off Our Own Sense of Superiority
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, there is a passage in this lesson that must be spoken honestly, because between adaptation and compromise lies a single, thin line, and what decides it is the self.

Missions history carries a painful lesson: some missionaries bound the gospel so tightly to their own home culture that converts were required to give up their given names, their mother tongue, even their dress, exchanging them for the missionary's own cultural forms. This "cultural imperialism" caused wounds that often took generations to heal. A self-centered heart easily turns "I know more" into "I am therefore entitled to decide," forgetting that the gospel enters a culture to set people free, not to reproduce the missionary's own familiar image.

Words that must never be spoken: "Our way of doing things is more advanced — just do it the way we do." "Adapting to local customs is only a formality; there's no need to take it that seriously." "I came here to solve your problems, not to learn from you." Truly healthy cross-cultural ministry takes off its own sense of superiority and walks, with a humble and teachable heart, into a world that was once unfamiliar.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "Our church habitually measures the fruit of a mission field by our own familiar cultural patterns, and rarely spends time understanding the field's real worldview." Language is only the surface layer of culture.

The second question: "Coworkers who are sent out often lack a heart for long-term commitment, and after a few brief months assume they now understand the whole culture." Building cultural intelligence requires genuine, long-term commitment.

The third question: "The relationship between the church and local believers easily and unconsciously becomes one of resource-provider over recipient, rather than equal partnership." Extending the right hand of fellowship is an equal division of labor, not a hierarchy of charity.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "I have come to teach you" for "I will learn from you first." Listening before teaching is the most basic courtesy and wisdom of entering a culture.

The second correction: exchange "reproduce the form I am familiar with" for "adjust the form, guard the core." What may change is the outer form; what may never change is the core truth of the gospel.

The third correction: exchange "one-sided giver" for "equal partner." Division of labor is not a hierarchy; a relay is not permanent leadership by one side.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Cross-Cultural Ministry
sections.html:
Facing the challenge of crossing cultures, different people respond in very different ways from the heart. Let me lay out four hearts side by side — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Holds a prejudiced displeasure toward a cultural group from the outset, even resenting that God has shown that group grace, as Jonah resented God's mercy on Nineveh: "I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful… therefore now, O LORD, please take my life from me." (Jonah 4:2, 3) The proud heart needs to be reminded: the object of God's mercy has never been limited by our own cultural bias.

The Fearful Heart

Shrinks back under group pressure, not daring to hold to convictions once clear in an unfamiliar cultural setting, as Peter withdrew from the Gentile believers for fear of the circumcision party: "He drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party." (Galatians 2:12) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: true unity is never purchased by silent retreat.

The Ashamed Heart

Instinctively wants to avoid crossing a cultural boundary, feeling unclean or unworthy, as Peter at first clung to his own distinction between clean and unclean: "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean." (Acts 10:14) Yet God keeps saying to us again and again: what God has made clean, do not call common.

The Wounded Heart

Has paid a great price in cross-cultural ministry, only to meet misunderstanding or even physical harm, leaving deep scars, as Paul carried the marks of beatings, blows, and dangers throughout his life: "Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one… three times I was beaten with rods." (2 Corinthians 11:24–25) Yet God is able to make these very scars the most powerful mark of gospel witness in the days ahead.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A missionary newly arrived on the field insisted that believers gather in the worship forms he himself was familiar with, and for years the fruit was thin, until he spent an entire year simply observing and learning the local music and rites — only then did worship truly come alive. He said, "I had been planting a seed I knew well, into soil I did not know at all."

The second. A coworker in cross-cultural service was harshly rebuked by a local partner after a cultural misunderstanding, and at one point became so discouraged he wanted to give up, until the church's prayer network walked alongside him. He readjusted his posture, learning to apologize first and explain afterward, and the relationship slowly mended. He said, "Holding on to grievance only builds a wall; only by bowing my head first do I get the chance to take it down."

The third. A mission agency had for many years let the sending church make every decision for the field, then changed strategy, gradually handing leadership back to local believers and stepping back into a supporting role. One of its leaders said, "We finally learned that the most beautiful moment in a relay race is passing the baton securely — not running all the way to the finish line by yourself."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing a mindset are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: this week, find someone from a different cultural background and quietly ask them three questions — simply listen, without rushing to correct or teach.

I declare, I will take off my cultural sense of superiority and become all things to all people, that I might win some.

I declare, I will listen first and teach second, so that the gospel is planted in real soil, not the soil of my own imagination.

I declare, I will build equal partnership with brothers and sisters from different cultural backgrounds, and not be a one-sided giver.

I declare, let Jesus be King, and let all my adaptation and adjustment be for the sake of the gospel; let all glory be given to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may we all learn Paul's wisdom — becoming all things to all people, doing everything for the sake of the gospel, that we might share with them in its blessings. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The three transformations are a road that goes downward. The first transformation drives the point into the mind. The second transformation carries it from the mind into the heart. The third transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the third transformation — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stays only an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority — if time is short, discuss at least this question in each transformation; ★★ = secondary priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked (Required) must not be skipped — it may be completed at home.

First Transformation | Internalized as a Concept (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the point of this lesson into a clear concept.

1. ★ Paul said, "I have become all things to all people," yet at the same time insisted he was "under the law of Christ." What does this show you about understanding "the form may change, the core may not"?

2. ★★ The theory of Cultural Intelligence includes four dimensions: metacognitive, cognitive, motivational, and behavioral. What does this show you about understanding cross-cultural competence as more than just language ability?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "The first lesson of cross-cultural ministry is often to grow quiet and listen for a long season." In your own words, explain why "listening before teaching" matters.

4. ★★ Paul, Barnabas, and the leaders in Jerusalem extended the right hand of fellowship — a division of labor, not a hierarchy. What does this show you about a healthy cross-cultural partnership?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "able to say it," not "answer beautifully." If someone's answer is fragmented, help organize it — don't finish it for them.

Second Transformation | Digested as Life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)

Purpose: through seeing, hearing, thinking, speaking, and acting, digest the concept into life.

[See] See Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — proud (a prejudiced displeasure toward a cultural group from the outset), fearful (shrinking back under group pressure, not daring to hold to a once-clear conviction), ashamed (instinctively wanting to avoid crossing a cultural boundary out of a sense of being unclean or unworthy), wounded (having paid a price in cross-cultural ministry only to meet misunderstanding or harm). Which one are you most like? What experience made you that way?

[Hear] Hear God Speak

6. ★★ For each of these four hearts, God has a word to say. Find the verse that corresponds to you, read it aloud, and then tell the group: where does this word touch you?

[Think] Think Through the Obstacle

7. ★★ Is there someone near you from a different culture or background whom you have not actually taken the time to listen to and understand their world?

[Speak] Say It Out Loud

8. ★ Finish this sentence in one line: "This lesson tore down which old idea I held about 'cross-cultural ministry'?" If your honest answer is "none," say that honestly too — that itself is an important discovery.

[Act] Take a Step

9. ★★ This week, what one concrete thing will you do to practice "becoming all things to all people"? Name the specific content.

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for the wounded and ashamed types — particularly anyone who has been misunderstood in cross-cultural service, or who avoids out of a sense of unworthiness. If someone weeps, pause the discussion and stay with them first — don't rush to give an answer. If it involves a deeper trauma, follow up individually after the meeting and help with referral if needed.

Third Transformation | Transformed into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily practice.

10. ★★ "Whatever I do, I do it all for the sake of the gospel." In your family, is there one thing this week that could become a concrete act of practicing humble learning across cultures?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "What may change is the form; what may never change is the core." How can you find a wise balance this week between adjusting and holding firm?

13. ★★★ Ten minutes a day: this week, spend ten minutes each day praying for a missionary or an unreached people group serving cross-culturally. Name the time slot you will practice this in.

14. ★★ The practice of 920: identify your "2" (a friend or coworker from a different cultural background), and this week do one concrete thing to show them genuine listening and care. Say their name out loud right now.

15. ★★★(Required)

Reproduction task: this week, in three sentences, tell this lesson to someone outside the group — "I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some. I do it all for the sake of the gospel." Write down right now who you will tell.

Closing (5 minutes)

In pairs, tell each other two things: whom you will learn to listen to across cultures this week, and whom you will tell about this lesson. Then pray for one another, asking the Lord to help us all learn to humbly become all things to all people.

ch53.title: Set Apart for Me — Cultivating the Church's Global Vision
ch53.partTitle: Part 11 — Global Missions and the Church's Calling
ch53.intro:
Grace and peace, brothers and sisters. In the last two lessons we talked about how every believer is already on the roster of the Great Commission, and how cross-cultural ministry means taking off our sense of superiority and learning with humility. Today we ask a question about the church as a whole: does a church's vision stop at its own four walls, or can it truly see the weight that every nation, every people, every tribe carries on God's heart? The church at Antioch, recorded in Acts 13, is the best answer to this question.

Acts 13:2–3: "While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, 'Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.' Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off."

sections.heading: 1. A Refugee Church Became the Birthplace of a Mission
sections.html: The origin of the church at Antioch is itself an extraordinary story. Acts 11 records that after the great persecution following Stephen's martyrdom, scattered believers fled to Antioch — a group of people with nowhere else to go — and yet in this foreign place they built a church that would one day become the very birthplace from which Paul and Barnabas were sent out. Acts 13:1 lists the leaders of this church, and the diversity is astonishing: Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus; Simeon was called Niger — the Greek Νίγερ, from the Latin word for "black," most likely marking him as a dark-skinned African believer; Lucius was from Cyrene in North Africa as well; Manaen had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch; and Saul was a Pharisee with rigorous rabbinic training. A group of people utterly different in background, class, and skin color, yet gathered in the same prayer meeting, heard the same voice of the same Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: 2. The Spirit Is the Sender; the Calling Comes in Ordinary Worship; a Full Cycle of Sending and Receiving
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, the vision for global missions is not something a church plans for itself — it is sent out directly by the Holy Spirit. "Set apart for me" — the underlying Greek ἀφορίσατε — casts the church at Antioch in the role of an obedient gardener, not an architect drawing up its own blueprint. Second, the moment this calling came was "while they were worshiping the Lord and fasting" — not at a special missions conference, but in the regular rhythm of daily worship. A global vision that is not lived in the rhythm of everyday worship is very hard to sustain for long. Third, the church at Antioch shows a complete cycle: Acts 11 records them sending relief for the famine in Jerusalem; Acts 13 has them sending Paul and Barnabas out; Acts 14 has them returning to Antioch, gathering the church, and reporting all that God had done through them — care, sending, and reporting back, none of which can be missing.

sections.heading: 3. Sent While Worshiping; Four Concrete Strategies; Confirmed by Contact Theory
sections.html:
The Greek word for "worshiping," λειτουργούντων, is the very root of the English word liturgy. In ancient Greece it originally described a citizen personally funding a public work or a theatrical production, carrying the sense of "costly public service." The Spirit chose to speak precisely within the ordinary rhythm of their "worshiping and fasting," not within a specially planned missions conference — a reminder to the church that a global vision propped up only by an annual missions Sunday can easily degrade into a single event rather than part of the church's daily breathing. Just as a family's healthy eating habits will never truly change if reinforced only by a once-a-year checkup, a global vision, too, must be woven into every week's prayer meeting, every sermon from the pulpit, and every small group's sharing.

Concretely, a church can ground its global vision through four strategies: a missions Sunday, giving distant peoples a concrete face; a prayer network, building a sustained connection between the congregation and the field; short-term mission teams, letting the congregation experience the field with their own hands and feet; and supporting missionaries, turning care into an institutionalized foundation. In 1954 the psychologist Gordon Allport proposed "Contact Theory," arguing that under conditions of equal status, shared goals, mutual cooperation, and institutional support, genuine contact effectively reduces prejudice and psychological distance between groups. These four strategies correspond exactly to the conditions of Contact Theory — a short-term mission team creates real contact under equal cooperation, while a prayer network and missionary support create institutionalized, sustained connection. Without concrete contact, a vision can only remain at the level of abstract knowledge.

It is worth noting that the list of five leaders at the church in Antioch echoes, from a distance, the 235 vision within the 321 framework — not isolated individuals, but interconnected companions, a passing on across generations, and a team of fivefold ministries, together carrying forward the vision God had entrusted to them. Only people who are free of problems and willing to live without self can truly develop the three layers of relationship — companionship, spiritual parents and children, and comrades in arms — and only such people can bear the weight of carrying the gospel to the whole earth. A vision that lives only in one person's passion will not go far; a vision woven into a team that watches over one another can go long and go deep.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — A Global Vision Is Not the Business of a Missions Committee; It Is the Breath of the Whole Church
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, there is a passage in this lesson that must be spoken honestly, because between outsourcing and owning lies a single, thin line, and what decides it is the self.

Many churches hand their missions vision to a single "missions committee" to carry alone, while other departments and most of the congregation comfortably exclude the matter from their own daily attention — as if a family handed the entire responsibility for healthy eating to the one member who does the grocery shopping, while everyone else eats exactly as they please, and the family's overall understanding of health never really changes. A self-centered church easily narrows the missions vision down to the business of one department, rather than the shared breath of the whole body.

Words that must never be spoken: "Missions belongs to the missions committee — it has nothing to do with my small group." "Our church's manpower is limited; let's take care of our own members first." "We hold a missions Sunday once a year — that already counts as taking missions seriously." A truly healthy global vision is woven into the church's weekly rhythm of prayer and worship — it is not an annual routine.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "Our church narrows the concern for global missions down to the business of one department, the missions committee, while most of the congregation has no real overlap with it at all." A vision that belongs to only one department can never grow into the breath of the whole body.

The second question: "Our church's concern for missions stays at the level of occasional fundraising or prayer reminders, lacking a sustained, institutionalized network of connection." Care without institutional support is easily forgotten in the busyness of life.

The third question: "Our church is used to serving the groups we already know well, groups similar to us in status, and lacks real contact and understanding with people from very different backgrounds." Real contact is the most effective path to dissolving prejudice and distance.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "the missions committee's business" for "the breath of the whole church." A global vision needs to be woven into every week's rhythm of prayer and worship.

The second correction: exchange "occasional concern" for "institutionalized connection." A prayer network and missionary support give care a sustained foundation.

The third correction: exchange "a distant people" for "real contact." A short-term mission team and a missions Sunday give an abstract vision a concrete face.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Vision
sections.html:
Facing the task of building a global vision, different people respond in very different ways from the heart. Let me lay out four hearts side by side — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Views a certain culture or group from the outset with a critical, condemning eye, as certain brothers from Jerusalem sharply criticized Peter for eating with Gentiles: "You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them." (Acts 11:3) The proud heart needs to be reminded: the scope of the Spirit's work has never been bound by the cultural lines we draw ourselves.

The Fearful Heart

At the very thought of investing resources in a distant, unfamiliar people, first worries there won't be enough for its own needs, as the disciples calculated in the face of thousands of hungry people: "Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?" (Mark 6:37) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: place what is limited into the Lord's hands, and He can make it more than enough.

The Ashamed Heart

Feels too small and insignificant, convinced that its own group is not qualified to carry a great vision or calling, yet the prophet declared to a people who saw themselves as no more than a worm: "Fear not, you worm Jacob, you men of Israel! I am the one who helps you, declares the LORD." (Isaiah 41:14) God delights in choosing what looks least significant to accomplish what He considers great.

The Wounded Heart

Once carried a great vision, only to be belittled and mocked by the very people closest to it, leaving deep scars, as David's own brother Eliab rebuked him for coming to face Goliath: "Why have you come down? And with whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your presumption and the evil of your heart." (1 Samuel 17:28) God is able to turn a vision despised by the closest kin into the most glorious testimony of the days ahead.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A church treated missions as the sole business of its missions committee for years, with no involvement from any other small group, until it changed course so that each small group took turns adopting a mission field to pray for. Only then did the whole church's temperature toward missions truly begin to rise. A small group leader said, "I used to think a global vision came from hearing one sermon — it turns out it's trained week by week in a small group."

The second. A brother had long felt he was nothing more than an ordinary office worker, not qualified to take part in something as great as missions, until the church invited him to use his own professional skill to remotely help a field with its administrative systems. Only then did he discover he had been part of God's missions blueprint all along. He said, "It turns out God didn't need me to become a missionary — He needed me to offer up the gift I already had."

The third. A church for years had mentioned distant peoples only once a year, on missions Sunday, and the congregation's feeling toward it stayed thin, until it arranged for members to personally join a short-term mission trip. Several members who returned spontaneously formed a prayer group. One participant said, "Once you've seen those faces, praying is no longer reciting an unfamiliar place-name — it's remembering real, specific people."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing a mindset are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: this week, formally add a missionary or a mission field to your own or your small group's regular prayer list, and keep praying for it for one full month.

I declare, a global vision is not only the business of the missions committee — it is my own breath as part of the body of the church.

I declare, I will turn my concern for distant peoples into a sustained, institutionalized connection, and no longer let it rest on a once-a-year reminder.

I declare, I will replace distant imagination with real contact, so that the vision has a concrete face.

I declare, let Jesus be King; may the Lord set me apart for the work He has called me to, whether to stay or to go far away; let all glory be given to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may every one of our churches follow the example of the church at Antioch — hearing the Spirit's sending within the rhythm of everyday worship, and letting the vision expand from our own four walls all the way to every nation on earth. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The three transformations are a road that goes downward. The first transformation drives the point into the mind. The second transformation carries it from the mind into the heart. The third transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the third transformation — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stays only an idea.

First Transformation | Internalized as a Concept (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the point of this lesson into a clear concept.

1. ★ The leadership list at the church in Antioch shows a stunning diversity of background, yet the Spirit sent out Paul and Barnabas from among them. What does this show you about a global vision not being bound by cultural lines?

2. ★★ The Spirit spoke at the moment the church at Antioch was "worshiping the Lord and fasting," not at a special missions conference. What does this show you about a global vision needing to be woven into daily worship?

3. ★★★ This lesson says: "Without concrete contact, a vision can only remain at the level of abstract knowledge." In your own words, explain the difference between "distant imagination" and "real contact."

4. ★★ The church at Antioch shows a complete cycle of care, sending, and reporting back. What does this show you about missions not being able to rest on just one part of that cycle?

Facilitator's reminder: the goal of this section is "able to say it," not "answer beautifully." If someone's answer is fragmented, help organize it — don't finish it for them.

Second Transformation | Digested as Life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)

Purpose: through seeing, hearing, thinking, speaking, and acting, digest the concept into life.

[See] See Yourself

5. ★★★ The message named four hearts — proud (views a certain culture or group from the outset with a critical, condemning eye), fearful (at the thought of investing resources in a distant people, first worries there won't be enough), ashamed (feels too small and insignificant, convinced its own group is unqualified to carry a great vision), wounded (once carried a great vision only to be belittled by the closest people). Which one are you most like? What experience made you that way?

[Hear] Hear God Speak

6. ★★ For each of these four hearts, God has a word to say. Find the verse that corresponds to you, read it aloud, and then tell the group: where does this word touch you?

[Think] Think Through the Obstacle

7. ★★ Right now, is your concern for global missions still at the level of abstract knowledge, or does it have a real face and a real name?

[Speak] Say It Out Loud

8. ★ Finish this sentence in one line: "This lesson tore down which old idea I held that 'a global vision is the missions committee's job'?" If your honest answer is "none," say that honestly too — that itself is an important discovery.

[Act] Take a Step

9. ★★ This week, what one concrete thing will you do to weave a global vision into the daily rhythm of your own life or your small group? Name the specific content.

Facilitator's reminder: questions 5 and 6 may touch wounds, especially for the wounded and ashamed types — particularly anyone whose vision has been belittled, or who has withdrawn out of a sense of smallness. If someone weeps, pause the discussion and stay with them first — don't rush to give an answer. If it involves a deeper trauma, follow up individually after the meeting and help with referral if needed.

Third Transformation | Transformed into Daily Life (about 25 minutes)

Purpose: through discussing practical application, transform life into daily practice.

10. ★★ "Set apart for me… for the work to which I have called them." In your family, is there one thing this week that could become a concrete act of practicing a global vision?

11. ★ Same question, different setting: what about your workplace or school?

12. ★★ The message said: "A vision needs real contact in order to dissolve prejudice and psychological distance." How can you create one instance of real cross-cultural contact this week?

15. ★★★(Required)

Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off." Write down right now who you will tell.

ch54.title: Only You — Resource Management and Support in Missions
ch54.partTitle: Part 11 — Global Missions and the Church's Calling
ch54.intro:
Grace and peace, brothers and sisters. In the last two lessons we talked about how every believer is on the roster of the Great Commission, and how a church cultivates a truly global vision. Today we take up a question that is often overlooked yet enormously important: what actually holds up the person standing on the front lines of missions? The relationship between Paul and the church at Philippi is the most beautiful example we have of resource management and support in missions.

Philippians 4:15, 18: "And you Philippians yourselves know that in the beginning of the gospel, when I left Macedonia, no church entered into partnership with me in giving and receiving, except you only… I have received full payment, and more. I am well supplied, having received from Epaphroditus the gifts you sent, a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God."

sections.heading: 1. A Friendship Recorded in a Ledger: Only You
sections.html: The founding of the church at Philippi is recorded in Acts 16, arising from Paul's Macedonian-vision calling and built through the purple-cloth merchant Lydia, the slave girl freed from a spirit of divination, and the jailer who kept the prison. Years later, writing to them from prison, Paul used an unusually specific phrase: "in giving and receiving" — the underlying Greek λόγον δόσεως καὶ λήμψεως, literally "an account of giving and receiving," was precise bookkeeping language from the commercial correspondence of the day. This is not a vague word of thanks; it is Paul's formal acknowledgment that between himself and the church at Philippi there existed a clear, recordable, mutually accountable partnership — not a fuzzy spiritual sentiment.

sections.heading: 2. An Invisible Support System; Costly Delivery; Health, Not Dependency
sections.html: Today's message turns on three cores. First, Paul, standing on the front line, was in fact standing on top of a vast, nearly invisible support system — the repeated support of the church at Philippi, the hospitality of Priscilla and Aquila who risked their own necks for him, Timothy, Titus, Luke, and Tychicus sharing his burdens, and countless churches praying for him without number. Second, true support often requires a costly, concrete act of delivery — Epaphroditus nearly gave his life to carry the Philippian church's gift into Paul's hands. Third, healthy resource management is built on mutual accountability and empowerment, not on manufacturing long-term, one-sided dependency — before Paul even thanked them for the gift, he first solemnly declared that the secret of his contentment did not lie in the amount of resources he had, but in the One who gave him strength.

sections.heading: 3. The Language of a Fragrant Offering; Empathy and Altruistic Motivation; Four Principles of Health
sections.html:
Paul called the gift the Philippian church sent "a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God" — the underlying vocabulary of fragrant aroma, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God, is exactly the technical language of the sacrificial regulations in Leviticus. Paul lifted a practical gift of resources to the height of sacrificial worship, thoroughly overturning a common myth — the idea that only those standing on the front line truly participate, while those who supply from behind are mere supporting characters. A church quietly giving from home and a missionary risking everything on the front line are, in God's eyes, equally an accepted offering.

The psychologist Daniel Batson proposed the "empathy-altruism hypothesis," distinguishing two motives for helping others: one is to relieve the discomfort we ourselves feel at seeing another person suffer; the other arises from a genuine, felt concern for that other person's actual situation. To truly stir up the latter requires a concrete, real understanding of the other person's circumstances, rather than an obligatory kind of charity. In his letter to the Philippians, Paul is specific about how he himself learned to be brought low and how to abound, having tasted both fullness and hunger — this concrete self-disclosure is exactly what stirs up genuine empathy rather than obligatory giving. Healthy resource management can be summed up in four principles: transparent reporting, so resource flows are clearly visible; mutual accountability, in which both giver and receiver bear responsibility; empowering the local, cultivating local ownership and leadership; and long-range strategic vision, constantly asking whether a given resource is moving toward self-sufficiency or deepening dependency.

Jesus Himself is the most complete demonstration of resource management. He fed five thousand with five loaves and two fish, generous enough that all ate and were satisfied with plenty left over, and yet He still instructed His disciples to gather up the leftover fragments so that nothing would be wasted — generosity and freedom from waste were never in tension in Him. He also freely accepted several women who supported Him and His disciples out of their own means, yet was never controlled or exploited by that provision. He said, "I am among you as the one who serves." (Luke 22:27) The ultimate root of truly healthy resource management is, in the end, not a system or a set of principles, but the humble, serving, generous-yet-unwasteful heart of Jesus Himself.

sections.heading: 4. The Hardest Part of This Lesson — True Support Is Not a Cheap Transfer; It Is Costly Participation
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, there is a passage in this lesson that must be spoken honestly, because between convenience and reality lies a single, thin line, and what decides it is the self.

Today's technology lets giving be completed with just a few clicks — a great blessing, without question — yet it can also easily let giving degenerate into an unfeeling routine: a sum of money is transferred, and we feel we have already done our part, without ever truly remembering the name behind it or offering one serious, considered prayer for that field. A self-centered heart easily reduces support to a mere number, forgetting that Epaphroditus nearly gave his own life to carry the Philippian church's love into Paul's hands.

Words that must never be spoken: "I've already given a sum of money — the rest is no longer my concern." "The missionary's needs are the mission agency's business to handle." "As long as the resources keep flowing in, that's the best kind of support." Truly healthy support connects giving with prayer, connects care with cost — it is never a cold transfer alone.

sections.heading: 5. Three Questions from Our Cultural Context
sections.html:
The first question: "Our church habitually treats giving as the whole of missions support, and rarely builds a sustained network of prayer and care alongside it." Giving without accompanying prayer and care is only a cold number.

The second question: "Our church has for years poured resources one-directionally into a certain mission field, without ever seriously assessing whether this is actually cultivating that field's capacity for self-sufficiency." Resources that only ever flow in, without empowering the local body, will in the end only deepen dependency.

The third question: "Our church generally believes only those standing on the front line truly count as taking part in missions, while the quiet contribution of those who stay behind is treated as second-class participation." The language of a fragrant offering applies equally to those who stay behind and faithfully supply.

sections.heading: 6. Living Out 321: Three Corrections
sections.html:
The first correction: exchange "a cold transfer" for "costly participation." True support connects to concrete care and prayer — it is not only a number.

The second correction: exchange "one-directional, ongoing supply" for "mutual accountability and empowerment." Constantly ask whether a given resource is moving toward self-sufficiency or deepening dependency.

The third correction: exchange "only the front line counts" for "the rear guard is equally a fragrant offering." Faithful supply from behind and sacrifice on the front line are equally accepted in God's eyes.

sections.heading: 7. Four Hearts, One Support System
sections.html:
Facing the task of resource management and support, different people respond in very different ways from the heart. Let me lay out four hearts side by side — perhaps you will see yourself in one of them.

The Proud Heart

Treats giving as a means of showing off its own piety and generosity, secretly hoping to be praised and noticed, as Ananias and Sapphira pretended to offer the full price of their property while secretly keeping back part of it, hoping to gain a good reputation: "With his wife’s knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles’ feet." (Acts 5:1–2) The proud heart needs to be reminded: what God sees is an honest heart, not the outward figure given.

The Fearful Heart

Out of fear that giving will leave it lacking, would rather hold its resources tightly and not truly invest in missions, as the servant who buried his talent, acting out of fear, dared not put to use what his master had entrusted to him: "I knew you to be a hard man… so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground." (Matthew 25:24–25) The fearful heart needs to be reminded: what the Master wants is faithful investment, not fearful burial.

The Ashamed Heart

Because its own resources are limited or its circumstances are difficult, feels unworthy and unqualified to support others, and so quietly withdraws, not daring to share its own struggle with anyone, as the woman with a flow of blood spent everything she had on physicians before, in fear and trembling, pressing through the crowd to touch the Lord's garment: "She had spent all her living on physicians and could not be healed by anyone… she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him." (Luke 8:43, 47) Yet God delights to bear witness before others to even the smallest offering of faith.

The Wounded Heart

Once poured out resources or effort, only to be forgotten or abandoned by the very people it supported, leaving deep scars, as Paul stood utterly alone at his first defense in Rome: "At my first defense no one came to stand by me, but all deserted me." (2 Timothy 4:16) Yet God is able, in the loneliest and most abandoned hour, to stand beside us Himself and grant us strength.

sections.heading: 8. Three True Stories
sections.html:
The first. A sister supported a missionary every month through a fixed online transfer, but for years never once wrote a letter, until the church organized a letter-writing event. Only then did she seriously come to understand that missionary's real circumstances for the first time. She said, "It turns out I had been supporting a name all along, without ever truly knowing the person."

The second. A church had for years continuously funded the entire building cost for a certain field, only to discover years later that the local congregation felt little sense of belonging or participation. It changed strategy, moving to matched support that also required the local congregation to give part of the funds themselves, and their sense of participation truly rose. A pastor said, "We finally understand — fully covering the cost is not the most generous love; empowering love is."

The third. A brother, because of tight financial circumstances at home, had for years felt he had no right to take part in missions giving, until his small group leader encouraged him to start with even a small amount and to keep praying for a missionary. He discovered that the weight of participation is not measured by the amount. He said, "I finally understand — a fragrant offering is judged by the heart, not by the sum."

sections.heading: 9. This Week's Practice and Declaration
sections.html:
The 321 vision reminds us that the eight steps of changing a mindset are: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, reproduction. Today I invite you to do one concrete thing: this week, write a specific letter of care or prayer to a missionary or a field you support — not simply give a sum of money.

I declare, I will turn a simple transfer into costly participation, connected to real care and prayer.

I declare, in supporting missions I will constantly ask myself whether this is moving toward self-sufficiency or deepening dependency.

I declare, I believe the faithful supply of those who stay behind is, in God's eyes, equally a fragrant offering alongside the sacrifice of the front line.

I declare, let Jesus be King; may all my resource management become an offering God receives and delights in; let all glory be given to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may we all learn the example of the church at Philippi, building through costly participation a healthy support system in which front and rear stand together in one heart, mutually accountable to one another. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.

sections.heading: 10. Small Group Discussion: The Three Transformations
sections.html:
Facilitator's note: The three transformations are a road that goes downward. The first transformation drives the point into the mind. The second transformation carries it from the mind into the heart. The third transformation carries it from the heart into daily life. If time is short, cover fewer questions rather than skip the third transformation — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stays only an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority — if time is short, discuss at least this question in each transformation; ★★ = secondary priority; ★ = discuss if time allows. The reproduction task marked (Required) must not be skipped — it may be completed at home.

First Transformation | Internalized as a Concept (about 20 minutes)

Purpose: through discussion, drive the point of this lesson into a clear concept.

1. ★ Paul used the phrase "an account of giving and receiving," precise bookkeeping language from commercial correspondence. What does this show you about missions support being a clear, accountable partnership?

2. ★★ Epaphroditus nearly gave his life to deliver the Philippian church's gift into Paul's hands. What does this show you about "true support is a costly delivery"?
