d17_01.a: This question mistakes “different roles” for “different worth.” Though the narrative focus of the text is on Moses, the decisive action that secured the victory was performed by Aaron and Hur—without them holding up his hands, Israel would have lost to Amalek. 1 Corinthians 12 states it plainly: “if one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together”—in the body, there is no unimportant member, only members with different functions. The hand that raised the staff needed to be seen; the hands that held it up needed to be seen just as much; and Joshua fighting down in the valley needed to be seen just as much too—this victory was won together by three roles, not a one-man performance.
d17_01.pos: After section 1 ‘His Hands Were Steady Until the Going Down of the Sun’

d17_02.q: Since ‘putting all the smartest people on one team actually made them finish last,’ shouldn't a church avoid choosing overly capable people as co-workers, and instead look for people who are somewhat more average, since they'll cooperate better?
d17_02.a: This question misdiagnoses the cause of the “Apollo Syndrome.” What Belbin identified as the problem was never too much intelligence, but too much of a posture in which “everyone wants to lead and win every argument”—that is a self-centered heart bent on winning, not an excess of ability. 1 Corinthians 12 clearly teaches that gifts are, by design, meant to differ and to need one another; God never intended the church to avoid capable people. What should truly be avoided is not ability, but a proud posture unwilling to cooperate and unwilling to let others shine too—when choosing co-workers, what should be valued is giftedness paired with a humble willingness to work together, not ability itself treated as the problem.
d17_02.pos: After section 3 ‘The Oil of Unity, Maturity in the Storm, and the Body That Needs One Another’

d17_03.q: ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them’—does that mean when I'm not praying together with a group of people, the Lord is not present with me when I'm alone?
d17_03.a: This question mistakes “united prayer carries a special promise” for “praying alone lacks God's presence.” What Jesus promises at the end of Matthew 28 is: “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (v. 20). This is a constant promise of presence given to every believer individually, unlimited by number. What Matthew 18:19–20 speaks of is a different, special promise—united, agreeing prayer in community carries a dimension of collective testimony and spiritual power that solitary prayer does not. These two passages are not competing or mutually exclusive; they are two complementary layers of truth: the Lord is always with you, and he also especially delights in and fulfills prayer offered in agreement.
d17_03.pos: After section 3 ‘The Oil of Unity, Maturity in the Storm, and the Body That Needs One Another’

d17_04.q: The lesson says ‘doing everything yourself’ shows a lack of trust in others, but some matters really are critically important—isn't it responsible for a leader to personally oversee them?
d17_04.a: This question equates “necessary oversight” with “doing everything personally.” In Exodus 18, what Jethro advised Moses was not to let go of everything entirely, but to appoint leaders of thousands and of hundreds to bear responsibility at each level, while difficult cases still came to Moses (18:22)—this is precisely healthy oversight: clearly discerning which matters truly need a leader's personal attention and which can be safely entrusted to others. The real problem is not “whether oversight exists,” but “insisting on doing everything oneself, no matter how large or small”—that is what this lesson calls the doing-everything-yourself posture, which confuses delegation with distrust.
d17_04.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson’

d17_05.q: Philippians says not to seek empty glory, but a church organization still needs titles and an order of division of labor—does setting up titles itself count as an expression of the flesh?
d17_05.a: This question equates “having a title” with “craving a title.” 1 Corinthians 14:40 says, “But all things should be done decently and in order”—the church needs clear offices and order so that gifts can each function in their place; this itself is a good design ordained by God, not a problem. What Philippians 2:3 rebukes is a heart of “selfish ambition” and “conceit”—treating a title as a token for showing off or competing. The key to discernment is not whether a title exists, but what is in the heart of the one who holds it: “How can this position serve people?” or “How can this position make me look more important than others?”
d17_05.pos: After the second question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d17_06.q: If I myself am currently in a weak, exhausted season and need to be supported, wouldn't demanding that I go support others first be the last straw that breaks me?
d17_06.a: This question mistakes “first ask whose hands I can hold up” for “you can never ask for help.” Galatians 6:2 says, “Bear one another's burdens”—“one another” is mutual, not a one-sided sacrifice. Even Moses himself grew weary and sat down; it was Aaron and Hur who took the initiative to bring a stone for him to sit on and to hold up his hands—Moses did not pretend he needed no help. The priority this lesson teaches has to do with not always waiting for others to support you first as a default posture, not demanding that you force yourself to support others when you are truly exhausted. Honestly saying that your own hands, too, are growing heavy is just as much a part of a team's genuine cooperation, not a sign of weakness.
d17_06.pos: After the first point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d17_07.q: Galatians says each one should test his own work and take pride in himself alone, not compare with others—but a church really does have differences in the size of people's gifts, so isn't refusing to compare just self-deception?
d17_07.a: This question confuses “honestly recognizing differences in gifts” with “using those differences to define one's own worth.” 1 Corinthians 12 clearly teaches that members' gifts genuinely differ from one another—this is God's deliberate design, not a fact that needs to be erased. Galatians 6:4 says, “But let each one test his own work”—the object of that testing is “Have I been faithful,” not “Am I stronger than he is.” Differences in gifts can be honestly acknowledged, but a person's worth is never determined by the size of their gift—it is determined by God's love and calling. The key to discernment is where your self-examination lands.
d17_07.pos: After the ‘shame type’ in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts’

d17_08.q: That pastor only let go because he was forced to by hospitalization from illness, and only then discovered his co-workers could actually carry things on their own—does this kind of ‘forced delegation’ really produce the same effect as delegation given willingly, out of trust?
d17_08.a: This question equates “an imperfect starting point” with “a meaningless outcome.” Neither Joseph being sold into Egypt nor David being pursued for years was a circumstance either of them chose—yet God still shaped their character and calling through it (Genesis 50:20, “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good”). God often uses unexpected or even crisis situations to accomplish what he already intended to accomplish. That pastor being forced into letting go was not an ideal starting point, but what matters is his response afterward—he chose to keep asking, “who could take my place in this,” turning a crisis into a new habit. That is genuine repentance and growth; it doesn't depend on whether the occasion was chosen or forced upon him.
d17_08.pos: After the first real-life example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d18_01.q: ‘Swearing to your own hurt and not changing’ sounds ideal, but if the original promise was made based on mistaken information, isn't stubbornly refusing to change it just rigid inflexibility?
d18_01.a: This question confuses “the character of keeping one's word” with “being unable to communicate honestly and adjust.” The situation described in Psalm 15 is one where, after making a promise, the cost turns out higher and the deal becomes unfavorable—yet the person keeps their word anyway. It speaks of the character of not breaking a commitment simply because circumstances have shifted in one's favor or not, not a prohibition against honest communication and renegotiation once a genuine mistake is discovered. Healthy promise-keeping includes two possibilities: one is keeping the original agreement even at a cost, and the other is candidly going back to the other party, explaining the situation, and renegotiating a new agreement both sides consent to. What is truly forbidden is disappearing without a word or unilaterally breaking the agreement—not honest, transparent communication and adjustment.
d18_01.pos: After section 1 ‘Who Shall Sojourn in Your Tent? Who Shall Dwell on Your Holy Hill?’

d18_02.q: If someone is very capable and very upright, just somewhat blunt in speech and not very considerate of others' feelings, does that mean their ‘benevolence’ is lacking, and therefore they can't be trusted?
d18_02.a: This question equates “speaking directly” with “lacking benevolence.” Proverbs 27:6 says, “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy.” An honest but unwelcome word may come precisely from sincere benevolence toward you, while someone full of flattering words may actually have ulterior motives. The “benevolence” in a trust model refers to whether this person's motives are genuinely for your good, not whether their manner of expression is pleasant. The key to discerning benevolence is whether this person will stand with you when you need them, not whether their tone is gentle.
d18_02.pos: After section 3 ‘Four Pillars, Three Components, Five Breaches’

d18_03.q: The lesson says a leader who insists on reviewing everything personally shows distrust—but before the early church appointed deacons, weren't they also examined and vetted by the apostles? Where is the line between vetting and distrust?
d18_03.a: This question confuses “a one-time careful selection” with “continuous, ongoing monitoring.” Acts 6 records that the people chose seven men “of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom”; the apostles' vetting was of their qualifications at the moment of selection. Once the selection was settled, the text goes on to record that they simply “appointed them over this business,” entrusting the actual ministry to them completely, without continuing to interfere in every detail. Healthy vetting happens before entrusting responsibility, as careful discernment of a person's character; the real problem is continuing to demand to review everything, no matter how small, after responsibility has already been entrusted—that is stretching a “one-time vetting” into permanent distrust.
d18_03.pos: After section 3 ‘Four Pillars, Three Components, Five Breaches’

d18_04.q: A prayer request mentions someone's difficulty so the group can pray for them together—where is the line between this and ‘gossip’? Does that mean prayer requests can never mention anything specific?
d18_04.a: This question confuses “praying for someone” with “casually disclosing someone else's private matters.” Proverbs 11:13 says, “Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered.” There are two layers to discernment here: first, has this person already agreed—or even personally asked—to have this shared as a prayer request; second, does what is shared stay limited to “the direction that needs prayer” without touching on details the person has not authorized to be made public. A healthy culture of prayer requests seeks the person's consent first, or phrases the need in general rather than specific terms; unrestrained “prayer requests” are often exactly the legitimate-sounding outlet for gossip that this lesson warns against.
d18_04.pos: After ‘gossip’ in section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson’

d18_05.q: After being let down by someone once, is it really unhealthy to become guarded toward everyone? Isn't protecting yourself from being hurt again a wisdom you should have?
d18_05.a: This question equates “wise boundaries” with “total closure.” Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.” Guarding one's heart is indeed a scriptural teaching, and that includes setting appropriate boundaries with people who are unsafe—that is wisdom, not distrust. But the problem this lesson points to is the total closure of “carrying everything alone and no longer daring to entrust anything to anyone”—a guardedness like that shuts out even the trustworthy people God has prepared for you, and ends up blocking the very way God intended to heal your heart through healthy relationships. Wise boundaries are selective caution, not indiscriminate closure.
d18_05.pos: After the third question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d18_06.q: Forgiveness is a decision and rebuilding is a process—but if the other person never shows any concrete action of repentance, am I still ‘required’ to rebuild a relationship with them?
d18_06.a: This question treats “forgiveness” and “rebuilding a trusting relationship” as the same thing. Forgiveness is an unconditional command Scripture gives every believer—Colossians 3:13 says that just as the Lord has forgiven us, so we must forgive others; this is a lesson we work out unilaterally before God and does not need to wait for the other person's repentance. But rebuilding trust and intimacy in a relationship follows a two-way pattern in Scripture—Luke 17:3–4 says, “if he repents, forgive him,” where a repentant response is the necessary condition for rebuilding the relationship. You can fully forgive someone who has not yet repented (no longer holding it against them before God, no bitterness in your heart), while wisely not yet re-entrusting deep trust to them—this is not unforgiveness; it is wisdom.
d18_06.pos: After the third point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d18_07.q: Having been betrayed by someone deeply trusted, the text says to cast your burden on the LORD—but practically speaking, should that person still be given another chance, or is complete separation the way to protect yourself?
d18_07.a: This question bundles “healing the wound” together with “deciding how to treat the person who hurt you” as if they had to be resolved all at once. These two things can actually be handled separately: casting your burden on the LORD refers to the inner release and healing you need, and it doesn't have to wait for a conclusion in the relationship with that person before it can begin; whether to give that person another chance, and how much trust to extend, is a separate decision requiring wisdom, time, and observation, and Scripture gives no one-size-fits-all formula for it. Romans 12:18 says, “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.” The phrase “if possible” already honestly acknowledges that in reality, some relationships may not be able to be fully restored—your healing does not need to wait for that answer to be settled first.
d18_07.pos: After the ‘wounded type’ in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts’

d18_08.q: Financial transparency is well-intentioned, but doesn't laying out every single transaction in the open harm the privacy and the ‘in secret’ spirit of those who give?
d18_08.a: This question confuses “a ministry's overall financial transparency” with “publicizing an individual's giving amount.” Matthew 6's teaching that “your left hand not know what your right hand is doing” concerns an individual not seeking recognition or boasting when they give, protecting the giver's personal motive and privacy. George Müller's practice of financial transparency, by contrast, concerns the public accounting of an organization's overall income and expenses—letting everyone know how the giving “as a whole” was used, not publicizing “who gave how much.” These are two different levels: an individual's giving motive can and should remain private; the overall use of funds should rightly be open and available for anyone to examine—the two are not in conflict.
d18_08.pos: After the third real-life example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d19_01.q: If shining is a declaration of identity rather than something achieved by effort, does that mean believers don't need to deliberately practice holiness—since the identity is already light, won't shining just happen naturally on its own?
d19_01.a: This question mistakes “identity precedes behavior” for “behavior no longer matters.” Matthew 5:16 comes right after “you are the light of the world,” and Jesus immediately says, “Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works.” Identity is the foundation, and good works are the fruit that naturally grows from that identity—but this fruit still needs to be lived out, still needs to be chosen, just as a branch that has already been grafted in and given new life still needs to abide in the vine in order to bear fruit (John 15). Identity makes shining possible—and it also makes it a calling—it does not make practice unnecessary; having identity first is what gives the motivation to keep practicing, identity does not replace practice.
d19_01.pos: After section 1 ‘No One Lights a Lamp and Puts It Under a Basket’

d19_02.q: Paul dares to say, ‘join in imitating me’—wouldn't that kind of confidence seem prideful? Shouldn't an ordinary believer avoid this attitude of ‘inviting people to imitate me’?
d19_02.a: This question equates “daring to invite others to imitate you” with “arrogance.” Paul's confidence has a clear foundation—in that very same letter he had just said of himself, “Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on” (Philippians 3:12); what he invites people to imitate is not a finished, perfect achievement, but an honest posture of running the race. The standard for discerning pride from healthy confidence is that sentence in Galatians 1:10: “Am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God?” If inviting people to imitate you is meant to point them toward Christ, giving them a visible living example, that is not pride; if it is meant to gather followers to yourself and build up your own name, that is the self-centered posture.
d19_02.pos: After section 3 ‘Mirror Neurons, Third-Degree Influence, and the Posture of Running’

d19_03.q: ‘A community's spiritual height rarely exceeds the life-height of its leader’—does that mean if a group's leader isn't good enough, the people following will never have any hope of surpassing him?
d19_03.a: This question confuses “a human leader as the ceiling” with “Christ as the ceiling.” Luke 6:40 says, “A disciple is not above his teacher,” describing the natural limit within a human-to-human relationship of imitation—but this lesson also points out that this verse “has a hopeful side: if the teacher keeps growing, the student's space keeps opening up”—if the leader on earth himself keeps growing in Christ, the ceiling keeps rising. More importantly, the ultimate object of our imitation was never only the human leader in front of us, but, as Hebrews 12:2 says, “looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith”—he has no ceiling, so a community's spiritual height is ultimately never limited by any one finite person.
d19_03.pos: After section 3 ‘Mirror Neurons, Third-Degree Influence, and the Posture of Running’

d19_04.q: If a father admits he was wrong in front of his children, won't that make the children feel their father has no authority and isn't worthy of respect?
d19_04.a: This question equates “authority” with “the illusion of never being wrong.” Truly lasting authority is built on a relationship of trust and love, not on an image that is always right and can never be challenged—the latter is fragile, and shatters completely the moment it is exposed; the former can withstand real breaches and can even be repaired. Jesus set the standard for greatness as “whoever would be first among you must be slave of all” (Mark 10:44)—servant-authority is not built by domination, but by self-giving and honesty. A father who dares to admit he was wrong in front of his children models exactly this true strength—admitting weakness does not lose authority; it builds authority on a firmer foundation.
d19_04.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson’

d19_05.q: Where exactly is the line between honoring and following the teaching and example of a spiritual elder, and ‘deifying’ them? How would I know if I've already crossed it?
d19_05.a: This question touches a real and necessary line to discern between healthy imitation and idolatry. Acts 17:11 records that the Bereans “received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so”—even facing the teaching of the apostle Paul himself, they still examined and verified it against Scripture daily, and this is the attitude Scripture commends. A practical test question is: when this elder's words diverge from Scripture, would you honestly be able to say “no”? If the answer is that you wouldn't dare, that may already have slipped past the line of healthy imitation into deification. Genuinely healthy following is one in which this elder himself keeps directing your gaze toward Scripture and toward Christ, not toward himself.
d19_05.pos: After the first question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d19_06.q: ‘Sustaining a good testimony by sheer willpower is a lamp running out of oil’—does that mean believers don't need self-discipline through willpower at all, and should only act when they ‘feel’ the Spirit's presence?
d19_06.a: This question sets “the Spirit's power” and “the human will” up as opposites. What Galatians 5:16–25 teaches is that “walking by the Spirit” and “putting to death the passions and desires of the flesh” happen together—the Spirit's power does not bypass a person's choosing will; it works through a renewed heart and through the choices a person is willing to make in obedience. The difference lies in the source of the power: relying on willpower alone to grit through is drawing on one's own strength to fight against sinful nature, and it eventually runs dry; drawing on the Spirit for oil means first receiving the Spirit's power, and then using that power to take action and practice—the result still requires action either way, only the source of the power differs.
d19_06.pos: After the second point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d19_07.q: ‘Feeling I'm too young to be qualified as an example’—isn't this a reasonable, humble self-awareness? Why does the text treat it as an attitude that needs to be challenged?
d19_07.a: This question confuses “humble self-awareness” with “avoiding a calling out of fear.” 1 Timothy 4:12 says, “Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.” When God called Timothy to be an example, he did not wait until Timothy was older and more mature—he called him to live out that example now, right where he was. Healthy humility honestly acknowledges there is still much to learn, while still being willing to obey the calling and act; unhealthy fear treats “I'm not qualified yet” as a reason to refuse the calling. The way to tell them apart is simple: humility drives you to depend on God even more as you act; fear only keeps you standing still.
d19_07.pos: After the ‘fear type’ in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts’

d19_08.q: That pastor was ‘stung’ into reconciling by something his child said—if the child hadn't said that, he probably would have kept being distant. Does repentance triggered this passively still count as real repentance?
d19_08.a: This question confuses “the trigger for repentance” with “the genuineness of repentance.” David's repentance in 2 Samuel 12 also only happened after the prophet Nathan confronted him face-to-face with a parable—if not for Nathan's words, “you are the man,” David might have gone on living in self-deception. The genuineness of repentance does not lie in whether the occasion that triggered it was something you discovered on your own or a reminder from an outside source, but in how you respond once reminded—whether you defend yourself and make excuses, or, like David in Psalm 51, submit completely and repent for real. God often uses the people and words he has prepared (even a child's simple question) as instruments of light—what matters is what you choose in that moment.
d19_08.pos: After the first real-life example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d20_01.q: Barnabas welcomed Saul when everyone else in the church was afraid of him—if Saul had later not truly repented and had instead taken advantage of the church's trust, wasn't this kind of ‘unexamined’ welcome by Barnabas too great a risk?
d20_01.a: This question overlooks the fact that the text itself records signs of examination—“but Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus” (Acts 9:27). Barnabas did not accept him with no examination at all—he first listened to Saul's full testimony before bringing him to the apostles. And grace itself does carry the real risk of being betrayed—in Luke 15, the father who saw his prodigal son far off ran and embraced him and kissed him, likewise embracing him while the evidence of his repentance was still very limited. Taking the risk of accepting someone is the very nature of grace, not an oversight unique to Barnabas.
d20_01.pos: After section 1 ‘Only Barnabas — A Life of Encouragement’

d20_02.q: The bucket-and-dipper theory sounds a lot like secular positive psychology—reducing the encouragement taught by faith down to a ‘psychological technique’—wouldn't citing it this way weaken the authority of Scripture's own teaching?
d20_02.a: This question mistakes “explaining scriptural truth in contemporary language” for “letting psychology replace scriptural authority.” Before this lesson cites the bucket-and-dipper theory, it has already cited Proverbs 12:25, “A good word makes [the heart] glad”—this ancient verse had already stated the same principle; the psychological research merely verifies and illustrates, in a modern way, wisdom Scripture had already revealed. The order is Scripture first, science confirming afterward, not science replacing Scripture. As the 321 vision often says, “follow the Spirit with your heart, don't rely on your own reasoning with your head”—citing insights from common grace to help people grasp God's word more concretely does not conflict with depending on the Spirit's guidance; it is a different expression of the same truth.
d20_02.pos: After section 3 ‘A Good Word Makes the Heart Glad, the Bucket and the Dipper, and the Science of Gratitude’

d20_03.q: The nine lepers who were healed but did not come back to give thanks—Jesus did not take back their healing—so does that mean gratitude actually isn't that important, since the grace was already given anyway?
d20_03.a: This question confuses “the validity of grace” with “the relational fruit that gratitude brings.” All ten men's bodies really were cleansed, and God did not take that back; but Jesus said one further thing to the Samaritan who came back, something the other nine never heard: “Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well” (Luke 17:19). This points to something deeper than bodily cleansing—a relationship built personally with Jesus himself. Gratitude is not the condition for grace to take effect, but it is the path that walks grace out into relationship; failing to give thanks does not cost you the grace you've already received, but it may cause you to miss that deeper blessing that is only received by turning back to the Lord's presence.
d20_03.pos: After section 3 ‘A Good Word Makes the Heart Glad, the Bucket and the Dipper, and the Science of Gratitude’

d20_04.q: Publicly praising a particular co-worker—won't that make other co-workers who quietly contribute without being specifically mentioned feel overlooked or compared unfavorably?
d20_04.a: This question points to a real risk in public praise that deserves to be honestly faced, not dismissed. This lesson itself reminds us to “criticize privately, face to face; praise publicly, far and wide”—but that does not mean praise can be given carelessly, without any wisdom. In practice, two things can be done deliberately: first, consciously take turns seeing different people, not always praising the most visible service; second, when praising, clearly give the credit to God (“I thank God for you”) rather than creating an atmosphere of comparison and ranking. This lesson gives a direction in principle, not an operating manual that disregards others' feelings—wise care in applying it is still needed.
d20_04.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson’

d20_05.q: If someone rarely offers praise and only corrects when something goes wrong, doesn't that just mean this person holds especially high standards and is being tough for the other person's own good?
d20_05.a: This question equates “high standards” with “a practice of only correcting, never building up.” The bucket-and-dipper theory reminds us that a bucket which is only ever dipped from and never filled will eventually run dry—a person who is only ever corrected and never affirmed, no matter how high the standard, often ends up discouraged and leaving, rather than being shaped into something better. Hebrews 3:13 says, “But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called ‘today,’ that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.” Healthy high standards hold correction and affirmation together—concretely affirming what's right, honestly pointing out what's wrong; correction with no affirmation at all is not a high standard, it is an empty bucket that gradually hardens the heart.
d20_05.pos: After the second question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d20_06.q: ‘I thank God for you’ sounds more spiritual than ‘you're amazing,’ but wouldn't saying it that way come across as too formulaic and not natural or sincere enough?
d20_06.a: This question mistakes “a specific way of expressing something” for “the only fixed formula.” This lesson's point that “I thank God for you” is better than “you're amazing” is about the underlying principle of encouragement “pointing to God” rather than “pointing to oneself”—it is not asking you to mechanically repeat that exact sentence. Sincerity matters far more than the phrasing—you can absolutely use your own natural, habitual way of speaking to express gratitude, as long as the focus of your heart clearly rests on God's grace rather than creating in the other person a dependence on or admiration for you. The principle is the skeleton; your sincerity and natural language are the flesh and blood—both need to be present together, or it will come across as hollow or formulaic.
d20_06.pos: After the first point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d20_07.q: James says jealousy and rivalry bring disorder, but seeing someone who worked less than I did receive more praise—is that feeling of ‘unfairness’ entirely sin? Couldn't it also be a reasonable longing for fairness?
d20_07.a: This question confuses “feeling a sense of unfairness” with “letting jealousy grow unchecked.” In Matthew 20's parable of the workers in the vineyard, the workers who came early do genuinely complain: “You have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat” (v. 12). Jesus does not deny the gap they feel; he gently points out instead, “Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me?” The feeling itself is not sin, and bringing that feeling honestly before God is not sin either; what becomes sin is letting that sense of unfairness ferment into bitterness, refusing to rejoice in another's good, refusing to speak words that build others up. The key to discernment is not whether you have this feeling, but how you handle it once you do.
d20_07.pos: After the ‘pride type’ in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts’

d20_08.q: Every meeting ending with a fixed practice of ‘invite everyone to specifically thank one group member’—won't this kind of structured, routine gratitude gradually become just a formality and lose its sincerity?
d20_08.a: This question touches a real tension present in any spiritual practice—structure can nurture a habit, but it can also degenerate into an empty ritual. But this lesson itself offers a clue for testing this: after six months, the group members said, “now we look forward to coming to the gathering more, because we know we'll be seen”—this statement shows that this fixed practice is bearing the fruit of genuine building-up, not empty formality. Any regular practice, including daily prayer or weekly worship, can slide into formality, and can also become a channel for training the heart—the difference is not whether there is a fixed structure, but whether the leader keeps paying attention and deliberately varying it, keeping the specific content of each occasion genuine and fresh rather than reciting from a script.
d20_08.pos: After the third real-life example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d21_01.q: The Great Commission has only one main verb, ‘make disciples’—so does that mean ‘go’ and ‘baptize’ aren't important, and can be treated as optional?
d21_01.a: This question mistakes “the grammatical main verb” for “the other verbs don't matter.” In the original grammar, “go,” “baptizing,” and “teaching” are participles, but they are the indispensable concrete means by which the goal of “make disciples” is accomplished—without going, there is no contact; without baptizing, there is no public commitment; without teaching them to obey, disciples remain merely seekers. These three participles are not optional decoration but the very path by which the main verb is achieved—much like saying “he ran to save someone”: “ran” isn't decoration for “save,” it's how the saving happens. The bullseye of the Great Commission is making disciples, but that bullseye is only hit through going, baptizing, and teaching obedience—leave any one out, and it's incomplete.
d21_01.pos: After section 1 ‘All Authority in Heaven and on Earth Has Been Given to Me’

d21_02.q: A system needs to answer four questions (where does the next step go, who walks with him, what counts as maturity, and who does he lead once mature)—won't this ‘institutionalize’ and ‘proceduralize’ an organic life relationship, losing spiritual freedom?
d21_02.a: This question equates “having a clear path” with “losing the freedom of life.” Jesus himself appointed twelve to “be with him” — this itself was a clear rhythm of discipleship, yet without a trace of rigidity: how he related to Peter and to John was clearly adjusted to each man's own temperament. A system functions like a trellis in a vineyard—the trellis itself doesn't bear fruit, but a branch with no trellis easily droops to the ground, rots, and gets trampled. A clear path is not meant to replace the Spirit's leading, but to prepare a stable space for the Spirit's work so that life doesn't end up scattered with nowhere to root—freedom and structure were never mutually exclusive opposites.
d21_02.pos: After section 2 ‘The Mission of Making Disciples, Jesus's System, and the Path of Multiplication’

d21_03.q: Deliberate practice needs a coach's real-time feedback—so if I truly can't find a suitable spiritual coach or discipleship partner nearby, does that mean I have no way to really grow?
d21_03.a: This question treats “one fixed coach” as the only channel for growth. Hosea 6:3 says, “Let us know; let us press on to know the LORD.” God's word itself is the most constant, always-available coach—the Spirit illuminating, reminding, and rebuking through Scripture is a resource every believer can draw on, unlimited by the availability of human companions. Beyond that, the brothers and sisters in a community, even when they are not formal discipleship coaches, can often become mirrors God uses in ordinary daily interaction and honest conversation. A season in which you truly cannot find a formal coach does not mean growth has stalled—only that the channel of growth has taken a different form.
d21_03.pos: After section 3 ‘Scaffolding, Deliberate Practice, and the Multiplication of Four Generations’

d21_04.q: Multiplication discipleship takes thirty years to reach a scale of a billion people—so should the church completely abandon large evangelistic crusades and rapid-growth methods, and only do discipleship?
d21_04.a: This question mistakes “which has more long-term staying power, addition or multiplication” for “addition has no value and should be abolished.” Acts 2 records three thousand baptized in a single day at Pentecost—that is precisely explosive, “addition”-style growth—and the text immediately continues that these three thousand “devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching,” entering the life of discipleship that very day. Addition and multiplication were never a competing either/or: large gatherings can scatter the seed of the gospel quickly and widely, while the multiplying system of discipleship is responsible for rooting, growing, and reproducing the seed that has been scattered. A healthy church has both—reaping through addition, rooting through multiplication.
d21_04.pos: After section 3 ‘Scaffolding, Deliberate Practice, and the Multiplication of Four Generations’

d21_05.q: Treating ‘each person’ individually takes a lot of time—so once a church grows large, is real discipleship simply impossible, leaving only large-group teaching as an option?
d21_05.a: This question overlooks the very solution this lesson itself proposes—the four-generation multiplication path is designed precisely to resolve the tension between “scale” and “individual attention.” The chain in 2 Timothy 2:2 doesn't require one pastor to personally shepherd every single person in the church individually; rather, the pastor individually shepherds a few faithful people, and those few each individually shepherd the next group, generation after generation spreading outward—no matter how large a church grows, each “one-on-one” or “one-on-a-few” node can still be genuine, in-depth, retail-level discipleship, without any one person having to shoulder wholesale-style teaching of everyone alone.
d21_05.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson’

d21_06.q: Beyond attending class and turning in assignments, what does ‘life follow-up’ actually look like in practice—does every single thing have to be followed up on to the end to count?
d21_06.a: This question mistakes “life follow-up” for “monitoring every last detail.” Real life follow-up is not centered on tracking every detail, but on asking one kind of question consistently and honestly: “What you heard and learned last time—did you actually go and do it? What difficulties did you run into?” James 1:22 says, “But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.” The point of follow-up is helping the other person continually move what they've heard into what they do, not managing every aspect of their life for them—a simple, regular rhythm of asking often drives the growth of life more solidly than exhaustive, detail-by-detail supervision.
d21_06.pos: After the first question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d21_07.q: Paul says, ‘our sufficiency is from God’—but in actual practice, don't you need to be equipped with methods and skills first before you dare to start leading someone?
d21_07.a: This question confuses “necessary preparation” with “perfect skill as the threshold for starting.” A reasonable amount of preparation is certainly helpful, but the starting point of the chain in 2 Timothy 2:2 is “faithful men who will be able to teach others also”—the emphasis is on faithfulness, not a full set of skills. Peter and John were “uneducated, common men” (Acts 4:13), yet were greatly used by God. A large part of the ability to lead someone is actually grown through the real process of leading them, learning and growing step by step by God's grace—if you wait until you feel your skills are fully complete before you dare begin, that day may never come; taking the first step in faithfulness is often exactly where real ability begins to grow.
d21_07.pos: After the ‘fear type’ in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts’

d21_08.q: That sister's rigid method caused the other person to leave the church—does that mean the responsibility for the failure of discipleship falls entirely on the one leading?
d21_08.a: This question confuses “a leadership approach that can be improved” with “the outcome being entirely the leader's fault alone.” In the parable of the sower in Luke 8, the same sower scatters the same seed onto four different kinds of soil, and the results are vastly different—the seed and the act of sowing are the same; the difference lies in the condition and response of the soil itself. This reminds us that the outcome of a discipleship relationship is never determined unilaterally—the willingness and response of the person being discipled is just as important a factor. A leader should certainly examine honestly whether their method needs adjusting, but they need not carry all of the other person's choices on their own shoulders alone—doing so would leave a person too afraid to ever try leading anyone again.
d21_08.pos: After the second real-life example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d22_01.q: Even Samuel got it wrong—so should a church select leaders by disregarding external qualifications (education, eloquence, appearance) entirely, and look only at the invisible heart?
d22_01.a: This question mistakes “you can't judge by appearance alone” for “external qualifications don't matter at all.” In Exodus 18, the list Jethro proposed includes “able men” as one of four qualifications, but it comes after the three character qualifications of fearing God, being trustworthy, and hating dishonest gain—Scripture never teaches that ability doesn't matter; it clearly points out that character takes priority over ability, and that outward impressions must never be allowed to replace the examination of the heart. Healthy selection looks at both, only the order cannot be reversed: first ask whether this person's character is trustworthy, then look at whether their gifting fits the role—rather than being won over at first sight by eloquence or appearance, skipping the examination of the heart.
d22_01.pos: After section 1 ‘The Eighth One Who Was Overlooked’

d22_02.q: The Peter Principle says people are often promoted to a position they can't handle—does that mean a church should avoid giving faithful servants greater responsibility, to keep them from being ‘promoted into failure’?
d22_02.a: This question mistakes “avoiding a mismatched promotion” for “simply not promoting anyone at all.” What the Peter Principle points to as the problem is not promotion itself, but the mismatched approach of “promoting someone who sings well to worship leader” — judging only by current performance without regard for differences in gifting; leading people and doing one thing well are two different gifts. The truly wise approach is not to leave faithful people standing still, but to honestly assess before promoting: does this person's gifting genuinely fit the abilities the new role requires, rather than simply equating “does the current job well” with “can lead.”
d22_02.pos: After section 3 ‘Four Signs, the Peter Principle, and the Heart of a Spiritual Parent’

d22_03.q: Elisha's ‘slaughtering the oxen and burning the plow equipment,’ cutting off any way back so decisively—does that mean everyone who is called must make some equally dramatic, no-turning-back gesture for it to count as a real response to the call?
d22_03.a: This question equates “the outward form of Elisha's response” with “a necessary condition for responding to a call.” When Peter, James, and John were called, the text says only that they “immediately left their nets and followed him” (Matthew 4:20)—no burning of boats, no destroying of fishing gear—and they would in fact go back to fishing later on (John 21). What is truly required is total surrender and following in one's heart, not some dramatic outward gesture. Elisha's choice to slaughter the oxen and burn the equipment was his own personal way of expressing his resolve to God; what God values is whether each person's heart genuinely hands over control, while the outward form that expression takes can vary according to each person's circumstances.
d22_03.pos: After section 3 ‘Four Signs, the Peter Principle, and the Heart of a Spiritual Parent’

d22_04.q: ‘Fear of being surpassed’ sounds like a negative emotion, but worrying that a successor lacks experience and fearing something might go wrong for the church—isn't that a responsible, reasonable consideration?
d22_04.a: This question confuses “a reasonable, cautious consideration” with “continually finding reasons to delay.” The key to discernment is not whether risk is being considered, but whether that consideration leads you to “actively prepare your successor” or becomes an excuse that keeps getting postponed. A practical test question is: over this past stretch of time, have I proactively arranged opportunities for him to gain experience and given him specific feedback, or have I just kept saying “he's not ready yet” without any concrete developmental action? Saul's hostility toward David did not come from cautious consideration—it was that upon hearing the people's praise, he “was very angry” (1 Samuel 18:8). True responsibility means treating risk as content for a development plan, not as a reason to refuse succession.
d22_04.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson’

d22_05.q: If a younger, not-yet-mature co-worker is given a chance to gain experience, and that really does lead to a mistake causing loss, whose responsibility should that be counted as?
d22_05.a: This question touches a real risk that inevitably accompanies developing new people, and deserves to be honestly faced. After Elijah called Elisha, he did not immediately hand over the whole prophetic office to him, but instead there was a long season in which Elisha “followed Elijah and served him” (2 Kings 3:11)—this is exactly the wisdom of “providing cover” that this lesson describes: letting him step into the role while still standing behind him, offering necessary guidance and oversight, rather than leaving him to bear everything alone with no preparation. Healthy development gradually reduces the proportion of hands-on accompaniment through tiered delegation, keeping risk within a bearable range, rather than avoiding all risk entirely—growth inevitably comes at some cost; wisdom lies in minimizing that cost, not avoiding it altogether.
d22_05.pos: After the second question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d22_06.q: ‘He must increase, but I must decrease’ was said by John the Baptist about Jesus—isn't applying this verse to succession between ordinary people pitching it too high, too idealized?
d22_06.a: This question mistakes “this verse's original object was Christ” for “it cannot be applied to relationships between people.” Philippians 2:3 says, “count others more significant than yourselves”—this is a principle Paul explicitly teaches for how believers are to treat one another, and John's statement about Jesus is precisely the ultimate example of that principle lived out. Applying it to the situation of succession is not meant to elevate a successor to a status equal with Christ, but to borrow John's posture of willingly stepping aside and rejoicing in another's flourishing as a measure of heart every leader handing off responsibility can imitate—the principle carries over, while the object and degree naturally adjust according to the actual relationship; it doesn't need to match word for word.
d22_06.pos: After the second point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d22_07.q: Psalm 27:14, ‘Wait for the LORD,’ sounds passive—so should someone called to take on greater ministry but who feels timid just keep ‘waiting’ indefinitely, without needing to proactively take the first step?
d22_07.a: This question mistakes “waiting that depends on God” for “inaction and delay.” “Wait for the LORD” in the Psalms never means doing nothing at all—it means placing the focus of your heart's dependence on God rather than on your own limited ability, and the result of this waiting is being “strong” — it is preparation for action, not a substitute for it. When God called Moses, he also gave him a specific, immediate next step (Exodus 3:10); while reminding Timothy not to neglect his gift, Paul also specifically instructed him to fan it into flame (2 Timothy 1:6). Waiting is the posture of the heart's dependence; taking the first step is the action that dependence naturally produces—the two are not in conflict.
d22_07.pos: After the ‘fear type’ in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts’

d22_08.q: That statement, ‘I see the hand of God on you,’ changed that sister's life forever—but if I say something similar to someone and nothing about them changes at all, does that mean my observation or what I said had no value?
d22_08.a: This question ties “speaking a word of encouragement” together with “the other person immediately showing obvious change” as the measure of value. In the parable of the sower, the same sower scatters the same seed, and it lands on different soils with vastly different results (Luke 8:5–15)—the value of the seed is not diminished just because some soils didn't respond. Whether an honest word of affirmation you speak bears immediately visible fruit is affected by many factors beyond your control, including the other person's current state of life and timing. Your responsibility is to sow faithfully—paying attention, speaking honestly—while when this seed sprouts, or even whether it quietly sprouts only years later, that sovereignty belongs to God, not to you.
d22_08.pos: After the third real-life example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d23_01.q: ‘Put some of your authority on him’ — this word ‘some’ sounds like giving only part, not all — does that mean the older generation can actually keep back some authority and not have to hand it over completely?
d23_01.a: This question mistakes “some” for “deliberately holding back and unwilling to fully delegate.” Numbers 27:21 goes on to record that Joshua, going forward, would still “stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before the LORD”—this shows that “some” describes a healthy, orderly distribution of authority (Joshua held real governing authority while still working within the established structure alongside the priest), not the older generation privately withholding authority. The real issue is not whether honor is granted in stages, structured by office, but whether the granting is public, genuine, and clearly visible—Moses gave thoroughly in the sense that he unreservedly established Joshua's authority before the whole assembly, not that he crammed every last bit of authority into Joshua alone.
d23_01.pos: After section 1 ‘Lest the Congregation of the LORD Be as Sheep That Have No Shepherd’

d23_02.q: Elisha asked for ‘a double portion of your spirit’ — this desire to ‘surpass the one before him’ — wouldn't that seem disrespectful toward the previous generation, too self-inflated?
d23_02.a: This question equates “longing for greater spiritual fruit” with “disrespect toward the previous generation.” Elisha's request was not spoken casually—it was made only after years of following Elijah and pouring water for his service (2 Kings 3:11)—that long-term service was itself the deepest form of respect for the previous generation. And a “double portion” in the Law was the right of the firstborn to inherit the estate (Deuteronomy 21:17); what Elisha asked for was not to replace Elijah's position, but to receive and continue the spiritual inheritance Elijah left behind, so that God's work would keep expanding through his hands. A truly humble heart toward succession is one that serves faithfully beforehand while also holding a faith-filled longing for greater fruitfulness in God's kingdom—the two are not in conflict.
d23_02.pos: After section 3 ‘Fruitfulness and Multiplication, a Double Portion of the Spirit, and the Relay of Generations’

d23_03.q: ‘Generational difference isn't a matter of who's right and who's wrong’ — does that mean a church, when facing disagreements over truth itself (not just cultural preference), should likewise treat it as generational difference and just accommodate it, without needing to debate what's right?
d23_03.a: This question confuses “differences in cultural style” with “disagreement over truth itself.” The generational difference this lesson speaks of refers to things like styles of worship or ways of communicating—things that naturally change over time and that Scripture gives no explicit rule about. Jude 3, however, clearly teaches that when it comes to the faith itself, believers are “to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints”—truth cannot be relativized just because generations differ. When Paul says in 1 Corinthians 9 that he “became all things to all people,” he too is speaking of flexibility in strategy and approach tailored to different people, not compromising on the content of truth. The key to discernment is: is this a truth Scripture clearly teaches, or a cultural expression Scripture gives no explicit rule about, which can be adapted to the times?
d23_03.pos: After section 3 ‘Fruitfulness and Multiplication, a Double Portion of the Spirit, and the Relay of Generations’

d23_04.q: Absalom's impatience and seizing the throne is clearly a bad example—but if the older generation truly refuses to hand over leadership for a long time and it's holding the church back, does the next generation really have no legitimate way to move the transition forward besides just ‘waiting’?
d23_04.a: This question mistakes “not seizing or grabbing power” for “doing absolutely nothing but passively waiting.” Although David was pursued by Saul for years, he consistently refused to raise his hand against Saul (1 Samuel 24)—yet he was not entirely passive either; he honestly expressed his situation through Jonathan (1 Samuel 20), and sought out the truth through appropriate timing and channels. Healthy and appropriate ways to move things forward include: honestly and respectfully communicating your own observations and burden face-to-face with the older generation, seeking the help of elders or overseers within the church's governance structure to mediate the conversation, and continuing to faithfully prepare in your own position—these are all legitimate paths. What is truly forbidden is doing what Absalom did: secretly winning people's hearts and seizing power through scheming.
d23_04.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson’

d23_05.q: Concretely, how do you tell whether something is a disagreement over truth, or just a difference in cultural style?
d23_05.a: This question raises a very practical issue in application, one worth building a clear habit around. A useful test is to ask honestly: does Scripture give an explicit command or a clear principle governing this matter? If it does—for example, the object of worship, the way of salvation, or moral boundaries—this falls within the realm of truth, not to be compromised due to generational or cultural differences. If Scripture gives no explicit rule and it is simply a habit or preference that has developed over time within a particular generation or cultural group—for example, what instruments are used in worship, dress expectations for gatherings, or how direct or indirect communication should be—this typically falls within the cultural realm, which can be adjusted according to time and place. The Jerusalem Council in Acts 15 operated exactly this way: the essence of the gospel (justification by faith) was not open to compromise, but whether Gentiles needed to keep all of Moses's ceremonial regulations was something that could be adjusted according to circumstance.
d23_05.pos: After the first question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d23_06.q: ‘Stepping back into the position of intercessor’ sounds like laying down all responsibility—so after stepping down, if the elder sees the successor clearly making a major wrong decision, are they completely forbidden from speaking up again?
d23_06.a: This question mistakes “stepping down” for “no longer being able to have any response at all.” The real meaning of stepping down is no longer holding final decision-making power or the office of governance—not cutting off every possibility of honest communication. Proverbs 27:6 says, “Faithful are the wounds of a friend.” An elder who has already stepped down can still express their observations and reminders privately and respectfully, speaking as a faithful friend would—the difference is that this reminder no longer carries the coercive force of an office; the final decision and the responsibility it carries now genuinely belong to the successor. A healthy stepping-down hands over “decision-making power,” without also withdrawing “care and honesty.”
d23_06.pos: After the first point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d23_07.q: Psalm 51:17 says, ‘a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise’ — but for someone who rushed ahead, grabbing at position and hurting the community's relationships, shouldn't they also make concrete restitution through action? Is inward regret alone enough?
d23_07.a: This question equates “the inward repentance God values” with “no need for concrete outward repair.” Psalm 51:17 speaks of the starting point of God receiving a repentant person—he does not despise a truly broken and contrite heart, and this is an indispensable first step of complete repentance. But after Zacchaeus met Jesus, the concrete expression of his repentance was: “if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19:8)—inward repentance naturally produces concrete outward correction and restoration. Truly complete repentance requires both layers: first a broken and contrite heart that God receives, and then, wherever within one's ability, honestly apologizing to those who were hurt, clarifying, and doing one's best to repair the relationship—regret of heart alone, with no action of repair, is incomplete repentance.
d23_07.pos: After the ‘shame type’ in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts’

d23_08.q: That senior pastor was forced to hand off leadership only because of illness—if his health had stayed fine all along, might he never have handed it off willingly for his whole life?
d23_08.a: This question honestly points to a common and worth-heeding pattern—many important changes really do happen only under the pressure of crisis. This lesson reminds us that healthy succession should not depend on crisis as its occasion, but should be practiced proactively and intentionally through the four actions of laying on hands, honoring, walking alongside, and blessing. God does indeed often use unwelcome circumstances like illness or accidents to push forward change that should have happened sooner—but that doesn't mean we can bank on this and simply wait for a crisis to force our hand. The real lesson of this example is an invitation for every reader to honestly ask themselves: am I also relying on the luck of “nothing has gone wrong yet” to delay a succession task that should actually begin proactively right now?
d23_08.pos: After the first real-life example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d24_01.q: Paul says he is suffering birth pains ‘again’ — meaning that after new birth, believers' Christlike shape hasn't yet grown to completion — so to what degree exactly does something count as ‘formed’? Is there an endpoint?
d24_01.a: This question mistakes “Christ being formed” for a task that can be fully completed and checked off in this life. Philippians 1:6 says, “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.” Paul clearly points out that the completion of this formative work happens at “the day of Jesus Christ”—that is, the moment the Lord returns and believers are glorified—not at some point in this present life. This reminder is not meant to discourage; rather it is a kind of freedom—you don't need to reach some “completed” standard in this life to feel secure; you simply keep being shaped in that direction, and the work of formation will only truly be complete on the day you stand face to face with the Lord.
d24_01.pos: After section 1 ‘What You Signed Was Not a Teaching Contract, But a Mother's Heart’

d24_02.q: ‘Neuroplasticity’ is brain science—comparing spiritual growth to the rewiring of neural circuits—won't that reduce a spiritual mystery to a purely physiological mechanism, losing the supernatural dimension of the Spirit's work?
d24_02.a: This question mistakes “using science to explain a mechanism God designed” for “denying the Spirit's supernatural work.” God made human beings as unified creatures of body, mind, and spirit; the brain rewiring its circuits through repeated practice is itself one of the ways God designed this creature to function—it is not a separate system competing with the Spirit's work. Just as eating leads to digestion and exercise strengthens muscles, neuroplasticity describes a natural law God set in place at the level of creation, while the Spirit's work is renewing, above and within this created mechanism, the invisible thoughts and spiritual life inside a person—science describes “how it works” as God designed it; Scripture reveals “who is truly at work behind it and gives it meaning”—these are different levels of truth, not mutually exclusive.
d24_02.pos: After section 3 ‘Neuroplasticity, the Tree by the Stream, and Abiding in Him’

d24_03.q: ‘Abiding in me’ sounds very abstract—practically speaking, with a whole day of work and household duties, how do you concretely ‘abide’?
d24_03.a: This question mistakes “abiding in the Lord” for a state that has to be continuous, unbroken, and cut off from the world. Brother Lawrence in the seventeenth century, washing pots and cooking in the kitchen for thirty years, practiced by deliberately, briefly turning his mind toward God in every ordinary, trivial task, simply “doing it for the love of God”—he said that he found God amid the noise of his kitchen just as truly as if he were kneeling at the altar. This shows that “abiding” does not require you to be constantly murmuring prayers or stopping whatever you're doing—it is a repeated, brief, always-available turning of the mind: meditating on a word from God while washing dishes, turning your thoughts to gratitude during your commute, entrusting yourself to God in a single sentence before a meeting—through countless small, repeated turnings, you live out the daily rhythm of abiding with the Lord.
d24_03.pos: After section 3 ‘Neuroplasticity, the Tree by the Stream, and Abiding in Him’

d24_04.q: Knowledge, busyness, and experience are all listed as ‘detours that disguise themselves well’—does that mean things like earnestly studying Scripture, committing to service, and attending conferences are all inherently problematic and should be reduced?
d24_04.a: This question mistakes “these things can be mistaken for the destination” for “these things are inherently problematic.” 1 Corinthians 8:1 says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up”—Paul does not deny the value of knowledge; he himself was a teacher full of scriptural knowledge. What he points to as the problem is that knowledge, without producing love, swells into pride. In the same way, earnestly studying Scripture, committing to service, and attending conferences are all normal and precious channels of grace given by God; what this lesson wants to point out is not that these practices should be reduced, but that we should honestly examine: are these practices actually producing the fruit of “becoming more like Christ,” rather than being mistaken for proof of spiritual maturity itself.
d24_04.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson’

d24_05.q: If a church measures commitment by how busy someone is in ministry, is that really entirely wrong? After all, Scripture also teaches diligent service—isn't laziness a problem too?
d24_05.a: This question confuses “diligent service itself is a virtue” with “using the level of busyness to measure spiritual commitment.” Romans 12:11 indeed says, “Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord”—diligent service is an explicit teaching of Scripture, and laziness really is a problem that needs to be dealt with. What this lesson wants to point out is not that there is too much service, but the habit of “using the busyness of service as an excuse to avoid quietly drawing near to God”—letting outward busyness replace the more fundamental task of building a genuine relationship with the Lord. True and healthy diligence is service that naturally flows out of the fruit borne from abiding in the Lord, not using a show of service to prove or cover up an inward spiritual emptiness.
d24_05.pos: After the second question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d24_06.q: Of the four channels—word, prayer, community, and obedience—if I really can't practice them regularly this season because of a special circumstance (illness, raising young children), does that necessarily mean my spiritual life will decline?
d24_06.a: This question treats “the ideal rhythm of practice” as the only standard by which God measures someone's spiritual life. Psalm 23 says, “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.” What David describes is precisely a situation where both resources and strength are extremely limited—what he relies on is not the regularity of his practices, but God's own personal presence. God well knows that in different seasons of life, the capacity a person has to give genuinely differs—what he values is your honest, best-effort heart of response to him in this season, not a mechanical requirement that you maintain the exact same frequency of practice under every circumstance. Once such a season has passed, you can honestly readjust and gradually restore a fuller rhythm, without needing to carry unnecessary guilt over a temporary reduction.
d24_06.pos: After the third point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d24_07.q: In Romans 7, Paul too experiences the struggle of ‘I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out’ — so does this cycle of ‘the more I practice spiritual disciplines, the more of a failure I feel’ mean the practice of spiritual disciplines itself is useless?
d24_07.a: This question mistakes “the ongoing process of struggling against sin” for “proof that the practice is futile.” The end of Paul's cry in that passage is not giving up the struggle, but “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (Romans 7:25)—the real point of this passage is turning one's gaze away from “gritting your teeth to overcome by your own strength” toward “depending on grace.” In fact, being able to honestly see the gap between “I want to do good but can't carry it out” is itself evidence that the Spirit is continually at work, shining light into the heart—a heart that feels completely numb, with no sense of struggle at all, would actually be far more concerning. True growth is not the day you no longer struggle at all, but growing increasingly quick, amid the struggle, to turn to grace, rather than grinding it out on your own.
d24_07.pos: After the ‘shame type’ in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts’

d24_08.q: That sister only started drawing near to the Lord in quiet after discovering she was ‘busy yet depleted’—but if a church's ministry needs are truly great and hands truly short, wouldn't deliberately setting aside quiet time affect other people who still need to be served?
d24_08.a: This question confuses “an apparent short-term reduction in output” with “what is genuinely beneficial to the community in the long run.” Jesus himself faced ministry demands far greater than any church co-worker's—crowds waited day after day for him to heal and teach, yet at the very height of his ministry he “would withdraw to desolate places and pray” (Luke 5:16). That word “yet” reminds us that withdrawing for renewal is not a selfish setting aside of responsibility, but a necessary prerequisite for sustained service—a life that only ever pours out without ever being replenished will eventually run dry, and at that point will have even less to give the community. In the short term, taking time for quiet may seem like doing a little less; in the long term, a serving life that doesn't run dry and keeps a flow of living water benefits the community far more than that temporary time of withdrawal ever costs.
d24_08.pos: After the second real-life example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d25_01.q: ‘The Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved’ sounds like growth is entirely God's sovereign work—does that mean a church doesn't need any evangelism strategy or growth plan at all?
d25_01.a: This question mistakes “growth's sovereignty belongs to God” for “people don't need to make faithful effort.” In that very same passage (Acts 2), the apostles were still actively teaching the truth, and believers were still actively living out a communal life of loving one another, breaking bread, and prayer—it was precisely this kind of faithful, concrete way of life that had “favor with all the people,” becoming the channel God used. 1 Corinthians 3:6–7 states it clearly: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.” God's sovereignty does not mean standing by with folded hands—it places a person's faithful planting and watering in their proper position: we are responsible for faithfully doing the work, while the sovereignty over the results is entrusted to God.
d25_01.pos: After section 1 ‘Three Thousand Immediately Entered the Life of Discipleship’

d25_02.q: Schwarz's research is a social-science survey that explains church growth using ‘quality characteristics’—won't this reduce spiritual revival to an ‘operable management formula,’ overlooking the sovereign work of the Spirit?
d25_02.a: This question mistakes “observing and describing the healthy channels God usually uses” for “replacing the Spirit's sovereignty with a formula.” Schwarz's central metaphor makes exactly this point: a farmer cannot pull a seedling to make it grow taller—he can only improve the soil; once the soil is good, growth happens on its own. This statement itself already acknowledges that the mystery of growth is not under the farmer's control—all the farmer can do is prepare a suitable environment. This kind of research is observing under what conditions the spiritual community God created generally grows more healthily; it is not claiming that following a formula will necessarily produce revival. Method and sovereignty were never mutually exclusive: faithfully preparing healthy soil while humbly looking to the God who makes the seed grow both need to be held together.
d25_02.pos: After section 3 ‘Natural Church Development, a Grain of Wheat, and the Faith of a Mustard Seed’

d25_03.q: Jesus pointed out that the crowd gathered because they had their fill of the loaves—so does a church using ‘practical benefits’ such as life care and community service to draw people fall into the same problem as that crowd who came ‘for the bread’?
d25_03.a: This question confuses “using practical service as a point of contact” with “stopping at meeting needs and never leading toward the gospel.” Matthew 5:16 says, “let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven”—concrete, practical good works were always meant by God as a channel through which people are meant to see and, in turn, give glory to God; Jesus himself also healed the sick and fed the crowds. The real problem is not providing practical help, but whether it stops there, never going on to lead people toward the cross and the discipleship of life. A healthy approach treats practical service as a bridge, not a destination—reaching people through action and building people up through truth need to be connected, not treated as opposites.
d25_03.pos: After section 3 ‘Natural Church Development, a Grain of Wheat, and the Faith of a Mustard Seed’

d25_04.q: If my church's numbers really have grown, but I'm not sure how much of that is transfer growth versus genuinely unbelieving people coming to faith, does that kind of growth count as ‘fake,’ and how should I tell the difference?
d25_04.a: This question reflects an honest attitude worth affirming, and this lesson itself has already given a concrete, usable tool for discernment. Rather than getting stuck on a question that can never be measured with one hundred percent precision, switch instead to the scorecard this lesson suggests, and begin honestly tracking three concrete numbers: how many people this year genuinely came to faith and were baptized, how many began entering discipleship and being built up, and how many who have already been built up have begun leading others. There doesn't need to be a perfect answer right away—what matters is building a habit of ongoing, honest self-examination. Having the right direction, and continually adjusting your focus toward it, matters far more than precisely sorting out “real” from “fake” in one pass—and that is far more in keeping with the spirit of this lesson.
d25_04.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson’

d25_05.q: Paul also mentions testimonies of the results of his own gospel preaching in 2 Corinthians—so is it also a kind of boasting that shouldn't happen when a church or pastor shares a testimony of their ministry's growth?
d25_05.a: This question confuses “sharing a testimony” with “proud comparison.” In 1 Corinthians 15:10, Paul describes having worked harder than all the other apostles, and immediately adds: “though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me.” The motive and focus of his sharing point clearly to God's grace, meant to encourage the reader's faith and give God the glory—not to prove himself superior to others. The key to discerning true boasting from healthy testimony-sharing is where the motive and focus of the words land: if the sharing is meant to direct people's attention to God's wondrous work and inspire others to imitate that faith, it is a healthy testimony; if the sharing is meant to compare numbers with others in order to show oneself as more blessed or more spiritual, that is the prideful-type heart this lesson warns against.
d25_05.pos: After the first question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d25_06.q: ‘I will build my church’ — does this verse mean the rise and fall of a church has nothing at all to do with whether I, as its leader, am faithful, since the Lord himself will take care of it anyway?
d25_06.a: This question confuses “God's ultimate preservation of the church's continued existence” with “an individual not needing to answer for their own faithfulness.” The promise in Matthew 16:18 speaks of the ultimate guarantee that the whole church, across all generations, will not be overcome by the gates of hell—this indeed does not depend on the performance of any single individual. But 1 Corinthians 3:8 says at the same time, “each will receive his wages according to his labor.” The church's overall continued existence being entrusted to the Lord's hand does not mean that any individual's faithfulness within it carries no weight—whether you are faithfully planting, watering, and building people up in the position you are called to will still be an account you give to the Lord one day; this responsibility is real and does not become irrelevant because of the church's ultimate security.
d25_06.pos: After the second point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d25_07.q: Luke 12:32, ‘Fear not, little flock,’ sounds like it's comforting people to accept the status quo—so does that mean a church no longer needs to pursue any kind of growth at all, and staying small is just fine?
d25_07.a: This question mistakes “removing the fear and inferiority that come from small numbers” for “forbidding hope or the pursuit of healthy growth.” This verse addresses the knot of feeling ashamed and unfavored by God because of small numbers—God himself declares that it is his good pleasure “to give you the kingdom,” and the point is to remove the anxiety of measuring identity and worth by numbers. A community no longer held hostage by that anxiety can respond more healthily and without strain to whatever God wants to do in it, whether that means staying small and focused or naturally expanding—this verse heals a mindset; it does not forbid hope. A heart no longer fearful or ashamed because of its numbers is best able to healthily welcome whatever blessing God gives, whether large or small.
d25_07.pos: After the ‘shame type’ in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts’

d25_08.q: That church invested ten years in discipleship before seeing solid results—if my church were to transition the same way, wouldn't more people who might otherwise have been drawn by lively activities be lost during those ten years?
d25_08.a: This question honestly points to a real short-term cost that may occur during a transition—this is exactly the concrete, real-world application of the tension described by the phrase “addition looks flashy at the start, multiplication has boundless staying power.” In the short term, turning toward solid discipleship may indeed not draw large crowds as immediately as lively activities do—this is something that needs to be honestly faced and communicated candidly with the congregation, not pretended away as if it cost nothing. But this lesson reminds us that the kingdom's ledger measures genuinely rooted life beyond “transfer” growth or “crowd-filling” growth—measured by a long-term view, it is better to choose a slower but solid harvest than to remain in a lively but fleeting crowd that doesn't stay. The process of transition requires wise communication and shepherding of the congregation's expectations, but the direction itself is worth holding to.
d25_08.pos: After the third real-life example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d26_01.q: God did not rebuke Elijah for asking to die—does that mean any time we feel depleted and want to give up on our calling, that feeling is completely justified and requires no self-examination?
