d50_03.a: This question raises an important reminder about discernment—the church's ministry, in the end, ought to be moved by the Spirit and carried out by faith, and shouldn't be reduced to a purely secularized methodology of management; this reminder is itself healthy and necessary. But the purpose of citing asset-based community development theory is not to replace spiritual leading with secular method—it borrows a phenomenon it precisely identifies: simply viewing people as objects of lack needing to be filled can easily let service degenerate into condescending charity, whereas Scripture itself has long taught that every person and every family has been given unique gifts and resources by God, and service should be about connecting gifts and building one another up, not one-directional giving. This theory happens to help the church turn a view of giftedness Scripture already holds into a concrete, actionable community ministry strategy, still exercised under the Spirit's leading and prayerful seeking, rather than replacing spiritual sensitivity.
d50_03.pos: After section 3 ‘Hospitality Alone, the Early Church's First Form, and Asset-Based Community Development’

d50_04.q: Many dual-income families, or families busy caring for young children or elderly parents, really do have almost no spare time or energy to proactively cultivate relationships with neighbors. Isn't it too harsh to categorize these families as ‘rusted-shut, isolated islands’ when they're already doing everything they can to cope with life's burdens?
d50_04.a: This question points to a real circumstance that needs to be treated gently—a family bearing heavy caregiving responsibilities, with almost no time or energy left, really shouldn't be held to the same standard as everyone else; this kind of harshness would be neither fair nor compassionate, and this deserves to be clearly affirmed. What this lesson warns against as “isolation” refers to a deliberate, long-term, unchanging posture of self-enclosure, not a requirement that every family must maintain a high level of community engagement at all times, under every circumstance. For a family currently in an especially heavy season of caregiving responsibility, healthy hospitality can take an extremely small, manageable form—a simple greeting, a brief message of care, the smallest connection within one's own capacity—not necessarily a concrete action like inviting someone over for a meal. What matters isn't the scale of the hospitality, but whether the heart still holds a willingness to connect, not being entirely closed off.
d50_04.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson — Don't Wait Until Someone Falls Before Opening Your Door for the First Time’

d50_05.q: If a church wants to truly put ‘asset-based’ community service into practice, discovering the gifts and resources of every family, that requires investing a great deal of time to get to know and take stock of every single family. For a small or mid-sized church with limited manpower, isn't this an unrealistic expectation, hard to truly carry out?
d50_05.a: This question points to a real limitation small and mid-sized churches genuinely face—systematically taking stock of every family's gifts, if done comprehensively and thoroughly, really does require considerable time and manpower investment, and this limitation deserves to be honestly acknowledged; not every church should be required to immediately build a complete, formal asset-mapping system. But putting this principle into practice doesn't necessarily require a large, formal system from the start—it can begin at the level of a small group or district, encouraging group leaders or district leaders to, in their day-to-day interaction and care, pay attention to and note down the gifts and resources each member has, gradually accumulating and connecting them, without needing to wait until there's enough manpower to build a complete system before beginning. The real key isn't how complete the system is, but whether one has already begun to see each family through the lens of “connecting assets” rather than “filling needs”—even if the start is small and incomplete, this shift in perspective is itself already an important step.
d50_05.pos: After the second question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d50_06.q: ‘Don't wait until you're ready to start blessing others’—this sounds very inspiring, but if a family itself still has obvious internal problems and struggles, such as a strained marriage or financial difficulty, shouldn't they deal with their own problems first before considering blessing their neighbors outward? Otherwise wouldn't that seem hypocritical or backward?
d50_06.a: This question raises a tension worth taking seriously in response—dealing with one's own internal problems first sounds logical and honest, and this instinct isn't entirely without merit. But this is exactly what makes this passage in Jeremiah so counterintuitive, and so profound—the exiled people's circumstance at that time was far more difficult and severe than an ordinary family's struggles, yet God did not wait until they had “dealt with their own problems first,” the difficulty of exile, before commanding them to seek the peace of the city—he required both things to happen at the same time. In fact, proactively blessing others outward is often not a reward that can only be given after internal problems are resolved—it's actually often one of the very means that helps a family break out of self-enclosure and regain hope and vitality. Of course, this doesn't mean a genuinely serious internal crisis that needs priority attention can be ignored—it's a reminder that you don't need to wait until everything is flawless before you're qualified to share a blessing outward; an imperfect but sincere blessing still has its own value.
d50_06.pos: After the first point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d50_07.q: Mephibosheth's sense of being unworthy and lowly came from his physical disability, being a descendant of Saul's house, and being at risk of being eliminated by David at any moment—this extreme circumstantial vulnerability seems quite different in nature from an ordinary person's hesitation to invite others into their home simply because their family is unremarkable or not presentable enough. Is using Mephibosheth's example as a comparison here a bit of a stretch?
d50_07.a: This question correctly points out a real difference in the objective severity of these two circumstances—what Mephibosheth faced was a politically life-and-death crisis, genuinely not something that can be simply equated in objective severity with an ordinary person's sense of inferiority over an unremarkable family situation, and this distinction deserves to be acknowledged. But the point of this lesson citing this passage isn't whether the two circumstances are objectively equally severe—it's the shared, subjective inner feeling behind both: feeling oneself to be “no better than a dead dog,” completely unworthy of favor and acceptance—this deep sense of unworthiness, regardless of whether its specific cause is a dire political situation or simple embarrassment over one's family circumstances, produces a strikingly similar psychological barrier and behavioral pattern. What God showed Mephibosheth was grace that disregarded his circumstances entirely and bestowed honor purely out of mercy—this quality of grace and invitation applies equally to anyone who feels unworthy for any reason.
d50_07.pos: After the ‘shame type’ heart in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts, One Door’

d50_08.q: That church used an ‘asset map’ approach and discovered members among the congregation with gifts like skilled baking or plumbing expertise—this sounds wonderful, but if connecting gifts to service becomes too specific and too functionalized, won't members feel like they're only being used within the church according to their ‘useful skills,’ actually losing the sense of value that comes from simply being accepted by God and the community?
d50_08.a: This question raises an important and nuanced warning—if connecting gifts is distorted into “your worth equals what function you can provide,” that really would depart from the core of the gospel, reducing a person to something merely instrumental, and this risk deserves to be taken very seriously, not dismissed lightly. Healthily implementing this connection of assets must first be built on the clearly established foundation that every person is already fully accepted and treasured simply for being a child God loves; the connection and use of gifts is a blessing and an opportunity for service received in addition, built on top of that foundation—it is not the threshold that determines whether a person is accepted. As the church promotes this kind of ministry connection, it needs to convey this order especially carefully—unconditional acceptance and love come first, and only then the discovery and connection of gifts; once this order is reversed, connecting gifts can indeed degenerate into the kind of functionalized evaluation this question worries about.
d50_08.pos: After the third example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d51_01.q: The text specifically records that some of the disciples ‘doubted,’ yet Jesus still issued the Great Commission—does that mean someone whose faith is weak, whose heart still holds doubt, can just as well take up the calling to missions, without needing to resolve their doubt first?
d51_01.a: This question confuses “doubt still being present” with “doubt not mattering at all.” The text honestly records that the disciples' doubt remained, and this gives great comfort to anyone still struggling inwardly—being called doesn't require waiting until you're fully convinced, with no doubt at all, before you can begin; but that doesn't mean doubt itself is unimportant and can simply be ignored. The real lesson is to imitate the disciples—choosing to obey and step out even while carrying doubt, and in the journey that follows, continually letting God, through experience and through community, strengthen that still-wavering faith bit by bit. Doubt is not a threshold that must be resolved before setting out—it is a traveling companion that can go along for the journey.
d51_01.pos: After section 1 ‘Sent from the Mountain: Doubt Still There, the Command Already Given’

d51_02.q: Paul uses the metaphor of the body for the church, with missionaries as the outstretched hand and everyone else as the body supplying blood—doesn't this metaphor imply that believers who stay to serve locally hold a lower status, playing only a secondary, supporting role, while the missionary is the one truly standing on the front line, the more important one?
d51_02.a: This question mistakes “a functional division of labor” for “a hierarchy of status”—exactly the misunderstanding the body metaphor itself is meant to strongly guard against. Paul clearly teaches in 1 Corinthians 12 that every member of the body, whether it seems prominent or hidden, is equally indispensable; the eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor can the hand say the same to the foot—the body supplying blood and the hand reaching out belong to the same living whole, and the body cannot function properly without either. The missionary standing on the front line certainly bears special challenges and cost, but the role of supplying, interceding, and sending is likewise a God-given, indispensable calling—the weight of the two in God's eyes was never measured by who stands further forward.
d51_02.pos: After section 2 ‘Every Believer Is on the List, the Order of Geographic Expansion, the Body's Shared Sending’

d51_03.q: Experimental research on the bystander effect observes how strangers respond to an emergency accident—a church's lack of action toward missions is often not because of this psychological mechanism of diffused responsibility, but simply because of unfamiliarity and a lack of relevant knowledge and channels. Isn't it an oversimplification of the problem's root to directly apply the bystander effect to explain this?
d51_03.a: This question correctly points out that the causes of a church congregation's lack of participation in missions may be diverse and complex—unfamiliarity and lack of access really are a common and real factor, and this deserves to be acknowledged rather than reduced to a single cause. Citing the bystander effect isn't claiming it's the only cause—it borrows this phenomenon to precisely describe a common collective mindset: even when a person has some burden or stirring about a matter, if they're within a community atmosphere of “someone else will surely do it,” that burden can easily be diluted and dissipate, never converting into concrete action. This reminder doesn't conflict with practical difficulties like a lack of knowledge or access—both can exist at the same time: the church needs to address the psychological collective silence of “assuming someone else will do it,” while also concretely providing knowledge and access to lower the practical barrier to participation—neither is dispensable.
d51_03.pos: After section 3 ‘Compassion Before Strategy, the Bystander Effect, and the Church's Silence’

d51_04.q: This lesson criticizes believers for saying, ‘I've already given some money, so I've fulfilled my responsibility’—but in reality, not everyone is suited to, or called to, go in person to the mission field. Isn't giving money precisely a fitting and appropriate way for most believers to participate, within their means? Why is it listed among the ‘things that must never be said’?
d51_04.a: This question correctly points out that giving money really is a form of participation within the reach and entirely appropriate for the vast majority of believers, and this shouldn't be denied or belittled—this lesson also isn't claiming everyone must go to the mission field in person. What's really identified as the problem isn't the act of “giving money” itself—it's the mindset implied behind that statement: “my responsibility has been fulfilled”—as though once a sum has been given, missions can be completely removed from one's own attention and prayer, with no ongoing connection whatsoever. Healthy participation can take the concrete form of giving money, while still continuing to pray for and stay concerned about that specific people group or missionary, rather than treating the gift as a one-time way of settling the matter, letting the mind withdraw from it entirely from then on.
d51_04.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson — The Great Commission Isn't Someone Else's Project, It Bears Every Disciple's Name’

d51_05.q: Isn't it reasonable for a church to treat missions as the dedicated work of a small number of called people? After all, a missionary really does need special equipping, training, and confirmation of calling—it's a professional service not just anyone can handle. Isn't ‘narrowing’ missions down to a dedicated role actually a responsible approach?
d51_05.a: This question correctly points out that becoming a full-time missionary long-term committed to the field really does require special equipping, training, and clear confirmation of calling—this kind of professional division of labor is itself reasonable and necessary, and shouldn't be denied. But what this lesson wants to address as “narrowing” isn't the fact that a full-time missionary needs special equipping—it's that most of the congregation, as a result, mistakenly assumes that since they aren't the ones called to that dedicated role, missions has nothing to do with them at all, giving up even the things everyone can do—praying, supporting, caring about a distant people group. Every name being on the Great Commission's list refers to exactly this broader level of participation—the full-time missionary carries the special calling of the front line, while every believer, at the same time, is on the line of prayer, provision, and care, each in their own office, none dispensable.
d51_05.pos: After the first question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d51_06.q: ‘Finding a specific people group or individual’ sounds good, but the number of unreached peoples in the world is enormous—if everyone only cares about one specific people group, won't that leave countless other equally needy groups overlooked? Doesn't this ‘specificity’ actually narrow the overall vision for missions?
d51_06.a: This question raises a scale-related question worth thinking through—if everyone only cares about one people group, as a whole this really can't cover the enormous need of all unreached peoples, and this concern has some merit. But the point of this lesson's emphasis on specificity is not requiring everyone to care about only a single people group for their whole life, narrowing their vision as a result—it's addressing the paralysis caused by “the vague masses,” where the object is so abstract and enormous that everyone feels it has nothing to do with them and there's nothing they can do. When every believer, every small group, every church each adopts a specific target and begins sustained prayer and care, the church as a whole, added together, can actually cover a far broader range than any single individual could reach alone—specificity doesn't narrow the vision; it lets the enormous overall vision truly be carried and put into practice through countless specific points of connection.
d51_06.pos: After the second point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d51_07.q: Peter's three denials of the Lord are an extremely serious betrayal—putting an ordinary believer's occasional weakness in everyday life, not boldly testifying to their faith, alongside a failure as major as Peter's—wouldn't that make ordinary weakness seem overly serious, or conversely make Peter's betrayal seem not serious enough?
d51_07.a: This question raises a difference in degree worth acknowledging—Peter's three denials really are an extremely serious, far-reaching failure recorded in Scripture, quite different in objective severity from an ordinary believer's occasional failure in daily life to boldly testify due to weakness, and this difference shouldn't be flattened. But this lesson's point in citing Peter's example is not comparing the severity of the failures—it's pointing to a more universal spiritual principle: no matter how serious or mild a person's past weakness in testifying to their faith has been, God's grace to forgive and use again is equally complete, with nothing held back. The extreme failure and the extreme restoration Peter experienced give those who feel deep shame over their own relatively minor weakness, and who no longer dare to be used by God, a more powerful hope—if even Peter could be restored and entrusted again with great responsibility, how much more someone with a lesser degree of weakness.
d51_07.pos: After the ‘shame type’ heart in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts, One Sending’

d51_08.q: That family only agreed to participate because the short-term mission team was suddenly short-handed, and they reluctantly said yes, which unexpectedly led to a positive transformation—does that mean a church can more actively ‘force’ believers who are afraid to step out into participating in short-term missions, using a similar approach to push everyone to overcome their fear, even if they're initially unwilling?
d51_08.a: This question raises an approach that needs a careful response—arranging for believers to participate in short-term missions through force or semi-force, even with good intentions, carries considerable risk and shouldn't be promoted as a general strategy. This family's story had a beautiful ending largely because of God's grace and this family's own eventual choice to embrace the opportunity, not because “forced arrangement” as a method guaranteed success—in a different circumstance, forcing someone not yet ready, or even carrying real psychological trauma or health concerns, to participate could very likely backfire, causing deeper resistance or harm. The healthy approach is a gentle but firm invitation, offering suitable, gradually progressive opportunities to participate (for example starting with prayer or brief contact), respecting each person's own pace of readiness, rather than treating this special case as a universally applicable operating manual.
d51_08.pos: After the second example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d52_01.q: Paul says, ‘to those under the law I became as one under the law... to win those under the law’—where exactly is the line drawn? If certain customs of a culture really do carry an obvious pagan-worship character, how should a missionary discern which are forms that can be adjusted, and which are the core that Paul insisted on holding to, ‘under the law of Christ,’ that cannot be given up?
d52_01.a: This question raises one of the most central, and least easily generalized, practical difficulties in cross-cultural ministry—even Paul himself gave no mechanical formula for this, and this needs to be honestly acknowledged rather than pretending there's a simple answer. But the wisdom left by the text and church history offers a few directions for discernment: any custom directly involving the object of worship, or directly contradicting Scripture's clear teaching (such as idol worship, violating the Ten Commandments), belongs to the core that cannot be given up; any neutral cultural form—clothing, language, artistic expression, social etiquette—even if unfamiliar at first glance, as long as it doesn't directly involve worship or violate truth, mostly belongs to the part that can be adjusted, or even ought to be respected and adopted. True discernment requires long-term listening and learning the real meaning of the local culture, not quickly making a judgment based on the missionary's own instincts shaped by their home culture—this is also why Paul specifically emphasizes “becoming” the other person first, in order to truly see clearly where this line lies.
d52_01.pos: After section 1 ‘A Confession in a Commercial City: I Am Willing to Change Myself to Win People’

d52_02.q: Cultural intelligence theory is a secular theory from the fields of modern management and cross-cultural communication, mainly aimed at helping multinational corporations improve their cross-cultural business performance. Applying this theory to missions work—won't that turn missions into something like a strategic operation of commercial expansion, losing the spiritual essence missions ought to have?
d52_02.a: This question raises an important reminder about discernment—the essence of missions, ultimately, is proclaiming Christ and serving the eternal needs of people's souls; it cannot be reduced to a strategy purely pursuing maximum performance, and this reminder itself deserves to be taken seriously. But citing cultural intelligence theory isn't meant to equate missions with commercial expansion—it borrows a phenomenon and framework of ability it precisely describes: cross-cultural effectiveness really is closely tied to whether a person has self-awareness, cultural knowledge, inner motivation, and the ability to actually adjust behavior—this phenomenon itself is a neutral observation, equally applicable whether in a business or a missions context. Paul himself is a model of extremely high cultural intelligence, and the ultimate purpose he used this wisdom to serve was always the sake of the gospel, that he might share with others in its blessings, not commercial gain—the tool is neutral; the heart and purpose behind using the tool determine whether it serves truth, or becomes another variant that is served by truth.
d52_02.pos: After section 2 ‘The Real Challenge Is Worldview, the Four Dimensions of Cultural Intelligence, Equal Partners Rather Than Givers’

d52_03.q: Peter's retreat in Antioch happened because he feared criticism from the circumcision party and yielded to group pressure—this was a weakness of his personal character. Isn't it wrongly repackaging a matter of personal courage into a cross-cultural issue to discuss this as ‘cross-cultural retreat’?
d52_03.a: This question raises a distinction worth clarifying—Peter's retreat on the surface really can be understood as simple lack of personal courage or weakness under group pressure, and this level shouldn't be overlooked. But this event carries cross-cultural meaning precisely because the specific scene of Peter's retreat involved exactly the sensitive intersection of Jewish culture and Gentile culture—he had already clearly received the revelation in the vision that Gentiles too were made clean, yet when facing people representing the group pressure of Jewish culture, he retreated back into his original culture's comfort zone and familiar circle. This exactly shows that individual character weakness and cross-cultural tension are often not two independent things—they are intertwined: group pressure often exerts its influence precisely through the tension of cultural identity, causing a person, even when clear in theological understanding, to still potentially retreat in behavior back to their own more familiar, safer cultural camp.
d52_03.pos: After section 3 ‘Peter's Retreat in Antioch, the Four Dimensions of Cultural Intelligence, and Listening Before Teaching’

d52_04.q: This lesson severely criticizes missionary approaches of ‘cultural imperialism’ that require converts to give up even their own name and native language—but historically some missionaries who did this were also acting from their sincere convictions at the time, believing that was the only way to thoroughly sever ties to past pagan belief. How should the church today view this history of well-intentioned but harmful practice? Wouldn't a wholesale rejection oversimplify their circumstances and struggles at the time?
d52_04.a: This question raises an important and nuanced reminder about historical evaluation—many missionaries who acted this way back then really were operating from sincere, even greatly costly commitment, and wholesale rejecting their motives and sacrifice, or simply judging them by today's standards, really would be unfair; this deserves to be acknowledged, and the complexity of history shouldn't be erased. But honestly facing the harm history caused, and having compassion for the sincere motives of the people at the time, can coexist—they don't need to replace each other. As the church looks back on this history today, the point isn't judging any individual missionary's heart—it's honestly acknowledging that even when done with good intentions, the practice of overly binding the gospel to a specific culture objectively did cause far-reaching harm, and learning from it to develop a more humble ministry approach that can better distinguish the cultural shell from the core of faith—this is a responsible attitude toward history, and also a responsible attitude toward ministry today and in the future.
d52_04.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson — Cultural Adaptation Is Not Compromising Truth, It Is Taking Off One's Own Sense of Superiority’

d52_05.q: This lesson criticizes ‘co-workers sent out who lack a heart for long-term commitment, assuming after a few months of brief contact that they understand an entire culture’—but in reality, churches and sending agencies often have real limitations of resources and manpower, unable to let everyone involved in cross-cultural service make a long-term commitment. Does that mean short-term contact and service have no value at all?
d52_05.a: This question raises a real resource limitation—not everyone has the circumstances or calling for long-term cross-cultural commitment, and this reality needs to be acknowledged; short-term service itself genuinely still has unique and important value, and shouldn't be wholesale denied. What this lesson really wants to address is not the form of “short-term service” itself—it's the overconfident, un-humble mindset of assuming, after brief contact, that one already understands an entire culture. Healthy short-term service can carry clear humility and self-awareness—understanding that what one has seen and known is only a tiny part of that culture, and therefore relying on and respecting even more the guidance of local co-workers or believers who have made a long-term commitment, rather than, based on a few weeks of experience, assuming one already has sufficient insight into the whole culture, even overriding local wisdom to make judgments or decisions on one's own.
d52_05.pos: After the second question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d52_06.q: ‘Equal partnership’ sounds ideal, but in reality, missionaries or churches from relatively resource-rich regions really do often have a clear advantage in funding, training, and technology. Does this objective imbalance of resources make truly equal ‘partnership’ hard to genuinely put into practice, staying only at the level of a slogan?
d52_06.a: This question honestly points to a real tension—the objective imbalance of resources really is a reality difficult to avoid in many cross-cultural partnerships, and pretending this imbalance doesn't exist would itself be dishonest; this deserves to be taken seriously. But what “equal” really refers to here isn't complete parity in the amount of resources—that really is difficult to achieve in reality—it's parity in decision-making power, dignity, and voice: local believers' wisdom, their understanding of their own circumstances, and their opinions on the direction of ministry are valued and respected equally, rather than the outside party automatically assuming a greater voice or decision-making power just because the other side has fewer resources. Galatians 2 describes Paul, Barnabas, and the Jerusalem leaders “giving the right hand of fellowship,” dividing the work rather than establishing a hierarchy—this is a concrete demonstration, in a circumstance of clearly unequal resources and status, of still choosing mutual respect and shared decision-making, showing that equal partnership isn't a naive slogan—it's an attitude and manner of governance that can still be deliberately chosen and continually practiced even amid the reality of unequal resources.
d52_06.pos: After the third point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d52_07.q: Peter retreated out of fear of the circumcision party—this kind of compromise under group pressure seems different in nature from the ordinary nervousness and anxiety that simply arise from fear of an unfamiliar environment, worrying about performing poorly; the former is more like a moral weakness, the latter perhaps just normal adjustment stress. Isn't it too broad to lump both situations into the same category of a ‘fear-type heart’?
d52_07.a: This question correctly points out that these two kinds of fear really do differ in nature—compromising and retreating on a matter of principle due to group pressure, versus normal adaptive anxiety that simply arises when facing an unfamiliar environment, ought to differ in their moral weight and how they're addressed, and this distinction deserves to be affirmed. But this lesson's use of the general term “fear-type heart” isn't meant to blur this difference—it points to a shared, root-level inner mechanism they have in common: when fear goes unnoticed, never brought before God to be dealt with, it can lead a person to retreat, avoid, and be unable to act according to clear conviction or calling, regardless of whether that fear is specifically aimed at group pressure or an unfamiliar environment. The practical exercise of discernment is first to honestly identify the specific nature and severity of one's current fear, and then, based on that discernment, decide whether what's needed is simple encouragement and adjustment, or a deeper facing of one's own weakness in compromising on a matter of principle.
d52_07.pos: After the ‘fear type’ heart in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts, One Cross-Cultural Ministry’

d52_08.q: That mission agency gradually returned leadership to local believers—that sounds like a wonderful vision, but if local believers are still relatively lacking in theological equipping and administrative management experience, wouldn't handing over leadership too early risk plunging the ministry into disorder, even causing it to drift from sound teaching? How should this risk be weighed?
d52_08.a: This question raises a real question of governance that needs to be carefully weighed—handing over power too early, without proper support in place, really could bring the risk of ministry disorder or theological drift, and this concern shouldn't be dismissed; “empowerment” doesn't mean letting go completely, immediately, with no structure at all. The healthy approach is to understand the handover of power as a deliberate, staged process of equipping and accompaniment—while returning leadership, continuing to invest in theological education, administrative training, and building a network of relationships that can be consulted, so that local leaders, even as they're empowered, also receive sufficient equipping and backup support, rather than reducing “empowerment” to simply washing one's hands and walking away. True wisdom doesn't lie in the either/or question of “should leadership be handed back or not”—it lies in how to design a handover process, based on the actual level of local readiness, that is responsible, gradual, and continues providing support all the while.
d52_08.pos: After the third example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d53_01.q: The Antioch church's list of leaders has a diverse background—does that mean if a church wants to cultivate a global vision, it must deliberately pursue diversity in its leadership team—for example, deliberately recruiting people of different ethnicities and backgrounds to serve as leaders—in order to truly generate a cross-cultural missions vision?
d53_01.a: This question mistakes the historical fact of “the Antioch church's leaders being diverse” for an operational formula that must be replicated. The diversity of the Antioch church's leadership team was a natural result of the diverse commercial and immigrant circumstances of that city itself, not a personnel policy they deliberately designed; the real point this passage emphasizes is not the ethnic proportion of the team's makeup—it's that a group of people with such different backgrounds could, in the same prayer gathering, together hear the voice of the same Spirit, demonstrating a unity that transcends cultural boundaries. A church with a relatively homogeneous congregation can likewise cultivate a genuine global vision through ongoing prayer, learning, and real contact with different groups—it doesn't necessarily need to first have a diverse leadership team before it's qualified to speak of a missions vision, though a diverse team certainly does help bring a broader perspective, an extra blessing, not the only path.
d53_01.pos: After section 1 ‘A Refugee Church Became the Birthplace of Missions’

d53_02.q: The Antioch church's vision was sent by the Spirit himself—does that mean when a church today advances missions ministry, it should also completely wait for some clear, supernatural stirring or revelation from the Spirit, and shouldn't proactively plan or advance any missions-related strategy unless such clear guidance appears?
d53_02.a: This question mistakes the spiritual principle “the Spirit is the sender” for “people shouldn't take any proactive planning or action.” The specific circumstance the text describes in which the Spirit spoke is that the whole Antioch church “was worshiping the Lord and fasting”—this is itself an active, ongoing, disciplined practice of worship, not passively doing nothing, simply waiting for a vision to fall from heaven. The way a church healthily responds to the Spirit's leading is precisely to continue faithfully committing to daily spiritual practices like prayer, worship, and intercession, while in this ongoing process of seeking, remaining sensitive and obedient to the Spirit's leading, and at the same time being able to, based on already-clear biblical principles (the universal call of the Great Commission), proactively plan concrete, workable missions strategies—proactive planning and obeying the Spirit's leading are not mutually exclusive; they happen together at the same time.
d53_02.pos: After section 2 ‘The Spirit Is the Sender, the Call Comes in Daily Worship, the Complete Cycle of Sending and Receiving’

d53_03.q: Allport's contact theory holds that under certain conditions, real contact can reduce prejudice—but this is social-psychological research on prejudice between general groups. Applying it to the spiritual matter of a church building a missions vision—doesn't that overlook the fact that resolving prejudice and spiritual life being renewed are, in essence, two different levels of change, unable to be simply compared?
d53_03.a: This question raises an important and nuanced distinction of levels—simply resolving prejudice in a psychological sense really isn't entirely the same thing as spiritual life being renewed, truly moved by the Spirit to develop compassion for all peoples; these belong to different levels, and this distinction deserves to be taken seriously, not simply conflated. But citing contact theory isn't claiming that real contact can replace or is equivalent to spiritual renewal—it borrows a phenomenon it precisely points to: abstract knowledge and imagination can hardly truly break down the distance and estrangement in a person's heart toward an unfamiliar group, while real contact is often an important medium God uses to soften the heart and prepare it to receive a deeper spiritual touch. A short-term mission trip or real cross-cultural contact doesn't itself guarantee spiritual renewal, but it often becomes the concrete setting in which the Spirit works and stirs compassion—the relationship between the two is complementary, not one replacing the other.
d53_03.pos: After section 3 ‘Sent Out in Worship, Four Concrete Strategies, Confirmation from Contact Theory’

d53_04.q: This lesson criticizes the practice of handing missions off to a missions committee to handle alone—but a church dividing labor and setting up different committees and departments is precisely so that professional matters have dedicated people responsible for them. Isn't the missions committee's existence exactly an embodiment of this kind of healthy division of labor? Why is it treated as a problem instead?
d53_04.a: This question correctly points out that establishing a missions committee, letting co-workers with a burden and expertise take dedicated responsibility for planning specific missions matters, is itself a healthy and necessary division of labor and shouldn't be denied—this lesson isn't arguing that the missions committee structure should be abolished either. What's really pointed out as the problem isn't “having a committee dedicated to coordinating missions matters” in itself—it's when this committee's existence becomes the reason other departments and most of the congregation completely exclude missions from their own daily attention—as though “there are dedicated people managing it now,” so they no longer need any participation or connection themselves. A healthy division of labor is one in which the missions committee is responsible for coordinating, planning, and providing resources and channels, while every small group and every member of the church is still encouraged and actually participates in prayer, care, and even short-term service—the missions committee is the engine that starts things up and coordinates, not the sole bearer of the responsibility.
d53_04.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson — Global Vision Isn't the Missions Committee's Job, It's the Whole Church's Breath’

d53_05.q: If a church wants to build the ‘sustained and institutionalized’ prayer network and missions concern this lesson describes, that requires investing considerable administrative manpower and time to maintain. For a small or mid-sized church with limited resources to begin with, is this something they can only shy away from? Is this calling only suited to large, well-resourced churches?
d53_05.a: This question points to a real limitation small and mid-sized churches genuinely face—building a well-developed, institutionalized prayer network, if it aims for the scale and refinement of a large church, really does require considerable resource investment, and this limitation deserves to be honestly acknowledged. But the core spirit of institutionalization isn't about the scale or complexity of the system—it's about being “sustained” rather than “occasional.” A small church can just as well put the spirit of institutionalization into practice in an extremely simple way—for example, a fixed monthly missions prayer time slot, a simple paper or group-chat prayer list, one co-worker responsible for regularly sharing field updates—none of this requires massive administrative resources, yet it can equally establish a connection of care that is ongoing rather than scattered and forgotten. Institutionalization doesn't mean complication—what matters is sustainability, not scale.
d53_05.pos: After the second question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d53_06.q: ‘Global vision needs to be woven into every week's rhythm of prayer and worship’—but if a church's worship gatherings and pulpit messages become long-term overly focused on this single topic of missions, won't that crowd out other equally important teaching and pastoral content, throwing the gathering off balance?
d53_06.a: This question raises a real balance issue requiring careful calibration—if worship gatherings and pulpit messages are completely dominated by a single topic, that really could crowd out other equally important, even more foundational teaching content; such an imbalance isn't the healthy model this lesson advocates, and this concern is reasonable and necessary. “Woven into the daily rhythm of worship” doesn't mean requiring every gathering, every message, to be centered on missions—it means that concern for missions can naturally and regularly—rather than only once a year—appear in prayer requests, testimony sharing, and brief reminders, becoming background music in the church's overall spiritual life, without necessarily occupying the main content of every single gathering. True wisdom is finding a rhythm and proportion that can sustain the warmth of a global vision without unbalancedly crowding out other important teaching—this requires the church's leaders to continually pray and exercise wise judgment.
d53_06.pos: After the first point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d53_07.q: An ordinary office worker feels unqualified to participate in something as significant as missions—this kind of self-assessment could also simply be an honest, accurate recognition of one's own gifts and calling; not everyone is suited to or called toward missions-related service. Doesn't categorizing this kind of self-awareness as a ‘shame-type heart’ that needs correcting overlook the value of honest self-knowledge itself?
d53_07.a: This question raises an important distinction—honestly recognizing that one is not the person called to be a front-line missionary is healthy, accurate self-knowledge, and shouldn't be treated as a problem; this deserves to be affirmed. What this lesson refers to as a shame-type heart is not this kind of honest discernment about a specific calling—it's a more fundamental, sweeping self-denial: deciding that the entire group or identity one belongs to is “not qualified” to bear any part in God's mission at all, and as a result giving up even things everyone can do, like praying, or using one's own existing professional skills to support and participate. The transformation of that office worker in the earlier example wasn't that he became a missionary—it was that he discovered that even though he wasn't called to be a full-time missionary, he could still offer up the professional gift he already had—this is exactly the key difference between healthy self-knowledge and shame-driven self-denial.
d53_07.pos: After the ‘shame type’ heart in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts, One Vision’

d53_08.q: That brother used his own professional skill to remotely help the field's administrative system—that's a very concrete way to contribute, but not everyone has professional skills directly applicable to a mission field—for example, the expertise of certain occupations is hard to convert into a contribution actually useful to the mission field. In this kind of situation, how can an ordinary member still participate concretely?
d53_08.a: This question points to a real circumstantial issue—not every professional skill can be directly and clearly converted into a contribution concretely helpful to a mission field; this reality really does exist, and not everyone can, like that brother, find a direct match between their professional skill and the field's needs; this needs to be acknowledged. But concrete participation was never limited to the one form of “professional skill happening to match the field's need”—sustained, concrete prayer is itself a profound and indispensable form of participation; care and encouragement through letters or messages can practically sustain a missionary serving alone in a foreign land; even simply learning about and understanding the circumstances and culture of an unreached people group is a meaningful form of commitment. The real point isn't whether one has a “convertible professional skill”—it's whether one is willing to sustainedly and concretely participate using whatever one already has, however ordinary it may seem, rather than simply not participating at all because a “perfectly matching” form of contribution can't be found.
d53_08.pos: After the second example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d54_01.q: Paul uses the commercial bookkeeping language of ‘giving and receiving’ to describe his relationship with the Philippian church—does this kind of commercially tinged wording mix a calculating, transactional commercial flavor into what should be a purely spiritual, love-driven giving relationship, weakening the selfless nature giving ought to have?
d54_01.a: This question raises a misunderstanding worth clarifying—the image of “bookkeeping” easily conjures associations with petty commercial calculation, and this association really does need to be carefully discerned, not rashly applied to a spiritual relationship of giving. But Paul's real purpose in using this commercial term is precisely the opposite—not commercializing a spiritual relationship, but elevating a relationship that might otherwise be lightly regarded as “casual, optional goodwill” to the level of “solemn, trustworthy, worthy of being taken seriously.” Just as a commercial ledger requires honesty, clarity, and accountability from both sides, Paul is saying that the exchange of resources between him and the Philippian church equally deserves to be treated this solemnly, seriously, and with mutual accountability—rather than equating “spiritual” with “casual, vague.” Truly healthy spiritual relationships should actually be as clear, trustworthy, and mutually accountable as the most reliable business partnership.
d54_01.pos: After section 1 ‘A Friendship Written in the Ledger: Giving and Receiving, Only You’

d54_02.q: Before thanking the Philippian church for their gift, Paul solemnly states that the secret of his contentment doesn't depend on the amount of resources—does that mean missionaries actually don't need the church's concrete supply of resources all that much, and can get by simply relying on spiritual contentment, so churches can reduce their emphasis on supplying missions resources as a result?
d54_02.a: This question mistakes what Paul expresses as “contentment” for “not needing concrete resource supply”—which runs exactly opposite to the overall context of the passage. In this very same passage, Paul solemnly thanks the Philippian church for their real, concrete resource gift, calling this supply a fragrant offering acceptable and pleasing to God—he never implies the church's supply is optional or unimportant. The contentment Paul expresses refers to his inward peace and joy not being controlled or determined by the amount of resources—whether in humble circumstances or in abundance, he can rely on the Lord who strengthens him; but this inward contentment is precisely not a reason to cancel the church's responsibility to supply—it shows that a healthy missionary can stand firm even when resources are scarce, while the church still bears the responsibility, and is blessed with the opportunity, to become a channel of blessing God uses through concrete supply.
d54_02.pos: After section 2 ‘The Invisible Support System, Costly Delivery, Health Rather Than Dependence’

d54_03.q: Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis distinguishes two kinds of helping motives, and this lesson implies that only help arising from genuine empathy is ideal—but in reality, many believers' initial giving to missions may genuinely come simply from wanting to relieve the inner discomfort they feel seeing photos of poverty or suffering. Does this ‘less ideal’ motive mean their giving is of lesser value, even unacceptable to God?
d54_03.a: This question raises an important issue that needs to be handled gently—the purity of a motive and whether the action itself is acceptable to God shouldn't be simply equated and used to pass judgment; if this makes someone feel their giving has lost its value because the motive wasn't pure enough, that isn't a healthy or biblical conclusion. The main purpose of Batson's research is to describe a phenomenon and help people understand how to inspire deeper, more lasting commitment—it isn't meant to judge or rank the spiritual worth of a giver. What God values is a heart willing to offer—even if the initial motive isn't entirely pure, this is still a real step in the journey of giving, just as the growth of much spiritual life often begins from an imperfect motive, gradually renewed and deepened by God. The healthy attitude isn't to judge harshly those whose initial motive wasn't deep enough—it's to encourage every giver, through more concrete understanding and connection, to let what may start as a shallower motive gradually grow into deeper, more lasting empathy and commitment.
d54_03.pos: After section 3 ‘The Sacrificial Language of a Fragrant Offering, Empathy and Altruistic Motivation, Four Healthy Principles’

d54_04.q: Technology has made giving more convenient, letting more people participate in giving support easily, with no barriers—this is actually a positive thing for expanding the overall participation base in missions resources. This lesson's description of ‘completing it with a few clicks’ sounds like it carries a negative tone—isn't that overly nostalgic, overlooking the real benefits technology brings?
d54_04.a: This question correctly points out that the convenient giving methods technology brings really have greatly lowered the barrier to participation, allowing many people who might otherwise have hesitated because of a cumbersome process to give and support—this is a real and valuable positive effect, and shouldn't be denied. What this lesson really wants to point out isn't opposition to convenient technology itself—it's a reminder not to let the convenient form replace the genuine care and prayer that giving ought to connect to—convenience can be the entry point of a giving action, but shouldn't become the endpoint of a giving relationship. The healthy approach is to make good use of the convenience technology brings to complete a concrete gift, while still deliberately, additionally investing time to know, pray for, and care about that specific missionary or field, letting convenient technology and genuine care go hand in hand, rather than letting convenience replace the depth of connection that ought to be there.
d54_04.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson — True Support Is Not a Cheap Transfer, It Is Costly Participation’

d54_05.q: This lesson questions whether ‘long-term, one-directional supply of resources to a mission field’ may deepen dependency—but for a region in extreme poverty, lacking basic infrastructure, if resources aren't supplied continuously and in large quantity, the local ministry probably can't even maintain basic operation. In this kind of situation, is insisting on promoting local self-sufficiency actually an unrealistic, even insufficiently compassionate demand?
d54_05.a: This question points to a real and important tension—for a region in extreme poverty or facing major structural limitations, rushing to promote complete self-sufficiency really could be an unrealistic demand that overlooks the real local circumstances, and this concern deserves to be taken seriously, not mechanically generalized. Healthy resource management doesn't demand immediate, complete self-sufficiency—it continually asks, “in the long run, is the use of this resource helping the local community build its own capacity and resources”—even in circumstances of extreme scarcity, this question still has meaning—for example, does the way resources are supplied also include skills training and capacity building, not only continuous delivery of goods; are local believers given a real voice and real participation in the decision-making process, rather than being merely passive recipients. The direction of long-term self-sufficiency and the currently necessary, continued supply can exist together—the former is a direction and a hope, not a threshold that must be reached immediately.
d54_05.pos: After the second question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d54_06.q: Won't a statement like ‘those in the rear are equally a fragrant offering’ make believers who stay in the rear too complacent, feeling that giving and praying is already enough, actually weakening the church's motivation to encourage more people to go to the front line in person, making the calling to the ‘front line’ feel less urgent?
d54_06.a: This question raises a balance that needs careful calibration—if “those in the rear are equally a fragrant offering” is overemphasized, it really could be misused as an excuse for settling into the status quo, no longer seriously considering the calling to go to the front line in person, and this risk deserves to be taken seriously. But the original intent of this reminder in this lesson isn't to weaken the urgency of the front-line calling—it's to correct a more fundamental misconception: the idea that only those standing on the front line are truly participating, while those in the rear are merely a secondary supporting role—this misconception could actually cause commitment in the rear to become perfunctory, lacking the seriousness and cost it ought to have. A healthy church culture should uphold both things at once—solemnly inviting and equipping those called to go to the front line, without lowering the urgency of that calling just because “those in the rear are equally accepted”; and at the same time solemnly regarding participation in the rear, requiring it too to carry real cost and commitment—rather than one weakening the other.
d54_06.pos: After the third point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d54_07.q: The parable of the servant who buried his talent originally speaks of faithful stewardship of the ability God entrusted—applying it to a concrete financial decision like ‘preferring to hold tightly onto resources for fear of lacking something oneself after giving them up’ seems like a bit of a stretch, since prudent financial planning, setting aside enough of a reserve for oneself and one's family, is itself wisdom Scripture also teaches, not entirely the same as the fear behind burying the talent.
d54_07.a: This question correctly points out an important distinction—prudently managing finances for oneself and one's family, keeping a reasonable reserve, is wisdom Scripture itself also teaches, like the ant preparing food—this really is different in nature from the burying in the parable of the talents, which comes from fear and a complete unwillingness to invest or put resources to use at all, and this distinction deserves to be affirmed. What this lesson cites this passage to point out isn't denying the wisdom of a reasonable reserve itself—it's pointing to a deeper tendency of mindset: when “prudence” becomes dominated by fear, turning into an instinctive resistance to any form of missions giving investment at all, preferring to offer nothing whatsoever—this has already gone beyond the scope of healthy financial planning and slid toward the burying the parable of the talents warns against, rooted in unbelief and fear. The key to discernment isn't whether one has a reserve—it's whether the heart is still willing, within a reasonable range, to invest and give by faith, or is completely ruled by fear, unwilling to put anything to use at all.
d54_07.pos: After the ‘fear type’ heart in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts, One Support System’

d54_08.q: That sister transferred money monthly, on a fixed schedule, to support a missionary, but never once wrote a letter, until a church letter-writing event let her truly get to know that person for the first time—this example seems to imply that without a church specially organizing this kind of activity, an ordinary believer would find it hard to spontaneously build this kind of deeper connection. Does that mean this ‘costly participation’ actually depends heavily on the church's organization and promotion, hard to sustain on individual initiative alone?
d54_08.a: This question points to an observation worth honestly acknowledging—for many believers, without the church providing a concrete channel, activity, or reminder, it really is harder to spontaneously take that step toward building a deeper connection; this reflects that human nature really does need a certain degree of external prompting and concrete opportunity, and this reality doesn't need to be seen as weakness or a problem—it can be an insight that's used wisely instead. What this example really reminds the church of isn't to harshly criticize individual believers for lacking initiative—it's to encourage church leaders to see the important role they themselves can play in this—by deliberately designing concrete activities, channels, and reminders, consciously lowering the barrier for the congregation to build deep connections, giving more believers like that sister, who might otherwise stay at the level of simply transferring money, the opportunity to be guided into more genuine, more costly participation—this is precisely the positive role the church's pastoral care and organization ought to play, not a flaw.
d54_08.pos: After the first example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’

d55_01.q: This passage in Daniel describes a twenty-one-day battle between an angel and the prince of Persia—does that mean a believer's prayer needs the battle of a heavenly messenger to be able to ‘arrive’ before God, and does that make God's power and sovereignty seem somehow limited, as though even God's own sending can be obstructed by the enemy?
d55_01.a: This question raises a theological issue that needs to be handled carefully—the text itself clearly says that from the very first day of Daniel's prayer, God had already answered and sent the messenger, showing that God's answer and power were complete and unobstructed from the very beginning; the obstruction happened in the process of the messenger delivering the answer, not because God himself was in any way limited or delayed. What this passage reveals isn't that God's sovereignty is limited—it's that it uncovers a spiritual reality invisible to the human eye: on the premise that God has already answered and is already sovereign, there is still a real spiritual battle taking place; the outcome of this battle was already settled by God's supreme sovereignty, but the process of the battle itself is still genuinely happening. The reminder this gives believers isn't to doubt God's power—it's to understand that there is sometimes an invisible spiritual process between a prayer being answered and the answer becoming visible, requiring sustained faith and patience.

d55_02.q: This lesson says, ‘every time the gospel breaks through a stronghold, resistance often intensifies along with it’—does that mean wherever ministry meets strong resistance and is especially difficult to advance, it necessarily means that place is exactly where a major breakthrough for the gospel is about to happen? Could this kind of interpretation be misused, rationalizing any form of difficulty as ‘proof that a breakthrough is coming’?
d55_02.a: This question raises an extremely important risk of misuse that must be taken seriously—if “meeting resistance equals an imminent breakthrough” is treated as a formula that can be limitlessly applied to any circumstance, that really could lead to an unhealthy reading, even causing people to overlook that some difficulties actually reflect a real need to adjust strategy, method, or timing, rather than simply being evidence of spiritual warfare in every case. Healthy discernment needs to rely simultaneously on seeking through prayer, the wisdom of community, and an honest assessment of circumstances—obstruction really may be an expression of spiritual warfare, and it may also simply reflect that the method needs adjusting, the timing isn't yet right, or God is using this to guide toward another direction. The real point of this lesson's reminder is to prevent believers from immediately interpreting every setback as “God is blocking this, I should give up”—an equally one-sided reaction—not to replace it with another equally one-sided interpretation—both extremes need to be balanced through prayer and the wisdom of community.
d55_02.pos: After section 2 ‘Strongholds Being Broken Down, Warfare Requires Equipment, Victory Has a Foundation’

d55_03.q: Beck's cognitive behavioral therapy is a secular method of modern psychotherapy, mainly dealing with emotional distress and mental health issues. Using it to explain the lesson of ‘taking back the mind’ in spiritual warfare—doesn't that oversimplify spiritual warfare into a purely psychological adjustment technique, overlooking the real evil spiritual forces truly present behind it?
d55_03.a: This question raises an important reminder about discernment—spiritual warfare really does involve real, genuinely existing evil spiritual forces beyond a purely psychological phenomenon; this is a reality Scripture clearly teaches and cannot be reduced or simplified into a purely psychological adjustment technique—this must be solemnly held to, with no compromise. Citing cognitive behavioral therapy isn't meant to deny the real spiritual entity behind spiritual warfare—it borrows a phenomenon it precisely describes: how distorted thought patterns affect a person's emotions and behavior—this observation at the phenomenon level can help believers more concretely identify what specific forms the enemy's attacks on the mind often take. Spiritual warfare simultaneously includes the real attack of spiritual entities and the concrete effects those attacks produce at the level of a person's mind; taking back a mind occupied by lies with God's truth is precisely the concrete action a person can and should take in response to this dual reality, and this doesn't conflict with acknowledging the real spiritual forces behind it.
d55_03.pos: After section 3 ‘The Battlefield of the Mind, the Full Armor Analyzed Piece by Piece, Prayer Running Through It All’

d55_04.q: This lesson lists among the ‘things that must never be said’ things like, ‘this battle is too hard, it's safer to retreat for now.’ But in reality, some circumstances really do call for wisely, temporarily retreating and adjusting strategy, rather than gritting through regardless of the cost. Isn't completely ruling out ‘retreat’ as an appropriate option too absolute, overlooking that a wise retreat is sometimes also the fitting choice?
d55_04.a: This question correctly points out that Scripture and church history are not without precedents of wise retreat, temporarily moving elsewhere—Paul himself, after meeting strong resistance in certain cities, also chose to move on to other places, showing that retreat itself isn't inappropriate under every circumstance, and this reminder deserves to be taken seriously. What this lesson warns against isn't a decision to “wisely evaluate and then choose to temporarily adjust or retreat,” confirmed through prayer and community—it's the kind of reaction driven purely by fear, based solely on the momentary feeling that “this battle is too hard,” hastily giving up without seeking through prayer or community confirmation. True healthy discernment brings every difficult decision before prayer and the wisdom of community to examine—is this really God guiding toward another direction through the door of circumstance, or simply cowardice retreating from the battle out of fear—the outward action of the two may look similar, but the inward motive and process are completely different.
d55_04.pos: After section 4 ‘The Hardest Passage in This Lesson — Wherever the Gospel Breaks Through, Obstruction Inevitably Follows’

d55_05.q: This lesson criticizes the church for ‘teaching the knowledge of putting on the armor, but rarely teaching that prayer is the power that runs through and activates all this equipment’—but in reality, many churches really do spend a great deal of time teaching the importance of prayer. Isn't this diagnosis too sweeping, overlooking that different churches' actual teaching may vary considerably?
d55_05.a: This question raises a fair reminder—the degree of investment different churches make in teaching prayer really does vary considerably, and treating this observation as a universal diagnosis that applies everywhere really does carry the risk of being too sweeping; this deserves to be acknowledged, and it shouldn't be generalized across the board. But what this passage in the lesson really wants to point out may not be the general question of “does the church teach the importance of prayer”—most churches really do teach that prayer matters—it's more precisely pointing out whether the teaching of the spiritual armor and the teaching of prayer are clearly connected, letting believers understand that prayer isn't a “seventh” piece of knowledge listed alongside the six pieces of armor, but the core power that runs through and activates the first six pieces, without which the whole set of armor is rendered useless. The value of this reminder isn't a blanket denial of the church's teaching on prayer—it's an invitation for every church to honestly examine whether it has taught this specific, tight connection between prayer and spiritual warfare clearly enough.
d55_05.pos: After the second question in section 5 ‘Three Issues in the Chinese Context’

d55_06.q: The metaphor of ‘iron lying still’ is vivid, but if a person is already praying diligently every day, and spiritual warfare still continues with no visible result or breakthrough, does this ongoing struggle mean there's something wrong with this person's prayer, or that the way they're wearing the armor isn't quite right?
d55_06.a: This question raises an extremely important question requiring gentle handling—continuing to pray yet seeing no immediate or obvious result absolutely cannot be simply interpreted as “something wrong with the prayer” or “the armor not worn correctly”; a judgment like that not only lacks a biblical basis, it could cause secondary harm to someone faithfully persevering through a difficult time, and this must be solemnly corrected. God already answered Daniel on the very first day of his prayer, yet the messenger was obstructed in the battle for a full twenty-one days—during those twenty-one days, Daniel didn't know how the battle behind the scenes was progressing, nor did he see any immediate result; all he could do was continue, faithfully, to pray, until the answer was made visible. The effect of spiritual warfare is often not revealed on a timetable people can immediately see; continuing to pray while temporarily seeing no breakthrough may be exactly the kind of Daniel-like faithful perseverance, not any form of failure or error—this requires great faith and patience, not rushing to find someone or something to blame for a delay that can't yet be seen.
d55_06.pos: After the second point in section 6 ‘Living Out 321: Three Corrections’

d55_07.q: Gideon's army was deliberately reduced by God down to just three hundred men—this was a specific action God took in a particular Old Testament historical event to display his own power. Applying this principle to today's missions ministry—does that mean a church should deliberately avoid organizing large-scale, well-resourced missions initiatives, and only ministries small in scale, low on resources count as truly relying on God rather than one's own strength?
d55_07.a: This question mistakes Gideon's story, which is about a spiritual principle concerning “the object one's heart depends on,” for an operational formula about “outward scale must be deliberately reduced.” God's purpose in reducing Gideon's army wasn't to declare that “smaller is more spiritual”—it was to expose the specific danger of pride in Israel's hearts, thinking “my own hand has saved me,” letting them see clearly that the key to victory lay in God's power, not in the size of their numbers. What this gives the church as a reminder isn't a demand to deliberately avoid organizing large-scale, well-resourced missions initiatives—abundant resources and manpower can equally be a blessing given by God, faithfully managed and used; the real lesson, regardless of the scale of the ministry or the amount of resources, is whether one's heart clearly knows that the foundation of ultimate victory is always God's power and presence, not dependence on the resources and strength held in human hands themselves.
d55_07.pos: After the ‘pride type’ heart in section 7 ‘Four Kinds of Hearts, One Battle’

d55_08.q: That member said, ‘what the enemy loves to attack most isn't my circumstances, it's that sentence in my head, “I can never change”’—directly attributing a recurring negative thought in one's own mind to the enemy's attack. Couldn't this kind of interpretation let a person shirk the responsibility they need to take for these thoughts, over-spiritualizing a thought pattern that simply needs one's own effort to adjust into the devil's work?
d55_08.a: This question raises an important balance that must be carefully maintained—indiscriminately attributing every negative thought directly to the devil's attack really could become an excuse to shirk personal responsibility, letting a person avoid honestly facing the parts of their own thought patterns that need adjustment and responsible effort to change—this warning is reasonable and necessary; over-spiritualizing really is a deviation that needs to be avoided. But Scripture also clearly teaches that a person's mind really can be a concrete battlefield where the enemy attacks and spreads lies—these two things, the need for personal, responsible effort, and acknowledging the reality of spiritual warfare, are not mutually exclusive; both can be true at the same time: a person still needs to responsibly practice and work to renew their own thinking, while also being able to honestly acknowledge that certain recurring, lie-like thoughts clearly at odds with God's truth may indeed have a component of spiritual warfare behind them, needing to be addressed both with God's word and with responsible self-awareness and effort—the two work together, not against each other.
d55_08.pos: After the third example in section 8 ‘Three Real-Life Examples’
